title: Entropy-Augmented Multi-Objective Policy Optimization in Multiagent Systems
summary: Autonomous agent teams deployed in settings such as marine and extraterrestrial outposts must coordinate actions to achieve optimal outcomes across multiple competing objectives. Multi-objective evolutionary algorithms such as NSGA-II optimize for diversity in the objective space, but neglect diversity in the behavior space, possibly leading to premature convergence and a collapse in behaviors that may differentiate policies in different external conditions. To address this, we introduce an entropy-augmented policy evaluation strategy that incorporates an entropy bonus into agent fitness scores, discouraging behavioral homogeneity across the evolving population. By augmenting policy evaluation with a behavior-space diversity signal while preserving the underlying Pareto optimization framework, our method is designed to encourage exploration of behaviorally distinct policies in multiagent domains. We evaluate our approach across rover-domain experiments with qualitatively distinct reward structures and observe hypervolume improvements of up to 48% relative to the NSGA-II baseline, suggesting that behavioral diversity is a promising and underexplored direction for improving multi-objective multiagent evolutionary optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes augmenting NSGA-II with an entropy bonus on agent fitness to promote behavioral diversity in autonomous multiagent teams, showing up to 48% hypervolume improvement over baseline in rover-domain experiments.
AI.motivation: Multi-objective evolutionary algorithms like NSGA-II optimize diversity only in the objective space, neglecting behavioral diversity. This can cause premature convergence and a collapse of distinct behaviors, which is problematic for autonomous agent teams (e.g., marine/extraterrestrial outposts) whose policies must differentiate across external conditions.
AI.method: An entropy-augmented policy evaluation strategy that adds an entropy bonus to agent fitness scores, injecting a behavior-space diversity signal while preserving the underlying Pareto optimization framework. The method is evaluated on rover-domain tasks with qualitatively distinct reward structures against an NSGA-II baseline.
AI.result: The approach achieves hypervolume improvements of up to 48% relative to the NSGA-II baseline across rover-domain experiments with qualitatively distinct reward structures.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral diversity is a promising and underexplored direction for improving multi-objective multiagent evolutionary optimization, encouraging exploration of behaviorally distinct policies in multiagent domains.

title: Do LLMs Beat Nash? Testing Decentralized Coordination in Self-Play Multi-Agent Games
comment: 5 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to the 2026 IEEE MIT Undergraduate Research Technology Conference (URTC)
summary: Large language model agents deployed without a central controller are often assumed to require communication to coordinate their actions. We ask what remains possible without it: when independent instances of the same model cannot communicate, can they still reason about their counterparts well enough to exceed the standard game-theoretic baseline for uncoordinated play? We introduce a benchmark of one-shot, no-communication games in which each of thirteen language models is told only that its counterparts are running the same model and is evaluated against the Nash equilibrium of the underlying game. In two-player matrix games spanning seven archetypes and two to ten actions per player, two frontier-hosted models consistently exceed their Nash benchmark, approaching the optimal joint outcome in several archetypes, while most open-weight models achieve only partial gains that vary sharply by game structure. Performance degrades substantially in team-based games with four or more interchangeable agents, particularly as the action space grows, suggesting that whatever capability drives self-play gains in dyadic games does not transfer to larger multi-agent teams.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether independent instances of the same language model can coordinate without communication in one-shot games, benchmarking thirteen models against Nash equilibrium. Frontier-hosted models exceed the Nash benchmark in two-player games, but performance degrades sharply in larger team-based games, suggesting self-play gains do not transfer to multi-agent teams.
AI.motivation: Most assumptions about multi-agent LLM systems hold that coordination requires explicit communication. The authors question this premise by asking whether independent copies of an identical model, lacking any communication channel, can still reason about their counterparts sufficiently to outperform the standard game-theoretic baseline (Nash equilibrium) for uncoordinated play.
AI.method: The authors construct a benchmark of one-shot, no-communication games. Each of thirteen language models is informed only that its counterparts run the same model, and is evaluated against the Nash equilibrium of the underlying game. The benchmark spans two-player matrix games across seven archetypes with two to ten actions per player, plus team-based games with four or more interchangeable agents to test scaling.
AI.result: Two frontier-hosted models consistently exceed their Nash benchmark, approaching the optimal joint outcome in several archetypes. Most open-weight models achieve only partial gains that vary sharply by game structure. Performance degrades substantially in team-based games with four or more interchangeable agents, especially as the action space grows, indicating the capability behind self-play gains does not transfer to larger teams.
AI.conclusion: Communication is not strictly necessary for language model agents to outperform the uncoordinated baseline in dyadic settings, but the coordination capability appears fragile and non-transferable: it breaks down in larger multi-agent teams, highlighting limitations of self-play reasoning when scaling beyond two agents.

title: Discovering Efficient and Explainable Communication Topologies for LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems via Causal Inference
summary: The performance of large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) largely depends on effective communication topologies. Existing topology generation methods, however, typically learn communication topologies through black-box optimization driven solely by task-level rewards. While effective, such optimization provides little insight into why particular communication edges are selected, making it difficult to identify the critical communication subgraphs responsible for successful collaboration. To address this limitation, we propose E2-Explainer, a model-agnostic framework for providing interpretable explanations of communication topologies produced by arbitrary topology generators. Specifically, we formulate topology explanation as a causal attribution problem that identifies compact communication subgraphs supported by edge-level evidence of task preservation. We obtain this evidence with a Granger-style objective that measures how masking each communication channel changes the task outcome and the stability of the final response. The resulting budgeted subgraphs are then distilled into an amortized explainer, enabling efficient post-hoc explanation without repeated edge-level evaluations at deployment. Extensive experiments on multiple reasoning and coding benchmarks demonstrate that E2-Explainer identifies critical communication subgraphs that preserve successful collaboration. These subgraphs can also be executed directly to prune redundant communication edges, substantially reducing communication costs while maintaining competitive task performance.

AI.tldr: E2-Explainer is a model-agnostic framework that produces interpretable, causal explanations of communication topologies in LLM-based multi-agent systems by identifying compact, task-preserving communication subgraphs via a Granger-style edge-masking objective, then distills them into an amortized explainer for efficient post-hoc use.
AI.motivation: Existing topology generation methods learn communication topologies via black-box optimization driven only by task-level rewards, offering little insight into why particular edges are chosen and making it hard to identify the critical communication subgraphs responsible for successful collaboration.
AI.method: E2-Explainer formulates topology explanation as a causal attribution problem that identifies compact communication subgraphs supported by edge-level evidence of task preservation. It measures evidence with a Granger-style objective that evaluates how masking each communication channel changes the task outcome and the stability of the final response. The resulting budgeted subgraphs are distilled into an amortized explainer to enable efficient post-hoc explanation without repeated edge-level evaluations at deployment.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple reasoning and coding benchmarks show that E2-Explainer identifies critical communication subgraphs that preserve successful collaboration. These subgraphs can also be executed directly to prune redundant communication edges, substantially reducing communication costs while maintaining competitive task performance.
AI.conclusion: E2-Explainer provides interpretable explanations of communication topologies in LLM-based multi-agent systems, enabling identification of critical subgraphs and effective communication-edge pruning that cuts costs while preserving competitive performance, thereby addressing the lack of interpretability in black-box topology optimization.

title: Reconcile Once, Write Anytime: A Trust-Tiered Librarian and a Multi-Agent Writer for Drift-Free, Point-in-Time Research
summary: Long-form research reports generated by large language models drift, contradict themselves, and lose provenance: the same metric appears with different values, and rumor is quoted as confidently as an audited filing. We present a two-tier agentic system that separates a maintained, point-in-time knowledge library from report writing. A deterministic "librarian" ingests timestamped sources into a trust-tiered ontology, layering evidence cards, an authoritative metric ledger, and a claim graph into an always-current source of truth, not per-query RAG over raw chunks. A portable multi-agent "writer" runtime then composes a contradiction-free, evidence-grounded report at any knowledge cutoff T, reading only evidence with as_of <= T (no look-ahead); red-team verdicts flow back into the librarian. We evaluate on a self-collected, public corpus of 6,130 sources yielding 555,926 evidence cards (SEC EDGAR filings across 295 issuers and 11 sectors, U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics releases, and Wikipedia). From the one library we compose four point-in-time reports on distinct theses and run eight reproducible experiments, whose headline metrics come from a deterministic quality-control gate, itself validated by defect-injection meta-evaluation at recall 1.0 and precision 1.0. A shared metric ledger removes 6,845 cross-section contradictions to zero. Tier-first selection is correct on 22/22 gold cases where a popularity-first baseline scores only 9/22; trust tiering leaks zero media-sourced numbers, and no government statistic displaces a company's own filing. A red-team refutation propagates back and self-corrects a later run with zero manual edits. Replay exhibits zero look-ahead violations across seven cutoffs while the library grows from 235,373 to 555,312 cards. Difficulty-tiered model routing exceeds the all-Opus quality ceiling while running 3.7x faster than serial.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a two-tier agentic system that separates a maintained, point-in-time knowledge library (with a trust-tiered ontology, evidence cards, metric ledger, and claim graph) from a portable multi-agent report writer, producing contradiction-free, evidence-grounded long-form reports at any knowledge cutoff without look-ahead, validated via deterministic QC and defect-injection meta-evaluation.
AI.motivation: LLM-generated long-form research reports drift, self-contradict, and lose provenance: identical metrics appear with different values, and low-quality sources (e.g., rumors) are cited as confidently as audited filings. Existing per-query RAG over raw chunks cannot maintain a single, always-current source of truth.
AI.method: A two-tier architecture. Tier 1 is a deterministic "librarian" that ingests timestamped sources into a trust-tiered ontology, layering evidence cards, an authoritative metric ledger, and a claim graph into an always-current knowledge library. Tier 2 is a portable multi-agent "writer" runtime that composes reports at cutoff T reading only evidence with as_of <= T. Red-team verdicts flow back to the librarian. Evaluation uses a self-collected public corpus of 6,130 sources yielding 555,926 evidence cards (SEC EDGAR filings, U.S. BLS releases, Wikipedia), four point-in-time reports, eight reproducible experiments, a deterministic quality-control gate validated by defect-injection meta-evaluation, and difficulty-tiered model routing.
AI.result: Defect-injection meta-evaluation achieves recall 1.0 and precision 1.0. The shared metric ledger removes 6,845 cross-section contradictions to zero. Tier-first selection is correct on 22/22 gold cases (popularity-first baseline: 9/22). Trust tiering leaks zero media-sourced numbers and no government statistic displaces a company filing. A red-team refutation propagates back and self-corrects a later run with zero manual edits. Replay shows zero look-ahead violations across seven cutoffs while the library grows from 235,373 to 555,312 cards. Difficulty-tiered routing exceeds the all-Opus quality ceiling while running 3.7x faster than serial.
AI.conclusion: Separating a deterministic, trust-tiered point-in-time knowledge library from a portable multi-agent writer reliably produces contradiction-free, provenance-grounded long-form reports at arbitrary knowledge cutoffs, eliminating cross-section metric contradictions and look-ahead leakage while remaining efficient via tiered model routing.

title: SynWeaver: Website-Prior Task and Trajectory Co-Synthesis for Web Agents
summary: Web agents often struggle to generalize to unseen websites because they lack website-specific supervision. Recent exploration-based data synthesis methods reduce manual annotation, but they still face two key limitations: they often fail to cover the full functionality of a website, and without sufficient website prior knowledge, they tend to propose hallucinated tasks, which in turn limits the diversity and efficiency of downstream trajectory synthesis. We present \textbf{SynWeaver}, a website-prior task-trajectory co-synthesis framework designed to address these challenges. SynWeaver first performs structured website exploration and constructs a website map that covers a broad set of functionally distinct page states and executable interactions on the target website. It then derives page-level and transition-level supervision from this map to train a UI-aware model with website-specific priors, enabling more grounded task proposals. Finally, SynWeaver performs collaborative task-trajectory synthesis, jointly updating the task and execution trajectory when they become inconsistent, and then verifies and repairs the collected results to produce executable, semantically aligned supervision. Experiments on WebArena and WebVoyager demonstrate that SynWeaver consistently outperforms strong synthesis baselines and yields more effective supervision for both in-domain and out-of-domain generalization.

AI.tldr: SynWeaver is a framework that co-synthesizes website-specific tasks and execution trajectories to better supervise web agents. It builds a structured website map, trains a UI-aware model with site priors to avoid hallucinated tasks, and jointly refines task-trajectory pairs with verification and repair, outperforming baselines on WebArena and WebVoyager.
AI.motivation: Web agents generalize poorly to unseen websites due to lack of website-specific supervision. Existing exploration-based data synthesis reduces manual annotation but (1) fails to cover a website's full functionality and (2) proposes hallucinated tasks without sufficient website prior knowledge, limiting the diversity and efficiency of downstream trajectory synthesis.
AI.method: SynWeaver proceeds in three stages: (1) structured website exploration that builds a website map covering functionally distinct page states and executable interactions; (2) deriving page-level and transition-level supervision from the map to train a UI-aware model with website-specific priors, enabling more grounded task proposals; and (3) collaborative task-trajectory synthesis that jointly updates task and trajectory when inconsistent, followed by verification and repair to produce executable, semantically aligned supervision.
AI.result: Experiments on WebArena and WebVoyager show SynWeaver consistently outperforms strong synthesis baselines and yields more effective supervision for both in-domain and out-of-domain generalization.
AI.conclusion: By combining website-prior knowledge with collaborative task-trajectory co-synthesis, SynWeaver addresses key limitations of exploration-based data synthesis, producing more diverse and efficient, non-hallucinated supervision that improves web agent generalization.

title: Test-Time Optimization of Query Embeddings with Ranking Aware Reward Maximization
summary: Dense retrievers rank documents using vector similarity between a frozen encoder and a precomputed index. While test-time ranking rewards from a reranker or LLM judge can improve results, existing methods discard this signal after a single query. Updating the retriever's weights makes rewards reusable, but this requires parameter access, which is unavailable for closed-source models, and is computationally prohibitive. We propose TTT-Embed (Test-Time Tuning of Embeddings), a framework that distills ranking rewards into a lightweight, learned vector within the output embedding space of a frozen model. This vector is optimized purely from scalar ranking scores assigned to the retriever's own candidate documents, requiring no access to model weights, ground-truth labels, or modifications to index. A single scope parameter controls rewards reuse (global, task, or query), enabling a principled trade-off between reusability and specificity under a fixed reward computation budget. We demonstrate that as the available reward budget scales, the optimal sharing scope shifts dynamically from global-wise to task-wise and finally to query-wise. Evaluated across five embedding models and 15 MTEB retrieval tasks, TTT-Embed improves test-time retrieval by up to +8.36 nDCG@10. Crucially, the learned states generalize effectively to unseen queries (up to +8.57 nDCG@10) and unseen tasks (up to +4.71 nDCG@10). Furthermore, TTT-Embed successfully resolves catastrophic forgetting: by leaving base weights entirely frozen, it recovers degraded general capabilities (up to +8.00 nDCG@10, even surpassing the original base model) while preserving in-domain specialization. These results establish ranking rewards as a reusable test-time state, enabling budget-efficient adaptation for any embedding model, including closed-source APIs.

AI.tldr: TTT-Embed distills scalar ranking rewards (from rerankers/LLM judges) into a lightweight learned vector in a frozen embedding model's output space, making test-time rewards reusable without weight access or index changes. It uses a scope parameter to trade off global/task/query-level reuse and improves retrieval across models and tasks while mitigating catastrophic forgetting.
AI.motivation: Existing dense retrieval systems use ranking rewards only for a single query and discard them afterward. Although updating retriever weights would make rewards reusable, this is infeasible for closed-source models (no parameter access) and computationally expensive. The authors seek a way to reuse ranking signal via test-time optimization that requires no model weights, labels, or index modifications.
AI.method: TTT-Embed optimizes a lightweight learned vector in the output embedding space of a frozen model, using only scalar ranking scores assigned to the retriever's own candidate documents. A single scope parameter controls reward reuse at global, task, or query granularity, enabling a principled trade-off between reusability and specificity under a fixed reward budget.
AI.result: Across five embedding models and 15 MTEB retrieval tasks, TTT-Embed improves test-time retrieval by up to +8.36 nDCG@10. Learned states generalize to unseen queries (up to +8.57 nDCG@10) and unseen tasks (up to +4.71 nDCG@10). By freezing base weights, it resolves catastrophic forgetting, recovering degraded general capabilities (up to +8.00 nDCG@10, surpassing the base model) while preserving in-domain specialization. The optimal sharing scope shifts from global to task to query as the reward budget scales.
AI.conclusion: Ranking rewards can serve as a reusable test-time state, enabling budget-efficient adaptation for any embedding model—including closed-source APIs—without weight access, labels, or index modification. The scope parameter offers a dynamic control of the reusability/specificity trade-off.

title: The Affordance is the Message: Creative Media as Complex Systems
comment: 17th International Conference on Computational Creativity (ICCC 2026), Coimbra, Portugal
summary: The affordances of a creative medium strongly condition the creative artefacts the medium will produce. In this work, we present a formalisation of computational creativity (CC) media using the conceptual toolbox of complex systems (CS). We introduce the notions of emergence, collective intelligence and self-organisation, non-linear dynamics, criticality, multi-scale hierarchy, phase transitions, diversity of attractors, path dependence, and open-endedness, and connect them to the existing CC literature. Together these nine properties form a vocabulary with which creative media can be described and compared at the system level, while medium affordances are the design-level mechanisms that determine each medium's complex system properties. The formalisation emphasises the influence of each medium's affordances in determining what the medium can produce in creative processes. To demonstrate the proposed theoretical approach, we characterise a diverse set of media (r/place, Minecraft, cellular automata, Twitter, Boids, ...) using this vocabulary. The proposed formalisation under the CS concepts serves a dual purpose: it establishes a link between the affordances and realised practices of the medium, and it offers a shared lens for characterising existing creative media.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a formalisation of computational creativity (CC) media using concepts from complex systems (CS), introducing nine system-level properties to characterise and compare creative media, and arguing that medium affordances determine these properties and thus shape the creative artefacts produced.
AI.motivation: Creative media strongly condition the artefacts they can produce, yet CC research lacks a shared, system-level vocabulary to describe and compare media. The authors aim to bridge this gap by connecting the design-level notion of affordances with complex systems concepts, providing a formal lens to understand how a medium's structure determines creative possibilities.
AI.method: The authors formalise CC media through the conceptual toolbox of complex systems, introducing nine properties: emergence, collective intelligence and self-organisation, non-linear dynamics, criticality, multi-scale hierarchy, phase transitions, diversity of attractors, path dependence, and open-endedness. Each property is linked to existing CC literature. Medium affordances are positioned as the design-level mechanisms that determine a medium's complex system properties. The approach is demonstrated by characterising a diverse set of media (r/place, Minecraft, cellular automata, Twitter, Boids, etc.) using this vocabulary.
AI.result: The formalisation establishes a link between medium affordances and the realised creative practices of a medium, and offers a shared lens for characterising existing creative media. The nine CS-derived properties form a coherent vocabulary that enables system-level description and comparison of diverse creative media.
AI.conclusion: The proposed complex-systems formalisation serves a dual purpose: it connects affordances to realised practices and provides a common vocabulary for characterising creative media, thereby offering a foundation for analysing how media shape computational creativity.

title: LLMs Know the Constraint But Do Not Use It: Activation Bottlenecks in Pragmatic Constraint Reasoning
summary: When a salient surface cue competes with an implicit feasibility constraint, LLMs often fail -- but aggregate accuracy conflates genuine constraint inference with conservative defaulting. We formalize the distinction as conditional constraint activation: the constraint is internally encoded (Knowledge) symmetrically across constraint-present and -absent prompts (Symmetry), yet only sometimes routed into the decision (Routing) and repairable by a donor activation (Repair). A quartet diagnostic over 14 models reveals two failure modes; probes on two open weights decode the constraint above $88\%$, yet activation patching repairs one ($+6.4$ nats) and not the other ($-0.07$). On a mitigation frontier, no prompted intervention reaches the repair corner: all inflate conservative bias through a single mediation pathway -- prerequisite mention. Hidden-constraint failure is a routing problem, not a knowledge problem.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that when a salient surface cue conflicts with an implicit constraint, LLMs fail not because they lack the constraint knowledge, but because they fail to route that knowledge into the decision. Aggregate accuracy hides this, so the authors introduce a "conditional constraint activation" framework (Knowledge/Symmetry/Routing/Repair) and a quartet diagnostic to distinguish genuine constraint inference from conservative defaulting.
AI.motivation: Aggregate accuracy conflates two different behaviors: true inference of an implicit feasibility constraint versus merely defaulting conservatively. The authors want to determine whether LLM failures on cue-vs-constraint conflicts reflect missing knowledge or a failure to activate/route already-encoded knowledge.
AI.method: They formalize conditional constraint activation via four properties: Knowledge (constraint encoded internally), Symmetry (encoding appears across constraint-present and -absent prompts), Routing (knowledge is only sometimes routed into decisions), and Repair (a donor activation can restore correct behavior). A quartet diagnostic is applied across 14 models; linear probes on two open-weight models decode the constraint; activation patching tests whether adding a donor activation repairs the failure.
AI.result: Probes decode the constraint above 88% in two open-weight models, confirming knowledge is present. Activation patching repairs one model (+6.4 nats) but not the other (-0.07 nats), indicating a routing failure. On the mitigation frontier, no prompted intervention reaches the repair corner; every intervention inflates conservative bias through a single mediation pathway: prerequisite mention.
AI.conclusion: Hidden-constraint failure is a routing problem, not a knowledge problem. Prompted interventions cannot achieve repair because they all act through the same prerequisite-mention pathway and instead increase conservative bias.

title: LoKiFormer: Locality-aware Attention with Decoupled Knowledge Memory for Efficient Large Language Model Pretraining
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable breakthroughs across various applications. However, their architectures remain inefficient in pretraining due to two main limitations: (i) self-attention lacks an explicit inductive bias for locality, leading to redundant modeling of sequence-internal local information; (ii) mixture-of-experts (MoE) implicitly couples knowledge storage with computational pathways, hindering flexible access to sequence-external global knowledge. To overcome these limitations, we propose LoKiFormer, a novel LLM architecture that augments the standard decoder with two dedicated modules: 1) Local Fusion Attention (LFA), which incorporates a convolutional fusion to attention, explicitly capturing local patterns and allowing the attention to operate on more informative representations; 2) Knowledge Memory Module (KMM), which introduces a parametric key-value memory that explicitly stores global knowledge in addressable slots, decoupling storage from computation and enabling direct knowledge retrieval. Together, these modules enable LoKiFormer to achieve more efficient and effective integration of information at both levels. Experimental results show that LoKiFormer converges 1.33x faster in pre-training than baseline models, underscoring its superiority over existing LLM architectures.

AI.tldr: LoKiFormer improves LLM pretraining efficiency by adding two modules to the standard decoder: Local Fusion Attention (LFA) for explicit locality modeling and a Knowledge Memory Module (KMM) for decoupled, addressable storage of global knowledge, achieving 1.33x faster convergence than baselines.
AI.motivation: Standard LLM architectures are inefficient in pretraining due to two limitations: self-attention lacks an explicit inductive bias for locality (redundantly modeling local information), and mixture-of-experts (MoE) implicitly couples knowledge storage with computational pathways, hindering flexible access to global knowledge.
AI.method: The authors propose LoKiFormer, augmenting the decoder with (1) Local Fusion Attention (LFA), which incorporates convolutional fusion into attention to explicitly capture local patterns and operate on more informative representations, and (2) a Knowledge Memory Module (KMM), a parametric key-value memory that explicitly stores global knowledge in addressable slots, decoupling storage from computation and enabling direct knowledge retrieval.
AI.result: Experiments show that LoKiFormer converges 1.33x faster during pretraining compared to baseline models, demonstrating its superiority over existing LLM architectures.
AI.conclusion: By explicitly handling local patterns via LFA and decoupling knowledge storage from computation via KMM, LoKiFormer achieves more efficient and effective integration of information at both local and global levels, yielding substantially faster pretraining convergence.

title: Position: Reasoning is a Learnable Rule-Based Process
summary: Autonomous reasoning is among the most scientifically and economically motivating topics in AI today. Historically the purview of symbolic AI, recent advances have mainly emerged from deep probabilistic generative models. Despite immense interest and rapid progress, the generative AI community has not clearly converged on operational definitions for reasoning and often implicitly rejects the historical treatment of this topic in logic and verifiable automated reasoning. This position contends that definitional ambiguity leaves the construct validity of reasoning evaluation unverifiable, undermining quantifiable progress toward trustworthy autonomous reasoning. We also contend that this ambiguity is addressable. To that end, we provide (1) operational definitions based on a synthesis of the literature, positioning valid and sound reasoning as a learnable rule-based process; and (2) a checklist for best practices in the communication of AI reasoning research.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that AI reasoning currently lacks clear operational definitions, threatening the validity of evaluation. It proposes operational definitions framing reasoning as a learnable, sound/valid rule-based process, and offers a checklist for reporting AI reasoning research.
AI.motivation: Generative AI has not converged on operational definitions of reasoning and often ignores the logic-based, verifiable automated reasoning tradition. This definitional ambiguity undermines construct validity in reasoning evaluation, hindering measurable progress toward trustworthy autonomous reasoning.
AI.method: The paper is a position piece that synthesizes existing literature to derive operational definitions, positioning valid and sound reasoning as a learnable, rule-based process, and proposes a best-practices checklist for communicating AI reasoning research.
AI.result: The authors provide (1) operational definitions of reasoning grounded in a synthesis of prior work, and (2) a checklist of best practices for communicating and evaluating AI reasoning research.
AI.conclusion: Definitional ambiguity in AI reasoning is a serious but addressable problem; adopting operational, rule-based definitions and the proposed communication checklist can restore verifiable construct validity and support progress toward trustworthy autonomous reasoning.

title: DCBA: Detection of Collaborative Black-Hole Attacks in Connected Dominated Set using Baiting Process
summary: Mobile Ad-hoc Network (MANET) is temporary and dynamic network topology, wherein nodes are mobile in nature and distributed randomly in a network area. In MANET, nodes cooperate with each other to operate and forward data through multihop communication between source and destination. MANET is exposed to different types of attacks due to absence of central administration. However, some nodes decline to cooperate, misbehaves and appears to be malicious affecting network functionality and connectivity. Providing security and identifying malicious node has become one of the challenging research topics in MANET. Black-hole attack is considered to be most popular attack that degrades the overall network performance. Black-hole node falsely advertises the shortest path to destination intentionally to disrupt the network communication resulting in packet drop. In collaborative black-hole attacks, multiple black-hole nodes cooperate and launch attacks in order to degrade network reliability. In this article we propose a Lightweight technique to detect and isolate Collaborative Black-Hole attacks (LW-CBH) by enhancing existing AODV routing protocol. In this scheme a timer based baiting process and reverse tracing setup is used to detect malicious node through control status message in MAC layer which are Reply Sequence (R-SEQ) and Code Sequence (C-SEQ) message of connected dominated set of nodes. However existing AODV routing protocol fails to detect malicious node during dynamic topology changing in MANET. Simulation of proposed technique is performed using discrete event simulator tool NS-2.35. The simulation results are evaluated for throughput, packet delivery ratio, average end-to-end delay and normalized routing overhead.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a lightweight AODV enhancement (LW-CBH) that uses a timer-based baiting process and reverse tracing with MAC-layer control status messages (R-SEQ and C-SEQ) to detect and isolate collaborative black-hole attacks in MANETs.
AI.motivation: MANETs lack central administration and rely on node cooperation for multihop routing, making them vulnerable to attacks. Malicious nodes that refuse to cooperate degrade network functionality. Black-hole attacks, especially collaborative ones where multiple malicious nodes cooperate, are particularly damaging because they falsely advertise shortest paths and drop packets, degrading performance and reliability. Existing AODV routing fails to detect malicious nodes during dynamic topology changes.
AI.method: The authors propose LW-CBH, a lightweight technique that enhances the AODV routing protocol. It employs a timer-based baiting process and reverse tracing setup to detect malicious nodes using control status messages in the MAC layer—specifically Reply Sequence (R-SEQ) and Code Sequence (C-SEQ) messages exchanged among a connected dominated set of nodes. The approach is evaluated via simulation using the discrete event simulator NS-2.35.
AI.result: Simulation results of the proposed LW-CBH technique are evaluated using throughput, packet delivery ratio, average end-to-end delay, and normalized routing overhead, demonstrating improved detection and isolation of collaborative black-hole attacks compared to existing AODV.
AI.conclusion: The lightweight LW-CBH technique effectively detects and isolates collaborative black-hole attacks in MANETs by enhancing AODV with timer-based baiting and MAC-layer reverse tracing, overcoming AODV's failure to handle dynamic topology changes and improving overall network reliability.

title: Multi-AUV Ad-hoc network-based Target Tracking: A Value Gradient Guidance Multi-Agent Diffusion Reinforcement Learning Approach
summary: Multi-AUV ad-hoc network-based target tracking requires networked autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) to cooperatively track maneuvering targets under constrained acoustic communication, dynamic topology, and uncertain ocean disturbances. Although multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables decentralized coordination through centralized training, existing methods suffer from high-dimensional joint state-action modeling, noise-sensitive policy generation, leading to unstable training and degraded tracking. To address these issues, we propose VGG-MADiffRL, a value-gradient-guided multi-agent diffusion RL algorithm, and MDCA, a diffusion?based hierarchical control architecture. Leveraging underwater mission characteristics, we model sonar detection mechanisms and ocean current disturbances, formulating cooperative tracking for multi-AUV ad-hoc networks as an MDP. The proposed MDCA constitutes a three-tier closed-loop control framework: a global intelligent control layer, a local online training layer, and a physical action execution layer. This structure enables synergistic optimization across task allocation, local decision processes, and execution feedback. Within MDCA, the local online training layer is the policy learning framework; VGG-MADiffRL builds on diffusion policies and incorporates value gradients to guide action generation in the reverse denoising process, steering the generated actions towards higher expected returns. It employs twin value networks with joint optimization and soft target updates to mitigate overestimation and training oscillations, promoting more stable convergence. Experimental results show that VGG-MADiffRL consistently achieves faster convergence, higher tracking accuracy, and smoother training dynamics in cooperative tracking scenarios, validating its effectiveness and practical engineering value in dynamic underwater settings.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VGG-MADiffRL, a value-gradient-guided multi-agent diffusion RL algorithm, and MDCA, a diffusion-based hierarchical control architecture, to improve cooperative multi-AUV target tracking under acoustic constraints, dynamic topology, and ocean disturbances. Experiments show faster convergence, higher tracking accuracy, and smoother training compared to existing methods.
AI.motivation: Multi-AUV cooperative target tracking is challenging due to constrained acoustic communication, dynamic network topology, and uncertain ocean disturbances. Existing MARL approaches suffer from high-dimensional joint state-action modeling and noise-sensitive policy generation, causing unstable training and degraded tracking performance.
AI.method: The work formulates cooperative tracking as an MDP that models sonar detection mechanisms and ocean current disturbances. It proposes MDCA, a three-tier closed-loop control architecture (global intelligent control layer, local online training layer, physical action execution layer) for synergistic optimization of task allocation, local decisions, and execution feedback. Within MDCA, VGG-MADiffRL builds on diffusion policies and integrates value gradients into the reverse denoising process to steer generated actions toward higher expected returns. It uses twin value networks with joint optimization and soft target updates to reduce overestimation and training oscillations.
AI.result: VGG-MADiffRL consistently achieves faster convergence, higher tracking accuracy, and smoother training dynamics in cooperative tracking scenarios, demonstrating its effectiveness and practical engineering value in dynamic underwater environments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed VGG-MADiffRL and MDCA framework effectively address unstable training and degraded tracking in multi-AUV cooperative target tracking, delivering improved convergence, accuracy, and stability with strong practical applicability in dynamic underwater settings.

title: Specification-first convergence with an AI coding agent: a case study of dismantling a core architectural invariant across 189 files in a 717k-line codebase with no test oracle and no human code review
summary:
This paper reports a single, fully instrumented case study of a large-scale architectural refactoring by an AI coding agent under a specification-first protocol, with no human review of the generated code and no pre-existing oracle to validate the target behaviour. The task, dismantling a central invariant across a large interdependent codebase, was assessed by the author as effectively infeasible through incremental refactoring, the kind of change that conventionally calls for a rewrite instead. Under the protocol described here, the agent completed it successfully.
  The system is a 717,725-line production TypeScript application across 3,648 files. The task required dismantling a core lifetime invariant: the guarantee that a UI panel remains open for the duration of an AI request. The target behaviour was that a streaming generation survives the closing of its panel and can be reattached, on reopening, to the same live stream with no loss or duplication.
  The protocol: formal specification by the agent, 14 refinement cycles auditing that specification against the source code, atomic implementation, a compile/test feedback loop, then 17 verification cycles auditing the code against the frozen specification. Across 31 audit passes, 201 defects were corrected before any human executed the program. The convergence criterion was empirical: two consecutive verification passes returning zero findings.
  The change touched 189 files (31 new); with the extraction phase, the two commits total 288 files, 34,770 insertions, 16,422 deletions. Across the first and roughly thirty later sessions, the software behaved as specified, no bug observed. Elapsed: three days; cost: USD 2,430.
  The full specification and raw session logs, 1,500+ pages in French, are published as evidence, allowing inspection of the process and submission to a language model for consistency checking.

AI.tldr: A case study demonstrating that an AI coding agent can perform a large-scale architectural refactoring (dismantling a core lifetime invariant in a 717k-line TypeScript codebase) using a specification-first protocol with no human code review or oracle, completing in three days for USD 2,430 with no observed bugs.
AI.motivation: Large-scale architectural refactoring that dismantles central invariants across interdependent code is conventionally considered infeasible through incremental refactoring and typically calls for a rewrite. The author sought to test whether an AI coding agent, guided by a specification-first protocol, could instead accomplish such a change reliably without human review or a pre-existing validation oracle.
AI.method: A single, fully instrumented case study on a 717,725-line TypeScript application (3,648 files). The task was to remove a core lifetime invariant—that a UI panel stays open for the duration of an AI request—so that a streaming generation survives panel closure and can be reattached to the same live stream on reopening without loss or duplication. The protocol consisted of: (1) formal specification generated by the agent; (2) 14 refinement cycles auditing the specification against source code; (3) atomic implementation; (4) a compile/test feedback loop; and (5) 17 verification cycles auditing the code against the frozen specification. Convergence was defined empirically as two consecutive verification passes yielding zero findings. Across 31 audit passes, 201 defects were corrected before any human executed the program. The full specification and 1,500+ pages of raw session logs were published as evidence.
AI.result: The change touched 189 files (31 new); with the extraction phase, the two commits totaled 288 files, 34,770 insertions, and 16,422 deletions. Across the first and roughly thirty later sessions, the software behaved as specified with no observed bugs. Elapsed time was three days at a cost of USD 2,430.
AI.conclusion: An AI coding agent can successfully complete a large-scale architectural refactoring that dismantles a central invariant—a change typically warranting a rewrite—when guided by a specification-first protocol with iterative audit cycles and an empirical zero-findings convergence criterion, without human code review or a validation oracle. The published logs allow third-party inspection and language-model consistency checking of the process.

title: Knowledge Synthesis Review Framework: Task-Level Benchmarking of LLM-Based Systems for Multi-Source Evidence Synthesis
summary: Evidence in rapidly evolving fields is fragmented across academic studies, industry reports, policy documents, and media sources that differ in quality, structure, and purpose, making timely synthesis difficult. Large language models (LLMs) may accelerate this work, but their reliability across the distinct cognitive tasks of a review remains uncertain. We introduce the Knowledge Synthesis Review (KSR), a human-in-the-loop framework that decomposes evidence synthesis into screening, extraction, analysis, and synthesis, benchmarks LLM-based systems on each task against expert reference standards, and routes each task to the best-performing system under continuous expert validation. We evaluated GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and NotebookLM on a 244-document benchmark subset drawn from a 1,893-document corpus on AI and work spanning four source types, against a gold standard with high inter-rater reliability (92.2% agreement, kappa = 0.80). No system led on all tasks. Claude Sonnet 4 achieved the highest screening accuracy (82.8%) and GPT-5 the highest recall (91.8%) at the expense of lower specificity. Extraction exceeded 90% agreement for titles and sources but degraded in author and reference fields. Performance declined most in interpretive analysis and cross-source synthesis, where expert judgment remained essential. A contamination check on post-cutoff documents showed no evidence that prior exposure inflated results. Applied to the full corpus, the routed workflow surfaced cross-source asymmetries and blind spots that single-source synthesis would miss, including worker well-being, small firms, and the Global South. KSR offers a transparent, auditable, model-agnostic framework for governing LLM assistance in research synthesis while preserving human accountability.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Knowledge Synthesis Review (KSR), a human-in-the-loop framework that benchmarks and routes LLM-based systems across four tasks of evidence synthesis (screening, extraction, analysis, synthesis). Evaluating four leading LLMs on a 244-document subset of an 1,893-document corpus on AI and work, it finds no single system dominates across tasks, with strong performance on screening and extraction but weaker results on interpretive analysis and cross-source synthesis, highlighting where expert judgment remains essential.
AI.motivation: Evidence in fast-moving fields is fragmented across academic studies, industry reports, policy documents, and media sources of varying quality, making timely synthesis difficult. LLMs could accelerate this work, but their reliability across the distinct cognitive tasks of a review is uncertain. The authors sought a transparent, auditable way to govern LLM assistance in research synthesis.
AI.method: The authors propose KSR, a framework that decomposes evidence synthesis into screening, extraction, analysis, and synthesis. It benchmarks LLM-based systems per task against expert reference standards and routes each task to the best-performing system under continuous expert validation. They evaluated GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and NotebookLM on a 244-document benchmark from a 1,893-document corpus on AI and work spanning four source types, using a gold standard with 92.2% agreement and kappa = 0.80. A contamination check on post-cutoff documents tested for prior exposure effects.
AI.result: No system led on all tasks. Claude Sonnet 4 had the highest screening accuracy (82.8%) while GPT-5 achieved the highest recall (91.8%) at lower specificity. Extraction exceeded 90% agreement for titles and sources but degraded on author and reference fields. Performance declined most in interpretive analysis and cross-source synthesis. The contamination check found no evidence that prior exposure inflated results. On the full corpus, the routed workflow surfaced cross-source asymmetries and blind spots (worker well-being, small firms, Global South) that single-source synthesis would miss.
AI.conclusion: KSR provides a transparent, auditable, model-agnostic framework for governing LLM assistance in research synthesis while preserving human accountability. Because no single LLM excels at all tasks, task-specific routing under expert validation is more reliable than using one model for the whole review, especially where interpretive analysis and cross-source synthesis still require expert judgment.

title: Visibility Asymmetry: How Vendor Attention Shapes Which EdTech Breakdowns Become Product-Visible
summary: Infrastructure scholarship in CSCW often treats breakdown as the moment when infrastructures become visible. However, in vendor-managed sociotechnical systems, not all breakdowns become visible to actors who have the capacity to repair them. Drawing on a retrospective qualitative study of a Chinese K-12 EdTech deployment, including 11 interviews, 5 classroom observations, and more than 28 days of field notes, this paper introduces visibility asymmetry: a sensitizing concept for understanding how similar local breakdowns encounter uneven conditions for being routed, recognized, and acted upon. The analysis traces a four-stage mechanism through which procurement categories sort schools into attention tiers; staffing and visit cadence follow those tiers; only some local problems travel through staff or administrator channels; and dashboards can re-code unresolved repair labor as evidence of adoption. By shifting attention from the occurrence of breakdown to the organizational channels through which breakdown becomes actionable, this paper extends CSCW work on infrastructure, articulation work, and repair. It concludes by discussing implications for feedback systems that can surface repair needs without expanding surveillance.

AI.tldr: Introduces "visibility asymmetry" to explain why similar local breakdowns in vendor-managed sociotechnical systems receive uneven attention and repair, based on a study of Chinese K-12 EdTech deployment.
AI.motivation: CSCW infrastructure scholarship treats breakdown as the moment infrastructure becomes visible, but in vendor-managed systems not all breakdowns reach actors capable of repair. The paper aims to explain this uneven visibility.
AI.method: Retrospective qualitative study of a Chinese K-12 EdTech deployment using 11 interviews, 5 classroom observations, and more than 28 days of field notes.
AI.result: Identifies a four-stage mechanism: procurement categories sort schools into attention tiers; staffing and visit cadence follow those tiers; only some local problems travel through staff/administrator channels; and dashboards re-code unresolved repair labor as evidence of adoption.
AI.conclusion: Shifts focus from breakdown occurrence to the organizational channels making breakdown actionable, extending CSCW work on infrastructure, articulation work, and repair; discusses implications for feedback systems that surface repair needs without expanding surveillance.

title: What Drives LLM Self-Reflection? A Controlled Ablation of Uncertainty Routing in Armed Conflict Forecasting
summary: Self-reflection is widely assumed to improve LLM reasoning, yet which component drives the gain remains poorly understood. We present a controlled six-condition ablation isolating four components of LLM self-reflection: evidence exposure, diagnostic scaffolding, taxonomy vocabulary, and action routing. Two precise null results converge on a single mechanism. First, structured diagnostic questions add no measurable value over unstructured reflection ($\text{F1} = 0.296$ vs $0.297$, $p = 1.000$, 95\% CI $[-0.041, +0.040]$). Second, presenting the full uncertainty taxonomy while collapsing the action space to a single generic action also adds no value ($Δ\text{F1} = +0.008$, overlapping 95\% CIs), ruling out taxonomy vocabulary as the mechanism. Typed action routing provides consistent directional gains ($\text{F1} = 0.379$ vs $0.296$); the conservative estimate controlling for taxonomy vocabulary is $Δ\text{F1} = +0.075$, and the overall gain over the single-shot baseline is significant by bootstrap CI ($Δ\text{F1} = +0.101$, 95\% CI $[+0.020, +0.185]$). The vocabulary-routing decomposition replicates on GPT-4o: taxonomy vocabulary adds no significant value over generic reflection ($p = 0.773$), while action routing provides significant gains ($p = 0.025$), confirming the mechanism holds across backbones. Gains concentrate on structurally novel conflicts: in Myanmar ($\text{F1}: 0.000 \rightarrow 0.353$) and Ukraine ($0.167 \rightarrow 0.500$), the vocabulary-only condition recovers no more than generic reflection while action routing breaks the degenerate prior. These findings identify typed action routing -- not diagnostic scaffolding or taxonomy vocabulary -- as a promising design principle for metacognitive LLM forecasting agents, while motivating larger-scale evaluation across conflict typologies.

AI.tldr: A controlled six-condition ablation isolates four components of LLM self-reflection and finds that typed action routing—not diagnostic scaffolding or taxonomy vocabulary—drives the measurable gains in reasoning, replicating across GPT-4o and concentrating on structurally novel conflicts.
AI.motivation: Self-reflection is widely assumed to improve LLM reasoning, but it is unclear which specific component of reflection produces the benefit. The authors aim to decompose self-reflection into isolable components and identify the actual mechanism responsible for performance gains.
AI.method: The study uses a controlled six-condition ablation design that isolates four components of LLM self-reflection: (1) evidence exposure, (2) diagnostic scaffolding, (3) taxonomy vocabulary, and (4) action routing. Each component is systematically toggled on or off, with statistical comparisons of F1 scores, p-values, and 95% confidence intervals (including bootstrap CIs). The vocabulary–routing decomposition is replicated on GPT-4o to test cross-backbone generalizability, and gains are examined across conflict typologies (Myanmar, Ukraine).
AI.result: Two null results converge: structured diagnostic questions add no value over unstructured reflection (F1 = 0.296 vs 0.297, p = 1.000), and presenting the full uncertainty taxonomy with a single generic action adds no value (ΔF1 = +0.008, overlapping CIs). Typed action routing yields consistent directional gains (F1 = 0.379 vs 0.296), with a conservative ΔF1 = +0.075 controlling for taxonomy vocabulary, and a significant overall gain over the single-shot baseline (ΔF1 = +0.101, 95% CI [+0.020, +0.185]). The decomposition replicates on GPT-4o (taxonomy: p = 0.773; routing: p = 0.025). Gains concentrate on structurally novel conflicts (Myanmar F1: 0.000→0.353; Ukraine 0.167→0.500), where vocabulary alone recovers no more than generic reflection.
AI.conclusion: Typed action routing—not diagnostic scaffolding or taxonomy vocabulary—is the promising design principle for metacognitive LLM forecasting agents, and larger-scale evaluation across diverse conflict typologies is warranted.

title: Which Site, and When: A Free-Satellite-Data Test of Himalayan Glacial Lake Bursts, Landslides, and Ice Floods
summary: Two free satellite signals carry real information about glacial-lake outburst risk in the Nepal Himalaya: radar interferometry sees a moraine dam slowly sagging, and satellite weather marks the weeks when a primed lake is under stress. A companion feasibility study found that deformation indicates which lake is destabilizing and weather indicates when it is at risk, but proposed no predictive model. To address this gap, we propose and evaluate models that predict which site is susceptible and when a trigger arrives. We test three related hazards on free data alone: large moraine- and ice-dammed bursts, rainfall-triggered landslides, and smaller floods from ponds on and around a glacier. Each hazard gets two questions, never blended. Using 589 dated outbursts from HMAGLOFDB and several thousand catalogued landslides, we match each event against similar but unfailed sites, and hold every model to a strong simple baseline under spatial cross-validation that withholds whole map tiles, so no model succeeds by recognising a trained-on neighbourhood. Antecedent weather times the trigger at ROC 0.73 for big bursts, 0.83 for landslides, and 0.82 for small floods. Terrain ranks susceptibility only in part: scored naively it appears near 0.9, largely because catalogued failures cluster in wetter ranges; matched against comparable nearby sites the honest figures are 0.76, 0.71, and 0.54 (no better than chance). The burst signal holds within single regions, reaching 0.89 in Nepal alone. Five deep-learning models do not decisively beat a simple gradient-boosted baseline. Three score marginally higher on landslides, a hint too small to confirm. For the lake hazards the baseline wins outright, reproduced by a three-rule decision tree on ruggedness and monsoon rainfall. We close with a ranked Nepal watchlist, a prioritisation aid, not a prediction, and note where free data reaches its limits.

AI.tldr: Using only free satellite data (InSAR-visible moraine dam deformation and satellite weather), the paper builds and evaluates models predicting glacial-lake outburst floods, rainfall-triggered landslides, and small glacier-pond floods in the Nepal Himalaya. Weather times the trigger well (ROC 0.73–0.83), terrain susceptibility is near-chance after matching comparable sites, a simple gradient-boosted baseline beats five deep-learning models, and the work ends with a ranked Nepal watchlist as a prioritisation aid.
AI.motivation: A prior feasibility study showed that radar interferometry (deformation) indicates which glacial lake is destabilizing and satellite weather indicates when it is at risk, but it proposed no predictive model. This paper fills that gap by proposing and rigorously evaluating models that predict both which site is susceptible and when a trigger arrives, using free data alone.
AI.method: Three related hazards are modeled separately, with two questions each (susceptibility and trigger timing), on free data: large moraine- and ice-dammed outbursts, rainfall-triggered landslides, and smaller glacier-pond floods. Using 589 dated outbursts from HMAGLOFDB and several thousand catalogued landslides, each event is matched against similar but unfailed sites. Every model is held to a strong simple baseline under spatial cross-validation that withholds whole map tiles, preventing learned-neighbourhood shortcuts. Five deep-learning models are compared against a simple gradient-boosted baseline; lake hazards are also distilled into a three-rule decision tree on ruggedness and monsoon rainfall.
AI.result: Antecedent weather times the trigger at ROC 0.73 for big bursts, 0.83 for landslides, and 0.82 for small floods. Terrain ranks susceptibility only in part: naive scoring appears near 0.9 due to clustered catalogues in wetter ranges, but matched against comparable nearby sites the honest figures are 0.76, 0.71, and 0.54 (the last no better than chance). The burst signal holds within single regions, reaching 0.89 in Nepal alone. Five deep-learning models do not decisively beat the gradient-boosted baseline; three score marginally higher on landslides (too small to confirm), while the baseline wins outright for lake hazards, reproduced by a three-rule decision tree.
AI.conclusion: Free satellite data can time the trigger reliably and rank susceptibility partially, with a simple interpretable model (three-rule decision tree) matching or beating deep learning for lake hazards. The authors close with a ranked Nepal watchlist framed strictly as a prioritisation aid rather than a prediction, and note where free data reaches its limits.

title: Diagnostic Foundation for Evaluating LLMs' Research Integrity as Co-Scientists
summary: Language models are increasingly deployed as co-scientists, yet their ability to uphold research integrity under institutional pressure remains unmeasured. We introduce IntegrityBench, a benchmark evaluating misconduct classification, ethical action reasoning and artifact-grounded decision making across 36 paired tasks under a 5-level implicit-explicit pressure protocol spanning 3 domains and 4 research stages. Evaluating 18 frontier model variants, we find that under peak pressure, models fail roughly 1 in 3 integrity-critical decisions, and neither scale nor reasoning ability reliably mitigates this. Explicit pressures induce compliance with misconduct, while implicit contextual reframing more often causes over-refusal of legitimate research tasks. Interestingly, models failing to classify research requests accurately perform equally or better on artifact-grounded decision making (85.7 vs. 79.4), suggesting the three facets are structurally dissociated and correct ethical action does not require accurate classification. Frontier models can thus appear helpful while harbouring integrity failures that create two distinct deployment risks: facilitating research misconduct and eroding trust in AI-assisted research.

AI.tldr: Introduces IntegrityBench, a benchmark testing language models' research integrity under institutional pressure, finding frontier models fail ~1 in 3 integrity-critical decisions at peak pressure and that the three evaluated facets are dissociated.
AI.motivation: Language models are increasingly used as co-scientists, but their capacity to uphold research integrity under institutional pressure is unmeasured, posing risks of facilitating research misconduct and eroding trust in AI-assisted research.
AI.method: IntegrityBench evaluates 36 paired tasks across a 5-level implicit-explicit pressure protocol spanning 3 domains and 4 research stages, assessing three facets: misconduct classification, ethical action reasoning, and artifact-grounded decision making. 18 frontier model variants are evaluated.
AI.result: At peak pressure, models fail ~1 in 3 integrity-critical decisions; scale and reasoning ability do not reliably mitigate failures. Explicit pressures induce compliance with misconduct, while implicit contextual reframing causes over-refusal of legitimate tasks. Models failing classification perform equally or better on artifact-grounded decisions (85.7 vs. 79.4), indicating the three facets are structurally dissociated.
AI.conclusion: Frontier models can appear helpful yet harbor integrity failures, creating two deployment risks: facilitating research misconduct and eroding trust in AI-assisted research. Correct ethical action does not require accurate classification, underscoring the need for integrity safeguards beyond surface-level helpfulness.

title: The energetic cost of mitigating AI attacks in cellular networks
comment: 7 pages, 6 figures, submitted to IEEE Communications Magazine
summary: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI), generally as Machine Learning (ML) algorithms, in all levels and aspects of cellular networks demonstrates the success of data-driven algorithms; for example, the Radio Intelligence Controller (RIC) of the O-RAN paradigm bestows the network with optimised radio resource allocation, load balancing or energy efficiency functions, among others. Nevertheless, this dependency on data opens new security vulnerabilities, as attackers can alter data properties and steer ML models to underperform or degrade. Conversely, the developed mitigation strategies are effective, but they generate a computational load which, in consequence, results in an energy cost generally overlooked, even in the current energy-awareness context. In this work, consumption of a defence technique is characterised, and the challenges raised by the triad of ML accuracy, robustness and energy efficiency are outlined.

AI.tldr: The paper examines how AI/ML integration in cellular networks (e.g., O-RAN's RIC) improves functions like resource allocation but introduces data-driven security vulnerabilities. It characterizes the energy consumption of ML defence/mitigation techniques and highlights the tension between accuracy, robustness, and energy efficiency.
AI.motivation: AI/ML increasingly drives cellular network functions, but this data dependency creates attack surfaces where adversaries can manipulate data to degrade ML models. Existing mitigation strategies work, yet their computational overhead imposes an energy cost that is typically neglected, especially given current energy-awareness priorities in networks.
AI.method: The work characterizes the energy consumption of a specific ML defence technique against data-altering attacks and outlines the challenges arising from the interaction of three objectives: ML accuracy, robustness (security), and energy efficiency within the network context.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates that ML defence mechanisms incur a non-negligible energy cost, and presents the trade-offs (the "triad") among accuracy, robustness, and energy efficiency as a key open challenge that is currently overlooked.
AI.conclusion: Effective ML defences against data manipulation attacks generate computational load and consequent energy costs that are generally ignored. Balancing ML accuracy, robustness, and energy efficiency is an emerging, unresolved challenge in AI-enabled cellular networks.

title: LLMs Are Not Good Strategists, Yet Memory-Enhanced Agency Boosts Reasoning
summary: Strategic reasoning in Large Language Models (LLMs) within long-horizon environments is often limited by inconsistent subgoals. In these settings, finite attention resources prevent the model from maintaining strategic coherence over thousands of steps. This limitation leads to strategic drift, where localized decisions fail to sustain a coherent trajectory across reasoning. To address this, we introduce EpicStar, a framework that enables agents to learn memory as policy to tackle long-horizon reasoning. Specifically, the agent maintains a bank of successful past episodes as a heuristic alongside a working memory to track short-term environmental changes. During inference, a dynamic gating mechanism determines whether to execute a retrieved action directly or to perform new reasoning through a contextual fusion of the retrieved episodes and current working memory. Utilizing StarCraft II as the testbed, we evaluated EpicStar against diverse opponent styles. It significantly outperforms baseline methods, achieving higher win rates while consuming an order of magnitude fewer tokens, and it maintains this advantage consistently across difficulty levels and opponent strategies. Our findings provide compelling evidence that structured cross-episode memory is essential for enabling LLM agents to perform robust, long-term strategic execution in dynamic, autonomous settings.

AI.tldr: EpicStar is a framework that gives LLM agents "memory as policy" to solve long-horizon strategic reasoning. It stores successful past episodes plus a working memory, uses a dynamic gating mechanism to reuse retrieved actions or reason anew, and on StarCraft II it wins more often than baselines while using roughly 10x fewer tokens.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle with long-horizon strategic reasoning because finite attention resources cause "strategic drift"—localized decisions fail to maintain coherent trajectories over thousands of steps, with inconsistent subgoals. The authors aim to overcome this by giving agents memory-based policy to sustain strategic coherence.
AI.method: EpicStar maintains a bank of successful past episodes as a heuristic and a working memory tracking short-term environmental changes. At inference, a dynamic gating mechanism decides whether to execute a retrieved action directly or perform new reasoning via contextual fusion of retrieved episodes and current working memory. StarCraft II serves as the testbed.
AI.result: EpicStar significantly outperforms baseline methods across diverse opponent styles, achieving higher win rates while consuming an order of magnitude fewer tokens, and maintains this advantage consistently across difficulty levels and opponent strategies.
AI.conclusion: Structured cross-episode memory is essential for enabling LLM agents to perform robust, long-term strategic execution in dynamic, autonomous settings.

title: Does It Render Everywhere? A Study of Cross-Environment Compatibility in MLLM-Generated Webpages
summary:
Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have been increasingly adopted to automate webpage generation from visual designs (e.g., screenshots). However, existing evaluations are limited to visual fidelity assessment under a fixed browser-device configuration. Such a setting overlooks the cross-environment rendering compatibility for real-world deployments.
  To address this gap, we present the first systematic empirical study of cross-environment compatibility in AI-generated webpages. Specifically, we construct WebCompat, a dataset of 2,032 annotated instances, comprising webpages generated by 8 representative AI tools, each rendered across 9 browser-and-device combinations. We analyze the prevalence of compatibility issues, their user-perceptible symptoms, and underlying code-level root causes. Our findings reveal that 68% of generated webpages exhibit at least one compatibility issue, underscoring the pervasive reliability concerns surrounding MLLM-generated front-end artifacts. The most prevalent symptoms are failures that disrupt the entire page layout (88.3%): pages shrink directly to fit the target screen with too small fonts, or exhibit scale mismatches that produce cut-off content. Failures localized to individual elements, such as image distortion or missing components, are comparatively less common (13.4%). Furthermore, although most MLLMs incorporate responsive design patterns into the generation, they fail to properly implement these codes.
  Guided by the findings, we develop XCompat, a lightweight offline compatibility issue detector that combines visual screenshots and the structural DOM tree for analysis. It achieves an F1 score of 0.903 on the WebCompat-test, outperforming the existing compatibility checking tools and LLM baselines. All datasets and tools are released to support future research on rendering reliability in MLLM-based front-end code generation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the first systematic study of cross-environment rendering compatibility of AI-generated webpages, introduces the WebCompat dataset (2,032 instances across 8 tools × 9 browser/device combos), finds 68% of generated pages have at least one compatibility issue, and proposes XCompat, an offline detector achieving F1=0.903.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of MLLM-generated webpages only assess visual fidelity under a single fixed browser-device configuration, overlooking cross-environment rendering compatibility needed for real-world deployment.
AI.method: Constructed WebCompat, a dataset of 2,032 annotated instances from 8 AI tools rendered across 9 browser-and-device combinations; analyzed prevalence, user-perceptible symptoms, and code-level root causes; then built XCompat, a lightweight offline detector combining visual screenshots with the structural DOM tree.
AI.result: 68% of generated webpages exhibit at least one compatibility issue. The most prevalent symptoms disrupt the entire page layout (88.3%), e.g., pages shrinking with too-small fonts or scale mismatches causing cut-off content; element-localized failures (image distortion, missing components) are less common (13.4%). Most MLLMs incorporate responsive design patterns but fail to implement the code correctly. XCompat achieves F1=0.903 on WebCompat-test, outperforming existing compatibility-checking tools and LLM baselines.
AI.conclusion: Cross-environment compatibility is a pervasive reliability problem in MLLM-generated front-end code. The WebCompat dataset and XCompat detector are released to support future research on rendering reliability in MLLM-based front-end code generation.

title: DrEM: Dual-Side Robust Ensemble Ranking from Noisy User Preference Predictions in Video Recommendation
summary: Industrial video recommendation systems typically adopt a multi-stage architecture. At the ensemble ranking stage, multi-dimensional user preference predictions (pxtrs) from an upstream multi-task model are fused into a unified ranking score to reflect user satisfaction. Since users' true satisfaction is difficult to observe directly, ensemble ranking models commonly use pxtrs both as input features and as a source for constructing proxy preferences. However, as outputs of an upstream prediction model, pxtrs inevitably contain prediction noise, which propagates to downstream learning across two sides. On the supervision side, noisy pxtrs may flip proxy preferences and introduce erroneous gradients. On the feature side, pxtr noise may propagate through model inputs and destabilize ranking scores. Existing ensemble ranking methods typically treat pxtrs as reliable signals and overlook such prediction noise. To address this, we propose DrEM, a dual-side robust ensemble ranking framework. Our DrEM introduces a risk-denoising robust loss that corrects the empirical risk using estimated preference flip probability. Meanwhile, it samples perturbations from the distribution of prediction noise and introduces a preference-preserving ranking consistency regularizer to improve feature-side output stability. Theoretically, we obtain an approximate distribution of the prediction noise and prove that the robust loss remains superior under flip probability estimation error. Extensive offline experiments and large-scale online A/B tests demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our DrEM.

AI.tldr: DrEM is a dual-side robust ensemble ranking framework for industrial video recommendation that mitigates prediction noise in pxtr (multi-task prediction) signals by (1) a risk-denoising robust loss correcting empirical risk via flip probability estimation, and (2) a preference-preserving ranking consistency regularizer using perturbations sampled from the prediction noise distribution. It is validated by offline experiments and large-scale online A/B tests.
AI.motivation: In multi-stage video recommendation systems, the ensemble ranking stage fuses pxtrs from an upstream multi-task model to form a unified ranking score. Since pxtrs are model outputs, they inherently contain prediction noise, yet existing methods treat them as reliable signals. This noise harms downstream learning on two sides: on the supervision side, noisy pxtrs can flip proxy preferences and inject erroneous gradients; on the feature side, pxtr noise propagates through inputs and destabilizes ranking scores. Existing ensemble ranking methods overlook this prediction noise.
AI.method: DrEM addresses prediction noise from both sides. For supervision, it introduces a risk-denoising robust loss that corrects the empirical risk using an estimated preference flip probability. For features, it samples perturbations from the estimated distribution of prediction noise and applies a preference-preserving ranking consistency regularizer to improve output stability. Theoretically, the authors derive an approximate distribution of the prediction noise and prove that the robust loss remains superior even under flip probability estimation error.
AI.result: Extensive offline experiments and large-scale online A/B tests demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of DrEM. Theoretically, the robust loss is shown to remain superior under flip probability estimation error.
AI.conclusion: DrEM effectively handles prediction noise in pxtrs for ensemble ranking in industrial video recommendation by jointly denoising the supervision signal and stabilizing feature-side outputs, yielding improved robustness and performance as validated by both offline and online evaluations.

title: Humans are Missing from AI Coding Agent Research
summary: Recent progress in AI coding agent research has led to rapid improvements in agents' ability to autonomously perform complex software engineering tasks, from editing large codebases to executing long-horizon development workflows. As these systems make strides, however, the primary bottleneck to practical usefulness increasingly shifts away from pure task-solving capability, and toward challenges in how users communicate with, supervise, and trust agents. In this position paper, we argue for a reorientation from autonomous to human-centered coding agents: systems designed not only to complete tasks, but to collaborate effectively with people. We identify four core interaction-level dimensions that characterize the human-agent task-solving loop: task alignment, verifiability, steerability, and adaptability. Finally, we outline concrete research directions to advance these dimensions, including user-involved coding environments, comprehensive verification mechanisms, and principled measures of human-agent interaction quality.

AI.tldr: This position paper argues that AI coding agent research should shift focus from autonomous task-solving toward human-centered collaboration, identifying four interaction-level dimensions (task alignment, verifiability, steerability, adaptability) and proposing research directions such as user-involved environments, verification mechanisms, and interaction-quality metrics.
AI.motivation: As AI coding agents become increasingly capable of autonomously handling complex software engineering tasks, the key bottleneck to practical usefulness is no longer task-solving ability but rather how users communicate with, supervise, and trust these agents.
AI.method: This is a position paper that reorients the research agenda from autonomous to human-centered coding agents. It proposes a conceptual framework decomposing the human-agent task-solving loop into four core interaction-level dimensions: task alignment, verifiability, steerability, and adaptability.
