However, these methods have not been successfully extended to diffusion-based language models, which generate text through iterative denoising rather than sequential token prediction. We propose LoRA-Diffusion, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning approach that applies low-rank decomposition to the denoising trajectory instead of model weights. Unlike weight-based LoRA, which modifies individual transformation matrices, our method learns low-rank perturbations to the entire diffusion path from noise to output. We introduce trajectory-level low-rank adapters that modify each denoising step, step-adaptive rank allocation across diffusion phases, and compositional multi-task learning that allows merging task-specific modules at inference without retraining. On SST-2, QNLI, and MRPC, we report token-level denoising validation accuracy over five random seeds. LoRA-Diffusion achieves the highest mean performance on SST-2 and strong performance on QNLI and MRPC. Joint multi-task training further shows that LoRA-Diffusion achieves the highest token-level accuracy among the evaluated methods. The approach reduces per-task storage compared with full fine-tuning and establishes a parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework for diffusion language models.

AI.tldr: LoRA-Diffusion adapts LoRA-style parameter-efficient fine-tuning from autoregressive models to diffusion language models by applying low-rank decomposition to the denoising trajectory (not model weights), with trajectory-level adapters, step-adaptive rank allocation, and compositional multi-task merging, achieving strong performance and reduced storage on SST-2, QNLI, and MRPC.
AI.motivation: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods like LoRA have greatly benefited autoregressive language models, but they have not been successfully extended to diffusion-based language models, which generate text via iterative denoising rather than sequential token prediction. The authors aim to bring the benefits of PEFT (fewer trainable parameters, task-specific customization, low storage) to diffusion language models.
AI.method: LoRA-Diffusion applies low-rank decomposition to the denoising trajectory rather than model weights. It introduces (1) trajectory-level low-rank adapters that modify each denoising step, (2) step-adaptive rank allocation that varies capacity across diffusion phases, and (3) compositional multi-task learning enabling task-specific modules to be merged at inference without retraining.
AI.result: Evaluated on SST-2, QNLI, and MRPC using token-level denoising validation accuracy over five random seeds, LoRA-Diffusion achieves the highest mean performance on SST-2 and strong performance on QNLI and MRPC. In joint multi-task training it attains the highest token-level accuracy among evaluated methods, while reducing per-task storage compared to full fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: LoRA-Diffusion establishes an effective parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework for diffusion language models, matching or exceeding baseline performance while drastically reducing per-task storage and supporting composable multi-task inference.

title: Dual Spatial-Temporal Attribution: Architecture-Aligned Post-Hoc Explainability for Recurrent Graph Anomaly Detection
comment: Under Review : The International Conference on Cooperative Information Systems (CoopIS)
summary: Deep learning detectors for anomalies in dynamic graphs have reached strong accuracy, yet they remain opaque: when an edge is flagged, the analyst receives a score but no reason. This opacity is untenable in the cooperative, regulated information systems where such detectors are deployed, where automated decisions must be auditable and trustworthy. We address this gap for AddGraph, the foundational GCN+GRU framework for edge-level anomaly detection in dynamic graphs, which to our knowledge has never been equipped with any form of explainability. We present a strictly post-hoc explainability framework, X-AddGraph, built on a Dual Spatial-Temporal Attribution (DSTA) mechanism whose three components are each aligned with one of AddGraph's architectural modules: a gradient-based relevance attribution over the current adjacency structure (spatial), a direct reading of the contextual attention weights already computed during inference (short-term temporal, at zero additional cost), and a gradient rollback through the recurrent hidden states (long-term temporal). Because the detector is frozen, detection performance is preserved exactly (Delta AUC = 0, verified empirically to ten decimal places). On the UCI Message benchmark, our trained AddGraph baseline reaches an average per-snapshot AUC of 0.8705, exceeding the originally published result; X-AddGraph reproduces every score identically while adding explanations where none existed. Evaluated across four edge populations - confident true positives, low-confidence true positives, false positives, and random samples - the long-term attribution identifies historical snapshots carrying significantly more counterfactual signal than random selection (0.127 vs. 0.074), a capability that no spatially-blind explainer can provide. We release our implementation for full reproducibility.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces X-AddGraph, a strictly post-hoc explainability framework for AddGraph—a GCN+GRU edge-level anomaly detector in dynamic graphs. It uses a Dual Spatial-Temporal Attribution mechanism aligned with AddGraph's modules to explain flagged edges without altering detection performance.
AI.motivation: Deep learning anomaly detectors for dynamic graphs achieve high accuracy but are opaque: they output scores without reasons, which is unacceptable in cooperative, regulated information systems requiring auditable and trustworthy automated decisions. AddGraph, the foundational GCN+GRU framework, has never had explainability, motivating this work.
AI.method: X-AddGraph is a strictly post-hoc framework built on a Dual Spatial-Temporal Attribution (DSTA) mechanism with three components aligned to AddGraph's modules: (1) gradient-based relevance attribution over the current adjacency structure (spatial); (2) direct reading of contextual attention weights computed during inference (short-term temporal, zero additional cost); (3) gradient rollback through recurrent hidden states (long-term temporal). The detector remains frozen, so performance is preserved exactly.
AI.result: On the UCI Message benchmark, the AddGraph baseline reaches an average per-snapshot AUC of 0.8705, exceeding the originally published result. X-AddGraph reproduces every score identically (Delta AUC = 0 verified to ten decimal places). Across four edge populations (confident true positives, low-confidence true positives, false positives, and random samples), long-term attribution identifies historical snapshots with significantly more counterfactual signal than random selection (0.127 vs. 0.074). The implementation is released for reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: X-AddGraph adds explanations to AddGraph while preserving detection performance exactly, providing a capability—long-term temporal attribution of counterfactual signal across historical snapshots—that spatially-blind explainers cannot offer, and supporting auditable, trustworthy anomaly detection in regulated systems.

title: Position: We Need Practical AI Alignment Methods to Mirror Human Reasoning
summary: AI systems are increasingly employed as decision aids, decision delegates, or autonomous decision-makers. This position paper argues that in many settings, particularly high-stakes decision-making, we need accurate cognitively-aligned AI systems that reason similarly to their users, and faithfully communicate their reasoning. We review evidence that cognitive alignment improves understandability and trustworthiness, and provide new survey data showing that many users find cognitive alignment "essential" when an AI's rationale for a judgment or action is important to them. We outline the gaps between existing alignment methods and what is needed to achieve cognitive alignment, and present a research agenda to address these gaps. We argue that cognitive misalignment represents a likely impediment to AI adoption in many envisioned applications, and that addressing it is important for creating AI systems on which users are both willing and justified to rely.

AI.tldr: This position paper argues that for high-stakes decision-making, AI systems should be "cognitively aligned"—reasoning like their users and faithfully communicating their reasoning—and lays out a research agenda to close the gap between current alignment methods and this goal.
AI.motivation: AI systems are increasingly used as decision aids, delegates, or autonomous decision-makers, especially in high-stakes contexts. The authors contend that cognitive misalignment—where AI reasons differently from users and communicates its reasoning poorly—undermines understandability and trustworthiness, and likely impedes AI adoption. They provide new survey data showing many users regard cognitive alignment as "essential" when an AI's rationale matters to them.
AI.method: This is a position paper. The authors (1) review existing evidence that cognitive alignment improves understandability and trustworthiness; (2) present new survey data on user attitudes toward cognitive alignment; (3) identify gaps between current alignment methods and what cognitive alignment requires; and (4) propose a research agenda to address those gaps.
AI.result: The authors identify key gaps between existing AI alignment methods and the requirements for cognitive alignment, and present a corresponding research agenda. Their survey indicates that many users consider cognitive alignment "essential" in settings where an AI's rationale for a judgment or action is important. They argue cognitive misalignment is a likely barrier to AI adoption in many envisioned applications.
AI.conclusion: Achieving cognitive alignment—reasoning similarly to users and faithfully communicating that reasoning—is important for creating AI systems on which users are both willing and justified to rely, particularly in high-stakes decision-making, and merits focused research attention.

title: PIPES: Securing Agent Perception with Provenance and Priors
summary: Tool-using agents consume external data from sources with different levels of trust, yet tool responses rarely identify who produced each component or what it should convey. We show that this gap enables state-corruption attacks, in which attacker-controlled content makes environmental claims beyond the informational authority of its response component and corrupts the agent's perceived environment, making the resulting action appear justified to existing guardrails. We introduce PIPES (Provenance-Informed, Prior-Enforced Screening), which screens response units using semantic priors and source provenance. PIPES uses static field contracts when schemas provide stable expectations, and conditions screening of open-ended content on the pre-response trajectory and trusted provenance metadata. It marks units that violate their semantic prior or the provenance hierarchy; deployments may remove, warn, block, or escalate detected violations. We instantiate atomic removal and evaluate PIPES against adaptive PAIR-style attacks. Across the three VitaBench and three AgentDyn splits with Gemma 4 31B IT as the target agent, PIPES reduces average attack success from 84.7% to 2.3%, while preserving average benign utility (92.5% with PIPES versus 90.6% without defense).

AI.tldr: Tool responses rarely indicate source provenance or intended meaning, enabling "state-corruption" attacks where attacker-controlled content makes illegitimate environmental claims. The paper introduces PIPES, a screening defense that uses semantic priors and provenance to filter response units, cutting attack success from 84.7% to 2.3% while preserving benign utility.
AI.motivation: Tool-using agents consume external data from sources with varying trust levels, but tool responses do not identify who produced each component or what it should convey. This gap allows state-corruption attacks in which attacker-controlled content makes claims beyond its informational authority, corrupting the agent's perceived environment so that harmful actions appear justified to existing guardrails.
AI.method: PIPES (Provenance-Informed, Prior-Enforced Screening) screens response units using semantic priors and source provenance. It applies static field contracts when schemas offer stable expectations, and conditions screening of open-ended content on the pre-response trajectory and trusted provenance metadata. PIPES marks units violating their semantic prior or the provenance hierarchy, allowing deployments to remove, warn, block, or escalate violations; the paper instantiates atomic removal. Evaluated against adaptive PAIR-style attacks.
AI.result: Across three VitaBench and three AgentDyn splits with Gemma 4 31B IT as the target agent, PIPES reduces average attack success from 84.7% to 2.3%, while preserving average benign utility (92.5% with PIPES versus 90.6% without defense).
AI.conclusion: PIPES effectively defends tool-using agents against state-corruption attacks by enforcing semantic priors and provenance hierarchy, nearly eliminating attack success while maintaining (and slightly improving) benign utility.

title: LigBench: A Unified and Human-Aligned Benchmark for LLM-based Research Idea Generation
summary: With the rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs), research idea generation has attracted increasing attention. Existing approaches enable LLMs to retrieve relevant literature and propose novel ideas for research areas. However, current evaluation practices for idea generation remain fragmented and lack objective standards, often relying on direct LLM scoring, which limits their ability to provide unified and reliable assessments across a coherent distribution of generated ideas. To address this challenge, we propose LigBench, an automated evaluation benchmark that enables fine-grained and reliable evaluation of AI research ideas, consistently applicable across different generation distributions. In addition, we introduce PAIR-IQ, a dataset tailored for training pairwise idea judgment models and serving as an auxiliary reference to support more objective comparative evaluation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LigBench achieves stable and interpretable evaluations, significantly improving alignment with expert judgments. Furthermore, models trained on PAIR-IQ exhibit enhanced ranking accuracy and robustness, establishing a principled standard for scalable and objective research idea assessment.

AI.tldr: The paper presents LigBench, an automated benchmark for fine-grained, reliable evaluation of AI research ideas, plus PAIR-IQ, a dataset for training pairwise idea-judgment models. Experiments show LigBench aligns better with expert judgments, and PAIR-IQ-trained models improve ranking accuracy and robustness.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of LLM-generated research ideas is fragmented and lacks objective standards, often relying on direct LLM scoring, which cannot provide unified, reliable assessments across diverse generation distributions.
AI.method: Propose LigBench, an automated evaluation benchmark enabling fine-grained and reliable evaluation across different generation distributions; introduce PAIR-IQ, a dataset tailored for training pairwise idea judgment models to support more objective comparative evaluation.
AI.result: LigBench achieves stable, interpretable evaluations with significantly improved alignment with expert judgments; models trained on PAIR-IQ show enhanced ranking accuracy and robustness.
AI.conclusion: The approach establishes a principled standard for scalable and objective research idea assessment.

title: How Powerful are LLMs in Generating Formal Program Specifications?
summary: Formal verification provides strong guarantees of software correctness, but its adoption is limited by the high cost of writing precise formal specifications. While recent large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities in theorem proving and verified code generation, their true ability to generate program specifications remains unclear. Existing evaluations require either verifying implementation conformance or proving semantic equivalence between specifications, both of which are formidably difficult and may conflate proof difficulty with specification quality. To address this problem, we introduce Coins, a Rocq based evaluation framework that assesses specification quality by instantiating specifications under evaluation on trusted test cases and generating concrete proof obligations. This design aligns with the asymmetric nature of formal reasoning, where successful proofs provide reliable evidence while proof failures are inherently ambiguous. Using Coins, we conduct a large scale study on HumanEval with a curated set of human written Rocq specifications. Our results show that specification generation remains a formidable challenge, and that verification complexity can obscure genuine differences in specification quality. Overall, we find that accurate specification evaluation, rather than model scaling alone, is central to understanding the power of LLMs for specification synthesis, and that test case based formal reasoning offers a more faithful and discriminative measure of progress.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Coins, a Rocq-based evaluation framework that measures LLM-generated specification quality by instantiating specifications on trusted test cases to produce concrete proof obligations, rather than requiring full implementation conformance or semantic equivalence proofs. A large-scale study on HumanEval shows specification generation is still difficult, and that verification complexity can mask real differences in specification quality, making test-case-based formal reasoning a more faithful measure of progress.
AI.motivation: Formal verification adoption is limited by the high cost of writing precise specifications. Although LLMs are strong at theorem proving and verified code generation, their true specification-generation ability is unclear. Existing evaluations either verify implementation conformance or prove semantic equivalence between specifications, both of which are extremely hard and conflate proof difficulty with actual specification quality.
AI.method: The authors build Coins, a Rocq-based evaluation framework that assesses specification quality by instantiating specifications under evaluation on trusted test cases and generating concrete proof obligations. This exploits the asymmetric nature of formal reasoning: successful proofs give reliable evidence, while proof failures are inherently ambiguous. They apply Coins in a large-scale study on HumanEval with a curated set of human-written Rocq specifications.
AI.result: Specification generation remains a formidable challenge for LLMs. The study finds that verification complexity can obscure genuine differences in specification quality, indicating that proof difficulty is not a reliable proxy for specification quality.
AI.conclusion: Accurate specification evaluation, rather than model scaling alone, is central to understanding LLM capabilities for specification synthesis. Test-case-based formal reasoning offers a more faithful and discriminative measure of progress than conformance checking or semantic equivalence.

title: STAR: Structured Tokenization and Target-Aware Interest Representation for PCVR Prediction
summary: Post-click conversion rate (PCVR) prediction is a core ranking task in industrial recommender systems. Modern ranking models must jointly capture heterogeneous non-sequential features, multi-behavior user sequences, and target-item-aware user interests, while remaining robust to high-cardinality sparse features, missing values, and train-inference inconsistencies. In this paper, we present STAR (Structured Tokenization and Target-Aware Interest Representation), a practical framework for the KDD Cup 2026 Tencent UniRec Challenge. STAR combines structured feature tokenization with target-aware interest representation on top of a HyFormer-style multi-sequence backbone. It introduces high-cardinality signal recovery, explicit user-item interaction tokens, target-aware sequence decoding, and a weighted user-item contrastive auxiliary objective inspired by InfoNCE. We further align the training and inference pipelines by reconstructing feature remapping tables and structural hyperparameters from the saved training configuration. Experiments on the challenge dataset identify the components that most reliably improve ranking AUC, while LogLoss is reported as a calibration diagnostic. The main ablation study shows a large gain from temporal context, with smaller but useful contributions from contrastive alignment, target-aware interest encoding, and high-cardinality sequence feature recovery.

AI.tldr: STAR is a practical framework for post-click conversion rate (PCVR) prediction in the KDD Cup 2026 Tencent UniRec Challenge, combining structured feature tokenization and target-aware interest representation on a HyFormer-style multi-sequence backbone, with additional components for high-cardinality recovery, contrastive alignment, and train-inference consistency.
AI.motivation: Modern ranking models for PCVR must jointly capture heterogeneous non-sequential features, multi-behavior user sequences, and target-item-aware interests while remaining robust to high-cardinality sparse features, missing values, and train-inference inconsistencies.
AI.method: STAR integrates structured feature tokenization with target-aware interest representation atop a HyFormer-style multi-sequence backbone. It introduces high-cardinality signal recovery, explicit user-item interaction tokens, target-aware sequence decoding, and a weighted user-item contrastive auxiliary objective inspired by InfoNCE. Training and inference pipelines are aligned by reconstructing feature remapping tables and structural hyperparameters from the saved training configuration.
AI.result: Experiments on the challenge dataset show that temporal context yields a large AUC gain, while contrastive alignment, target-aware interest encoding, and high-cardinality sequence feature recovery provide smaller but useful contributions. LogLoss is reported as a calibration diagnostic rather than a primary metric.
AI.conclusion: STAR delivers a practical, robust PCVR ranking solution, with the main ablation study confirming temporal context as the dominant contributor and smaller complementary gains from contrastive alignment, target-aware interest encoding, and high-cardinality sequence feature recovery.

title: Transforming Interactions in Thesis Supervision: An Exposé-First Workflow in Higher Education
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures; accepted as Work in Progress at Mensch und Computer 2026 (MuC 2026)
summary: At the studied research institute, one professorship oversees approximately 20 theses per semester, while day-to-day supervision is distributed among doctoral and postdoctoral researchers. To manage this supervision demand, the institute uses an exposé-first workflow in which students prepare a research proposal before entering the main thesis-writing phase. This paper asks how students, supervisors, and administrators experience the exposé-first workflow as a structured process for early thesis preparation, and how it redistributes responsibility, supervision, and administrative coordination work across roles and two digital platforms. Based on a mixed-methods study analyzed through Frauenberger et al.'s four reflective design lenses, the findings show that the exposé-first model made thesis preparation more structured by turning early research planning into a staged process of proposal writing, feedback, and approval. Students reported that this process helped them clarify research goals and take ownership of their research plans at an early stage. However, the workflow redistributed rather than reduced work: supervisors shifted toward iterative feedback, feasibility checking, and preliminary quality assurance, while administrators carried much of the coordination across platforms, deadlines, submissions, and feedback. The paper contributes an analysis of exposé-first thesis preparation as a sociotechnical workflow, showing how workflow redesign can improve structure while leaving essential administrative coordination work underrecognized.

AI.tldr: A study of an exposé-first thesis supervision workflow at a research institute finds it improves structure and student ownership of research planning, but redistributes rather than reduces work—shifting supervisors toward iterative feedback and quality checks while administrators absorb coordination across digital platforms, a load that remains underrecognized.
AI.motivation: One professorship oversees roughly 20 theses per semester, with day-to-day supervision delegated to doctoral and postdoctoral researchers. To handle this supervision load, the institute adopted an exposé-first workflow requiring a research proposal before the main thesis phase. The paper investigates how students, supervisors, and administrators experience this structure and how it redistributes responsibility, supervision, and coordination across roles and two digital platforms.
AI.method: A mixed-methods study analyzed through Frauenberger et al.'s four reflective design lenses, examining the exposé-first workflow as a sociotechnical process spanning multiple roles and two digital platforms.
AI.result: The exposé-first model made early research planning more structured by turning it into a staged sequence of proposal writing, feedback, and approval. Students reported clarified research goals and early ownership of their plans. However, the workflow redistributed rather than reduced work: supervisors shifted toward iterative feedback, feasibility checking, and preliminary quality assurance, while administrators carried much of the coordination across platforms, deadlines, submissions, and feedback.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes an analysis of exposé-first thesis preparation as a sociotechnical workflow, showing that redesign can improve structure while leaving essential administrative coordination work underrecognized.

title: AnchorSIPS: A Synthetic Dataset and Evaluation Resource for Evidence-Supported Psychosis-Risk Symptom Measurement
summary: Progress on AI for psychosis-risk assessment is limited by a data-access bottleneck. Real clinical interviews are difficult to share because of privacy, governance, and consent constraints. We present AnchorSIPS, a synthetic dataset of 10K structured psychosis-risk interviews with transcript-grounded measurement targets. Each interview is modeled on Mini-SIPS, a clinician-administered psychosis-risk interview. It captures history, 24 symptom questions, follow-up evidence for items the patient affirms, decisions about delusion-like symptoms (unusual beliefs), hallucination-like symptoms (unusual perceptions), and disorganized communication, exclusion of clear psychotic-level symptoms ("frank psychosis"), and a final attenuated psychosis syndrome (APS) diagnosis, a high-risk state of milder or early psychotic symptoms. The APS diagnosis is not a standalone label. It depends on earlier endorsements, supporting follow-up details, symptom-class decisions, and the frank-psychosis check. Every intermediate decision is anchored to its supporting transcript turns. AnchorSIPS is generated by a plan-then-realize pipeline. A hidden case sheet specifies the patient's clinical state, a deterministic planner fixes the interview structure, and an LLM realizes only the patient utterances under validation and bounded repair. Fixing labels and structure before generation avoids the inter-turn inconsistencies typical of multi-turn LLM dialogue. Across seven LLM baselines, models recover coarse decisions but fail to extract follow-up details or cite supporting transcript turns, so final-label performance overstates interview competence. AnchorSIPS is intended for research on evidence extraction, transcript-grounded measurement, and uncertainty under partial disclosure.

AI.tldr: AnchorSIPS is a 10K synthetic dataset of structured psychosis-risk interviews, generated via a plan-then-realize pipeline to enable transcript-grounded AI research and expose shortcomings in current LLM performance on interview-based measurement.
AI.motivation: Progress on AI for psychosis-risk assessment is bottlenecked by restricted access to real clinical interviews due to privacy, governance, and consent constraints. There is a need for a shareable, realistic dataset that supports transcript-grounded measurement and reliable evaluation.
AI.method: A plan-then-realize pipeline generates 10K synthetic interviews modeled on Mini-SIPS. A hidden case sheet defines the patient's clinical state, a deterministic planner fixes interview structure and labels, and an LLM realizes only patient utterances with validation and bounded repair. Each interview captures history, 24 symptom questions, evidence follow-ups, delusion-/hallucination-like symptom decisions, disorganized communication, frank-psychosis exclusion, and an APS diagnosis, with every intermediate decision anchored to supporting transcript turns.
AI.result: Across seven LLM baselines, models recover coarse decisions but fail to extract follow-up details and cannot cite supporting transcript turns. This indicates final-label performance overstates actual interview competence.
AI.conclusion: AnchorSIPS provides a resource for studying evidence extraction, transcript-grounded measurement, and uncertainty under partial disclosure, highlighting that label-level accuracy alone is insufficient to judge LLM competence in clinical interview tasks.

title: Personalized Scorer Modeling: A Learning-Based Framework for Deriving Robust Sleep Stage Labels from Multiple Experts
summary: Sleep stage classification is important for the diagnosis and management of sleep disorders, yet most automatic staging studies evaluate models against a single reference hypnogram despite known inter-scorer variability. This study investigates whether multi-scored datasets can be used to construct more reliable reference labels from the collective behavior of multiple experts. We use the publicly available DOD-H and DOD-O datasets. EEG (C3-M2) and chin EMG signals were segmented into 30-s epochs, and 30 features were extracted from each modality, yielding 60 features for EEG+EMG. We propose a learning-based hypnogram (LBH) that models the stage-specific behavior of each scorer using confusion matrices derived from machine-learning models. After column normalization, these matrices estimate the probability of each true sleep stage given each scorer's label; probabilities are aggregated across scorers to assign the final label for each epoch. LBH was evaluated with random forest, support vector machine, and multilayer perceptron classifiers under EEG-only and EEG+EMG settings, and compared with the dataset hypnogram (DH) and best-scorer hypnogram (BSH). LBH consistently improved overall performance. The best results were obtained with random forest and EEG+EMG, reaching 86.07% accuracy, 85.46% precision, and 85.29% F1-score on DOD-H, and 86.04% accuracy, 85.21% precision, and 84.70% F1-score on DOD-O. These findings suggest that personalized scorer modeling can improve reference hypnogram construction without discarding information from individual experts.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a learning-based hypnogram (LBH) method that aggregates multiple sleep scorers' labels using per-scorer confusion matrices to build more reliable reference labels, improving multi-class sleep stage classification accuracy over single-expert references.
AI.motivation: Most automatic sleep staging studies evaluate against a single reference hypnogram, despite known inter-scorer variability among experts. The authors seek to leverage multi-scored datasets to construct more reliable reference labels from the collective behavior of multiple experts, rather than discarding or relying on a single scorer's annotation.
AI.method: Using the public DOD-H and DOD-O datasets, 30-s epochs of EEG (C3-M2) and chin EMG were segmented and 30 features were extracted per modality (60 total for EEG+EMG). The proposed learning-based hypnogram (LBH) models each scorer's stage-specific behavior via confusion matrices derived from machine-learning classifiers. After column normalization, these matrices estimate P(true stage | scorer's label); probabilities are aggregated across scorers to assign the final epoch label. LBH was evaluated with random forest, support vector machine, and multilayer perceptron classifiers under EEG-only and EEG+EMG settings, and compared against the dataset hypnogram (DH) and best-scorer hypnogram (BSH).
AI.result: LBH consistently improved overall performance across all classifiers and modalities. Best results used random forest with EEG+EMG: on DOD-H 86.07% accuracy, 85.46% precision, 85.29% F1-score; on DOD-O 86.04% accuracy, 85.21% precision, 84.70% F1-score.
AI.conclusion: Personalized scorer modeling can improve reference hypnogram construction without discarding information from individual experts, suggesting that aggregating multi-scorer labels via confusion-matrix-based probability modeling yields more reliable sleep staging references.

title: Don't Want Your LLM to Recommend Nuclear Strike? Try Asking It in Japanese
summary: Large language models are increasingly used in strategic and advisory contexts, yet their safety alignment is typically evaluated in English only. We test nine models from six providers and ask whether the language of a prompt can change a model's decision in a high-stakes scenario. We use single-turn game-theoretic vignettes in which a model advises a nuclear-armed nation on whether to strike a defenseless opponent. The prompt is intentionally amoral and strategically identical across languages. We find that Japanese prompts reduce launch rates in the Claude model family: Claude Sonnet 4.6 drops from 40% to 0% in scenarios where the strike is unnecessary and from 93% to 17% in contested scenarios, with minimal effect when the strike is strategically rational. The effect extends to Gemini Pro 3.1 (53% to 13%). A cross-language experiment isolates the mechanism: when instructed to reason in Japanese in an English prompt, launch rates drop from 93% to 37%. It is the language the model is asked to reason in, not the language of the input, that drives the effect. When reasoning in Japanese, models spontaneously generate moral vocabulary (''moral cost'', ''millions of lives'') that is entirely absent from the prompt. Five other models show no language effect, but they launch in nearly every condition regardless of language. The effect requires a model that already hesitates in English. These results show that LLM safety behavior is language-dependent, and that evaluating in English alone can miss both risks and safeguards encoded in other languages.

AI.tldr: LLM safety alignment varies by language: prompting some models to reason in Japanese sharply reduces their willingness to recommend nuclear strikes in game-theoretic vignettes, while most other models launch regardless of language.
AI.motivation: Safety alignment in LLMs is typically evaluated only in English, but these models are deployed in multilingual strategic and advisory contexts. The authors ask whether the language of a prompt—and specifically the language of reasoning—can materially change a model's decisions in high-stakes scenarios.
AI.method: The authors tested nine models from six providers using single-turn game-theoretic vignettes in which a model advises a nuclear-armed nation on whether to strike a defenseless opponent. The prompt is amoral and strategically identical across languages. They measured launch rates across English and Japanese, varied whether the strike was strategically rational, unnecessary, or contested, and ran a cross-language experiment requiring reasoning in Japanese while the prompt remained in English.
AI.result: Japanese prompts reduce launch rates in the Claude model family (Sonnet 4.6 falls from 40% to 0% when the strike is unnecessary, and from 93% to 17% in contested scenarios), with minimal effect when the strike is strategically rational. The effect extends to Gemini Pro 3.1 (53% to 13%). A cross-language experiment shows that instructing reasoning in Japanese within an English prompt drops launch rates from 93% to 37%, and models spontaneously generate moral vocabulary (e.g., "moral cost", "millions of lives") absent from the prompt. Five other models show no language effect but launch in nearly every condition. The effect requires a model that already hesitates in English.
AI.conclusion: LLM safety behavior is language-dependent, driven by the language of reasoning rather than input. English-only evaluations can miss both risks and safeguards encoded in other languages.

title: RealmEye: Virtual Machine Introspection for Arm CCA Realm VMs
summary:
Confidential VMs (CVMs) have become the dominant substrate for sensitive cloud workloads, from financial services to privacy-preserving AI inference. The hardware isolation that protects these CVMs from a malicious cloud also blinds their owners to what runs inside them: kernel rootkits planted via network or supply-chain attacks can hide processes, tamper with kernel data, and exfiltrate model weights under the cover of the same isolation that defends the VM. Tenants therefore need to inspect a running CVM from outside, yet classical VM introspection (VMI) presupposes a trusted Hypervisor, which CVMs exclude from the TCB. The state-of-the-art CVM-VMI system, 00SEVen, restores introspection on AMD SEV-SNP via an in-VM agent at a privileged tier (VMPL0), a mechanism that does not exist on Arm CCA, leaving Realm VMs without any introspection solution.
  We present RealmEye, the first VMI system for Arm CCA Realm VMs. RealmEye places the entire introspection logic inside the Realm Management Monitor (RMM) at R-EL2, achieving hardware-enforced separation between the monitor and the monitored VM: no agent runs inside the Realm, and the Realm remains unmodified. RealmEye reads Realm memory and registers, suspends the VM for consistent snapshots, and traps page-level accesses, without relying on any in-VM interface. A periodic, self-driven trigger mode keeps scan timing internal to the RMM, preventing the Hypervisor from colluding with in-Realm rootkits. Results are returned to the remote owner over a hardware-attested channel, and a CCA driver backend lets existing tools such as LibVMI and DRAKVUF interoperate with RealmEye unchanged. On the Arm FVP, RealmEye detects process hiding and syscall-table hooking by Diamorphine, and its in-RMM cost is linearly predictable from primitive invocation counts.

AI.tldr: RealmEye is the first VM introspection (VMI) system for Arm CCA Realm VMs, implementing all introspection logic inside the Realm Management Monitor (RMM) at R-EL2 to achieve hardware-enforced separation without any in-VM agent or modification to the Realm.
AI.motivation: Confidential VMs protect workloads from a malicious cloud but hide their contents from their owners, allowing in-VM rootkits to hide processes, tamper with kernel data, and exfiltrate secrets. Existing CVM-VMI solutions assume a trusted hypervisor or require a privileged in-VM agent (e.g., 00SEVen's VMPL0 on AMD SEV-SNP), and no introspection solution exists for Arm CCA Realm VMs, which lack the VMPL mechanism.
AI.method: RealmEye places the entire introspection logic inside the RMM at R-EL2, giving hardware-enforced separation from the monitored VM. It reads Realm memory and registers, suspends the VM for consistent snapshots, and traps page-level accesses with no in-VM interface. A self-driven trigger mode keeps scan timing internal to the RMM to prevent hypervisor collusion with in-Realm rootkits. Results are returned over a hardware-attested channel, and a CCA driver backend lets LibVMI and DRAKVUF interoperate unchanged.
AI.result: On the Arm FVP, RealmEye detects process hiding and syscall-table hooking by the Diamorphine rootkit. Its in-RMM overhead is linearly predictable from primitive invocation counts.
AI.conclusion: RealmEye provides the first practical, hardware-enforced out-of-VM introspection for Arm CCA Realm VMs, restoring tenant visibility without trusting the hypervisor or modifying the guest, while preserving compatibility with existing introspection tools.

title: Can Formal Specifications Be Synthesized from Tests Alone?
summary: Formal specifications offer strong guarantees, but remain costly to write manually. Recent LLM-based approaches automate this by inferring specifications from source code, yet their reliance on white-box access poses barriers to industrial adoption due to intellectual property risks and deployment costs. Our approach uses LLMs to infer candidate specifications solely from test code and dynamic execution traces: the LLM observes only the program interface, selected inputs, and corresponding outputs or state changes, while the implementation internals remain hidden. Candidate specifications are validated locally using bounded model checking, with feedback guiding iterative refinement. Initial results on the SpecGenBench benchmark suggest that tests can guide LLMs towards meaningful Java Modeling Language specifications, while also highlighting checker compatibility and diagnostic feedback as key challenges for reliable refinement.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a black-box LLM-based method that infers Java Modeling Language (JML) specifications from test code and execution traces only, without exposing implementation internals, and iteratively refines candidates via bounded model checking.
AI.motivation: Manually writing formal specifications is costly. Existing LLM-based specification-inference approaches require white-box access to source code, which creates intellectual property risks and high deployment costs, hindering industrial adoption. The authors seek a method that infers specifications while keeping implementation internals hidden.
AI.method: The approach uses LLMs to infer candidate specifications solely from test code and dynamic execution traces. The LLM only observes the program interface, selected inputs, and corresponding outputs or state changes. Candidate specifications are validated locally using bounded model checking, with the checker's feedback used to guide iterative refinement of the candidates.
AI.result: Initial results on the SpecGenBench benchmark suggest that tests can guide LLMs toward meaningful JML specifications. The work also identifies checker compatibility and the quality of diagnostic feedback as key challenges to achieving reliable refinement.
AI.conclusion: Test-driven, black-box specification inference is a promising direction toward practical, privacy-preserving automation of formal specification generation, but further work is needed to address checker compatibility and diagnostic-feedback limitations for reliable iterative refinement.

title: Generative Universal Multimodal Retrieval with Dual-role Identifiers
summary: Generative information retrieval (GIR) has emerged as a compelling alternative to the conventional index-retrieve-then-rank retrieval pipeline by training a generator to produce the identifiers of relevant items directly. Despite its promise, a number of open challenges still remain. First, constrained left-to-right decoding is vulnerable to prefix-level errors and local optima. Second, most prior GIR research remains largely unimodal, leaving instruction-aware retrieval across text, image, and mixed image-text items underexplored. Third, although discrete identifier-based GIR offers higher efficiency, its retrieval accuracy still lags behind that of the cutting-edge dense-vector-based retrieval methods. Motivated by these challenges, we propose DrIG, a novel Generative framework for universal multimodal retrieval featuring Dual-role Identifiers, which supports diverse retrieval tasks across multiple modalities and domains. Each candidate is assigned a single residual-quantized identifier that serves two complementary roles. In its sequential role, the identifier is decoded autoregressively, where the first token explicitly models modality and the remaining tokens capture progressively finer semantics. In its set-based role, the same tokens are reinterpreted as an unordered set to provide a prefix-independent relevance prior, which guides constrained beam search and alleviates local-optimum errors. Extensive experiments on the M-BEIR benchmark and the text-to-image evaluation datasets show that:(1)DrIG consistently outperforms state-of-the-art generative multimodal baselines across diverse tasks, while hybrid reranking achieves a favorable efficiency-effectiveness trade-off against strong dense retrievers. (2)Ablation and scaling analyses reveal how the base LMM, beam size, reranking depth, and fusion strategy affect retrieval performance, providing practical guidance for system design.

AI.tldr: DrIG is a generative universal multimodal retrieval framework using dual-role identifiers that decodes identifiers autoregressively (sequential role) and reinterprets them as an unordered set (set-based role) to guide constrained beam search, outperforming SOTA generative multimodal baselines on M-BEIR and text-to-image benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Generative information retrieval (GIR) faces three open challenges: (1) constrained left-to-right decoding suffers prefix-level errors and local optima; (2) prior GIR research is mostly unimodal, leaving instruction-aware retrieval across text, image, and mixed image-text items underexplored; (3) discrete identifier-based GIR lags behind dense-vector retrieval in accuracy despite offering higher efficiency.
AI.method: DrIG assigns each candidate a single residual-quantized identifier with two complementary roles: a sequential role where the identifier is decoded autoregressively (first token models modality, remaining tokens capture progressively finer semantics), and a set-based role where the same tokens form an unordered set providing a prefix-independent relevance prior that guides constrained beam search to mitigate local-optimum errors. It supports universal multimodal retrieval across modalities/domains and hybrid reranking.
AI.result: On M-BEIR and text-to-image evaluation datasets, DrIG consistently outperforms state-of-the-art generative multimodal baselines across diverse tasks, and hybrid reranking achieves a favorable efficiency-effectiveness trade-off against strong dense retrievers. Ablation and scaling analyses show how the base LMM, beam size, reranking depth, and fusion strategy affect retrieval performance.
AI.conclusion: DrIG effectively addresses prefix-error vulnerability, multimodality, and accuracy gaps in GIR through dual-role identifiers, delivering superior generative multimodal retrieval performance and practical guidance for system design.

title: Analysis of Motor Signatures of Social Adaptation in Autism for Efficient Human-Centric Systems
summary: Dance imitation integrates motor planning, sensorimotor integration, and social cognition, offering a sensitive framework to characterize motor behavior in autism. In this work, we explore a computational analysis framework to identify potential biomarkers that allow the design and development of improved medical and human-machine systems. We analyzed 3D motion capture data from autistic and neurotypical adults performing dance imitation under solo and socially-framed duo conditions. Methodologically, using Dynamic Time Warping, we quantified movement consistency and propose the Social Context Sensitivity Index (SCSI) to measure modulation of variability by social framing. These features were then used on a classifier to discriminate subjects into autistic or neurotypical groups. Results show that neurotypical adults exhibited increased movement variability in socially-framed imitation, especially in upper and lower limbs, whereas autistic adults maintained consistent movement across contexts. Classification achieved 79.2% balanced accuracy in distinguishing groups. These findings suggest that social context sensitivity in motor imitation constitutes a robust biomarker of autism-related motor behavior, highlighting the importance of social modulation in motor assessments and informing the development of inclusive human-centric technologies.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes 3D motion capture data from autistic and neurotypical adults performing dance imitation in solo vs. social duo contexts. It introduces Dynamic Time Warping-based movement consistency metrics and a Social Context Sensitivity Index (SCSI), then classifies groups with 79.2% balanced accuracy, finding reduced social-context modulation of movement in autism.
AI.motivation: Dance imitation integrates motor planning, sensorimotor integration, and social cognition, offering a sensitive framework to characterize autism-related motor behavior. The goal is to identify computational biomarkers that enable better medical diagnostics and human-machine system design.
AI.method: 3D motion capture data were collected from autistic and neurotypical adults during dance imitation under solo and socially-framed duo conditions. Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) quantified movement consistency, and a novel Social Context Sensitivity Index (SCSI) measured how social framing modulates movement variability. These features were fed into a classifier to discriminate autistic vs. neurotypical groups.
AI.result: Neurotypical adults showed increased movement variability in socially-framed imitation (especially upper and lower limbs), while autistic adults maintained consistent movement across contexts. Classification achieved 79.2% balanced accuracy in distinguishing the two groups.
AI.conclusion: Social context sensitivity in motor imitation constitutes a robust biomarker of autism-related motor behavior, underscoring the importance of social modulation in motor assessments and supporting the development of inclusive human-centric technologies.

title: Reliability-Aware Sexism Detection: Combining DPO with Annotator Agreement and Token-Level Confidence Scoring
summary: The detection of online sexism remains an open problem. Sexism detection is inherently subjective, yet most existing systems reduce multi-annotator labels to a single majority decision and treat all instances uniformly. This ignores two informative signals: annotator agreement and model uncertainty. We propose RA-DPO (Reliability-Aware Direct Preference Optimization), which integrates annotator agreement, model confidence, and a token-level uncertainty signal into a single reliability score. RA-DPO uses this score to select high-value preference pairs during training and to support inference-time abstention, which allows the model to trade coverage for accuracy. We evaluate RA-DPO on 6,920 multilingual posts from EXIST 2023, fine-tune OpenAI gpt-4o base via DPO, and validate on two open-weight 3B models (Llama, Qwen). Results show that training on the top 30% most reliable pairs matches full-data DPO, which indicates that reliability-aware selection can reduce training cost without sacrificing performance. At inference, selective prediction reaches 96.2% accuracy at 50% coverage in the true-agreement setting and 88.7% in the deployable predicted-agreement setting, both exceeding the 85.3% no-agreement baseline. These results suggest that accounting for annotation uncertainty is beneficial for both efficient training and reliable deployment in subjective classification.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RA-DPO, a reliability-aware training and inference method for subjective sexism detection that combines annotator agreement, model confidence, and token-level uncertainty. It shows reliability-aware data selection matches full-data DPO performance while enabling selective prediction that improves accuracy through abstention.
AI.motivation: Sexism detection is inherently subjective, but existing systems reduce multi-annotator labels to a single majority vote and treat all instances uniformly, discarding two informative signals: annotator agreement and model uncertainty. This ignores valuable information that could improve both training efficiency and deployment reliability.
AI.method: RA-DPO (Reliability-Aware Direct Preference Optimization) integrates annotator agreement, model confidence, and a token-level uncertainty signal into a single reliability score. The score selects high-value preference pairs during DPO training and enables inference-time abstention (selective prediction) to trade coverage for accuracy. The method is validated by fine-tuning OpenAI gpt-4o base via DPO and testing on two open-weight 3B models (Llama, Qwen).
AI.result: On 6,920 multilingual posts from EXIST 2023: training on the top 30% most reliable pairs matches full-data DPO performance; selective prediction reaches 96.2% accuracy at 50% coverage in the true-agreement setting and 88.7% in the deployable predicted-agreement setting, both exceeding the 85.3% no-agreement baseline.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for annotation uncertainty benefits both efficient training and reliable deployment in subjective classification tasks, enabling reduced training cost without performance loss and improved accuracy through abstention at inference.

title: Geometric and Behavioral Stratification in Transformer Residual Streams
comment: 63 pages, 10 figures, 15 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/nelsonguda/pdsf-residual-geometry
summary:
Trained transformer models develop privileged bases: coordinate axes whose statistics differ from the rest of the residual stream. But what kind of direction does such a basis select? We investigate the prediction direction, the unembedding direction of the token a model currently predicts, and find that it functions as a content-defined privileged anchor. Measured with respect to this anchor, residual-stream variation is geometrically and behaviorally stratified by proximity to the prediction.
  The stratification holds in all eighteen models tested (dense and mixture-of-experts, 7B-120B, base and instruction-tuned). A narrow, scale-invariant prediction interface concentrates readout-relevant structure, while the vast prediction-distal complement expands with model scale. Because the prediction direction sits nearly orthogonal to the principal variance axes, variance-based analyses recover this organization only partly, and the shortfall grows with prompt heterogeneity.
  Anchoring reveals a steep geometric gradient: prediction-proximal regions are highly structured and cluster related prompts, while the complement is flatter and anti-discriminates among prompt groups. The interface is a narrow slice but functionally decisive. Disrupting the variance directions closest to the prediction causes immediate divergence and frequent task-frame shifts; disrupting the next level down delays divergence and preserves framing. The complement is weakly readout-aligned per direction yet causally and temporally load-bearing, and behavior is driven by direction rather than magnitude.
  These results establish the prediction direction as a privileged anchor distinct from previously described coordinate axes, and give a geometric account of how high-dimensional computation coexists with linear readout.

AI.tldr: Transformer models develop a "prediction direction" — the unembedding direction of the currently predicted token — that acts as a content-defined privileged anchor. Residual-stream variation is stratified by proximity to this anchor, revealing a narrow prediction interface where readout-relevant structure concentrates, with a flat complement that expands with scale.
AI.motivation: Prior work identified "privileged bases" in transformer residual streams but left open what kind of direction such a basis selects. The authors aim to characterize the prediction direction as a content-defined anchor and explain how high-dimensional computation coexists with linear readout.
AI.method: The authors measure residual-stream variation with respect to the prediction direction (the unembedding vector of the model's current prediction) across eighteen models — dense and mixture-of-experts, 7B–120B, base and instruction-tuned. They analyze geometric and behavioral stratification by proximity to the prediction, compare against variance-based analyses (principal variance axes), and perform causal/temporal perturbation experiments at different proximity levels.
AI.result: The stratification by prediction proximity holds in all eighteen models. A narrow, scale-invariant prediction interface concentrates readout-relevant structure, while the prediction-distal complement grows with scale. The prediction direction is nearly orthogonal to principal variance axes, so variance-based analyses only partly recover the organization. Prediction-proximal regions are highly structured and cluster related prompts; the complement is flatter and anti-discriminates among prompt groups. Disrupting variance directions closest to the prediction causes immediate divergence and task-frame shifts; disrupting the next level delays divergence and preserves framing. The complement is weakly readout-aligned per direction yet causally and temporally load-bearing, with behavior driven by direction rather than magnitude.
AI.conclusion: The prediction direction constitutes a privileged anchor distinct from previously described coordinate axes, providing a geometric account of how high-dimensional computation coexists with linear readout in transformers.

title: Dual-Flow Transformers: Decoupling the Primary Prefill Path from Additional Decode Computation
summary: As large language models serve more requests, cumulative inference cost is becoming increasingly important relative to one-time training cost. The two inference phases stress hardware differently: prompt prefill is parallel and typically compute-bound, whereas autoregressive decode is sequential and often memory-bandwidth-bound. Conventional width or depth scaling increases both costs together because every added layer is evaluated in both phases. We ask whether additional learned computation can instead be allocated to continuation prediction while preserving the prompt-wide primary computation and a single persistent key-value (KV) cache. We introduce the Dual-Flow Transformer. Its primary flow is a complete causal language model that processes the prompt and writes the KV cache. The auxiliary flow is omitted during prompt processing and activated only from the final prompt position onward, adding continuation-prediction computation without writing persistent state or influencing the primary flow. The two flows share major attention, MLP, and output matrices, while using separate token embeddings and lightweight coupling. Sharing weights and the primary cache also creates opportunities to reuse loaded weights and cached keys and values during grouped execution. Across matched-token comparisons, Dual-Flow achieves lower validation loss across architectures and data configurations. In MoE models, the separation makes primary and auxiliary expert fan-outs independent controls over prompt cost, continuation cost, and predictive quality. We study two regimes: increasing decode computation at fixed prefill expert computation, and reallocating a fixed decode expert budget between the two flows. These experiments expose a prefill-decode-quality trade-off and demonstrate the potential of phase-specific expert allocation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Dual-Flow Transformer, which separates computation between the prompt (prefill) phase and continuation (decode) phase by adding an auxiliary flow that only runs during decoding, sharing weights and KV cache with a primary causal LM without affecting prompt processing.
AI.motivation: LLM inference cost is dominated by two phases with opposing hardware bottlenecks: parallel, compute-bound prefill versus sequential, memory-bandwidth-bound decode. Conventional width/depth scaling inflates both costs simultaneously since every added layer runs in both phases. The authors ask whether extra learned computation can be directed specifically at continuation prediction while preserving prompt-wide primary computation and a single persistent KV cache.
AI.method: The Dual-Flow Transformer uses a primary flow (a full causal LM that processes the prompt and writes the KV cache) and an auxiliary flow omitted during prefill and activated only from the final prompt position onward. The auxiliary flow adds decode-side computation without writing persistent state or influencing the primary flow. Both flows share major attention, MLP, and output matrices but use separate token embeddings and lightweight coupling. In MoE variants, primary and auxiliary expert fan-outs become independent controls.
AI.result: Across matched-token comparisons, Dual-Flow achieves lower validation loss across architectures and data configurations. In MoE models, separating flows makes primary and auxiliary expert fan-outs independent levers for prompt cost, continuation cost, and quality. Experiments expose a prefill-decode-quality trade-off and show promise for phase-specific expert allocation.
AI.conclusion: Dual-Flow enables targeted allocation of learned computation to the decode phase, decoupling continuation quality from prefill cost and demonstrating the potential of phase-specific expert allocation to improve inference efficiency-quality trade-offs.

title: Beyond Source: An Empirical Study of Python Bytecode Security Risks
summary: Python package security is largely source-centric, yet Python runtimes can execute bytecode directly through .pyc files, compiled-only modules, and marshalled code objects, creating an inspection-execution gap. We present an empirical study of Python bytecode as a security artifact. We measure bytecode exposure in PyPI distributions, evaluate practical analyzability using version-aware tooling, assess CPython runtime robustness under adversarial bytecode, and test source-level reproduction of bytecode findings. Across 1,034,843 collected PyPI artifacts, we identify 7,388 bytecode-containing artifacts, including 228,578 .pyc files and 28,193 artifact-local source-less .pyc files. For modern CPython 3.8-3.14 bytecode, at least one selected decompiler emits source for 204,901 of 204,904 in-scope files, a result measuring emission rather than verified functional equivalence. Tools are non-robust: observed PyPI bytecode triggers managed-code exceptions and timeouts, while adversarial mutated bytecode also drives decompilers into native process failures; together these outcomes yield 17 distinct robustness signatures. Fuzzing produces 1,009 stack-deduplicated runtime findings dominated by pointer-dereference symptoms; 261 groups exhibit potential memory-corruption characteristics, and at least 91.7% of groups reach execution beyond the documented-unsafe ingestion boundary. None reproduce from ordinary Python source. Bytecode is thus a visible ecosystem artifact, a practical analysis target, and a security-relevant interpreter input whose behavior need not match source-level behavior.

AI.tldr: An empirical study of Python bytecode as a security artifact, showing it is widespread in PyPI, practically decompilable by modern tooling, and a security-relevant interpreter input that triggers non-robust tool behavior and memory-corruption-like runtime failures not reproducible from source.
AI.motivation: Python package security is source-centric, but runtimes can execute bytecode (.pyc files, compiled-only modules, marshalled code objects) directly, creating an inspection-execution gap where what gets inspected (source) differs from what gets executed (bytecode). The paper aims to quantify and characterize this gap empirically.
AI.method: Large-scale empirical measurement across 1,034,843 collected PyPI artifacts to quantify bytecode exposure (counting .pyc files and source-less .pyc files); evaluation of decompiler emission coverage using version-aware tooling on CPython 3.8-3.14 bytecode; robustness testing of decompilers/CPython runtime against observed and adversarially mutated bytecode; and fuzzing CPython with stack-deduplicated findings classified for memory-corruption characteristics and reach past the documented-unsafe ingestion boundary, plus source-level reproduction attempts of bytecode findings.
AI.result: Found 7,388 bytecode-containing artifacts among 1,034,843 PyPI artifacts, with 228,578 .pyc files and 28,193 artifact-local source-less .pyc files. At least one selected decompiler emitted source for 204,901 of 204,904 in-scope files (emission, not verified functional equivalence). Tooling proved non-robust: observed PyPI bytecode caused managed-code exceptions and timeouts, and mutated bytecode drove native process failures, yielding 17 distinct robustness signatures. Fuzzing produced 1,009 stack-deduplicated findings dominated by pointer-dereference symptoms, 261 groups with potential memory-corruption characteristics, and at least 91.7% reached execution beyond the documented-unsafe ingestion boundary. None reproduced from ordinary Python source.
AI.conclusion: Bytecode is a visible ecosystem artifact, a practical analysis target, and a security-relevant interpreter input whose behavior need not match source-level behavior, so security analysis must account for the bytecode layer rather than relying solely on source.

title: Refine After Generation: Toward Correct and Concise Patches in LLM-based Program Repair
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) have advanced automatic program repair (APR) to the point where agentic systems routinely resolve real-world, repository-level issues. Yet the generated patch has received little scrutiny beyond whether it passes tests.
  In this paper, we identify patch verbosity as a major yet overlooked concern in LLM-based APR. Characterizing 28 state-of-the-art approaches on SWE-bench Verified, we find that even successful patches are consistently larger and more complex than developer patches, with the median approach producing 121.78% more total changes, 80.91% more net changes, and 43.99% higher cyclomatic complexity. We further show that this verbosity is rooted in capability-oriented design choices such as iterative refinement and broad context, and can hardly be reduced by surface-level controls such as output format or minimality prompts. Motivated by these findings, we formulate post-generation patch refinement and propose RECAP, a lightweight, plug-and-play adapter that attaches to existing repair frameworks after generation. RECAP's refiner is trained via supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization with distilled reasoning traces, on a dataset of patch pairs we construct from multiple sources. Across four host systems, prompting, commit-untangling, and minimality-aware baselines reduce patch size only by sacrificing 49 to 217 resolved instances. In contrast, RECAP achieves a substantially better size-correctness tradeoff, cutting average total changes from +242.14% to +4.24% and net changes from +348.24% to -39.75% relative to developer patches while preserving or improving resolution by up to 42 instances. Our results indicate that minimality cannot be simply reduced to syntactic compression, and that decoupling minimization from generation offers a practical path to more reviewable repairs.

AI.tldr: LLM-based automated program repair produces patches that are much larger and more complex than human developer patches. The paper proposes RECAP, a post-generation refinement adapter that dramatically reduces patch verbosity while preserving or improving issue resolution, achieving a far better size-correctness tradeoff than existing controls.
AI.motivation: While LLM-based APR systems are highly effective at resolving real-world issues, generated patches have been judged largely by whether they pass tests. The authors identify patch verbosity as a major overlooked concern: even successful patches are consistently larger and more complex than developer patches, making them harder to review. They show this verbosity stems from design choices (iterative refinement, broad context) and is resistant to surface-level fixes like formatting or minimality prompts.
AI.method: The authors characterize patch verbosity across 28 state-of-the-art APR approaches on SWE-bench Verified. Motivated by these findings, they formulate post-generation patch refinement and introduce RECAP, a lightweight plug-and-play adapter attached after generation. RECAP's refiner is trained via supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization with distilled reasoning traces, using a dataset of patch pairs constructed from multiple sources.
AI.result: Across 28 approaches, the median system produces 121.78% more total changes, 80.91% more net changes, and 43.99% higher cyclomatic complexity than developer patches. Prompting, commit-untangling, and minimality-aware baselines reduce patch size only at the cost of 49 to 217 lost resolved instances. In contrast, RECAP cuts average total changes from +242.14% to +4.24% and net changes from +348.24% to -39.75% relative to developer patches, while preserving or improving resolution by up to 42 instances across four host systems.
AI.conclusion: Patch minimality cannot be reduced to syntactic compression. Decoupling minimization from generation via post-generation refinement (RECAP) offers a practical path to more reviewable, correct repairs without sacrificing resolution performance.

title: When Should Multi-Round RAG Stop? Structured Stopping Judgments and Retrieval Reduction in Search-R1
summary: Multi-round retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) must decide when to stop searching as evidence accumulates. Because the deployed policy is determined by the first STOP on each trajectory, this is a sequential selection problem rather than an independent state-classification task. We adapt S2G-RAG's structured sufficiency-and-gap judgment to a frozen Search-R1 pipeline and train a Qwen3.5-2B judge on 3,009 states from 900 disjoint HotpotQA questions. Search-R1's reasoner, retriever, corpus, prompt, and search budget remain unchanged, while the judge checkpoint and stopping threshold are selected on grouped validation and frozen before confirmatory evaluation. On the confirmatory test set, the resulting policy reduces retrieval calls by 77 (3.70\%) relative to Native Search-R1, while Official Exact Match decreases by 0.625 percentage points. Thus, the trained S2G-style structured judge reduces retrieval while broadly preserving answer accuracy. The result does not imply unchanged or improved accuracy, safe stopping, or lower total inference cost.

AI.tldr: This paper adapts S2G-RAG's sufficiency-and-gap judgment into a frozen Search-R1 pipeline, training a Qwen3.5-2B judge on 3,009 states to learn when to stop multi-round retrieval. The resulting policy cuts retrieval calls by 3.70% while reducing Exact Match by only 0.625 points, broadly preserving accuracy at lower retrieval cost.
AI.motivation: Multi-round RAG requires deciding when to stop retrieving as evidence accumulates. Because the deployed behavior is determined by the first STOP on each trajectory, stopping is a sequential selection problem, not an independent per-state classification task. The goal is to reduce redundant retrieval calls while preserving answer accuracy.
AI.method: The authors adapt the structured sufficiency-and-gap judgment from S2G-RAG to a frozen Search-R1 pipeline. They train a Qwen3.5-2B judge on 3,009 states sampled from 900 disjoint HotpotQA questions. The Search-R1 reasoner, retriever, corpus, prompt, and search budget remain unchanged; only the judge checkpoint and stopping threshold are tuned on grouped validation and then frozen for confirmatory evaluation on a held-out test set.
AI.result: On the confirmatory test set, the trained S2G-style judge reduces retrieval calls by 77 (3.70%) relative to Native Search-R1, while Official Exact Match decreases by 0.625 percentage points. This shows reduced retrieval cost with broadly preserved answer accuracy.
AI.conclusion: A trained structured sufficiency-and-gap judge can reduce retrieval calls in Search-R1 without any change to the underlying reasoner, retriever, corpus, prompt, or budget, while largely maintaining answer accuracy. However, the result does not imply unchanged or improved accuracy, safe stopping, or lower total inference cost.

title: Legally Mandated, but Still Inaccessible: Digital Tensions in Older Adults' Use of Norwegian Web Services
summary: Norway is among the most digitalized countries in the world, where access to essential services increasingly depends on digital systems. Although universal design of ICT is legally required across public and private sectors, ensuring cognitive accessibility for older adults involves more than technical compliance. We analyzed responses from 294 participants aged 55 to 90 to examine the barriers they encounter when using digital services. Our findings identify four tensions, namely navigational, semantic, procedural, and temporal, which reveal how accessibility barriers emerge through misalignments between service design, system assumptions, and older adults' capabilities. Together, these tensions show that checklist-based compliance does not necessarily translate into lived accessibility when engaging with mandatory or near-mandatory digital services. We discuss the need to move beyond minimum compliance frameworks toward accessibility approaches that better support older adults' independent participation in digital society.

AI.tldr: A survey of 294 Norwegian older adults (ages 55–90) reveals four tensions—navigational, semantic, procedural, and temporal—showing that legal ICT accessibility compliance does not guarantee real-world accessibility for older users of mandatory digital services.
AI.motivation: Norway is highly digitalized and essential services depend on digital systems, yet universal design of ICT is legally required without guaranteeing cognitive accessibility for older adults. The authors aim to expose how accessibility barriers persist beyond minimum technical compliance.
AI.method: The study analyzed responses from 294 participants aged 55 to 90 regarding barriers they encounter when using digital services, and identified tensions through analysis of these experiences.
AI.result: Four tensions were identified: navigational, semantic, procedural, and temporal. These reveal that accessibility barriers emerge from misalignments between service design, system assumptions, and older adults' capabilities. Checklist-based compliance does not translate into lived accessibility for mandatory or near-mandatory digital services.
AI.conclusion: There is a need to move beyond minimum compliance frameworks toward accessibility approaches that better support older adults' independent participation in digital society.

title: Thought-Aware KV Cache Compaction for Reasoning via Adaptive Attention Matching
summary: Reasoning language models generate lengthy chain-of-thought (CoT) sequences whose key-value (KV) cache grows linearly and becomes a memory bottleneck during decoding. Existing compaction methods treat reasoning trajectories as flat token sequences and apply uniform compression, ignoring the hierarchical structure of CoT reasoning where different steps vary drastically in importance. We propose \textbf{Thought-Aware Attention Matching (TAM)}, which exploits this structure through three mechanisms: (i)~thought segmentation that decomposes the trajectory into reasoning blocks, (ii)~adaptive budget allocation that assigns compression budget based on each segment's importance and size, and (iii)~pivotal token protection that preserves high-attention reasoning anchors. We prove that the allocation rule is optimal under a convex error model and that cumulative error under sequential compaction remains bounded. Experiments on AIME 2024 and MATH-500 with Qwen3-4B show that TAM improves accuracy over uniform compaction at the same memory footprint, with periodic compaction bounding peak memory to 3.1--3.2\,GB (a 65\% reduction) while maintaining competitive accuracy.

AI.tldr: TAM is a KV-cache compaction method for reasoning LMs that exploits CoT's hierarchical structure via thought segmentation, adaptive budget allocation, and pivotal token protection to reduce memory while preserving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Reasoning language models produce long chains-of-thought whose KV cache grows linearly, becoming a memory bottleneck. Existing methods treat CoT as flat token sequences and apply uniform compression, ignoring that different reasoning steps vary greatly in importance.
AI.method: TAM uses three mechanisms: (1) thought segmentation decomposing the trajectory into reasoning blocks; (2) adaptive budget allocation assigning compression budget per segment based on importance and size; (3) pivotal token protection preserving high-attention reasoning anchors. The allocation rule is proven optimal under a convex error model, and cumulative error under sequential compaction is shown bounded.
AI.result: On AIME 2024 and MATH-500 with Qwen3-4B, TAM improves accuracy over uniform compaction at equal memory footprint. Periodic compaction bounds peak memory to 3.1–3.2 GB (a 65% reduction) while maintaining competitive accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting the hierarchical structure of chain-of-thought reasoning enables more effective KV-cache compaction, achieving large memory savings with preserved accuracy compared to uniform compression.

title: Exemplar-based objective classification of gust-induced loads across multiple flight conditions
summary: Is it possible to find an objective classification criterion that organizes the complexity of gust-induced loads across many flight conditions? And one that remains as interpretable as a labelling based on coarse parameters, such as the flight attitude? Our approach encodes a large number of experimental observations through a machine-learned representation and applies a summarization procedure to select a minimal subset of highly significant exemplars. The exemplars provide a similarity-based objective classification criterion of all the observations, they can be more conveniently inspected by experts and can become subject of more refined experiments. We demonstrate the approach on a database of 3480 pressure-load measurements induced by random gusts on a flying-wing model across six flight attitudes. We find nine fundamental response types that recur across multiple attitudes; analysis of a type's transient response enables physical intuition into the underlying fluid mechanics.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an objective, similarity-based classification of gust-induced pressure loads using machine-learned representations and exemplar summarization, avoiding reliance on coarse labels like flight attitude. Applied to 3480 measurements on a flying-wing model, it identifies nine recurring fundamental response types that enable physical interpretation of the fluid mechanics.
AI.motivation: To find an objective classification criterion that organizes the complexity of gust-induced loads across many flight conditions, while remaining as interpretable as coarse parameter-based labelling (e.g., flight attitude).
