AI.method: Encode experimental observations via a machine-learned representation, then apply a summarization procedure to select a minimal subset of highly significant exemplars. These exemplars provide a similarity-based, objective classification criterion for all observations.
AI.result: On a database of 3480 pressure-load measurements from random gusts on a flying-wing model across six flight attitudes, the method found nine fundamental response types that recur across multiple attitudes; analysis of a type's transient response provides physical intuition into the underlying fluid mechanics.
AI.conclusion: A machine-learned, exemplar-based summarization yields an objective and interpretable classification of gust-induced loads, revealing nine recurring response types that transcend flight attitude and support physical understanding of the underlying flow physics.

title: Learning to Adapt Cross-Domain Preferences via Meta-LoRA for LLM Personalization
summary: Cross-domain zero- or few-shot personalization aims to generate user-preferred responses in unseen conversational domains from only a handful of target-domain interactions. Existing adaptation methods struggle to calibrate update magnitude under sparse evidence and thus overfit, whereas history-transfer methods often entangle user preferences with source-domain artifacts, yielding unreliable personalization priors and negative transfer. To calibrate adaptation to evidence quality, we propose PAC-Bayes-regularized Meta-LoRA, which uses a meta-learned LoRA initialization as both the adaptation start and prior center, while adjusting update strength according to support-set size and predictive uncertainty. This limits overfitting under sparse or ambiguous evidence while permitting stronger personalization as evidence grows. Controlled adaptation alone does not determine which preferences should transfer across domains or how they should be expressed. We therefore functionally decompose personalization priors into user and domain components, using a human-readable prompt for stable preferences and topology-preserving soft tokens for domain-specific hidden-space conditioning. Experiments across multiple benchmarks and personalization tasks show consistent gains over strong baselines. On HiCUPID, our method reduces cross-domain win-rate degradation by 47.9% relative to the best competing baseline and improves win rate by 110.2% under unseen-user cold start.

AI.tldr: The paper tackles cross-domain zero/few-shot personalization by combining PAC-Bayes-regularized Meta-LoRA (adaptive updates calibrated to evidence quality) with a functional decomposition of priors into user (stable, prompt-based) and domain (topology-preserving soft tokens) components, achieving large gains in win-rate and reduced degradation across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Cross-domain zero/few-shot personalization must generate user-preferred responses in unseen domains using very few target interactions. Existing methods fail because adaptation approaches overfit under sparse evidence (poorly calibrated update magnitude), while history-transfer methods entangle user preferences with source-domain artifacts, producing unreliable priors and negative transfer. The work aims to calibrate adaptation to evidence quality and decouple transferable user preferences from domain-specific artifacts.
AI.method: The authors propose PAC-Bayes-regularized Meta-LoRA, which uses a meta-learned LoRA initialization as both the adaptation starting point and prior center, and adjusts update strength based on support-set size and predictive uncertainty. This limits overfitting under sparse/ambiguous evidence while allowing stronger personalization as evidence increases. Additionally, personalization priors are functionally decomposed into user and domain components: stable user preferences are captured via a human-readable prompt, while domain-specific hidden-space conditioning uses topology-preserving soft tokens.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple benchmarks and personalization tasks show consistent gains over strong baselines. On HiCUPID, the method reduces cross-domain win-rate degradation by 47.9% relative to the best competing baseline and improves win rate by 110.2% under unseen-user cold start.
AI.conclusion: By combining PAC-Bayes-regularized Meta-LoRA (evidence-quality-calibrated adaptation) with functional decomposition of personalization priors into user and domain components, the approach reliably transfers user preferences across domains, mitigates overfitting and negative transfer, and achieves substantial improvements in cross-domain personalization, particularly under sparse evidence and cold-start conditions.

title: Discovering Persistent Behavioural Patterns for Interpretable Blockchain Forensics
summary: Public blockchain data enables large-scale DeFi-related analysis, but many existing approaches are application-specific, difficult to scale, or hard to interpret. This research proposes a scalable, application-agnostic framework for \emph{persistent behavioural pattern discovery} from large-scale blockchain activity. It constructs behaviour sentences enriched with contract, token and market context, then applies a two-step embedding process: sentence-level embeddings capture individual actions, while sequence-level embeddings capture user behaviour over time. An interpretable behavioural profiler characterizes discovered communities through behavioural motifs, routines, temporal dynamics, entity exposure, and suspiciousness evidence. Evaluation on Ethereum using over 30 million transactions shows that the framework uncovers both routine and malicious behavioural patterns, including decentralised exchange (DEX) trading, NFT activity, phishing, bot operations, oracle manipulation, and rug-pull schemes. Importantly, many patterns remain stable across independent observation windows, enabling the identification of long-term behaviours beyond a single analysis period. The proposed framework combines scalability, interpretability, and persistence analysis, supporting blockchain forensic investigation, behavioural attribution, and threat discovery.

AI.tldr: A scalable, application-agnostic framework that embeds blockchain user actions and sequences into interpretable behaviour profiles, enabling discovery of both routine and malicious patterns across large-scale Ethereum data with persistence over time.
AI.motivation: Existing DeFi/blockchain analysis approaches are application-specific, hard to scale, or difficult to interpret, limiting large-scale behavioural discovery and long-term longitudinal analysis.
AI.method: Constructs behaviour sentences enriched with contract, token, and market context; applies two-step embeddings (sentence-level for individual actions, sequence-level for user behaviour over time); uses an interpretable behavioural profiler to characterize communities via motifs, routines, temporal dynamics, entity exposure, and suspiciousness evidence.
AI.result: On Ethereum with 30M+ transactions, the framework uncovered routine and malicious patterns including DEX trading, NFT activity, phishing, bot operations, oracle manipulation, and rug-pull schemes; many patterns remained stable across independent observation windows, confirming long-term persistence.
AI.conclusion: The framework combines scalability, interpretability, and persistence analysis, supporting blockchain forensics, behavioural attribution, and threat discovery.

title: Integration-First Structural Coverage for Embedded Software:Trace-Based Evidence, Hybrid Runtime Analysis, and Cross-Variant Consolidation
summary: Structural coverage is widely used as evidence that testing is complete, yet in embedded projects it is predominantly collected at unit level, simply because that is where instrumentation and observability are inexpensive. This produces a mismatch. The most representative completeness signal would come from integration and system tests executed on the device under test, but classical instrumentation perturbs timing, memory footprint and concurrency behaviour, while purely trace-reconstructed coverage loses reliability for decisions and conditions as soon as the compiler optimizes aggressively. We address this mismatch from both ends. On the process side we describe an integrationfirst coverage strategy that treats integration and system tests as the baseline measurement and drives the residual gaps through an explicit closure loop, so that completeness is established as covered or justified rather than as covered alone. On the technical side we use embedded trace as the observation path and add hybrid runtime analysis (hRA): a minimal, semantics-preserving observability scaffolding that keeps decision and condition boundaries distinguishable in the trace stream of an optimized (-O3) build, while all coverage state and counting remain off-target. This converts object-to-source mapping from a heuristic reconstruction into reviewable evidence and makes branch, condition and MC/DC measurement practical on release-like binaries. Finally we describe Hyper Coverage, a consolidation layer that merges evidence across test levels, test runs, variants and build configurations, and that exposes source lines which remain untested in every relevant variant.

AI.tldr: The paper tackles the mismatch between where structural coverage is cheaply collected (unit level) and where it is most meaningful (integration/system tests on real hardware). It proposes an integration-first coverage process combined with "hybrid runtime analysis" (hRA) that preserves decision/condition observability even in -O3 optimized trace-based builds, plus a "Hyper Coverage" layer consolidating evidence across runs, variants, and configurations.
AI.motivation: Structural coverage is used as evidence of testing completeness, but in embedded projects it is mostly measured at unit level due to low instrumentation cost, even though integration and system tests executed on the device are the most representative completeness signal. Classical instrumentation perturbs timing, memory, and concurrency, while trace-reconstructed coverage loses reliability for decisions/conditions under aggressive compiler optimization (-O3). The goal is to resolve this mismatch.
AI.method: Two-pronged approach: (1) a process-side "integration-first coverage strategy" that uses integration/system tests as the baseline, drives residual gaps through an explicit closure loop, and establishes completeness as "covered or justified." (2) A technical side using embedded trace as the observation path with "hybrid runtime analysis" (hRA) — a minimal, semantics-preserving observability scaffolding that keeps decision and condition boundaries distinguishable in the trace stream of an optimized (-O3) build, with all coverage state/counting done off-target. This turns object-to-source mapping into reviewable evidence and enables branch, condition, and MC/DC measurement on release-like binaries. Additionally, a "Hyper Coverage" consolidation layer merges evidence across test levels, runs, variants, and build configurations, exposing source lines untested in every relevant variant.
AI.result: The approach makes branch, condition, and MC/DC measurement practical on release-like (-O3 optimized) binaries via trace without runtime instrumentation perturbation. It converts object-to-source mapping from heuristic reconstruction into reviewable evidence and produces a consolidation layer (Hyper Coverage) that identifies source lines remaining untested across all relevant variants, test levels, runs, and configurations. Completeness becomes expressible as "covered or justified" rather than "covered alone."
AI.conclusion: The mismatch between low-cost unit-level coverage and representative integration/system coverage can be addressed from both process and technical ends. An integration-first strategy with an explicit closure loop, combined with trace-based hybrid runtime analysis for optimized binaries and a Hyper Coverage consolidation layer, enables reliable and representative structural coverage evidence on release-like embedded builds.

title: Structure then Query: Enabling Precise Analytical Queries over Unstructured Documents
summary: Unstructured documents constitute the majority of enterprise and web data. With the rapid development of large language models(LLMs), researchers have started to build data systems that analyze unstructured textual documents like operating on databases. However, because mainstream retrieval methods still relies on fuzzy matching based on vector similarity, accurately obtaining information and performing structured analysis and reasoning remains a major challenge. To address these limitations, AnnoIndex introduces two core fundamental components. The first is Annotation Index. The system uses a module called SchemaLoop to automatically create hierarchical annotation schemas from the raw corpus, and then uses lightweight language model to extract specific values. It turns scattered unstructured text into a materialized, structured index that enables low-cost filtering and querying. The annotation index avoids the black-box matching of vector similarity and amortizes attribute extraction costs from online queries to a one-time build. The second innovation is a Structured Query Engine. It compiles user questions into execution plans based on SQL extension. It first uses the Annotation Index for precise documents filtering, then gradually applies extraction operations in ascending order of cost, resorting to LLMs only for the remaining minimal fraction of the corpus that require deep semantic understanding. The extracted attributions are merged into the annotation index, reducing the cost of future queries. Experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that AnnoIndex consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving the highest average F1 score (0.87) while maintaining robust performance on complex multi-hop join and progressive reasoning queries.

AI.tldr: AnnoIndex is a data system that indexes unstructured documents by automatically building hierarchical annotation schemas and extracting structured attributes, then answering queries through an SQL-extended structured query engine that minimizes costly LLM calls—achieving state-of-the-art F1 (0.87) on real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Unstructured text dominates enterprise/web data, but mainstream retrieval relies on fuzzy vector-similarity matching, which makes precise information extraction, structured analysis, and reasoning difficult. The goal is to enable database-like operations over unstructured documents with low cost and high accuracy.
AI.method: AnnoIndex has two core components: (1) Annotation Index—SchemaLoop automatically creates hierarchical annotation schemas from the raw corpus, and lightweight language models extract specific values to materialize a structured index, amortizing extraction cost into a one-time build; (2) Structured Query Engine—compiles questions into SQL-extension execution plans, first filters documents via the Annotation Index, then applies extraction operations in ascending cost order, invoking LLMs only on the minimal remaining fraction needing deep semantics, and merges extracted attributes back into the index for future reuse.
AI.result: On three real-world datasets, AnnoIndex consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving the highest average F1 score of 0.87 and maintaining robust performance on complex multi-hop join and progressive reasoning queries.
AI.conclusion: By replacing black-box vector matching with a materialized annotation index and a cost-aware structured query engine, AnnoIndex enables accurate, low-cost structured analysis and reasoning over unstructured documents, significantly surpassing existing approaches.

title: InvisIto: Weaving Unobtrusive Infrared Markers for Ubiquitous Textile Interaction
comment: 11 pages. To appear in the Proceedings of the 39th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST 2026)
summary: Textiles are increasingly explored as media for interacting with digital information. However, many of the existing approaches rely on visible tags, printed overlays, or electronic modules that compromise the fabric's aesthetic and tactile qualities. To address this, we present InvisIto, a method for weaving visually unobtrusive yet machine-readable infrared markers directly into fabrics using near-infrared (NIR)-absorbing yarns. Although these yarns look similar to standard fibers in ambient light, they produce strong contrast in NIR imaging. Our method includes: (1) a design tool that helps users easily embed infrared markers into weaving drafts, (2) five disguising strategies that further reduce marker visibility under ambient light, and (3) a camera-based detection pipeline for decoding and tracking the woven markers. InvisIto supports both woven QR codes for data encoding and woven ArUco markers for binary input and deformation tracking. We demonstrate applications across hand weaving, Jacquard weaving, and industrial fabrication, showing that InvisIto supports scalable interaction and fabrication from bespoke artifacts to mass production.

AI.tldr: InvisIto weaves visually unobtrusive infrared markers into fabrics using NIR-absorbing yarns, enabling machine-readable tags (QR codes and ArUco markers) that are invisible under ambient light but visible in NIR imaging, with design tools, disguising strategies, and a detection pipeline supporting applications from hand weaving to industrial production.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches for embedding digital information into textiles rely on visible tags, printed overlays, or electronic modules that compromise the fabric's aesthetic and tactile qualities. The authors aim to preserve fabric appearance and feel while enabling machine-readable interaction.
AI.method: The method uses near-infrared (NIR)-absorbing yarns that look similar to standard fibers under ambient light but create strong contrast in NIR imaging. It comprises: (1) a design tool to embed infrared markers into weaving drafts, (2) five disguising strategies that reduce marker visibility under ambient light, and (3) a camera-based detection pipeline for decoding and tracking woven markers. It supports woven QR codes for data encoding and woven ArUco markers for binary input and deformation tracking.
AI.result: The approach successfully produces woven, visually unobtrusive infrared markers that remain machine-readable in NIR imaging. Applications were demonstrated across hand weaving, Jacquard weaving, and industrial fabrication, showing scalability from bespoke artifacts to mass production.
AI.conclusion: InvisIto demonstrates a scalable, unobtrusive way to integrate machine-readable markers into textiles without compromising aesthetics or tactility, enabling interactive fabric applications from custom handmade pieces to industrial-scale manufacturing.

title: Can Spectral-Clipping Enable Better Learning While Forgetting Less for Low-Rank Adaptation?
summary: In recent years, low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has emerged as a significant paradigm that freezes pre-trained weights and introduces small, learnable adapters instead of fine-tuning the full set of parameters. In this work, we uncover several key insights regarding the singular components of network parameters based on Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). Firstly, the principal singular components with large singular values in pre-trained network parameters can be effectively reused during fine-tuning, whereas the minor components with smaller singular values are more task-specific and require substantial adaptation. Secondly, we first establish the theoretical connection that the uncontrolled growth of singular values in LoRA adapters leads to the forgetting of pre-trained knowledge -- a well-known issue referred to as catastrophic forgetting. Building on these observations, we propose SCLoRA, which injects parameterized singular components with spectral clipping into the pre-trained model in a way that is aware of the spectral distribution of the pre-trained model. SCLoRA effectively adapts to new tasks by focusing updates on components that require adaptation, while simultaneously alleviating catastrophic forgetting. We conduct extensive experiments and demonstrate that SCLoRA not only improves downstream performance but also effectively retains pre-trained knowledge.

AI.tldr: SCLoRA is a spectral-aware low-rank adaptation method that injects parameterized singular components with spectral clipping into pre-trained models, reusing principal singular components while adapting minor ones to improve downstream performance and reduce catastrophic forgetting.
AI.motivation: LoRA freezes pre-trained weights and adds small learnable adapters instead of full fine-tuning. The authors aim to understand how singular components of network parameters (via SVD) behave during fine-tuning, and to address catastrophic forgetting—where uncontrolled growth of singular values in LoRA adapters causes loss of pre-trained knowledge.
AI.method: The work analyzes network parameters using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), revealing that principal singular components (large singular values) can be reused during fine-tuning while minor components (small singular values) are task-specific and need substantial adaptation. It establishes a theoretical connection between uncontrolled singular value growth in LoRA adapters and catastrophic forgetting. Based on this, SCLoRA injects parameterized singular components with spectral clipping, aware of the pre-trained model's spectral distribution, focusing updates on components requiring adaptation while constraining spectral growth.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that SCLoRA improves downstream task performance while effectively retaining pre-trained knowledge, alleviating catastrophic forgetting.
AI.conclusion: SCLoRA demonstrates that leveraging the spectral structure of pre-trained weights—reusing principal components and adaptively updating minor components with spectral clipping—yields better downstream performance and mitigates catastrophic forgetting compared to standard LoRA.

title: Learning Under Treatment-Induced Label Indeterminacy with Expert Annotations of Counterfactual Outcomes: A Case Study in Neurological Prognostication
summary: Clinical prediction models are often developed as if the outcome of interest were cleanly observed for every patient. This assumption fails when treatment decisions make the clinically relevant outcome permanently unobservable. As a case study of this problem, we consider post-cardiac-arrest neurological prognostication using a cohort of 2,497 patients, including 1,429 patients whose outcomes were rendered indeterminate by treatment decisions. These patients with indeterminate outcomes were reviewed by independent clinical experts, who provided their guesses of counterfactual outcomes about what would have happened to the patients. We refer to these patients as uncertain cases. We also have patients for whom we observe their clinically relevant outcomes; we refer to these patients as certain cases. We propose a framework for evaluating prediction models that explicitly splits the evaluation between certain and uncertain cases. Here, we cannot easily evaluate both types of cases in a uniform manner as the available target labels differ. We then propose a simple prediction model that uses target labels from both certain and uncertain cases in a manner that allows us to trade off between them. Across the proposed neural model and a collection of tabular baselines, models with similar certain-case AUROC can nevertheless differ substantially in both certain-case Brier score and their probability estimates for uncertain cases. Improving alignment with target labels of uncertain cases for our proposed model generally comes at the cost of worse accuracy on certain cases, highlighting an explicit tradeoff that standard evaluation conceals. These results show that when treatment decisions determine whether clinically meaningful outcomes remain observable, conventional evaluation metrics can miss important failure modes in the very patients for whom prognostic support matters most.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the problem that clinical prediction models are often trained and evaluated as if outcomes were observed for all patients. Using post-cardiac-arrest prognostication as a case study, it proposes an evaluation framework that separates "certain" (observed outcome) and "uncertain" (outcome made unobservable by treatment decisions, with expert-guessed counterfactuals) cases, and a model that trades off between labels from both.
AI.motivation: Treatment decisions can permanently render the clinically relevant outcome unobservable (e.g., withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment after cardiac arrest), so outcomes are not "cleanly observed." Standard evaluation that ignores or mishandles these indeterminate cases misses important failure modes in exactly the patients for whom prognostication matters most.
AI.method: A framework that explicitly splits evaluation between certain cases (observed clinically relevant outcomes) and uncertain cases (outcomes rendered indeterminate by treatment decisions, with independent clinical experts providing counterfactual outcome guesses). Rather than evaluating both groups uniformly, the authors propose a simple prediction model using target labels from both certain and uncertain cases with a mechanism to trade off between them, compared across a neural model and tabular baselines.
AI.result: Models with similar certain-case AUROC differed substantially in certain-case Brier score and in probability estimates for uncertain cases. Improving alignment with uncertain-case target labels generally reduced accuracy on certain cases, revealing an explicit tradeoff that standard evaluation conceals.
AI.conclusion: When treatment decisions determine whether clinically meaningful outcomes remain observable, conventional evaluation metrics can hide critical failure modes. Evaluation and model development should explicitly account for certain and uncertain cases, acknowledging the tradeoff between them.

title: Research Assistant: AstraZeneca's Agentic System for R&D
summary: We describe Research Assistant, an internal LLM-based system developed at AstraZeneca to help scientists and clinicians explore biomedical questions across a broad range of data sources. The system provides a chat-style interface that brings together evidence from scientific literature, knowledge graphs, chemistry, clinical trials, safety resources, expression data, and internal experimental systems. It supports both a fast mode for direct question answering and a multi-step mode for more complex research tasks. Responses are grounded in retrieved evidence and linked back to the original sources, allowing users to review and further explore the underlying data. In this technical note, we outline the system architecture, the main design choices behind the product, and lessons learned from deploying it at scale to support day-to-day R&D workflows across AstraZeneca.

AI.tldr: AstraZeneca built "Research Assistant," an internal LLM-based chat system that lets scientists and clinicians query biomedical questions across literature, knowledge graphs, chemistry, clinical trials, safety data, expression data, and internal experiments, with grounded, source-linked answers and both fast and multi-step modes; the note describes its architecture, design choices, and deployment lessons.
AI.motivation: To help AstraZeneca scientists and clinicians efficiently explore biomedical questions across a broad, heterogeneous range of data sources and support day-to-day R&D workflows.
AI.method: An LLM-based chat-style system that integrates evidence from scientific literature, knowledge graphs, chemistry, clinical trials, safety resources, expression data, and internal experimental systems. It offers a fast mode for direct question answering and a multi-step mode for complex research tasks. Responses are grounded in retrieved evidence and linked back to original sources for verification and further exploration.
AI.result: Deployment of an internal Research Assistant at scale across AstraZeneca, with grounded, source-linked answers supporting both quick queries and multi-step research tasks across diverse biomedical data sources.
AI.conclusion: The technical note outlines the system architecture, key design decisions, and lessons learned from large-scale deployment, demonstrating a practical LLM-based assistant for real-world biomedical R&D workflows.

title: Labels Are Not Endpoints: Treatment Leakage and Construct Validity in MCP Agent Security Evaluation
summary: Security evaluations of tool-using agents often equate stored labels with behavioral facts. We audit a preserved campaign by tracing 10,200 execution rows to 180 model-bound requests, 45 semantic requests, and 15 observable stimuli. Two schema treatments were delivered, but the planned external payload-family corpus was not. The historical grader exhibited direct treatment leakage: treatment metadata gated the ATTACK_SUCCESS class, so fixed behavior could change class under treatment relabeling. A treatment-blind reconstruction corrects 58 historical ATTACK_SUCCESS or HIJACK_ATTEMPT labels to authorized benign completions while preserving three verified protected-data transfers and one separate unauthorized-forwarding case. The locked v2 census contains exactly zero ATTACK_SUCCESS records, while the forwarding case remains a HIJACK_ATTEMPT at a semantic boundary concerning objective completion. A dual-reviewer blinded concordance review of all 96 requests deemed structurally interpretable by locked v2 produced identical reviewer-consensus classes but differed from the locked codebook on four construct-boundary cases. We contribute a seven-link Integrity Chain and an executable, scope-bounded endpoint-integrity linter. The result is a campaign-bounded measurement audit, not a population attack-rate, model-ranking, defense-efficacy, or causal estimate.

AI.tldr: An audit of a preserved tool-using-agent security campaign reconstructs the labeling pipeline and finds that stored labels leaked treatment metadata, causing unreliable attack-success classifications; a treatment-blind reconstruction relabels most historical "attacks" as benign, and a locked census contains zero attack-success records, yielding a campaign-bounded measurement audit rather than general attack-rate claims.
AI.motivation: Security evaluations of tool-using agents often treat stored labels as ground-truth behavioral facts. The authors question this equivalence by auditing a preserved campaign to determine whether historical labels faithfully reflect actual agent behavior or instead encode pipeline artifacts such as treatment leakage.
AI.method: A trace-based audit of 10,200 execution rows, decomposed into 180 model-bound requests, 45 semantic requests, and 15 observable stimuli. Two schema treatments were delivered, while the planned external payload-family corpus was not. A treatment-blind reconstruction reclassifies outcomes, a dual-reviewer blinded concordance review examines 96 structurally interpretable requests in the locked v2 census, and a seven-link Integrity Chain with an executable scope-bounded endpoint-integrity linter is contributed.
AI.result: The historical grader showed direct treatment leakage (treatment metadata gated the ATTACK_SUCCESS class). The treatment-blind reconstruction corrected 58 historical ATTACK_SUCCESS or HIJACK_ATTEMPT labels to authorized benign completions, while preserving three verified protected-data transfers and one unauthorized-forwarding case. The locked v2 census contains exactly zero ATTACK_SUCCESS records; the forwarding case remains a HIJACK_ATTEMPT at a semantic boundary. Blinded dual-reviewer consensus was identical across all 96 requests but differed from the locked codebook on four construct-boundary cases.
AI.conclusion: The analysis is a campaign-bounded measurement audit that corrects label leakage and boundary inconsistencies, explicitly not a population attack-rate, model-ranking, defense-efficacy, or causal estimate.

title: Does Fixing Break Security? An Empirical Study of Security Degradation in Iterative LLM-Driven Infrastructure-as-Code Repair
comment: 20 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at the 20th International Symposium on Empirical Software Engineering and Measurement (ESEM 2026). To appear in LIPIcs Vol. 394
summary: Background: Iterative feedback loops are the dominant paradigm for improving LLM-generated Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC): validators such as Checkov and terraform validate feed error signals back for successive repair attempts. Prior work reports cumulative-best metrics, which are non-decreasing by construction, so the raw per-iteration security trajectory has never been examined for IaC. Aims: We study security regression (a previously-passing CIS Benchmark check that fails after a repair iteration) to determine whether and how often iterative LLM repair degrades security while fixing other issues. Method: We analyze 5,968 scenario timelines from the IaC-Eval benchmark, each one scenario run through one configuration for up to 5 repair iterations. The 15 configurations (six model-specific RAG, nine model-aggregated non-RAG, three temperatures each) yield 4,440 iteration transitions with Checkov data on both sides. We track 30 individual CIS check IDs and classify root causes from code diffs, under two detection modes: standard (inclusive) and strict (exclusive check failures only). Results: Under standard detection, 13.8% of scenarios (24.8% of transitions) exhibit at least one regression. Under strict detection the rate falls to 3.3% of scenarios (5.2% of transitions), indicating most apparent regressions are multi-resource measurement artifacts. Resource restructuring (79.0%) is the dominant root cause. Regression transitions show 2.6x more code churn (Cohen's d=0.90) and 4.9x higher strict-mode check volatility (d=1.49). Of standard-mode regressions, 36.6% self-correct within an average of 1.2 iterations; iteration 3 is the optimal stopping point. Conclusions: Iterative IaC repair does introduce security regressions, but the conservative, defensible rate is about 3.3% of scenarios. Our findings motivate security-aware feedback-loop design and actionable iteration-budget guidance.

AI.tldr: This paper studies whether iterative LLM repair of Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) introduces security regressions. Analyzing 5,968 scenarios from IaC-Eval across 15 configurations and up to 5 repair iterations, it finds that 13.8% of scenarios show regressions under standard detection but only 3.3% under strict detection, indicating most apparent regressions are measurement artifacts. Resource restructuring is the dominant root cause, and iteration 3 is identified as the optimal stopping point.
AI.motivation: Prior work on LLM-generated IaC repair reports only cumulative-best metrics, which are non-decreasing and therefore mask the raw per-iteration security trajectory. The authors aim to determine whether and how often iterative repair degrades security (a previously-passing CIS Benchmark check failing after repair) while fixing other issues.
AI.method: The authors analyze 5,968 scenario timelines from the IaC-Eval benchmark, each run through one of 15 configurations (six model-specific RAG, nine model-aggregated non-RAG, three temperatures each) for up to 5 repair iterations, yielding 4,440 iteration transitions with Checkov data on both sides. They track 30 CIS check IDs and classify root causes from code diffs under two detection modes: standard (inclusive) and strict (exclusive check failures only).
AI.result: Under standard detection, 13.8% of scenarios (24.8% of transitions) exhibit at least one regression; under strict detection this drops to 3.3% of scenarios (5.2% of transitions). Resource restructuring (79.0%) is the dominant root cause. Regression transitions show 2.6x more code churn (Cohen's d=0.90) and 4.9x higher strict-mode check volatility (d=1.49). Of standard-mode regressions, 36.6% self-correct within an average of 1.2 iterations.
AI.conclusion: Iterative IaC repair does introduce security regressions, but the conservative, defensible rate is about 3.3% of scenarios. The findings motivate security-aware feedback-loop design and actionable iteration-budget guidance, with iteration 3 as the optimal stopping point.

title: MindMemOS: A Portable and Self-Evolving Memory Operating Layer for AI Agents
summary: Memory is a core component of AI agents, enabling them to accumulate experience, maintain personalization, and adapt over long-term interactions. However, existing memory systems often remain fixed after development, limiting their ability to adapt their memory models, organization strategies, and procedural knowledge through continued use. We present MindMemOS, a portable and self-evolving memory operating layer that organizes open-world information using a unified entity property timestructure. MindMemOS supports scenario-adaptive memory modeling, higher-order pattern discovery, autonomous memory refinement, and continuous skill evolution. Its MindMemEvolve algorithm employs validation-driven evolutionary search to optimize memory schemas for target scenarios, whiledreaming consolidates accumulated memories by merging redundant records and resolving conflicts. In addition, implicit corrective feedback serves as a human-in-the-loop signal for identifying and revising potentially inaccurate or misaligned memories. Its MindSkillEvolve algorithm further transforms agent execution trajectories into reusable and progressively refined skills. MindMemOS achieves 94.03% accuracy on LOCOMO and 70.63% on PersonaMem. MindSkillEvolve improves SpreadsheetBench success by 9.2 percentage points over the initial-skill baseline.

AI.tldr: MindMemOS is a self-evolving memory operating layer for AI agents that organizes open-world information via a unified entity–property–time structure, enabling adaptive memory modeling, memory refinement via evolutionary search and "dreaming" consolidation, human-in-the-loop correction, and skill evolution from execution trajectories.
AI.motivation: Existing AI agent memory systems remain fixed after development, limiting their ability to adapt memory models, organization strategies, and procedural knowledge through continued use. The paper aims to create a memory system that can evolve and self-improve over long-term interactions.
AI.method: MindMemOS is a portable memory operating layer built on a unified entity–property–time structure. It includes scenario-adaptive memory modeling, higher-order pattern discovery, autonomous memory refinement, and continuous skill evolution. Its MindMemEvolve algorithm uses validation-driven evolutionary search to optimize memory schemas for target scenarios and employs "dreaming" to consolidate memories by merging redundant records and resolving conflicts. Implicit corrective feedback provides a human-in-the-loop signal to revise inaccurate or misaligned memories. MindSkillEvolve transforms agent execution trajectories into reusable, progressively refined skills.
AI.result: MindMemOS achieves 94.03% accuracy on LOCOMO and 70.63% on PersonaMem. MindSkillEvolve improves SpreadsheetBench success by 9.2 percentage points over the initial-skill baseline.
AI.conclusion: MindMemOS demonstrates a self-evolving memory operating layer that effectively adapts memory schemas, consolidates experiences, incorporates corrective feedback, and evolves skills, yielding strong performance on memory benchmarks (LOCOMO, PersonaMem) and measurable gains on SpreadsheetBench.

title: Not All Nudges Land: Behavioral Controllability and Elaboration Quality in AI-Supported Journaling
summary: AI journaling tools can tailor prompts to a person's own sensed behavior, but it is unclear which behaviors respond to them. We analyzed 369 journal entries from an eight-week passive sensing study. An LLM labeled each entry as expressing an intention to change a behavior or not, and we measured follow-through against 26 sensor features with a 3-day before/after comparison. Responsiveness depended most on whether a behavior involves other people. Behaviors that depend on others improved in only 15 to 22% of cases, while behaviors a person can act on alone improved more often, up to 50 to 63%, though unevenly. How users wrote mattered less. No single text feature separated improved from unimproved entries; writing carried signal only within specific behaviors, most clearly for text messaging and for longer, more personal intention entries. The sample is small, so we treat these as exploratory patterns that point to where AI journaling nudges are most likely to work.

AI.tldr: An exploratory analysis of 369 AI journal entries from an 8-week passive sensing study found that whether a journaled intention led to actual behavior change depended mainly on whether the behavior involved other people, not on how the entry was written. Solo behaviors improved up to 50–63% of the time, while social behaviors improved only 15–22%.
AI.motivation: AI journaling tools can generate prompts tailored to a person's sensed behavior, but it is unclear which behaviors actually respond to such prompts. The authors sought to identify what distinguishes intentions that lead to real behavioral follow-through from those that do not.
AI.method: The authors analyzed 369 journal entries from an eight-week passive sensing study. An LLM labeled each entry as expressing an intention to change a behavior or not. Follow-through was then measured against 26 sensor features using a 3-day before/after comparison. They examined whether textual features of the writing or the type of behavior predicted improvement.
AI.result: Responsiveness depended most on whether the behavior involved other people. Behaviors requiring others improved in only 15–22% of cases, whereas solo behaviors improved up to 50–63% (though unevenly). How users wrote mattered less: no single text feature separated improved from unimproved entries. Writing carried signal only within specific behaviors, most clearly for text messaging and for longer, more personal intention entries.
AI.conclusion: The small sample size means the findings are treated as exploratory patterns rather than definitive conclusions. They suggest AI journaling nudges are most likely to work for behaviors a person can act on alone, pointing to where such interventions may be most effective.

title: Vision-Language Models are Fragile Multilingual Associators
summary: Vision-language models must associate visual entities with textual attributes. Whether these associations or concept bindings remain stable when the language of the input changes is unexplored. We introduce M$^2$BIND, a benchmark varying the language of the context and query across multiple languages. We evaluate binding both extrinsically through task performance metrics and intrinsically through causal interventions. We find that binding is not language-invariant: cross-family and cross-script settings trigger significant binding collapse, with the model's internal binding computation shifting to later layers and losing causal strength. Closely related languages preserve associations comparatively better. In a broader sense, our findings indicate how VLMs deployed globally in multilingual settings cannot be assumed to maintain the same association quality observed in monolingual evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces M²BIND, a benchmark testing whether vision-language models keep concept bindings (the association between visual entities and textual attributes) stable across languages. It finds bindings fail significantly across language families/scripts, though closely related languages preserve them better.
AI.motivation: Whether vision-language models' concept bindings remain stable when the language of the input changes is unexplored, despite VLMs being deployed globally in multilingual settings. The authors aim to investigate this binding stability across languages.
AI.method: Introduce M²BIND, a benchmark that varies the language of both context and query across multiple languages. Binding is evaluated in two complementary ways: extrinsically via task performance metrics, and intrinsically via causal interventions tracing where and how strongly binding is computed inside the model.
AI.result: Binding is not language-invariant. Cross-family and cross-script settings trigger significant binding collapse; the model's internal binding computation shifts to later layers and loses causal strength. Closely related languages preserve associations comparatively better.
AI.conclusion: VLMs deployed globally in multilingual settings cannot be assumed to maintain the same association quality observed in monolingual evaluation, highlighting a robustness gap in concept binding across languages.

title: When Can You Trust Offline Evaluation of Equal-Cost Top-k Allocation? A Controlled, Reproducible Benchmark and Practitioner's Guide
summary: Organizations decide whom to treat under a budget and want to know what a targeting rule would have earned before deploying it. Off-policy evaluation promises this from logged data, but the deployable rule is a deterministic top-k policy: it removes all averaging over actions, so weak overlap hits the estimate directly. We benchmark six estimators across five datasets and two known-effect sweeps, and validate the mechanisms against a non-simulated paired reference. First, weak overlap is governed by logger-target action alignment, not by logging sharpness alone: what governs support is the logger's probability of the target's actions. Sharpening a logger built from the target's own score barely moves overlap over the tested range; action-level disagreement collapses it. Effective sample size ranks this risk across logging environments, but is weak at ranking candidates within the single log a practitioner holds, and its cut point does not transfer. Second, the optimizer's curse is not fixed by cross-fitting the outcome nuisance. When the rule is fit on the data used to evaluate it, cross-fitting the nuisance alone leaves the reuse bias in place and makes it worse. Honest policy-level splitting avoids the reuse by targeting the learning procedure's value -- a change of estimand, not a de-biasing of the full-sample policy. Third, propensity-estimation error is the largest degradation we measure: an out-of-fold estimate hurts IPS more than any other stress we apply, leaves doubly-robust estimation almost unchanged, and can invert the overlap diagnostic itself. Logging is synthesized and propensities floored at 0.02, so every failure occurs with bounded weights; the floor also reduces the two tuned hybrids to their untuned parents, leaving four practically distinct estimators, and all exact-value surfaces are synthetic or semi-synthetic. We release the benchmark; public data only.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks six off-policy estimators for deterministic top-k targeting rules across five datasets, finding that weak overlap is driven by logger-target action alignment rather than logging sharpness, cross-fitting the outcome nuisance does not fix but worsens the optimizer's curse, and propensity-estimation error is the largest source of degradation, even with bounded weights.
AI.motivation: Organizations deploying budget-constrained targeting rules need to know what a rule would have earned before deployment, but off-policy evaluation of deterministic top-k policies exposes estimators to weak-overlap bias because there is no averaging over actions. The paper aims to understand the failure mechanisms of off-policy evaluation under such deterministic rules and identify which estimators are practically robust.
AI.method: The authors benchmark six estimators (including IPS and doubly-robust variants, with two tuned hybrids reduced to their untuned parents by propensities floored at 0.02) across five datasets and two known-effect sweeps, validating mechanisms against a non-simulated paired reference. They manipulate logger-target action alignment versus logging sharpness, apply cross-fitted outcome nuisance estimation versus honest policy-level splitting, and inject out-of-fold propensity-estimation error, using effective sample size to assess overlap risk. Logging is synthesized with propensities floored at 0.02, and exact-value surfaces are synthetic or semi-synthetic.
AI.result: First, weak overlap is governed by the logger's probability of the target's actions (action-level alignment), not by logging sharpness alone: sharpening a logger built from the target's own score barely changes overlap, while action-level disagreement collapses it. Effective sample size ranks risk across logging environments but is weak at ranking candidates within a single log and its cut point does not transfer. Second, the optimizer's curse is not fixed by cross-fitting the outcome nuisance; reusing the evaluation data to fit the rule leaves reuse bias in place and worsens it. Honest policy-level splitting avoids the reuse by targeting the learning procedure's value, a change of estimand rather than a de-biasing of the full-sample policy. Third, propensity-estimation error is the largest measured degradation: an out-of-fold propensity estimate hurts IPS more than any other stress, leaves doubly-robust estimation almost unchanged, and can invert the overlap diagnostic itself. All failures occur with bounded weights due to the 0.02 floor.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark reveals that the main threats to off-policy evaluation of deterministic top-k rules are action-level overlap between logger and target and propensity-estimation error, not logging sharpness, and that cross-fitting the outcome nuisance does not address the optimizer's curse but honest policy-level splitting changes the estimand instead. With propensities floored, only four estimators remain practically distinct. The benchmark is released using public data only.

title: Large Language Models Can Follow Instructions, But Not Many at Once: Phase Transitions in Compositional Constraint Satisfaction
comment: 35 pages, 7 figures, 13 tables. Reviewed in the ARR May 2026 cycle
summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed in settings that require simultaneous adherence to multiple explicit constraints - reasoning structure, safety boundaries, output schemas. Individual constraints are handled proficiently, but the compositional regime, where many must hold jointly, remains poorly characterized: how rapidly does performance degrade, what governs the degradation, and can the collapse be mitigated? We introduce Constraint Saturation Evaluation (CSE), a procedurally generated benchmark that systematically varies the number of simultaneous constraints (k), with every constraint scored by a deterministic, rule-based verifier and zero LLM-judge involvement: 15 models, 36 constraint types, 369,753 checks at k=1-12. Three findings emerge. First, per-constraint pass rate decays gradually and predictably, while the chance of satisfying all k constraints collapses - a model passing individual constraints at ~41% at k=8 succeeds on all eight just 5.7% of the time. Second, constraints do not degrade equally: structural constraints lose 2x more baseline capability per added constraint than lexical ones, ordered by a comprehension-maintenance gap that separates constraints requiring sustained tracking from binary decisions immune to composition. Third, failures are nearly independent, which is what makes the accumulation multiplicative; the residual coupling that does exist tracks shared output features rather than pairwise interference - a wrong sentence count fails every constraint that reads it. Reliable instruction following breaks down beyond 5-6 simultaneous constraints: probe-level success falls below 50% at 7 constraints for the strongest model, and at 3 or fewer for 12 of 15.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Constraint Saturation Evaluation (CSE), a procedurally generated benchmark testing how LLMs degrade when asked to satisfy many constraints simultaneously. Across 15 models and 36 constraint types (369,753 checks at k=1-12), it finds per-constraint pass rates decay gradually while joint satisfaction collapses multiplicatively (e.g., 41% per-constraint at k=8 yields only 5.7% all-pass). Structural constraints degrade ~2x faster than lexical ones, failures are nearly independent with residual coupling driven by shared output features, and reliable instruction following breaks down beyond 5-6 constraints.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed under multiple simultaneous explicit constraints (reasoning structure, safety boundaries, output schemas). While individual constraints are handled well, the compositional regime—where many constraints must hold jointly—remains poorly characterized: how fast performance degrades, what governs it, and whether the collapse can be mitigated.
AI.method: The authors build Constraint Saturation Evaluation (CSE), a procedurally generated benchmark that systematically varies the number of simultaneous constraints k. Every constraint is scored by a deterministic, rule-based verifier with zero LLM-judge involvement. The study covers 15 models, 36 constraint types, and 369,753 checks at k=1-12.
AI.result: Three findings: (1) per-constraint pass rate decays gradually and predictably, but the probability of satisfying all k constraints collapses—models passing individual constraints at ~41% at k=8 succeed on all eight only 5.7% of the time; (2) constraints degrade unequally—structural constraints lose 2x more baseline capability per added constraint than lexical ones, separated by a comprehension-maintenance gap (sustained tracking vs. binary decisions immune to composition); (3) failures are nearly independent (hence multiplicative accumulation), with residual coupling tracking shared output features rather than pairwise interference—e.g., a wrong sentence count fails every constraint that reads it. Reliable instruction following breaks down beyond 5-6 constraints: probe-level success falls below 50% at 7 constraints for the strongest model, and at 3 or fewer for 12 of 15 models.
AI.conclusion: Constraint composition is a distinct and severe failure mode for LLMs: joint satisfaction collapses multiplicatively even when individual constraints hold moderately well, with structural constraints disproportionately affected due to a comprehension-maintenance gap. The near-independence of failures and the dominant role of shared output features suggest that mitigation should target sustained tracking and output-feature correctness rather than pairwise constraint interactions.

title: Adversarial Robustness in Smishing Detection: A Comparative Analysis of Adversarial Fragility in Classical vs. Transformer-Based Detection Systems
summary: Smishing detection systems are commonly trained and evaluated on clean, monolingual text. In low-resource settings, however, attackers frequently circumvent these systems through character obfuscation, cross-lingual code-switching, and structural perturbation. This study evaluates adversarial robustness for five model architectures: three classical lexical models (Random Forest, XGBoost, CNN+BiLSTM) and two multilingual transformers (mBERT, XLM-RoBERTa), using a dataset of 27,037 messages. Classical models are subjected to black-box generic attacks, while transformers are evaluated with attention-guided targeting. Each model is tested across three attack types and intensity levels, with performance measured by the Robustness Degradation Ratio (RDR). The results reveal a distinct architectural boundary: classical models experience near-catastrophic failure under character obfuscation and structural perturbation (RDR up to 0.988), whereas transformers demonstrate significantly greater resilience (RDR up to 0.351), with structural perturbation representing their most pronounced vulnerability. Effect-size analysis (Cliff's d) indicates a substantial difference between the two model categories. Within the transformer group, XLM-RoBERTa, despite achieving a higher clean-text baseline, exhibits greater degradation than mBERT. These findings demonstrate that clean-text performance is not a reliable predictor of adversarial robustness. Statistical validation using Mann-Whitney U and Friedman tests confirms that these patterns are attributable to model architecture rather than sampling. The results underscore the necessity for architecture-specific defences and frame smishing detection as an adversarial cybersecurity challenge rather than a static classification task.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates adversarial robustness in smishing detection across five models (Random Forest, XGBoost, CNN+BiLSTM, mBERT, XLM-RoBERTa) under three attack types, finding classical models suffer near-catastrophic degradation (RDR up to 0.988) while transformers are far more resilient (RDR up to 0.351), and that clean-text accuracy does not predict robustness.
AI.motivation: Smishing detectors are typically trained and tested on clean, monolingual text, but attackers in low-resource settings evade them via character obfuscation, cross-lingual code-switching, and structural perturbation, making adversarial robustness assessment essential.
AI.method: The authors benchmark five architectures—three classical lexical models (Random Forest, XGBoost, CNN+BiLSTM) under black-box generic attacks and two multilingual transformers (mBERT, XLM-RoBERTa) under attention-guided targeted attacks—on 27,037 messages across three attack types and intensity levels, measuring Robustness Degradation Ratio (RDR), effect size via Cliff's d, and statistical validation via Mann-Whitney U and Friedman tests.
AI.result: A clear architectural boundary emerges: classical models show near-catastrophic failure under character obfuscation and structural perturbation (RDR up to 0.988), while transformers are notably more resilient (RDR up to 0.351), with structural perturbation as their main weakness. Cliff's d indicates a substantial difference between categories, and within transformers, XLM-RoBERTa degrades more than mBERT despite a higher clean-text baseline, showing clean-text performance does not predict robustness. Statistical tests attribute the patterns to architecture rather than sampling.
AI.conclusion: Smishing detection should be framed as an adversarial cybersecurity challenge requiring architecture-specific defences rather than a static classification task, since clean-text accuracy is an unreliable predictor of adversarial robustness.

title: LLM-Assisted Dynamic Threat Analysis for Attacker-Reachable Software Weaknesses in Autonomous Vehicles
summary: Autonomous vehicles depend on large safety-critical software stacks, where weaknesses reachable from adversarial inputs may affect steering, braking, or other control decisions. Static analysis can identify candidate sites, but dynamically confirming exploitability requires executable test artifacts that are difficult to construct manually. We investigate whether large language models (LLMs) can automate this process for Autoware, an open-source autonomous-driving stack. We perform compiler-precise static analysis across 185 packages, identifying 1,375 decision rules, 2,274 validation checks, and 482 input-to-safety-output flows, from which we derive a weakness taxonomy and sample 740 reachable sites. Two local open-weight LLMs, a no-static-context ablation, and a naive-template baseline generate 3,700 artifact sets, which are compiled against the real build under sanitizers, repaired through compiler-in-the-loop feedback, and fuzzed when executable. The main result is a build-integration failure taxonomy showing that 80% of first-shot compilation failures arise from dependency wiring rather than program logic. The reasoning model compiled 64% of harnesses on the first attempt, compared with 6% for the code-specialized model. Repair achieved full object-compileability for the reasoning model only through extensive stubbing; fewer than half of its harnesses reached the fuzzer, and all 37 observed crashes originated in stubbed code rather than Autoware. No candidate weakness was dynamically confirmed within budget. These results show that build integration, not candidate generation or fuzzing, is the primary barrier to reliable LLM-assisted dynamic analysis of full autonomous-vehicle software stacks.

AI.tldr: LLMs can generate candidate test harnesses for safety-critical Autoware code, but build integration (dependency wiring) — not candidate generation or fuzzing — is the dominant barrier; no weakness was dynamically confirmed, and all crashes came from stubbed code.
AI.motivation: Autonomous vehicles rely on large safety-critical stacks where adversarial-input-reachable weaknesses can affect steering/braking. Static analysis finds candidate sites, but dynamically confirming exploitability needs executable test artifacts that are hard to build manually. The paper asks whether LLMs can automate harness generation for Autoware.
AI.method: Compiler-precise static analysis across 185 Autoware packages identified 1,375 decision rules, 2,274 validation checks, and 482 input-to-safety-output flows, yielding a weakness taxonomy and 740 sampled reachable sites. Two local open-weight LLMs (a reasoning model and a code-specialized model), a no-static-context ablation, and a naive-template baseline generated 3,700 artifact sets, compiled against the real build under sanitizers, repaired via compiler-in-the-loop feedback, and fuzzed when executable.
AI.result: A build-integration failure taxonomy shows 80% of first-shot compilation failures stem from dependency wiring, not logic. The reasoning model compiled 64% of harnesses first-shot vs 6% for the code-specialized model. Full object-compileability was achieved only with extensive stubbing; under half of reasoning-model harnesses reached the fuzzer, and all 37 observed crashes originated in stubbed code, not Autoware. No candidate weakness was dynamically confirmed within budget.
AI.conclusion: Build integration is the primary barrier to reliable LLM-assisted dynamic analysis of full autonomous-vehicle software stacks, more so than candidate generation or fuzzing.

title: CRAFT: LLM-Based Iterative Refinement for Temporal Reasoning over Clinical Narratives
summary: Understanding the temporal progression of symptoms in clinical narratives is critical for disease monitoring, safety surveillance, and causality assessment. Clinical narratives, however, rarely provide explicit temporal anchors. Current approaches to temporal information reasoning focus predominantly on pairwise relation classification across multi-visit and timestamp-rich records, leaving the reconstruction of structured symptom trajectories from individual anchor-sparse reports largely unaddressed. We propose CRAFT, an LLM framework that pairs a generator with a constraint-based verifier to iteratively produce and refine stage-wise symptom timelines through targeted feedback. We conduct evaluation on MedTempo, a new benchmark of 5,347 vaccine adverse-event narratives spanning three COVID-19 vaccine types, with expert-validated temporal stage annotations for 3,166 reports. Experiments across four LLM backbones demonstrate that CRAFT consistently improves temporal ordering accuracy, with ablation analysis isolating the contribution of generator and verifier components across model capability levels.

AI.tldr: CRAFT is an LLM framework combining a generator with a constraint-based verifier to iteratively construct stage-wise symptom timelines from anchor-sparse clinical narratives, evaluated on the new MedTempo benchmark of 5,347 vaccine adverse-event reports.
AI.motivation: Clinical narratives rarely contain explicit temporal anchors, and existing temporal reasoning methods focus mainly on pairwise relation classification in timestamp-rich, multi-visit records. Reconstructing structured symptom trajectories from individual anchor-sparse reports remains largely unaddressed, yet it is critical for disease monitoring, safety surveillance, and causality assessment.
AI.method: CRAFT pairs a generator LLM with a constraint-based verifier, iteratively producing and refining stage-wise symptom timelines through targeted feedback (constraint checking and correction loops).
AI.result: Evaluated on MedTempo (5,347 vaccine adverse-event narratives across three COVID-19 vaccine types, 3,166 with expert-validated temporal stage annotations), CRAFT consistently improves temporal ordering accuracy across four LLM backbones; ablation studies isolate the contributions of the generator and verifier components across model capability levels.
AI.conclusion: CRAFT effectively reconstructs structured symptom trajectories from anchor-sparse clinical reports, outperforming baselines across multiple LLM backbones and demonstrating the value of generator-verifier iteration for temporal information reasoning.

title: Surprise2Refine: Axis-Centered Exploration-To-Refinement for Agent-Assisted Creative Scaffolding
summary: Designers require different design spaces across creative stages: broad during exploration, and targeted during refinement. Yet existing agent-driven tools assume a fixed or continuously expanding space, leaving designers to manage and navigate it themselves. Informed by a formative study with five designers, we propose an axis-centered workflow that adaptively broadens and narrows the design space to support structured exploration and refinement. We implemented this workflow in Surprise2Refine, a prototype that allows users to build and reshape an nxn design space through a set of axis-centered interactions as their creative intent evolves. A within-subjects study with 14 designers shows that Surprise2Refine enhances users' sense of control, supports tracking of scaffolding paths, and improves the perceived creativity of design outcomes. We further distill design insights to guide future agent-assisted tools for creative scaffolding.

AI.tldr: Surprise2Refine introduces an axis-centered workflow that adaptively widens and narrows an n×n design space, helping designers explore broadly and refine precisely with improved control, path tracking, and perceived creativity.
AI.motivation: Designers need different design space scopes at different creative stages—broad for exploration, targeted for refinement—but existing agent-driven tools assume a fixed or continuously expanding space, forcing designers to manually manage and navigate it.
AI.method: Based on a formative study with five designers, the authors propose an axis-centered workflow and implement it in Surprise2Refine, a prototype enabling users to build and reshape an n×n design space through axis-centered interactions as their creative intent evolves. A within-subjects study with 14 designers evaluates the prototype.
AI.result: Surprise2Refine enhances users' sense of control, supports tracking of scaffolding paths, and improves the perceived creativity of design outcomes.
AI.conclusion: The adaptive broadening and narrowing of design spaces via axis-centered interactions effectively scaffolds creative work, and the distilled design insights guide future agent-assisted creative scaffolding tools.

title: Steering the Language Axis: From Linear Decodability to Causal Control
summary:
Despite the impressive multilingual capabilities of Large Language Models, the latent dynamics dictating language selection remain poorly understood. In this work, we ask whether language identity is merely linearly decodable from hidden states, or if it can be causally controlled by a compact activation direction. We conduct an exhaustive causal intervention analysis across multiple model families, including Qwen 3.5-2B and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, isolating PCA-derived "language axes" to perform steering and ablation experiments across 1.26 million generations on the FLORES-200 dataset.
  Steering along these geometric directions reliably forces language switching in both cross-script (English to Chinese) and same-script (English to Spanish) settings, whereas equal-magnitude random perturbations yield virtually no effect. Our layerwise analysis reveals that language commitment is highly localized and explicitly language-pair-dependent. While English to Chinese switching resists early intervention and steers easily in the later layers, the English-Spanish transition shifts earlier, displaying a distinct, bimodal sensitivity. Furthermore, targeted ablation uncovers a fundamental reversion to English: once the language signal is removed, the model falls back to English regardless of the input prompt. Ultimately, these findings demonstrate that language decision boundaries function during inference as causally active features that are direction-dependent and layer-specific.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a model's output language can be causally controlled by steering hidden activations along a compact "language axis," with effects that are layer-localized and language-pair-specific, and that ablating the language signal causes a fallback to English.
AI.motivation: Language identity is linearly decodable from LLM hidden states, but it is unclear whether this is merely a correlational readout or a causally controllable feature. The authors seek to move beyond linear probing to test whether a compact activation direction can causally dictate language selection.
AI.method: The authors perform exhaustive causal intervention analysis across Qwen 3.5-2B and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct. They isolate PCA-derived "language axes" and apply steering and ablation experiments over 1.26 million generations on the FLORES-200 dataset, testing cross-script (English→Chinese) and same-script (English→Spanish) transitions, comparing against equal-magnitude random perturbation controls, and measuring layerwise steering and ablation sensitivity.
AI.result: Steering along geometric language directions reliably forces language switching in both cross-script and same-script settings, while random perturbations have virtually no effect. Language commitment is highly localized and language-pair-dependent: English→Chinese resists early intervention and steers easily only in later layers, whereas English→Spanish shifts earlier and shows a distinct bimodal sensitivity. Targeted ablation reveals a reversion to English once the language signal is removed, regardless of the input prompt.
AI.conclusion: Language decision boundaries during inference act as causally active, direction-dependent, and layer-specific features, not merely passively decodable signals. This demonstrates that language selection is robustly controllable through compact geometric interventions.

title: Exploring Oversmoothing with Householder Matrices
summary: Deep graph neural networks(GNNs) suffer from oversmoothing- a progressive collapse of node representation towards a low information subspace as network depth increases because the normalized graph propagation operator is repeatedly applied directly to the hidden representations. In this work we study Householder Graph Neural Network (HouseGNN). Rather than updating the hidden state like standard GCN, HouseGNN uses the aggregated neighbourhood message solely to estimate a reflection direction; the node embedding is then updated by a Householder reflector followed by GroupSort, yielding a piecewise orthogonal layer that preserves Euclidean norm at every node and at every depth. We prove three core properties: (i) every internal layer preserves the node-wise Euclidean norm; (ii) the Householder reflector is scale scale and sign-invariant in the message; and (iii) pairwise distance between nodes can change through mismatch between node-wise orthogonal operators.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Householder Graph Neural Network (HouseGNN), which replaces standard GCN hidden-state updates with a Householder reflector driven by the aggregated neighborhood message, followed by GroupSort, yielding piecewise orthogonal layers that preserve node-wise Euclidean norms at every depth, thereby mitigating oversmoothing in deep GNNs.
AI.motivation: Deep GNNs suffer from oversmoothing, where node representations progressively collapse toward a low-information subspace as depth increases because the normalized graph propagation operator is repeatedly applied directly to the hidden representations. The work seeks an architectural solution that avoids this collapse by keeping updates norm-preserving rather than smoothing.
AI.method: HouseGNN estimates a reflection direction from the aggregated neighborhood message instead of directly updating the hidden state. The node embedding is then updated via a Householder reflector followed by GroupSort, producing a piecewise orthogonal layer. The authors prove three properties: (i) every internal layer preserves node-wise Euclidean norm; (ii) the Householder reflector is scale- and sign-invariant in the message; and (iii) pairwise distances between nodes can change through mismatch between node-wise orthogonal operators.
AI.result: The analysis establishes that HouseGNN layers are norm-preserving per node at every depth, are invariant to the scale and sign of the aggregated message, and can alter pairwise node distances via mismatched node-wise orthogonal operators, distinguishing it from standard GCN propagation.
AI.conclusion: HouseGNN provides a principled, norm-preserving alternative to standard GCN updates that counters oversmoothing by using reflections over direct propagation, while maintaining invariance to message scale/sign and enabling expressive distance changes between nodes.

title: Beyond Handcrafted Security: Towards Self-Evolving Defense for LLM Agents
summary: The expanding operational capabilities of large language model (LLM) agents introduce sophisticated security threats. Runtime defenses have emerged as an effective approach to mitigating these risks by integrating security mechanisms into the agent execution loop. However, existing runtime defenses rely heavily on manually designed interventions and lack a principled framework for their construction and maintenance. In this work, we first develop a harness-level formulation of runtime defense that systematically characterizes how harness mechanisms enable defense construction and provides a unified view of existing runtime defense interventions from a harness perspective. Building on this formulation, we propose HARD (Harness-based Autonomous Runtime Defense Evolution), a self-evolving runtime defense framework that automatically identifies appropriate intervention strategies and iteratively improves defense artifacts based on observed failure traces. HARD transforms runtime defense development from manual engineering into an autonomous evolution process, and extensive experiments demonstrate that it improves security performance over existing handcrafted defenses while preserving benign task utility. Our findings highlight autonomous defense evolution as a promising new paradigm for securing deployed LLM agents, enabling agents to identify defense weaknesses and continuously improve their protection mechanisms.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes HARD, a self-evolving runtime defense framework for LLM agents that autonomously identifies intervention strategies and iteratively improves defense artifacts based on failure traces, framing runtime defense through a harness-level formulation. Experiments show HARD improves security over handcrafted defenses while preserving benign task utility.
AI.motivation: LLM agents' expanding capabilities introduce sophisticated security threats. Existing runtime defenses rely on manually designed interventions and lack a principled framework for construction and maintenance, motivating a systematic and automated approach to runtime defense.
AI.method: The authors first develop a harness-level formulation of runtime defense that characterizes how harness mechanisms enable defense construction and unifies existing interventions. They then propose HARD (Harness-based Autonomous Runtime Defense Evolution), which automatically identifies suitable intervention strategies and iteratively improves defense artifacts using observed failure traces, turning defense development into an autonomous evolution process.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that HARD improves security performance over existing handcrafted defenses while preserving benign task utility. The findings establish autonomous defense evolution as a promising paradigm for securing deployed LLM agents.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous defense evolution offers a promising new paradigm for securing deployed LLM agents, enabling them to identify defense weaknesses and continuously improve protection mechanisms, moving beyond manual engineering of runtime defenses.

title: CAPRI: Contract-Aware Proof Repair for Isabelle
comment: 17 pages, 1 figure, 7 tables. Submitted to SBMF 2026. Reproducibility artefact available on Zenodo
summary: We address the use of large language models (LLMs) to help discover Isabelle proofs. An Isabelle build establishes that the submitted theory is accepted, but not that an LLM changed only what the developer authorised. We present CAPRI, a contract-aware repair workflow in which Isabelle checks the proof and an independent checker enforces a machine-readable edit contract. Prompts, proposals, candidate repositories, diagnostics, verdicts, and hashes are retained for audit. We evaluate five workflows on twelve failed proofs from four developments, with three replicates per task and condition, giving 180 runs and 138 valid repairs. Of 144 terminal candidates accepted by Isabelle, six had modified protected text; all arose in iterative workflows that could edit a complete theory. A proof-body-only interface produced 29/36 valid repairs and no contract violations, compared with 31/36 for the corresponding full-theory workflow. One-shot repair produced 22/36, while a later prospectively frozen iterative workflow produced 32/36; these figures compare complete workflows rather than individual mechanisms. A separate post hoc OpenRouter campaign found no improvement in the designated Luna comparisons. A Sol configuration with matched demonstrations produced 33/36 repairs, compared with 29/36 in the frozen OpenAI Responses condition, but the difference was not statistically significant in a one-sided exact McNemar test ($p=0.0625$).

AI.tldr: CAPRI is a contract-aware Isabelle proof-repair workflow that pairs Isabelle's acceptance check with an independent, machine-readable edit contract checker to ensure LLMs only modify developer-authorised text, retaining full audit trails. Across 180 runs testing five workflows on twelve failed proofs, it found 138 valid repairs and few contract violations, with proof-body-only editing matching full-theory editing in repair rate while eliminating protected-text violations.
AI.motivation: LLMs can help discover Isabelle proofs, but an Isabelle build only proves a theory was accepted—it does not guarantee the LLM modified only what the developer authorised. This creates a trust/verifiability gap: a model could tamper with protected or pre-approved content and still pass compilation. The authors want a workflow that both validates correctness and enforces authorisation boundaries on LLM edits.
AI.method: They introduce CAPRI, a contract-aware repair workflow.
