Isabelle checks the proof (acceptance), while an independent checker enforces a machine-readable edit contract that limits which parts of the theory may be modified. Prompts, proposals, candidate repositories, diagnostics, verdicts, and hashes are logged for audit. They evaluate five workflows (one-shot repair, iterative full-theory editing, proof-body-only editing, and two later/other configurations) on twelve failed proofs from four developments, with three replicates per task and condition (180 runs total). They also ran a post hoc OpenRouter campaign and a Sol configuration with matched demonstrations; statistical comparison used a one-sided exact McNemar test.
AI.result: Out of 180 runs, 138 produced valid repairs. Of 144 terminal candidates accepted by Isabelle, only six had modified protected text, all from iterative workflows that could edit a complete theory. The proof-body-only interface yielded 29/36 valid repairs with zero contract violations, versus 31/36 for full-theory editing. One-shot repair produced 22/36; a later frozen iterative workflow produced 32/36. The post hoc OpenRouter campaign found no improvement in designated Luna comparisons. The Sol configuration with matched demonstrations produced 33/36 repairs versus 29/36 for the frozen OpenAI Responses condition, but this difference was not statistically significant (one-sided exact McNemar p = 0.0625).
AI.conclusion: A contract-aware repair workflow can enforce authorisation boundaries during LLM-assisted Isabelle proof discovery while preserving repair capability. Restricting LLM edits to the proof body eliminates contract violations at essentially no cost to repair rate, and the iterative workflows outperform one-shot repair. No statistically significant advantage was found for the Sol configuration over the frozen OpenAI Responses condition, highlighting the need for robust, reproducible evaluation of LLM proof-repair mechanisms.

title: HybridRAG-BN: A Retrieval-Augmented Framework with Fine-Tuned Verification for Bangla KBQA
comment: Developed for the IEEE Computer Society CUET Student Branch
summary: Knowledge-base question answering (KBQA) systems rely on effective retrieval and reasoning mechanisms to generate accurate answers from external knowledge sources. However, developing reliable KBQA systems for low-resource languages such as Bangla remains challenging due to limited retrieval-focused research, scarce language resources, and difficulties in grounding generated responses in external knowledge. In this work, we propose HybridRAG-BN, a retrieval-augmented framework for Bangla KBQA that integrates hybrid retrieval using BM25 and BGE-M3, answer generation using the GGUF version of Gemma-4-31B-Instruct, and a LoRA-fine-tuned Gemma-4-31B-Instruct model for answer verification and refinement. To further improve robustness, the framework incorporates a post-processing stage that addresses unresolved cases through fallback answer replacement and DuckDuckGo-assisted retrieval. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, achieving token-level F1 scores of 0.71654 and 0.72912 on the public and private leaderboards, respectively, securing first place in the competition.

AI.tldr: The paper presents HybridRAG-BN, a retrieval-augmented KBQA framework for low-resource Bangla that combines hybrid retrieval (BM25 + BGE-M3), Gemma-4-31B-Instruct generation, and a LoRA-fine-tuned verifier, achieving first place with token-level F1 scores of 0.71654 (public) and 0.72912 (private).
AI.motivation: Developing reliable knowledge-base question answering (KBQA) systems for low-resource languages like Bangla is difficult due to limited retrieval-focused research, scarce language resources, and the challenge of grounding generated answers in external knowledge.
AI.method: HybridRAG-BN integrates hybrid retrieval using BM25 and BGE-M3, answer generation with the GGUF version of Gemma-4-31B-Instruct, and a LoRA-fine-tuned Gemma-4-31B-Instruct model for answer verification and refinement. A post-processing stage handles unresolved cases via fallback answer replacement and DuckDuckGo-assisted retrieval.
AI.result: The framework achieved token-level F1 scores of 0.71654 on the public leaderboard and 0.72912 on the private leaderboard, securing first place in the competition.
AI.conclusion: HybridRAG-BN effectively addresses Bangla KBQA through hybrid retrieval and verification, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance and validating the approach's robustness for low-resource settings.

title: NavSight in the Wild: Understanding Real-World Use of a Mobile Augmented Reality Application for People with Low Vision in Outdoor Navigation
summary: The ability to navigate outdoors safely and independently is crucial yet challenging for people with low vision (PLV). While various augmented reality (AR) systems for low vision have been designed and evaluated in ideal lab environments, no research has investigated their real-world feasibility and challenges. We present NavSight, a mobile AR application that assists PLV in outdoor navigation by recognizing important outdoor objects (e.g., curb, vehicle) and rendering real-time visual augmentations. Through a seven-day diary study with 12 PLV in real-world settings, we characterize the impact of NavSight on scene perception, users' configuration strategies on what objects to augment and how to augment them across scenarios, how users made sense of and responded to recognition errors, and the social acceptability of using NavSight in public. We further identify environmental factors affecting recognition, such as weather conditions, lighting and shadows, and nonstandard road markings and textures, as well as usability issues in daily use. We discuss these real-world challenges and derive design implications for future AI-powered assistive AR systems for outdoor use.

AI.tldr: NavSight is a mobile AR app for people with low vision (PLV) that recognizes outdoor objects and renders real-time visual augmentations. A seven-day diary study with 12 PLV examined its real-world impact on scene perception, object/augmentation configuration strategies, responses to recognition errors, and social acceptability, revealing environmental factors and usability issues that inform future assistive AR design.
AI.motivation: People with low vision need safe, independent outdoor navigation, but existing AR assistive systems have only been evaluated in ideal lab environments. No prior research has investigated their real-world feasibility and challenges, leaving a gap between idealized performance and daily, messy outdoor conditions.
AI.method: The authors built NavSight, a mobile AR application that recognizes important outdoor objects (e.g., curbs, vehicles) and renders real-time visual augmentations. They conducted a seven-day diary study with 12 PLV in real-world settings to evaluate its use in everyday life.
AI.result: The study characterized NavSight's impact on scene perception; users' configuration strategies for which objects to augment and how, across scenarios; how users interpreted and reacted to recognition errors; and the social acceptability of using the app in public. It also identified environmental factors affecting recognition (weather, lighting/shadows, nonstandard road markings/textures) and usability issues in daily use.
AI.conclusion: Real-world deployment reveals challenges not visible in lab studies. The authors derive design implications for future AI-powered assistive AR systems for outdoor use, emphasizing robustness to environmental variability and addressing social and usability concerns.

title: HC-RAG: Evidence-Centric Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Heterogeneous Financial Filings
summary: Financial question answering over annual reports requires more than retrieving semantically similar passages. It often involves identifying relevant companies and fiscal years, locating standardized filing sections, collecting textual and tabular evidence, and checking answers against the original documents. Existing RAG systems, however, usually flatten long filings into unordered chunks, pay limited attention to the typed structure of financial reports, and use fixed text-table fusion strategies without considering query intent. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{HC-RAG}, a hierarchical cross-modal retrieval-augmented generation framework for evidence-centric financial QA. HC-RAG organizes filings into a typed financial evidence graph with documents, sections, text units, table units, and metadata nodes. It retrieves evidence through document-section-unit paths, aligns textual and tabular evidence in a shared retrieval space, and routes evidence according to four semantic intents: calculation, trend, fact, and comparison. We further introduce \textbf{Multi-Doc-2025}, a benchmark containing 2,327 expert-verified QA pairs from 179 SEC 10-K filings of 87 S\&P 500 companies across fiscal years 2022--2024, with labels for intent, difficulty, and structural evidence attributes. Experiments on public financial QA benchmarks and Multi-Doc-2025 show that HC-RAG improves both answer quality and evidence localization, especially in long-document, table-related, and cross-document settings. HC-RAG outperforms RAPTOR by 6.6 F1 points on DocFinQA and GraphRAG by 10.9 F1 points on Multi-Doc-2025. Evidence-level analysis and ablation studies show that the improvements mainly come from more accurate section localization, table grounding, cross-document evidence aggregation, and intent-aware text-table routing.

AI.tldr: HC-RAG is a hierarchical, cross-modal RAG framework for evidence-centric financial QA that organizes SEC filings into a typed evidence graph, uses document-section-unit retrieval paths with shared text-table alignment, and routes evidence by query intent. It introduces Multi-Doc-2025 benchmark and shows substantial F1 gains over RAPTOR and GraphRAG.
AI.motivation: Financial QA over annual reports requires more than semantic passage retrieval; it needs to identify relevant companies and fiscal years, locate standardized filing sections, gather textual and tabular evidence, and verify answers. Existing RAG systems flatten long filings into unordered chunks, ignore the typed structure of financial reports, and use fixed text-table fusion without accounting for query intent.
AI.method: HC-RAG organizes filings into a typed financial evidence graph with document, section, text unit, table unit, and metadata nodes. It retrieves evidence through document-section-unit paths, aligns textual and tabular evidence in a shared retrieval space, and routes evidence according to four semantic intents: calculation, trend, fact, and comparison. The paper also introduces Multi-Doc-2025, a benchmark of 2,327 expert-verified QA pairs from 179 SEC 10-K filings of 87 S&P 500 companies (FY 2022-2024), labeled for intent, difficulty, and structural evidence attributes.
AI.result: HC-RAG improves answer quality and evidence localization, especially in long-document, table-related, and cross-document settings. It outperforms RAPTOR by 6.6 F1 points on DocFinQA and GraphRAG by 10.9 F1 points on Multi-Doc-2025. Gains come from more accurate section localization, table grounding, cross-document evidence aggregation, and intent-aware text-table routing.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical typed structure, cross-modal shared retrieval space, and intent-aware evidence routing are key to improving evidence-centric financial QA. HC-RAG delivers consistent gains over strong baselines, with ablation and evidence-level analysis confirming the contribution of each component.

title: GENADA: efficient generative time series adversarial attack framework
summary: Deep learning models are widely used for time series analysis in domains such as healthcare, finance, energy systems, and environmental monitoring. However, these models remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where small input perturbations cause severe degradation in predictive performance. Commonly used gradient-based attacks, iterative first-order methods, are computationally burdensome, as they repeatedly backpropagate through the victim model to compute input gradients during a number of iterative refinement steps. We propose a GENerative ADversarial Attack (GENADA) that learns a generative model to produce deceptive perturbations directly in a single forward pass and a procedure to train it. Variants include single-step and iterative generative attack schemes. The validation considers attacks on several neural models and datasets in the time-series domain, a controlled, low-dimensional setting. Empirically, GENADA achieves comparable attack quality to strong baselines while requiring less time to generate perturbations during inference.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GENADA, a generative adversarial attack that produces deceptive time-series perturbations in a single forward pass, achieving comparable attack quality to gradient-based baselines while being significantly faster at inference.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models for time series are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Existing gradient-based (iterative first-order) attacks are computationally expensive because they require repeated backpropagation through the victim model over many refinement iterations. The paper aims to reduce this computational burden while preserving attack effectiveness.
AI.method: GENADA learns a generative model (and a training procedure for it) that directly produces deceptive perturbations in a single forward pass, eliminating repeated gradient computations. It offers single-step and iterative generative attack variants. Validation is performed in a controlled, low-dimensional setting across multiple neural models and time-series datasets.
AI.result: Empirically, GENADA achieves attack quality comparable to strong baselines (iterative gradient-based attacks) while requiring considerably less time to generate perturbations during inference.
AI.conclusion: A learned generative attack (GENADA) can match the effectiveness of iterative gradient-based attacks on time-series models while substantially reducing inference-time computation, offering an efficient alternative for adversarial evaluation of time-series deep learning models.

title: Governed Persistent Memory: Source-Bound State Semantics and Fail-Closed Release for Long-Horizon Agents
comment: 23 pages, 2 figures, 11 tables. Includes a sealed end-to-end governed-memory service evaluation with an ungoverned local Qwen2.5-7B comparison
summary:
Long-term agent memory is usually treated as select--store--retrieve, but retrieval does not decide whether contradictory, superseded, retracted, deleted, or stale records may support an outgoing claim. We introduce Governed Persistent Memory (GPM), an auditable bitemporal state-transition model with source-bound admission, derived lifecycle state, current public barriers, and fail-closed structured release. Five executable clauses cover ledger integrity, source binding, conflict isolation, non-revival after retraction or deletion, and exact claim closure over a fresh view at one verified head.
  On a prespecified hash-frozen 3,600-case GPM-ReleaseBench, GPM matches all complete outcomes; the strongest of three intentionally simple complete policies matches 1,800/3,600 and makes unmatched releases on 50% of violation cases. A separate sealed end-to-end service evaluation exercises real ingestion and release across eight query families. In its publicly disclosed V3 arm, the governed lane is correct on 2,400/2,400 clusters versus 600/2,400 for ungoverned local Qwen2.5-7B; it repairs all 1,800 baseline failures with no regression (one-sided 95% lower bounds 99.875% and 99.834%). A later V5 reseal over Chinese- and English-command arms, with generation-date pinning and no post-freeze reducer amendment, again obtains 2,400/2,400 per arm. A production-code-independent finite model explores 331,776 semantic and 1,990,656 query states without a full-contract counterexample, and a 100,000-trace three-engine differential yields zero mismatches.
  These are bounded contract and implementation results, not open-world model accuracy or evidence of world truth. Governed answers in the sealed service evaluation are deterministic service outputs; the 7B result is the ungoverned comparison, not a claim that a language model itself became perfectly accurate.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Governed Persistent Memory (GPM), an auditable bitemporal state-transition model that constrains how long-term agent memory supports outgoing claims, using source-bound admission, lifecycle state, and fail-closed release. It evaluates GPM on a benchmark and a sealed end-to-end service evaluation, showing governed lanes achieve near-perfect correctness versus ungoverned baselines, while scoping results to bounded contract/implementation guarantees rather than open-world truth.
AI.motivation: Classical long-term agent memory is framed only as select--store--retrieve, with no mechanism to decide whether contradictory, superseded, retracted, deleted, or stale records may legitimately support an outgoing claim. This leaves agents vulnerable to emitting claims grounded in invalid or stale memory, motivating a governed memory model that enforces admissible evidence and claim closure.
AI.method: GPM is a bitemporal state-transition memory model with five executable clauses: ledger integrity, source binding, conflict isolation, non-revival after retraction/deletion, and exact claim closure over a fresh view at one verified head. It applies source-bound admission, derived lifecycle state, current public barriers, and fail-closed structured release. Evaluation uses a prespecified hash-frozen 3,600-case GPM-ReleaseBench, a sealed end-to-end service evaluation with eight query families, a production-code-independent finite model (331,776 semantic and 1,990,656 query states), and a 100,000-trace three-engine differential test.
AI.result: On GPM-ReleaseBench, GPM matches all complete outcomes, while the strongest of three simple policies matches only 1,800/3,600 and makes unmatched releases on 50% of violation cases. In the sealed V3 arm, the governed lane is correct on 2,400/2,400 clusters versus 600/2,400 for ungoverned Qwen2.5-7B, repairing all 1,800 baseline failures with no regression (one-sided 95% lower bounds 99.875% and 99.834%). A later V5 reseal over Chinese- and English-command arms again obtains 2,400/2,400 per arm. The finite model finds no full-contract counterexample, and the three-engine differential yields zero mismatches.
AI.conclusion: GPM provides deterministic, auditable governance of agent memory, substantially outperforming simple policies and ungoverned baselines on bounded contract and implementation tests. However, these are contract/implementation results, not evidence of open-world model accuracy or world truth; the 7B ungoverned result is a comparison, not a claim that a language model became perfectly accurate.

title: ATOBench: Tracing How Autonomous Penetration-Testing Agents Verify Vulnerabilities When Target Evidence Lies
summary: Autonomous penetration-testing agents rely on target responses. These responses guide both subsequent actions and the final report. A deceptive response can therefore redirect both the attack trajectory and the agent's verification process. However, final reports reveal little about how an agent interprets conflicting evidence, changes course, decides to stop, or turns observations into a vulnerability claim. We introduce ATOBench, an evaluation framework that makes this verification process observable. ATOBench injects registered response transformations at runtime and pairs each transformed episode with a native episode under the same environment. Each pair is aligned at the first affected response. A source-linked reconstruction then follows later actions, evidence recovery, stopping, and report support. Three frozen observation contracts cover exploit proof, resource ownership, and reusable artifacts. We evaluate five model routes over 450 episodes. The analysis shows that increased activity can mask a broken verification chain, while successful recovery depends on finding usable evidence and preserving it through reporting. ATOBench turns deceptive target observations into a reproducible probe of evidence handling in autonomous penetration testing. This process-level view extends offensive pentest agent evaluation beyond final outcomes by revealing how untrusted observations shape actions, verification, and reporting.

AI.tldr: ATOBench is an evaluation framework that makes the verification process of autonomous penetration-testing agents observable by injecting deceptive target responses at runtime and comparing transformed vs. native episodes, revealing how untrusted observations shape actions, evidence recovery, stopping, and final reports.
AI.motivation: Autonomous pentest agents depend on target responses to guide actions and final reports, yet a deceptive response can redirect both the attack and verification. Existing final-report-based evaluation reveals little about how an agent interprets conflicting evidence, changes course, decides to stop, or converts observations into vulnerability claims, creating a need for process-level observability.
AI.method: ATOBench injects registered response transformations at runtime and pairs each transformed episode with a native episode under the same environment, aligned at the first affected response. A source-linked reconstruction tracks later actions, evidence recovery, stopping, and report support. Three frozen observation contracts cover exploit proof, resource ownership, and reusable artifacts. The framework is evaluated across five model routes over 450 episodes.
AI.result: Increased activity can mask a broken verification chain, while successful recovery depends on finding usable evidence and preserving it through reporting. The framework converts deceptive target observations into a reproducible probe of evidence handling in autonomous penetration testing.
AI.conclusion: ATOBench extends offensive pentest agent evaluation beyond final outcomes by providing a process-level view of how untrusted observations shape actions, verification, and reporting, making deceptive responses a reproducible probe of evidence handling.

title: EviReform: Evidence-Guided Query Reformulation for Multi-Hop Graph Retrieval
summary: Multi-hop retrieval must recover passages that provide sufficient evidence together. An initial passage often resolves an entity or relation implicit in the question, making the missing evidence easier to describe only after retrieval begins. Graph retrieval improves access to related evidence through stored corpus structure, but its retrieval signal is commonly derived from the original question. Complementary evidence must then be reached through stored relations even when an observed passage provides a more direct semantic cue. We introduce EviReform, which separates revising the retrieval request from aggregating evidence in the graph. Retrieved source passages formulate residual queries for the unresolved information need. The original and residual retrieval signals are normalized separately, combined, and propagated between propositions that share entities. On 2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue, EviReform exceeds the strongest baseline by up to 5.59 Recall@5 points and 4.50 F1 points. These results show that observed evidence can guide graph retrieval toward the part of a supporting chain left underspecified by the original question. Code is available at https://github.com/XrazyMee/EviReform.

AI.tldr: EviReform improves multi-hop graph retrieval by letting initially retrieved passages formulate revised "residual" queries, which are combined with the original query and propagated over a proposition graph to find complementary evidence.
AI.motivation: Multi-hop questions often leave entities or relations implicit, so the missing evidence is hard to describe before retrieval starts. Existing graph retrieval relies mainly on the original question's signal and must reach complementary evidence through stored relations, even when an already-retrieved passage offers a more direct semantic cue.
AI.method: EviReform separates request revision from evidence aggregation: retrieved source passages generate residual queries for the unresolved information need; original and residual signals are normalized separately, combined, and propagated between propositions sharing entities.
AI.result: On 2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue, EviReform beats the strongest baseline by up to 5.59 Recall@5 points and 4.50 F1 points.
AI.conclusion: Observed evidence can steer graph retrieval toward the underspecified part of a supporting chain, substantially improving multi-hop retrieval performance. Code is available at https://github.com/XrazyMee/EviReform.

title: Considering Contribution Statements in Visualization and HCI Research
summary: Contribution statements are an increasingly common way to make research labor visible, reduce academic malfeasance, and provide broader transparency. Despite this potential value, they remain uncommon in visualization and HCI. To explore this gap, we conducted an online study with (N=21) visualization and HCI researchers. We find a range of differing opinions about the utility of contribution statements, which are set against a background of tensions relating to contribution frameworks that inadequately fit contribution types in HCI and especially visualization, power dynamics between authors, bias in authorship perceptions, and the tedium of providing yet another form of documentation. From these factors, we offer a modest recommendation to authors: consider contribution statements. There are contexts when they may usefully explicate work, and others where they can cause author-team conflict or become a burdensome chore. Regardless of whether they are used by readers or not, we suggest that scaffolded mechanisms for reflecting on contribution roles are valuable both for public accountability and internal alignment. To institutions, we recommend that contribution statements be exempt from page or word limits, and that flexible templates and examples be provided to authors, but that they continue to not be required. By surfacing these perspectives, we seek to open a dialogue about what constitutes authorship, how our community might move toward more equitable and transparent attribution practices, and where the visualization and HCI communities might be uniquely equipped to help.

AI.tldr: This paper examines why contribution statements remain uncommon in visualization and HCI research. Through an online study with 21 researchers, it surfaces divergent opinions shaped by poorly fitting contribution frameworks, power dynamics, authorship bias, and documentation fatigue. The authors recommend authors consider using contribution statements, suggest institutions exempt them from page limits and offer flexible templates without making them mandatory, and call for a broader dialogue on equitable authorship attribution.
AI.motivation: Contribution statements promise to make research labor visible, reduce academic malfeasance, and increase transparency, yet they are rarely used in visualization and HCI. The authors seek to understand this gap and open a conversation about what constitutes authorship and how the communities can move toward more equitable, transparent attribution practices.
AI.method: An online study was conducted with N=21 visualization and HCI researchers to gather their perspectives on contribution statements. The qualitative findings were synthesized to identify tensions around contribution frameworks, author power dynamics, authorship perception bias, and documentation burden.
AI.result: Participants held a range of differing opinions on contribution statements. Key tensions identified include: contribution frameworks that inadequately fit HCI and especially visualization contribution types; power dynamics between authors; bias in authorship perceptions; and the tedium of additional documentation. Some contexts benefit from contribution statements, while others risk conflict or burdensome overhead.
AI.conclusion: The authors advise researchers to consider contribution statements, noting they can usefully explicate work but may also cause conflict or burden. They recommend scaffolded mechanisms for reflecting on contribution roles for accountability and internal alignment. To institutions, they recommend exempting contribution statements from page/word limits, providing flexible templates and examples, while keeping them non-mandatory. They call for dialogue on authorship and more equitable, transparent attribution, highlighting where visualization and HCI communities may be uniquely equipped to contribute.

title: StorySpark: Module-wise Evolutionary Search for Story Premise Generation
summary: A story premise is the creative spark from which a full narrative can grow. Yet LLM-based story generation has mostly emphasized later-stage planning, controllability, coherence, and prose expansion, while premise-level ideation remains comparatively underexplored. We introduce StorySpark, a module-wise evolutionary search framework for story premise generation. StorySpark operates over interpretable narrative modules such as background, persona, event, ending, and twist, treating each active module not as a static field to fill once, but as a local search space conditioned on the partial premise built so far. For each module, it generates alternatives, evaluates them in context, refines them through feedback-driven mutation and recombination, preserves complementary strengths with Pareto-guided selection, and reallocates frontier capacity to balance branch coverage with promising directions. Multi-view automatic and human evaluations show that StorySpark produces stronger final premises than competitive baselines, with especially consistent gains in originality; when expanded with the same story writer, its premises also lead to higher-quality downstream stories while maintaining completeness, fascination, and diverse usable narrative directions.

AI.tldr: StorySpark is an evolutionary search framework that generates stronger story premises by treating narrative modules (background, persona, event, ending, twist) as iterative local search spaces, evaluated and refined through feedback-driven mutation, Pareto-guided selection, and frontier reallocation, outperforming baselines in premise quality and downstream story generation.
AI.motivation: LLM-based story generation has focused on later-stage planning, controllability, coherence, and prose expansion, while premise-level ideation—the creative spark from which a narrative grows—remains underexplored. The authors aim to fill this gap by improving how story premises are generated.
AI.method: StorySpark uses a module-wise evolutionary search framework over interpretable narrative modules (background, persona, event, ending, twist). Each active module is treated as a local search space conditioned on the partial premise built so far. For each module, the framework generates alternatives, evaluates them in context, refines them through feedback-driven mutation and recombination, preserves complementary strengths via Pareto-guided selection, and reallocates frontier capacity to balance branch coverage with promising directions.
AI.result: Multi-view automatic and human evaluations show StorySpark produces stronger final premises than competitive baselines, with especially consistent gains in originality. When expanded with the same story writer, its premises lead to higher-quality downstream stories while maintaining completeness, fascination, and diverse usable narrative directions.
AI.conclusion: Premise-level ideation is a valuable and underexplored stage of LLM story generation. StorySpark demonstrates that a module-wise evolutionary search approach can produce original, high-quality premises that also improve downstream story quality, reducing the burden on later-stage generation.

title: Scaling Automatic Research Agents via World Models
summary: Automating empirical research is a long-standing direction of AI. Recent automatic research (AutoResearch) agents bring this goal within reach, as modern LLMs show the capability to independently implement solutions and learn from the execution outcomes. Behind these gains, post-training (especially RL) plays a central role. In this paper, we identify a fundamental tension when scaling RL for these agents: the two components of every AutoResearch trajectory (agent generation and environment execution) scale in very different manners, since all generation shares compute through batching, while each execution occupies its exclusive sandbox and real machine time. As a result, the environment execution dominates the training cost and becomes the bottleneck as trajectories grow. To resolve this tension, we propose World Model RL (WMRL), which replaces environment execution with a world model to remove this bottleneck. Additionally, the world model can be imperfect, as its rewards are corrupted by bias and noise. Therefore, we further equip WMRL with two mitigations, Online Debiasing and Inverse-Variance Denoising, which offset the bias and suppress the noise respectively. Theoretically, we prove that both mitigations of WMRL strictly improve the convergence guarantee. Empirically, WMRL accelerates training by 3-4x on various tasks at different agent scales, while exceeding the performance of standard RL baselines. Moreover, our post-trained 4B and 9B agents outperform much larger open-weight agents of 48B and 120B on held-out benchmarks. Beyond AutoResearch, WMRL also transfers to post-training embodied VLA policies, which demonstrates the generalizability of our method.

AI.tldr: RL post-training for AutoResearch agents is bottlenecked by real environment execution cost. World Model RL (WMRL) substitutes environment execution with a world model, and adds Online Debiasing and Inverse-Variance Denoising to correct the imperfect model's reward bias/noise, yielding 3-4x faster training, better convergence, and superior small agents that outperform much larger open-weight models.
AI.motivation: Modern LLMs enable AutoResearch agents that autonomously implement solutions and learn from execution outcomes, with RL post-training central to their gains. However, scaling RL exposes a fundamental tension: agent generation scales efficiently via batching (shared compute), whereas environment execution requires exclusive sandboxes and real machine time, so execution cost dominates and becomes the bottleneck as trajectories grow.
AI.method: The authors propose World Model RL (WMRL), replacing expensive real environment execution with a learned world model to remove the execution bottleneck. Because the world model's rewards are corrupted by bias and noise, they add two mitigations: (1) Online Debiasing, which offsets bias, and (2) Inverse-Variance Denoising, which suppresses noise. They provide theoretical proofs that both mitigations strictly improve convergence guarantees and validate the approach empirically across tasks and agent scales.
AI.result: WMRL accelerates training by 3-4x across tasks at different agent scales while exceeding standard RL baseline performance. Post-trained 4B and 9B agents outperform much larger open-weight agents of 48B and 120B on held-out benchmarks. The method also transfers to post-training embodied VLA policies, demonstrating generalizability beyond AutoResearch.
AI.conclusion: WMRL resolves the scaling tension in RL post-training for AutoResearch agents by substituting environment execution with a world model, with principled debiasing and denoising mitigations. The approach yields substantial training speedups, better convergence, superior small agents beating far larger models, and generalizes to embodied VLA policy post-training.

title: $\varepsilon$-MemEvo: Adaptive Cross-Task Memory Transfer for LLM Program Evolution
summary: LLM-based program evolution systems such as FunSearch and AlphaEvolve have shown strong ability to discover novel algorithms, but typically optimize each task in isolation, discarding search experience after completion. We introduce $\varepsilon$-MemEvo, a framework for cross-task knowledge transfer in LLM program evolution. $\varepsilon$-MemEvo stores prior experience as task-agnostic tactic memories: compact natural-language summaries of successful algorithmic strategies rather than raw code, enabling transfer across tasks with different APIs and evaluators. To avoid negative transfer from semantically mismatched memories, $\varepsilon$-MemEvo uses an adaptive injection gate that decides whether retrieved memories should be injected, and at what intensity. We evaluate $\varepsilon$-MemEvo on 8 diverse optimization benchmarks spanning mathematical optimization and systems engineering, using a content-level Leave-One-Out protocol that excludes target-task memory entries. On the primary GPT-5 backbone, $\varepsilon$-MemEvo improves AUCC over AdaEvolve on all 8 tasks, with a mean relative gain of +8.7%, and improves early-stage convergence by +9.4% on average. Ablations show that naive memory injection can fail catastrophically, while adaptive gating remains safe across all five ablation tasks. The data-updated posterior is interpretable in observed states: it favors skip during improving search and shifts from skip to hint across early and late plateaus. These gains incur less than 1% computational overhead.

AI.tldr: ε-MemEvo enables cross-task knowledge transfer in LLM-based program evolution by storing experience as task-agnostic tactic memories (natural-language summaries of strategies) and using an adaptive injection gate to control memory injection, achieving +8.7% mean AUCC gain and +9.4% early-stage convergence improvement over AdaEvolve across 8 benchmarks with <1% overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM program evolution systems (FunSearch, AlphaEvolve) optimize each task in isolation and discard search experience after completion. The goal is to reuse prior search experience across tasks (which may have different APIs and evaluators) while avoiding negative transfer from semantically mismatched memories.
AI.method: ε-MemEvo stores prior experience as task-agnostic tactic memories—compact natural-language summaries of successful algorithmic strategies rather than raw code—enabling transfer across tasks. It employs an adaptive injection gate that decides whether retrieved memories should be injected and at what intensity, to avoid negative transfer. Evaluation uses 8 optimization benchmarks (mathematical optimization and systems engineering) under a content-level Leave-One-Out protocol excluding target-task memory entries, primarily on GPT-5.
AI.result: On the primary GPT-5 backbone, ε-MemEvo improves AUCC over AdaEvolve on all 8 tasks with a mean relative gain of +8.7% and improves early-stage convergence by +9.4% on average. Ablations show naive memory injection can fail catastrophically, while adaptive gating remains safe across all five ablation tasks. The posterior favors skipping during improving search and shifts from skip to hint across early and late plateaus. Overhead is less than 1%.
AI.conclusion: Cross-task experience transfer via compact tactic memories with adaptive gating provides consistent, safe, and interpretable performance gains in LLM-based program evolution at negligible computational cost.

title: OmniSphinx: Active Mix Networks (Extended Version)
summary: Mix networks are an important tool to implement anonymous communication, which protects not just the content but also the metadata of messages. Over time, various packet formats for mix networks have been proposed, usually with single, specific goals in mind. These formats are incompatible with each other, requiring separate software and infrastructure to be set up. In this paper, we propose a new format, OmniSphinx, which solves this issue. In OmniSphinx, senders embed code in their packets that determines how they must be processed. The resulting active mix network can emulate any other mix format within a single deployment. Our empirical evaluation shows that emulation in OmniSphinx incurs reasonable overhead compared to native execution for typical mix network use cases: For Sphinx, the most compact format, computation time increases by around 90μs, while headers increase by 33% in size.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes OmniSphinx, a new mix network packet format that embeds processing code in packets, enabling a single deployment to emulate any other mix format.
AI.motivation: Existing mix network packet formats are incompatible with each other, each designed for specific goals, and require separate software and infrastructure to deploy. The authors aim to unify these formats within a single active mix network.
AI.method: OmniSphinx is an active mix network format in which senders embed code in their packets that determines how each packet must be processed by the mix nodes, allowing the network to emulate any other mix format within one deployment.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows reasonable emulation overhead: for Sphinx (the most compact format), computation time increases by about 90μs and header size increases by 33% compared to native execution.
AI.conclusion: OmniSphinx successfully enables a single mix network deployment to emulate arbitrary mix packet formats with acceptable overhead, addressing the incompatibility problem among existing formats.

title: Smart Contract Invariants Protect Against Cybercriminals
summary: Blockchains are among the most adversarial environments in computing. Billions are stolen by cybercriminals who exploit vulnerabilities. This is an open problem and no concept or technique has proven to really make a difference. In this paper, we claim that the classical notion of program invariant is perhaps the most powerful solution to the problem. We devise anoriginal experimental protocol to 1) study how invariants would have protected against past real-world attacks and 2) whether state-of-the-art automated tools can find them. The experimental toolchain is sophisticated. It is based on INVARIANTEVAL, a benchmark of 28 real Ethereum exploits, each paired with a human-authored invariant that blocks the attack. We validate every invariant with PONDEREPLAY, a replay framework that re-executes transactions in order to prove the correctness and soundness of smart contract invariants. We demonstrate that smart contract invariants block all the cybercriminal attacks in INVARIANTEVAL, fully validated by replaying 108,637 historical transactions. Our large-scale experiments clearly demonstrate that smart contract invariants protect against cybercriminals.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that program invariants are a highly effective solution to smart contract vulnerabilities, introducing INVARIANTEVAL (a benchmark of 28 real Ethereum exploits with human-authored invariants) and PONDEREPLAY (a replay framework), and shows invariants block all attacks, validated across 108,637 historical transactions.
AI.motivation: Blockchains are highly adversarial environments where billions are stolen by cybercriminals exploiting smart contract vulnerabilities, and no existing concept or technique has proven genuinely effective at solving this open problem.
AI.method: The authors propose using the classical notion of program invariants and devise an experimental protocol with two components: INVARIANTEVAL, a benchmark of 28 real Ethereum exploits each paired with a human-authored invariant that blocks the attack, and PONDEREPLAY, a replay framework that re-executes transactions to prove the correctness and soundness of smart contract invariants.
AI.result: The smart contract invariants blocked all cybercriminal attacks in INVARIANTEVAL, and this was fully validated by replaying 108,637 historical transactions, demonstrating that invariants protect against real-world attacks.
AI.conclusion: Program invariants are a powerful and validated solution for protecting smart contracts against cybercriminals, with the benchmark and replay framework providing strong experimental evidence of their effectiveness.

title: RAGSieve: Self-Referenced Local Contrast for Knowledge-Poison Detection in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation treats an external corpus as inference evidence, allowing injected documents to promote attacker-chosen claims. Existing detectors depend on trusted references, specific attack artifacts, or global thresholds sensitive to corpus topology. We present RAGSieve, a self-referenced detection framework that constructs its reference from the inspected system. RAGSieve-Query (RSQ) performs query-local contrast, scoring top-five candidates against ranks 6-20 of the same retrieval to detect answer-anchor concentration and carrier transitions. RAGSieve-Graph (RSG) performs corpus-local contrast, comparing each document's semantically similar but lexically distinct neighbors with its local baseline to detect coordinated density before queries arrive. Across three QA datasets and six poisoning constructions, RSQ achieves 95.2% AUROC and detects 82.2% of poison at 5% clean-document removal, versus 81.1%/52.5% for GMTP. RSG achieves 93.3%/79.8%, versus 79.4%/37.6% for CleanBase. Joint deployment reduces attack success from 67.4% to 14.0% while retaining 41.3% F1 on unpoisoned retrieval, demonstrating practical protection at both corpus ingestion and query time without poison labels or trusted corpora. Source code is available at https://github.com/XrazyMee/RAGSieve.

AI.tldr: RAGSieve is a self-referenced detection framework for retrieval-augmented generation poisoning attacks, operating at both query time (RSQ) and corpus ingestion time (RSG) without needing trusted references or poison labels.
AI.motivation: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems can be manipulated by injected documents that promote attacker-chosen claims, and existing detectors rely on trusted references, specific attack artifacts, or global thresholds sensitive to corpus topology — all of which are impractical or fragile. The authors aim to build a detector that constructs its own reference from the inspected system itself.
AI.method: RAGSieve consists of two components. RAGSieve-Query (RSQ) performs query-local contrast by scoring the top-five retrieved candidates against ranks 6-20 of the same retrieval, detecting answer-anchor concentration and carrier transitions. RAGSieve-Graph (RSG) performs corpus-local contrast by comparing each document's semantically similar but lexically distinct neighbors with its local baseline to detect coordinated density before queries arrive.
AI.result: Across three QA datasets and six poisoning constructions, RSQ achieves 95.2% AUROC and detects 82.2% of poison at 5% clean-document removal (vs 81.1%/52.5% for GMTP). RSG achieves 93.3% AUROC and 79.8% detection (vs 79.4%/37.6% for CleanBase). Joint deployment reduces attack success from 67.4% to 14.0% while retaining 41.3% F1 on unpoisoned retrieval.
AI.conclusion: RAGSieve demonstrates practical protection at both corpus ingestion and query time without poison labels or trusted corpora, significantly outperforming baseline detectors (GMTP and CleanBase) in AUROC and poison detection rate while preserving reasonable retrieval quality on clean data.

title: PolyPresentation: A Multimodal AI Platform for Slide-Aware Iterative Presentation Practice
summary: Presentations are essential for students, researchers, and professionals to communicate ideas persuasively, yet delivering them effectively requires repeated practice that coordinates content, delivery, visual materials, and audience interaction. Existing AI-assisted rehearsal tools provide scalable feedback, but they often treat presentations as single-run delivery performances, offering limited support for linking feedback to the slide deck or planning what to practice in the next iteration. To address this gap, we introduce PolyPresentation, a multimodal AI platform for slide-aware iterative presentation practice. PolyPresentation organizes slide-by-slide practice, full rehearsal, audience Q&A, and feedback into a unified practice loop, using slide-grounded evidence to help presenters diagnose performance issues and prepare for subsequent practice. We evaluate PolyPresentation through a rubric-based comparison with four baseline systems on 20 academic presentation rehearsals, and additionally assess its alignment with human ratings. Results suggest that PolyPresentation provides more actionable, context-aware, and practice-oriented support for improving presentations. The demonstration video is available at https://youtu.be/MmWj9O_PJxw.

AI.tldr: PolyPresentation is a multimodal AI platform that turns presentation practice into a slide-aware iterative loop—combining slide-by-slide practice, full rehearsal, Q&A, and feedback grounded in slide evidence—outperforming four baselines on 20 academic presentations in actionable, context-aware support.
AI.motivation: Effective presentations require repeated practice coordinating content, delivery, visuals, and audience interaction. Existing AI rehearsal tools treat presentations as single-run performances, offering limited linkage of feedback to specific slides and little guidance on what to practice next, creating a gap in iterative, slide-aware training.
AI.method: PolyPresentation organizes slide-by-slide practice, full rehearsal, audience Q&A, and feedback into a unified practice loop. It uses slide-grounded evidence to diagnose performance issues and plan subsequent practice. The system is evaluated via a rubric-based comparison against four baseline systems on 20 academic presentation rehearsals, plus an assessment of alignment with human ratings.
AI.result: PolyPresentation provides more actionable, context-aware, and practice-oriented feedback than the four baseline systems, with results indicating better support for improving presentations and alignment with human ratings.
AI.conclusion: The slide-aware iterative practice loop of PolyPresentation addresses the limitations of single-run rehearsal tools, offering stronger actionable and context-aware support, as validated on 20 academic rehearsals and human-rating alignment; a demonstration video is publicly available.

title: From Refuse to Richness: Rubric Rewards for Long-Form Hallucination Reinforcement Learning
summary: Rewards that penalize unsupported claims can improve grounding in long-form generation, but they can also teach models to answer less. We study this refusal-to-richness trade-off in long-form hallucination RL. Instead of using global richness proxies such as length, claim count, detail, or pairwise relevance, we represent each question with a key-point rubric that specifies the required and optional information a useful answer should cover. These rubrics define coverage directly and are used both for evaluation and as reward signals. Across grounding-only, proxy-based, rubric-only, and combined rewards, we find a stable trade-off: strict grounding rewards improve support but suppress coverage, while unconstrained rubric rewards improve coverage but weaken grounding. A soft combination of grounding, rubric coverage, and relevance gives the best balance in our experiments, improving in-distribution support while transferring better to out-of-distribution checklist tasks than either grounding-only or rubric-only rewards.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the trade-off between refusal and richness in long-form hallucination RL, where grounding penalties improve support but reduce answer coverage. It introduces key-point rubrics that directly specify required/optional information, and finds that combining grounding, rubric coverage, and relevance yields the best balance and out-of-distribution transfer.
AI.motivation: Rewards penalizing unsupported claims improve grounding but can cause models to answer less (refusal-to-richness trade-off). Existing richness proxies (length, claim count, detail, pairwise relevance) are global and indirect, motivating a direct, per-question specification of what a useful answer should cover.
AI.method: Represent each question with a key-point rubric specifying required and optional information a useful answer should cover. Use these rubrics both for evaluation and as reward signals. Compare grounding-only, proxy-based, rubric-only, and combined rewards in long-form hallucination RL, including a soft combination of grounding, rubric coverage, and relevance.
AI.result: A stable refusal-to-richness trade-off emerges: strict grounding rewards improve support but suppress coverage; unconstrained rubric rewards improve coverage but weaken grounding. The soft combination of grounding, rubric coverage, and relevance achieves the best balance, improving in-distribution support and transferring better to out-of-distribution checklist tasks than grounding-only or rubric-only rewards.
AI.conclusion: Direct coverage via key-point rubrics is more meaningful than global richness proxies, but grounding and richness are fundamentally in tension. A soft combined reward (grounding + rubric coverage + relevance) best balances the trade-off and generalizes better out-of-distribution.

title: Prof-K: Probabilistic One-Pass Filtering for Efficient Top-k Selection
summary: Top-k selection is a fundamental computational primitive with applications spanning databases, information retrieval, signal processing, and modern machine learning workloads, including sparse activations and attention pruning. As data sizes grow, existing approaches become inefficient: exact methods incur high memory and compute overhead, while approximate methods often rely on brittle heuristics that degrade under adversarial or heavy-tailed inputs. In this paper, we introduce Prof-K, a fast, scalable, and distribution-agnostic top-k algorithm with probabilistic correctness guarantees. Prof-K performs a single-pass filtering procedure: a small random sample estimates an adaptive threshold, the N input elements are streamed once into a compact buffer, and an exact top-k routine on this buffer recovers the true top-k elements with probability at least 1 - $ε$, where $ε$ > 0 is user specified. We derive high-probability guarantees for correctness and buffer size, together with an approximately optimal sample size that minimizes overhead as a function of N and k. Empirically, Prof-K achieves 1.5x-10x speedups over the highly optimized PyTorch topk and recent RadiK implementations, with the largest gains in the large-scale, small-to-moderate-k regime where prior methods struggle most. Unlike previous approaches, these guarantees hold independently of the input distribution, ensuring robustness to adversarial settings. By relaxing the recall target (e.g., recovering 95% of the true top-k values), Prof-K additionally provides a principled accuracy-speed trade-off. We further demonstrate its impact on training BatchTopK Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), where top-k selection constitutes a significant portion of the training cost.

AI.tldr: Prof-K is a fast, single-pass, distribution-agnostic top-k selection algorithm with probabilistic correctness guarantees, achieving 1.5x–10x speedups over PyTorch topk and RadiK, especially in the large-scale, small-to-moderate-k regime.
AI.motivation: Top-k selection is a fundamental primitive in databases, information retrieval, signal processing, and machine learning (e.g., sparse activations, attention pruning). As data sizes grow, exact methods incur high memory/compute overhead, while approximate methods rely on brittle heuristics that fail under adversarial or heavy-tailed inputs. There is a need for a fast, scalable algorithm with rigorous, distribution-independent guarantees.
AI.method: Prof-K performs a single-pass filtering procedure: a small random sample estimates an adaptive threshold, the N input elements are streamed once into a compact buffer, and an exact top-k routine on the buffer recovers the true top-k elements with probability at least 1 - ε. The authors derive high-probability guarantees for correctness and buffer size, plus an approximately optimal sample size minimizing overhead as a function of N and k. A relaxation of the recall target (e.g., 95% of true top-k) provides an accuracy-speed trade-off.
AI.result: Prof-K achieves 1.5x–10x speedups over highly optimized PyTorch topk and recent RadiK implementations, with the largest gains in the large-scale, small-to-moderate-k regime where prior methods struggle most. Its guarantees hold independently of the input distribution, ensuring robustness in adversarial settings. The method is demonstrated on BatchTopK Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) training, where top-k selection is a major cost component.
AI.conclusion: Prof-K provides a fast, scalable, distribution-agnostic top-k algorithm with probabilistic correctness guarantees, robustness to adversarial/heavy-tailed inputs, and a principled accuracy-speed trade-off through recall relaxation, yielding substantial speedups in large-scale settings and practical impact on SAE training.

title: CAS: A Causal Attribution Score for Local and Global Explainable Artificial Intelligence
summary: Predictive explanation methods attribute a model output; they do not, by themselves, attribute an intervention effect on the real-world outcome. We introduce the Causal Attribution Score (CAS), a compact score architecture for causal explanation. CAS starts from an identified interventional coalition game, allocates the joint intervention contrast with causal Shapley contributions, and converts those raw outcome-scale effects into Local CAS, Signed Local CAS, and two complementary Global CAS summaries. The innovation is not a new Shapley formula, but a local-to-global causal reporting layer with an explicit intervention target. In the known-truth benchmark, eight repeated primary-interaction simulations (n = 2,200 each, three actions) gave mean Local CAS MAE of 0.107 for coalition-aware CAS, compared with 0.173 for one-at-a-time normalisation and 0.213 for a global normalised absolute ATE vector. The paired advantage over one-at-a-time normalisation increased from -0.003 under additivity to 0.091 under strong interactions. On both empirical DoubleML datasets, 401(k) eligibility/net financial assets (n = 9,915) and Pennsylvania reemployment bonus/unemployment duration (n = 5,099), predictive SHAP/TreeSHAP rankings differed materially from Feature-CAS rankings of treatment-effect modifiers. In Pennsylvania, dep1 (exactly one dependent) moved from predictive global rank 13 to Feature-CAS rank 2 and was the leading local Feature-CAS modifier. These results isolate the added value of separating what predicts the outcome from what explains heterogeneity in an estimated causal effect.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Causal Attribution Score (CAS), a causal-explanation score that attributes intervention effects rather than model outputs, combining interventional Shapley contributions with local-to-global reporting layers targeting an explicit intervention.
AI.motivation: Predictive explanation methods (e.g., SHAP) attribute a model's output but fail to attribute real-world intervention effects. The authors aim to separate what predicts an outcome from what explains heterogeneity in an estimated causal effect, providing causal explanations tied to an explicit intervention target.
AI.method: CAS starts from an identified interventional coalition game, allocates the joint intervention contrast using causal Shapley contributions, and converts raw outcome-scale effects into Local CAS, Signed Local CAS, and two complementary Global CAS summaries. The novelty lies in a local-to-global causal reporting layer with an explicit intervention target rather than a new Shapley formula. Evaluation uses known-truth simulations (eight repeated primary-interaction simulations, n=2,200 each, three actions) and empirical DoubleML datasets (401(k), n=9,915; Pennsylvania reemployment, n=5,099).
AI.result: In known-truth benchmarks, coalition-aware CAS achieved mean Local CAS MAE of 0.107 versus 0.173 for one-at-a-time normalisation and 0.213 for a global normalised absolute ATE vector. The paired advantage over one-at-a-time normalisation grew from -0.003 under additivity to 0.091 under strong interactions. On empirical datasets, predictive SHAP/TreeSHAP rankings differed materially from Feature-CAS rankings; in Pennsylvania dep1 (exactly one dependent) moved from predictive rank 13 to Feature-CAS rank 2 and was the leading local Feature-CAS modifier.
AI.conclusion: CAS successfully isolates the added value of distinguishing outcome prediction from causal-effect heterogeneity explanation, demonstrating superior accuracy over baseline normalisation methods and revealing treatment-effect modifiers that predictive rankings miss.

title: Vero: Can AI Agents Build Formally Verified Software Repositories?
summary: AI agents are increasingly used for programming, but do not provide any guarantee on the correctness of generated code. Verified code generation, in which an agent produces both an implementation and a machine-checked proof of its specification, offers a stronger path toward trustworthy AI-generated software. Existing benchmarks in this direction either focus on individual functions or only evaluate proof generation with provided implementations. It is still an open question whether agents can make coherent implementation and proof choices across real multi-module codebases. To bridge this gap, we introduce Vero, the first benchmark to evaluate joint implementation and proof synthesis at the repository level. Vero contains 43 multi-module instances sourced from real-world repositories spanning Python, Dafny, Verus, and Coq, and covering diverse domains from cryptographic protocols to distributed systems. Each instance consists of a multi-module Lean 4 repository with predetermined API interfaces, manually curated formal specifications, and reference implementations, supporting both proof-only and code-and-proof evaluation modes. To improve benchmark reliability, Vero also includes an audit mechanism where agents are allowed to formally prove unsatisfiability of provided specification or incorrectness of reference code, which surfaces and corrects latent code and specification errors during curation. We evaluate frontier coding-agent configurations with Lean toolchain access. The strongest agent fully solves only 27 of 43 instances and closes no specifications on the hardest repositories. Vero provides a concrete testbed for measuring progress toward repository-scale verified software synthesis, where current agents still fall short. We release the benchmark, curation pipeline, and evaluation harness at https://github.com/sunblaze-ucb/vero.

AI.tldr: Vero is the first repository-level benchmark for evaluating joint implementation and formal proof synthesis in verified code generation, containing 43 multi-module instances across Python, Dafny, Verus, and Coq (ported to Lean 4), with an audit mechanism to catch latent spec/code errors. Frontier agents solve only 27/43 instances, showing verified software synthesis at repository scale remains unsolved.
AI.motivation: AI coding agents generate code without correctness guarantees. Verified code generation (implementation plus machine-checked proof) offers a path to trustworthy software, but existing benchmarks only test individual functions or proof generation given a provided implementation. It is unknown whether agents can make coherent implementation and proof choices across real multi-module codebases.
AI.method: The authors build Vero: 43 multi-module instances sourced from real-world repositories spanning Python, Dafny, Verus, and Coq, covering domains from cryptographic protocols to distributed systems. Each instance is a multi-module Lean 4 repository with predetermined API interfaces, manually curated formal specifications, and reference implementations, supporting both proof-only and code-and-proof modes. A novel audit mechanism lets agents formally prove unsatisfiability of a provided specification or incorrectness of reference code, surfacing and correcting latent errors during curation. They evaluate frontier coding-agent configurations with access to Lean toolchain.
AI.result: The strongest agent fully solves only 27 of 43 instances and closes no specifications on the hardest repositories. This demonstrates current agents still fall far short of repository-scale verified software synthesis.
AI.conclusion: Vero provides the first concrete testbed for measuring progress toward repository-scale verified software synthesis, where current agents still fall short. The benchmark, curation pipeline, and evaluation harness are released publicly.

title: GEM: A Generative Embedding Model Bridging Reasoning and Retrieval
summary: Modern LLMs excel at reasoning and instruction following, enabling users to express complex and diverse information needs. However, conventional retrievers largely rely on surface-level matching between queries and documents, resulting in a growing gap between how users express their needs and how retrievers interpret them. In this paper, we present GEM, a generative embedding model that augments retrieval through its own knowledge by explicitly reasoning about user intent and relevance criteria. GEM unifies generation and embedding within a single model: it first reasons over the query, then appends an embedding token to encode the enriched context for retrieval. \zhili{Evaluated on reasoning-intensive and instruction-following retrieval tasks, GEM demonstrates the effectiveness of its reasoning-augmented retrieval, outperforming its non-reasoning variant and matching baselines using substantially larger models.} Furthermore, GEM's generative nature allows test-time compute scaling via prompting to further enhance retrieval performance. Our code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/GEM.

AI.tldr: GEM is a generative embedding model that unifies reasoning and retrieval, explicitly reasoning about user intent before encoding an embedding token, and achieves strong retrieval performance while enabling test-time compute scaling via prompting.
AI.motivation: Conventional retrievers rely on surface-level query-document matching, which fails to capture the complex, diverse, and instruction-rich information needs that modern LLM users express. The goal is to close the gap between how users state needs and how retrievers interpret them by leveraging the model's own knowledge and reasoning.
AI.method: GEM (Generative Embedding Model) combines generation and embedding in a single model. It first reasons over the query to understand user intent and relevance criteria, then appends a special embedding token that encodes the enriched, reasoned context to produce a retrieval embedding.
AI.result: On reasoning-intensive and instruction-following retrieval tasks, GEM outperforms its non-reasoning variant and matches baselines that use substantially larger models. Its generative nature also allows test-time compute scaling through prompting, further improving retrieval performance.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning-augmented retrieval via a unified generative embedding model effectively bridges the intent-expression gap in retrieval, delivering competitive or superior performance with smaller models and offering scalable test-time performance gains.

title: How LLMs Respond to Escalating Delusions: Four Longitudinal Trajectories of Model Behavior
summary: The widespread use of LLMs among psychiatric populations has raised concerns regarding their safety and potential iatrogenic impact in the context of AI psychosis. While growing literature conceptualizes AI psychosis and documents case studies, empirical evidence tracing AI-exacerbated psychotic processes remains scarce. We propose and test a longitudinal qualitative evaluation design, supported by automated metrics, to assess mainstream LLMs' potential to exacerbate psychosis. Fifteen widely used LLMs were prompted across 30 days using the same 30-message script, simulating progression from mild anomalous experiences to psychotic ideation. Four trained evaluators independently rated 449 model-days, assessing (1) recognition stage (from naive engagement to stabilized clinical framing), (2) interpretative confidence, and (3) intervention profile (from education to treatment recommendation). Two computational metrics-entrainment and modality-were devised to increase evaluation reliability. Direct recommendations to disengage from the LLM were flagged and re-coded via adjudication using a strict two-level definition. Across model generations and vendors, we identified four response trajectories: (1) premature medicalization and disengagement (Claude Haiku 4.5); (2) recognition without safeguarding, marked by LLM self-sufficiency in offering help (GPT Instant/Thinking); (3) delayed and unstable recognition, marked by late, non-progressive conceptualization (Claude Opus 3/4/4.1, Claude Haiku 3.5, GPT-4o, Gemini 3.1 Pro); and (4) delusion co-construction through active engagement with delusional content (Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash, DeepSeek-V3, Claude Sonnet 4). Our findings indicate that LLMs' potential to exacerbate AI psychosis should be operationalized as a combination of recognition timing, stability, and intervention accuracy and evaluated longitudinally, focusing on temporal dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper empirically tests whether mainstream LLMs exacerbate "AI psychosis" by longitudinally prompting 15 LLMs over 30 days with a script progressing from mild anomalous experiences to psychotic ideation, then rating model responses on recognition stage, interpretative confidence, and intervention profile using human evaluators plus two new computational metrics (entrainment and modality).
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used by psychiatric populations, raising safety concerns about iatrogenic effects in "AI psychosis"; however, while conceptual and case-study literature exists, there is scarce empirical evidence tracing AI-exacerbated psychotic processes, leaving a gap in evidence-based assessment of LLM risk.
AI.method: A longitudinal qualitative evaluation design with automated metrics: 15 widely used LLMs were prompted over 30 days using an identical 30-message script simulating progression from mild anomalous experiences to psychotic ideation. Four trained evaluators independently rated 449 model-days on (1) recognition stage (from naive engagement to stabilized clinical framing), (2) interpretative confidence, and (3) intervention profile (from education to treatment recommendation). Two computational metrics, entrainment and modality, were devised to improve reliability, and direct disengagement recommendations were re-coded via a strict two-level adjudication definition.
AI.result: Four response trajectories emerged across model generations and vendors: (1) premature medicalization and disengagement (Claude Haiku 4.5); (2) recognition without safeguarding, marked by LLM self-sufficiency in offering help (GPT Instant/Thinking); (3) delayed and unstable recognition with late, non-progressive conceptualization (Claude Opus 3/4/4.1, Claude Haiku 3.5, GPT-4o, Gemini 3.1 Pro); and (4) delusion co-construction through active engagement with delusional content (Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash, DeepSeek-V3, Claude Sonnet 4).
AI.conclusion: LLMs' potential to exacerbate AI psychosis should be operationalized as a combination of recognition timing, stability, and intervention accuracy, and evaluated longitudinally with a focus on temporal dynamics rather than static single-turn behaviors.

title: SDAM: Structure-Difference-Aware Memory Evolution for Complex Text-to-SQL
summary: Text-to-SQL aims to convert natural language questions into executable SQL queries. While memory-based agent system improves complex SQL generation, existing memory design neglect historical experience and suffer from weak structure analysis, shallow semantic understanding, and poor schema alignment. To address these challenges, we propose SDAM. Specifically, SDAM identifies potential errors via a structure-difference aware reasoning tree, extracts deep semantic rules through contradiction-aware reflection, and enhances structural consistency using a schema-grounded memory evolution mechanism to bind memory with database schemas. We integrate SDAM into a Text-to-SQL framework named SDAM-SQL. Experiment shows that SDAM-SQL achieves 2.0 and 0.4 improvement on BIRD-dev and Spider-test compared with mainstream Text-to-SQL methods, showing the effectiveness of SDAM-SQL.

AI.tldr: SDAM is a memory-based approach that improves Text-to-SQL by using structure-difference aware reasoning, contradiction-aware reflection, and schema-grounded memory evolution, integrated into SDAM-SQL, which outperforms mainstream methods on BIRD-dev and Spider-test.
AI.motivation: Existing memory-based agent systems for Text-to-SQL neglect historical experience and suffer from weak structure analysis, shallow semantic understanding, and poor schema alignment, limiting complex SQL generation.
AI.method: SDAM introduces three mechanisms: (1) a structure-difference aware reasoning tree to identify potential errors, (2) contradiction-aware reflection to extract deep semantic rules, and (3) a schema-grounded memory evolution mechanism that binds memory with database schemas to enhance structural consistency. These are integrated into a framework called SDAM-SQL.
AI.result: SDAM-SQL achieves improvements of 2.0 on BIRD-dev and 0.4 on Spider-test compared with mainstream Text-to-SQL methods.
AI.conclusion: SDAM-SQL effectively enhances Text-to-SQL performance by addressing memory design limitations, demonstrating its effectiveness over mainstream approaches.

title: Represent, Then Generate: Multimodal-Conditioned Time-Series Generation under Irregular Missingness
summary: Continuous physiological time series underpin modern clinical monitoring, yet many of the most informative signals are invasive, expensive, or simply unavailable for a given patient. Conditional generation offers a remedy: an absent signal can be synthesized from co-recorded signals and routine clinical variables. Existing generators, however, are built around a single conditioning modality and degrade when forced to handle the heterogeneous, irregularly missing mix of time-variant signals and static covariates seen in practice. We propose ReCoGen (Represent Conditions, then Generate), a two-stage framework that decouples multimodal condition representation from target generation. Stage I trains one masked autoencoder per modality, distilling each time-variant condition into a compact and missingness-tolerant token sequence. Stage II trains a flow-matching generator that fuses these tokens with static conditions to synthesize the target signal. Across three physiological benchmarks, including continuous glucose monitoring on AI-READI and arterial blood pressure generation on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV, ReCoGen attains the best downstream utility on all sixteen (dataset, task, metric) settings, surpassing six representative conditional generators; on thirteen of them its utility also reaches or exceeds the utility measured on the real signal, a reference we read as an approximate anchor rather than a ceiling. Ablations trace the gains to the conditioning path: learnable cross-attention over the frozen per-modality encoders, and a dual token-plus-AdaLN route for the static conditions. ReCoGen thus turns routinely collected signals into informative surrogates for invasive or unavailable ones, a step toward less invasive, lower-cost continuous clinical monitoring.

AI.tldr: ReCoGen is a two-stage conditional generation framework for synthesizing missing physiological signals. Stage I trains per-modality masked autoencoders to turn each time-variant condition into compact, missingness-tolerant tokens; Stage II trains a flow-matching generator that fuses these tokens with static covariates to synthesize the target signal. It achieves the best downstream utility across all sixteen settings and often matches or exceeds real-signal utility.
AI.motivation: Many informative physiological signals are invasive, expensive, or unavailable. Conditional generation could synthesize an absent signal from co-recorded signals and clinical covariates, but existing generators are built around a single conditioning modality and degrade on the heterogeneous, irregularly missing mix of time-variant signals and static covariates seen in practice.
AI.method: ReCoGen decouples multimodal condition representation from target generation. Stage I trains one masked autoencoder per modality, distilling each time-variant condition into a compact and missingness-tolerant token sequence. Stage II trains a flow-matching generator that fuses these tokens with static conditions (via a dual token-plus-AdaLN route and learnable cross-attention over frozen per-modality encoders) to synthesize the target signal.
AI.result: Across three physiological benchmarks (continuous glucose monitoring on AI-READI; arterial blood pressure generation on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV), ReCoGen attains the best downstream utility on all sixteen (dataset, task, metric) settings, surpassing six representative conditional generators. On thirteen settings its utility reaches or exceeds the utility of the real signal (treated as an approximate anchor, not a ceiling). Ablations attribute gains to learnable cross-attention over frozen per-modality encoders and the dual token-plus-AdaLN static-condition route.
AI.conclusion: ReCoGen turns routinely collected signals into informative surrogates for invasive or unavailable signals, advancing less invasive, lower-cost continuous clinical monitoring.

title: Trie Automata for Constrained Decoding over Large Finite Sets
summary: Large language models increasingly need to generate structured outputs that conform to predefined schemas, with one common constraint being selection from a finite set of valid strings. Current constrained decoding systems handle this through general-purpose grammar compilation, which becomes prohibitively slow as the number of valid values grows into the thousands, a cardinality wall. We introduce the trie automaton, a specialized mechanism that exploits finite-set structure (shared prefixes, bounded depth, known cardinality) via Aho-Corasick multi-pattern matching to precompute per-node token masks. The trie achieves 7X faster per-step valid-token computation (0.65 us vs. 5.8 us) compared to XGrammar, one of the primary backends in vLLM and SGLang, and 2--6.5X faster compilation at K >= 300. Because precomputed masks enable a stateless serving path that bypasses the guided decoding pipeline, this advantage compounds in batch serving: end-to-end vLLM throughput reaches 219 req/s vs. XGrammar's 7.5 req/s at batch size 256 (29X). The 29X combines the algorithmic speedup with integration-path savings that only precomputed masks can unlock. Across seven tokenizer families (32K--262K vocabulary), the trie maintains sub-100ms compilation up to K = 10,000 and flat per-step cost regardless of set size, while guaranteeing 100% output validity.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the trie automaton, a specialized constrained decoding mechanism for selecting valid outputs from finite string sets.
