It precomputes per-node token masks via Aho-Corasick matching, avoiding general-purpose grammar compilation. It achieves 7X faster per-step token computation, 2-6.5X faster compilation for large sets, and 29X higher batch throughput in vLLM versus XGrammar, while guaranteeing 100% output validity.
AI.motivation: LLMs increasingly must generate outputs constrained to finite sets of valid strings, but existing constrained decoding systems use general-purpose grammar compilation that slows prohibitively as valid values grow into the thousands—a "cardinality wall." There is a need for a mechanism that scales efficiently with set size.
AI.method: The trie automaton exploits finite-set structure (shared prefixes, bounded depth, known cardinality) using Aho-Corasick multi-pattern matching to precompute per-node token masks. These masks enable a stateless serving path that bypasses the guided decoding pipeline, unlocking integration-path savings in batch serving.
AI.result: The trie achieves 7X faster per-step valid-token computation (0.65 us vs. 5.8 us) versus XGrammar, and 2-6.5X faster compilation at K >= 300. End-to-end vLLM throughput reaches 219 req/s vs. XGrammar's 7.5 req/s at batch size 256 (29X). Across seven tokenizer families (32K-262K vocabulary), it maintains sub-100ms compilation up to K = 10,000 and flat per-step cost regardless of set size, while guaranteeing 100% output validity.
AI.conclusion: The trie automaton overcomes the cardinality wall by combining an algorithmic speedup (precomputed token masks via Aho-Corasick) with integration-path savings (stateless serving bypassing the guided decoding pipeline), yielding large throughput gains and guaranteed validity for finite-set constrained decoding in LLM serving systems.

title: InSPECtor: Improving SLEIGH Processor Specification Veracity via Proxy
comment: Extended version published at USENIX Security (USENIX Security'2026). Code available at: https://github.com/Sleigh-InSPECtor/
summary:
Processor specifications underpin critical security and program- analysis tools such as disassemblers, decompilers, and emulators, yet, their correctness is rarely examined. Errors in specifications distort program behaviour, obscure vulnerabilities, and enable analysis-evasion techniques. Validating processor specifications is a non-trivial task. Our study is a significant undertaking to enable, for the first time, the systematic validation of open-source SLEIGH language specifications, predominantly used by Ghidra. We design and implement a testing framework based on an automated oracle validation strategy by proxy. Our approach leverages the structure encoded in a specification itself to enumerate decodable instruction forms and generate targeted initial states. Then differentially test the successful decoding and emulation of those instructions by comparing emulators exercising the processor specification against hardware references.
  Applying InSPECtor across diverse, open-source specifications---x86-64, AArch64, ARM/Thumb, RISC-V, MSP430---embedding differences in specification styles, author preferences, and instruction set architecture designs, we uncovered over 38,920 discrepancies that led to 125 unique bugs with proposed fixes, identifying decoding and semantic defects as well as cross-vendor inconsistencies. We distill our findings into 8 concrete recommendations to drive future improvements. Our work underscores the importance of specification correctness and provides a practical tool to substantially improve the fidelity of SLEIGH processor specifications, strengthening the reliability of downstream security and analysis tools.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces InSPECtor, a testing framework for systematically validating open-source SLEIGH processor specifications (used by Ghidra) via differential oracle testing against hardware references, uncovering 38,920+ discrepancies and 125 unique bugs across five ISAs.
AI.motivation: Processor specifications underpin security and program-analysis tools (disassemblers, decompilers, emulators) but their correctness is rarely examined. Specification errors distort program behavior, hide vulnerabilities, and enable analysis-evasion techniques, so there is a pressing need for systematic validation of SLEIGH specifications.
AI.method: The authors design InSPECtor, an automated oracle-validation-by-proxy testing framework. It exploits the structure encoded in a specification to enumerate decodable instruction forms and generate targeted initial states, then differentially tests successful decoding and emulation by comparing specification-driven emulators against hardware references.
AI.result: Applying InSPECtor to x86-64, AArch64, ARM/Thumb, RISC-V, and MSP430 specifications revealed over 38,920 discrepancies leading to 125 unique bugs with proposed fixes, including decoding and semantic defects and cross-vendor inconsistencies. Findings are distilled into 8 concrete improvement recommendations.
AI.conclusion: Specification correctness is critical, and InSPECtor provides a practical tool to substantially improve the fidelity of SLEIGH processor specifications, strengthening the reliability of downstream security and program-analysis tools.

title: QuoteBench: How Matched Scores Can Hide Command-Path Failures
summary: LLM coding agents issue Bash commands through interfaces that may serialize, wrap, and reparse model output. Matched execution scores alone cannot distinguish command-generation errors from failures introduced after generation. QuoteBench measures this boundary with exact final-state validation on 56 one-shot tasks from 14 incident-derived families, crossing the generation contract with the execution transport around one deliberately unescaped added parser. Escaping at the interpolation point reproduces each replayed reply's raw-path outcome, so any recovery under a disclosed boundary must come from the model changing its generation. Across eight same-window configurations, replaying the same reply through the added parser lowers success by 55.4 to 73.2 percentage points; disclosure recovers 30.4 to 60.7 points for six configurations, and zero or slightly negative for the other two. Raw generation is nearly saturated at the frontier; boundary adaptation is what still separates models. GPT-5.6-sol's matched gap of -3.6 points hides -64.3 points of damage and +60.7 points of compensation. The deployment configuration reorders models: one reversal among 26 comparable pairs is unambiguous and four more sit on single-task margins. Evaluations of command-issuing agents should report the model configuration, generation contract, execution path, operating point, and final-state validator rather than treat a matched score as an intrinsic model property.

AI.tldr: QuoteBench exposes how LLM coding agents' Bash command generation interacts with the execution transport boundary. Using 56 one-shot tasks from 14 incident-derived families with a deliberately unescaped parser, it shows that replaying identical replies through the added parser reduces success by 55.4–73.2 points, while disclosure-only recovery (with no model changes) recoups 30.4–60.7 points in most configurations. Matched scores conceal large damage and compensation, and deployment configuration can reorder model rankings.
AI.motivation: Matched execution scores cannot distinguish whether failures come from command-generation errors (the model) or from the post-generation transport/serialization layer (the infrastructure). Existing evaluations conflate these two sources, treating a unified score as an intrinsic property of the model when it actually reflects an unexamined boundary between generation and execution.
AI.method: QuoteBench constructs a fixed dataset of 56 one-shot tasks drawn from 14 incident-derived families. It systematically crosses two variables: the generation contract (what the model is told about output format) and the execution transport (how output is serialized, wrapped, and reparsed). A deliberately unescaped parser is added at the interpolation point. Replay experiments send the exact same model reply through different transports to isolate boundary effects from generation effects. Validation uses exact final-state comparison, and disclosure conditions reveal the boundary to the model without any replay-side changes, so any recovery must come from the model altering its generation.
AI.result: Across eight same-window configurations, replaying the identical reply through the added parser lowers success by 55.4 to 73.2 percentage points. Disclosure recovers 30.4 to 60.7 points for six configurations and zero or slightly negative for two. Raw generation is nearly saturated at the frontier, so boundary adaptation—not raw capability—separates models. GPT-5.6-sol shows a matched gap of only -3.6 points, yet this conceals -64.3 points of damage plus +60.7 points of compensation. Reordering under the deployment configuration yields one unambiguous reversal among 26 comparable pairs and four more on single-task margins.
AI.conclusion: A matched score is not an intrinsic model property; it is the product of the model configuration, generation contract, execution path, operating point, and final-state validator. Evaluations of command-issuing agents must report all of these components separately rather than presenting a single aggregate number, since boundary effects dominate the remaining variance at the frontier and can reverse model rankings.

title: Tracing Methamphetamine abuse in under-treatment drivers: How biomechanical and oculomotor features help detect at-risk drivers?
summary: While the detrimental impacts of driving under the influence of stimulants such as methamphetamine are well-documented, the driving performance of individuals currently under-treatment has received considerably less attention. This study compared the behavior of individuals with a history of stimulant abuse (across two distinct treatment phases) with a control group of healthy drivers using a driving simulator. Oculomotor and biomechanical data were continuously collected via an eye-tracker and a Kinect sensor, respectively. These parameters were utilized to train a K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classification model designed to detect high-risk behavioral patterns in drivers undergoing methamphetamine rehabilitation. Through the evaluation of various feature combinations and neighborhood configurations, the optimized model successfully discriminated between normal drivers and those with a history of abuse with an accuracy of 90%. Detecting at-risk drivers through technologies embedded in Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) by continuously monitoring physiological and behavioral parameters, facilitates a proactive safety strategy. Issuing real-time alerts to the driver, passengers, and external monitoring networks can ultimately mitigate the risk of traffic collisions.

AI.tldr: This study uses driving-simulator data (eye-tracking and Kinect biomechanics) to train a KNN classifier that detects high-risk driving patterns in methamphetamine rehabilitation patients, achieving 90% accuracy versus healthy controls, and proposes integrating such detection into ADAS for proactive safety alerts.
AI.motivation: While driving under the active influence of stimulants (e.g., methamphetamine) is well-studied, the driving performance of individuals currently undergoing rehabilitation/treatment remains underexplored. The authors aim to fill this gap and enable early identification of high-risk drivers to prevent collisions.
AI.method: A driving simulator compared three groups: two distinct treatment phases of individuals with a stimulant-abuse history and a healthy control group. Oculomotor data (eye-tracker) and biomechanical data (Kinect sensor) were continuously collected. These parameters were used to train a K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classification model; various feature combinations and neighborhood configurations (k values) were evaluated to detect high-risk behavioral patterns.
AI.result: The optimized KNN model successfully discriminated between normal drivers and those with a history of stimulant abuse, achieving 90% classification accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Detecting at-risk drivers via technologies embedded in Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) through continuous monitoring of physiological and behavioral parameters enables a proactive safety strategy. Real-time alerts to the driver, passengers, and external monitoring networks can help mitigate the risk of traffic collisions.

title: Mimicry without understanding: the origins of decision bias in large language models
summary: Large Language models (LLMs) were found to be susceptible to a host of social, affective, and cognitive biases. We examined two mechanisms through which such biases can be generated even when human preferences (in the training data) are not biased or when they are correctly categorized as being biased. The first is faulty mimicry of preferences based on human behavior: this involves LLMs inferring human preferences even when behaviors are logically unrelated to preferences. The second is mimicry of explicitly biased human behaviors. In four studies focusing on economic biases, we find that ChatGPT-4o and Qwen exhibited social proof biases even when prompted with reports of human behaviors that were clearly non-indicative of individuals' actual preferences. LLMs also displayed loss aversion when it was explicitly described as a bias. Indeed, when prompted with detailed scientific reports, the extent of the bias (i.e., loss aversion) in the scientific report predicted LLMs' own subsequent bias. Scientific papers of biases can thus become self-fulfilling prophecies, at least when it comes to LLMs' responses. The current study goes beyond fleshing out LLM biases and sheds light on the underlying component processes.

AI.tldr: LLMs exhibit social, affective, and cognitive biases even when training data or behavioral cues are uninformative or explicitly labeled as biased. Two mechanisms are identified: faulty mimicry of preferences from logically unrelated behaviors, and direct mimicry of explicitly biased behaviors. Models displayed social proof and loss aversion biases whose magnitude tracked the bias levels described in scientific reports, making such reports self-fulfilling prophecies.
AI.motivation: To understand how LLMs generate biases even when human preferences in training data are not biased or are correctly categorized as biased, moving beyond merely cataloging biases to examining the underlying component processes.
AI.method: Four studies focused on economic biases using ChatGPT-4o and Qwen. The authors tested two mechanisms: (1) faulty mimicry of human behavior, where LLMs infer preferences from behaviors logically unrelated to preferences; and (2) mimicry of explicitly biased human behaviors, such as loss aversion described as a bias. They also varied the extent of bias in detailed scientific reports to predict the LLMs' subsequent bias.
AI.result: ChatGPT-4o and Qwen exhibited social proof bias even when prompted with human behaviors clearly non-indicative of actual preferences. They also displayed loss aversion when it was explicitly labeled as a bias. The degree of bias described in scientific reports predicted the magnitude of the LLMs' subsequent bias, demonstrating that scientific papers about biases can become self-fulfilling prophecies for LLM responses.
AI.conclusion: LLM biases can arise from faulty mimicry of human behavior and from mimicking explicitly labeled biases. This goes beyond documenting biases to revealing the component processes by which they are generated, with implications for interpreting and mitigating bias in language models.

title: Predicting When Random Low-Dimensional Reparameterizations Train Neural Networks
summary: Neural networks can often be trained or fine-tuned through random low-dimensional reparameterization, where a small latent vector is mapped into a full parameter update by a frozen random map. This raises a practical question: how large must the latent search space be to reach a low-loss region? We first express the known accessibility transition in an equivalent conic form, centered for compact convex targets at the statistical dimension of the polar cone. Our main theoretical contribution is an orientation-resolved quadratic master formula that predicts the random-slice residual from both the curvature spectrum and the reference-to-solution displacement profile. It yields a self-consistent isotropic-orientation predictor and, in a conservative radius-only specialization, recovers the earlier Gaussian-width quadratic bound. Building on this analysis, we introduce Random Mapping Networks (RaMaN), which instantiate the predicted latent dimension using structured Hadamard or seed-regenerated Gaussian maps. These constructions avoid the O(dP) storage of dense random maps and reduce optimizer-state memory from O(P) to O(d). We also develop matrix-free curvature approximations and sweep-free dimension selection. Across controlled quadratic and neural-curvature experiments, the orientation-resolved predictor closely tracks measured transition locations and outperforms orientation-agnostic approximations when displacement direction matters. End-to-end experiments further show sharp, protocol-dependent training transitions across image and language models.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how large a low-dimensional latent space must be for random reparameterization of neural network training to reach a low-loss region. It derives a conic-form accessibility transition and an orientation-resolved quadratic master formula predicting the required latent dimension, then introduces Random Mapping Networks (RaMaN) using structured Hadamard or seed-regenerated Gaussian maps for memory-efficient training.
AI.motivation: Neural networks can be trained or fine-tuned via random low-dimensional reparameterization, but it is practically important to know the minimal latent dimension needed to reach a low-loss region. Existing accessibility-transition analyses are largely orientation-agnostic and ignore how the displacement direction relative to curvature spectrum affects the required subspace size; memory costs of dense random maps (O(dP) storage and O(P) optimizer state) are also prohibitive.
AI.method: First, the known accessibility transition is reformulated in an equivalent conic form, centered for compact convex targets at the statistical dimension of the polar cone. The main contribution is an orientation-resolved quadratic master formula predicting the random-slice residual from the curvature spectrum and the reference-to-solution displacement profile. This yields a self-consistent isotropic-orientation predictor and, in a conservative radius-only specialization, recovers the earlier Gaussian-width quadratic bound. The authors then build Random Mapping Networks (RaMaN) that instantiate the predicted latent dimension using structured Hadamard or seed-regenerated Gaussian maps, plus matrix-free curvature approximations and sweep-free dimension selection.
AI.result: Across controlled quadratic and neural-curvature experiments, the orientation-resolved predictor closely tracks measured transition locations and outperforms orientation-agnostic approximations when displacement direction matters. The structured maps avoid O(dP) storage and reduce optimizer-state memory from O(P) to O(d). End-to-end experiments show sharp, protocol-dependent training transitions across image and language models.
AI.conclusion: Random low-dimensional reparameterization has a predictable, orientation-dependent accessibility transition governed by the curvature spectrum and displacement profile. The proposed RaMaN framework uses this prediction to achieve memory-efficient training with structured maps, accurately matching transition locations and enabling protocol-dependent training behavior in image and language models.

title: Reasoning Jury: Multi-Model Consensus for Evaluating Reasoning Traces
summary: Improving reasoning LLMs requires the ability to judge the quality of long reasoning traces for effective reasoning data curation, strong training signals during reinforcement learning, and an in-depth understanding of reasoning behaviors during model performance evaluation. Additionally, surfacing reasoning mistakes that the model makes would enable improving the model's performance at runtime through providing feedback. Due to the difficulty of this complex task on long reasoning traces, single-model judges (even frontier models) do not do well at identifying reasoning defects. Additionally, leveraging frontier models during online training of reasoning LLMs is generally prohibited due to guardrails in terms of use. In this work, we introduce Reasoning Jury, a system that replaces the single judge with a jury of LLMs and a moderated consensus mechanism, to improve the fidelity of judgments for identifying reasoning defects. In reasoning jury, defects of a reasoning trace and their severity are surfaced through a deliberation where a moderator conducts a discussion amongst the jury where the jurors critique each other's judgments and get to modify their initial votes. The moderator derives a consensus through deliberation amongst jurors or consolidation of judgements. We show that Reasoning Jury with a jury of open-weight models (e.g., gpt-oss-120b) is able to significantly outperform frontier models (opus-4.6, sonnet-4.6, and gemini-3.1-pro) at correctly identifying reasoning defects. Besides accuracy performance improvements, the aggregated cost of the jury (initial verdicts, deliberations, consolidation, etc.) is a fraction (8 to 15%) of the cost of running frontier models in LLM-as-a-judge setup. We also show how these judgements can be leveraged to understand failure modes of reasoning LLMs on benchmarks, which allows much deeper understanding of a model's performance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "Reasoning Jury," a system that replaces single LLM judges with a jury of open-weight models moderated through a deliberation-and-consensus mechanism to reliably identify defects in long reasoning traces, outperforming frontier models at a fraction of the cost.
AI.motivation: Improving reasoning LLMs requires judging the quality of long reasoning traces for data curation, RL training signals, and performance evaluation, as well as surfacing reasoning mistakes for runtime feedback. However, single-model judges (even frontier models) perform poorly on this complex task, and using frontier models during online training is typically prohibited by terms-of-use guardrails.
AI.method: Reasoning Jury uses a jury of LLMs plus a moderated consensus mechanism. A moderator conducts a deliberation among jurors, who critique each other's judgments and may revise their initial votes; the moderator then derives consensus through deliberation or consolidation of judgments, surfacing defects and their severity in a reasoning trace.
AI.result: Reasoning Jury built from open-weight models (e.g., gpt-oss-120b) significantly outperforms frontier models (opus-4.6, sonnet-4.6, gemini-3.1-pro) at correctly identifying reasoning defects. Its aggregated cost (initial verdicts, deliberations, consolidation) is only 8–15% of the cost of running frontier models in an LLM-as-a-judge setup. The judgments also reveal failure modes of reasoning LLMs on benchmarks, enabling deeper performance understanding.
AI.conclusion: A deliberative jury of open-weight LLMs with moderated consensus provides higher-fidelity defect identification in long reasoning traces than single frontier-model judges, at substantially lower cost, while enabling richer analysis of reasoning failure modes.

title: Operationalizing Cyber Threat Intelligence with GraphRAG
summary: When a security researcher publishes a report on a cyberattack, detection engineers are supposed to turn it into working detection rules. In practice, most automated attempts at this only extract the simplest clues from the report --- bad IP addresses, domain names, and file hashes --- and turn them into block lists. This is a weak strategy, because attackers can change these simple clues within hours or days, so the resulting detections stop working almost as soon as they are deployed. Security teams describe this idea with the Pyramid of Pain. This project asks whether feeding a report into a knowledge-graph retrieval system, Microsoft GraphRAG, rather than a standard vector-similarity retrieval system (Naive RAG), produces detection plans that rely more on these durable, top-of-pyramid clues. Both systems are given the same report, the same generation instructions, and the same language model to write the final plan; only the retrieval step differs. In a detailed case study of one APT28 report, the GraphRAG plan kept firing at 100\% of its detections after every IP address, domain, and file hash in the report was rotated, while the Naive RAG plan kept firing at only 29\%. Repeating the comparison across nine real CTI reports from four vendors confirms the same pattern: GraphRAG plans consistently reach higher, harder-to-evade levels of the pyramid, even when the two systems end up close on total score. The results support treating knowledge-graph-aware retrieval as the architecturally correct foundation for automatically generating SOC-deployable hunting plans, while showing that the wording of the generation prompt matters almost as much as the retrieval back-end itself.

AI.tldr: The paper compares knowledge-graph-based retrieval (Microsoft GraphRAG) against naive vector-similarity retrieval for automatically turning cyber threat intelligence reports into detection rules, finding GraphRAG produces more durable, top-of-pyramid detections that survive indicator rotation.
AI.motivation: Existing automated approaches to converting security reports into detections extract only volatile low-level indicators (IPs, domains, hashes), which attackers can change within hours or days, causing detections to fail quickly. The authors aim to determine whether a knowledge-graph retrieval system can produce detection plans built on durable, harder-to-evade behavioral indicators higher on the Pyramid of Pain.
AI.method: The study feeds threat reports into two retrieval back-ends—Microsoft GraphRAG (knowledge-graph-aware) and Naive RAG (standard vector similarity)—while holding constant the report, generation instructions, and language model used to write the final detection plan, so only the retrieval step differs. It performs a detailed case study on one APT28 report, rotating every IP, domain, and file hash and measuring how many detections still fire, then repeats the comparison across nine real CTI reports from four vendors.
AI.result: In the APT28 case study, the GraphRAG plan kept 100% of its detections firing after all indicators were rotated, versus only 29% for the Naive RAG plan. Across the nine-report comparison from four vendors, GraphRAG plans consistently reached higher, harder-to-evade levels of the Pyramid of Pain, even when total scores were similar. Prompt wording also significantly influenced results.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge-graph-aware retrieval is the architecturally correct foundation for automatically generating SOC-deployable hunting plans, as it yields more durable, top-of-pyramid detections. However, the study also emphasizes that prompt wording matters nearly as much as the retrieval back-end itself.

title: CogChat: Knowledge Graph-Augmented Conversational AI with Heterogeneous Graph Transformer for Cognitive Grounding in Design Generation
summary: LLM-based chat systems have become valuable tools for design practice, enabling rapid ideation and flexible task support. Yet these systems process designer utterances as generic sequences, maintaining context through recency rather than through any model of how the speaker organizes knowledge. In design conversation, this gap compounds as relational context decays between turns, identical words go unresolved across designers, and the conversation loops or restarts rather than deepens. We present CogChat, a real-time chat framework that grounds conversational AI in a personal heterogeneous knowledge graph constructed from each designer's input. The system extracts typed entities and relations into a heterogeneous graph, then applies a HGT (Heterogeneous Graph Transformer) to select structurally relevant nodes for response generation and to generate both intentional and exploratory probing questions. Technical evaluation shows that HGT-based entity selection outperforms both ungrounded LLM interaction and naive KG augmentation, which introduces noise that degrades response quality. A within-subjects study with nine professional designers indicates that grounding conversation in a relationally structured, designer-specific semantic context improves context retention, personalized intent interpretation, and conversational depth while reducing cognitive load. These findings suggest that structuring a designer's expressed concepts and relations as a dynamic knowledge graph can preserve relational context that fades across turns, pointing toward a graph-grounded approach to long-term context management in LLM-based interaction.

AI.tldr: CogChat grounds LLM chat in each designer's personal heterogeneous knowledge graph, using a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer to select relevant context and generate probing questions, improving context retention, intent interpretation, and conversational depth while reducing cognitive load.
AI.motivation: LLM-based chat systems treat designer utterances as generic sequences and maintain context by recency, lacking any model of how the speaker organizes knowledge. This causes relational context to decay between turns, identical words to go unresolved across designers, and conversations to loop or restart instead of deepening.
AI.method: CogChat extracts typed entities and relations from each designer's input into a personal heterogeneous knowledge graph, then applies a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer (HGT) to select structurally relevant nodes for response generation and to produce both intentional and exploratory probing questions. A within-subjects study with nine professional designers was conducted, alongside technical evaluation against ungrounded LLM interaction and naive KG augmentation.
AI.result: HGT-based entity selection outperformed both ungrounded LLM interaction and naive KG augmentation (which introduces noise that degrades response quality). The nine-designer user study showed improved context retention, personalized intent interpretation, and conversational depth, with reduced cognitive load.
AI.conclusion: Structuring a designer's expressed concepts and relations as a dynamic knowledge graph preserves relational context that fades across turns, supporting a graph-grounded approach to long-term context management in LLM-based interaction.

title: Class-Structure Preservation Beats Diversity: A Comprehensive Benchmark of Text Augmentation Methods for Imbalanced Text Classification
summary: With the rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs), generative data augmentation has attracted considerable attention for imbalanced text classification in natural language processing. However, no empirical benchmark to date has compared LLM-based augmentation against the embedding-space SMOTE-style retrieval (EmbSMOTE), a strong classical reference for imbalanced classification. In this study, a controlled benchmark of 11 augmentation methods, spanning classical perturbation, embedding-space retrieval, and LLM-based generation, is newly constructed on seven public text classification datasets covering class counts $K=2$-$28$ and imbalance ratios of 1.1 to over 500, evaluated with five random seeds per cell using macro F1, Welch's $t$-tests, five distributional metrics, and an LLM-family sensitivity analysis based on Qwen3-8B. The experimental results reveal that all LLM-based methods are statistically equivalent or inferior to EmbSMOTE, with the performance gap widening monotonically as imbalance increases and reaching $Δ\text{F1}_\text{macro}\!\approx\!0.063$ on GoEmotions-28. Furthermore, it is observed that surface-level uniqueness has negligible correlation with downstream performance, whereas LLM-specific artifacts, such as text elongation and label-distribution uniformization, are negatively associated with classification accuracy. Compared with six LLM-based and four classical augmentation baselines, these results demonstrate that the effective variable is not surface-level diversity but class-conditional structural fidelity, namely the degree to which augmented samples preserve the class-conditioned geometry of the training distribution. Accordingly, retrieval-based oversampling should be adopted as the default for imbalanced multi-class classification, and a higher empirical bar should be required before LLM-based augmentation is deployed in practice.

AI.tldr: A controlled benchmark of 11 augmentation methods across 7 text classification datasets finds that all LLM-based augmentation methods perform no better than embedding-space SMOTE (EmbSMOTE), with the gap widening as class imbalance increases. The key driver of performance is class-conditional structural fidelity, not surface-level diversity.
AI.motivation: LLM-based generative data augmentation is widely adopted for imbalanced text classification, but no empirical benchmark has compared it against EmbSMOTE, a strong classical reference method. The authors aim to fill this gap and identify what actually drives downstream performance.
AI.method: A controlled benchmark of 11 augmentation methods (classical perturbation, embedding-space retrieval, and LLM-based generation) on 7 public text classification datasets with class counts K=2-28 and imbalance ratios from 1.1 to over 500. Evaluation uses 5 random seeds per cell with macro F1, Welch's t-tests, five distributional metrics, and an LLM-family sensitivity analysis (Qwen3-8B).
AI.result: All LLM-based methods are statistically equivalent or inferior to EmbSMOTE, with the gap widening monotonically as imbalance increases, reaching ΔF1_macro ≈ 0.063 on GoEmotions-28. Surface-level uniqueness has negligible correlation with performance, while LLM-specific artifacts (text elongation, label-distribution uniformization) correlate negatively with accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The effective variable is not surface-level diversity but class-conditional structural fidelity—how well augmented samples preserve the class-conditioned geometry of the training distribution. Retrieval-based oversampling (EmbSMOTE) should be the default for imbalanced multi-class classification, and a higher empirical bar should be required before deploying LLM-based augmentation.

title: The Boolean Power of ReLU
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, comes with AI declaration
summary: We prove that, on finite simple undirected graphs equipped with a single Boolean node feature, the Boolean queries expressible in $Σ$-MPLang, for any collection $Σ$ of eventually constant activation functions and with arbitrary real coefficients, form a strict subclass of the Boolean queries expressible in ReLU-MPLang. We thereby settle a recently posed open problem: whether ReLU-MPLang is more powerful than trReLU-MPLang when it comes to Boolean queries. In particular, this implies that ReLU-GNNs are strictly more expressive than {TrReLU,id}-GNNs with respect to Boolean queries on Boolean-featured graphs.

AI.tldr: The paper proves a strict expressiveness separation: on finite simple undirected graphs with a single Boolean node feature, Boolean queries expressible in Σ-MPLang (for any collection Σ of eventually constant activation functions, with arbitrary real coefficients) form a strict subclass of those expressible in ReLU-MPLang. This settles an open problem by showing ReLU-MPLang is more powerful than trReLU-MPLang for Boolean queries.
AI.motivation: To settle a recently posed open problem concerning the relative power of graph neural network (GNN) languages: specifically, whether ReLU-MPLang is strictly more powerful than trReLU-MPLang when restricted to Boolean queries. Understanding this separation clarifies the expressiveness advantage of ReLU activations over truncated ReLU (trReLU) and identity activations in message-passing GNNs.
AI.method: The authors work within the MPLang framework (message-passing language for GNNs) over finite simple undirected graphs with a single Boolean node feature. They show that every collection Σ of eventually constant activation functions yields a Boolean query class strictly contained in the Boolean queries of ReLU-MPLang, using arbitrary real coefficients. The proof establishes that any Σ-MPLang Boolean query can be separated from some ReLU-MPLang Boolean query, demonstrating a strict containment hierarchy and thereby contrasting ReLU against trReLU and identity activations.
AI.result: The Boolean queries of Σ-MPLang form a strict subclass of the Boolean queries of ReLU-MPLang for any collection Σ of eventually constant activation functions. Consequently, ReLU-MPLang is strictly more powerful than trReLU-MPLang for Boolean queries, and ReLU-GNNs are strictly more expressive than {trReLU, id}-GNNs on Boolean-featured graphs.
AI.conclusion: ReLU-based message-passing GNNs possess strictly greater expressiveness than GNNs using eventually constant activations such as truncated ReLU or identity, at least for Boolean queries on Boolean-featured graphs. This conclusively resolves the open problem and highlights a fundamental expressiveness gap favoring the ReLU activation function.

title: Auditable agentic AI for evidence-grounded thyroid ultrasound diagnosis and reporting
summary: Thyroid ultrasound diagnosis requires coordinated lesion localization, measurement, risk stratification and reporting, yet most AI systems address these tasks in isolation and provide limited support for clinical review. We present ThyroidXAgent, a clinician-interactive agentic AI system that coordinates specialized diagnostic tools and stores their outputs as an auditable case-level evidence record. The system was developed using OpenThyroidDB, a multicentre, multitask resource integrating approximately 0.3 million ultrasound images and 24,000 paired reports, and was evaluated on 28,458 non-overlapping test cases, including 8,721 cases from 35 centres in the private NHC-MISD-TUS cohort. Across heterogeneous datasets, ThyroidXAgent achieved a mean Dice score of 87.21 percent for nodule segmentation and a mean AUROC of 0.9466 for benign-malignant classification. The same workflow supported lymph-node metastasis prediction and follicular versus papillary thyroid carcinoma classification, with AUROCs of 0.864 and 0.805, respectively. For report generation, evidence-grounded assembly outperformed multimodal language-model baselines across three cohorts. ThyClinScore, a lesion-level clinical semantic metric introduced here, showed the strongest correlation with a location-aware language-model judge. ThyroidXAgent improved physician classification accuracy, increased report diagnostic consistency from 70.3 percent to 86.2 percent, and reduced segmentation and reporting time by 35.9 percent and 27.4 percent, respectively. These findings support auditable, clinician-correctable agentic AI for thyroid ultrasound diagnosis and reporting.

AI.tldr: ThyroidXAgent is a clinician-interactive agentic AI system that integrates specialized diagnostic tools for thyroid ultrasound into a unified, auditable workflow. Trained/evaluated using OpenThyroidDB (~0.3M images, 24K reports) and tested on 28,458 cases, it achieved strong segmentation (Dice 87.21%) and benign-malignant classification (AUROC 0.9466), improved report generation, raised physician diagnostic consistency from 70.3% to 86.2%, and cut segmentation/reporting time by 35.9%/27.4%.
AI.motivation: Thyroid ultrasound diagnosis requires coordinated lesion localization, measurement, risk stratification, and reporting, but most AI systems handle these tasks in isolation and offer limited support for clinical review. The authors aim to build a unified, clinician-interactive system with audible, correctable evidence to support the full diagnostic workflow.
AI.method: They developed ThyroidXAgent, an agentic AI system that coordinates specialized diagnostic tools and stores outputs as an auditable case-level evidence record. Development used OpenThyroidDB, a multicentre multitask dataset (~0.3M ultrasound images, 24,000 paired reports). Evaluation covered 28,458 non-overlapping test cases including 8,721 cases from 35 centres in the private NHC-MISD-TUS cohort. The workflow supported nodule segmentation, benign-malignant classification, lymph-node metastasis prediction, follicular vs papillary classification, and evidence-grounded report generation. They introduced ThyClinScore, a lesion-level clinical semantic metric correlated with a location-aware language-model judge, and conducted physician-in-the-loop studies.
AI.result: Across heterogeneous datasets: mean Dice 87.21% for nodule segmentation; mean AUROC 0.9466 for benign-malignant classification; AUROC 0.864 for lymph-node metastasis prediction; AUROC 0.805 for follicular vs papillary carcinoma classification. Evidence-grounded report assembly outperformed multimodal language-model baselines across three cohorts. ThyClinScore showed strongest correlation with a location-aware language-model judge. With thyroidXAgent, physician classification accuracy improved; report diagnostic consistency rose from 70.3% to 86.2%; segmentation time reduced 35.9%; reporting time reduced 27.4%.
AI.conclusion: The results support auditable, clinician-correctable agentic AI for thyroid ultrasound diagnosis and reporting, demonstrating benefits in accuracy, consistency, and workflow efficiency.

title: A Commitment-Based Hybrid Post-Quantum Cryptographic Model for Multi-File Cloud Storage
summary: Cloud storage clients increasingly require authentication that remains secure against future quantum-capable adversaries, motivating hybrid constructions that combine classical primitives with standardized post-quantum alternatives. Extended naively to multi-file upload, such constructions incur a per-file lattice signing cost that dominates authentication time and becomes prohibitive at realistic batch sizes. This paper presents a commitment-based hybrid post-quantum model that addresses this bottleneck. It comprises AES-256-GCM bulk encryption, a hybrid X25519 with ML-KEM-768 key encapsulation mechanism, and a hybrid Ed25519 with ML-DSA-65 dual signature, computed over a SHA3-256 batch commitment. The commitment binds all ciphertexts in a batch to a single fixed-size digest that is signed once, reducing the number of post-quantum signature invocations per batch from n to one, independent of batch size; the remaining encryption and hashing is bounded by fast symmetric throughput. On a commodity client platform, averaged over 20 repetitions, this holds signing-phase time near-constant as the batch grows while the per-file baseline scales linearly. At n = 1000, the model reduces signing-phase time by factors of 629, 606, and 725 for 100 KB, 1 MB, and 10 MB files respectively, against a per-file dual-signing baseline sharing every other primitive.

AI.tldr: A commitment-based hybrid post-quantum scheme reduces per-batch post-quantum signature operations from n to one by binding all ciphertexts to a single SHA3-256 digest, drastically cutting multi-file upload signing time.
AI.motivation: Cloud storage clients need authentication secure against future quantum adversaries, but naively extending hybrid post-quantum constructions to multi-file upload incurs a per-file lattice signing cost that dominates and becomes prohibitive at realistic batch sizes.
AI.method: The model combines AES-256-GCM bulk encryption, a hybrid X25519 with ML-KEM-768 key encapsulation mechanism, and a hybrid Ed25519 with ML-DSA-65 dual signature computed over a SHA3-256 batch commitment that binds all ciphertexts to one fixed-size digest signed once, reducing post-quantum signature invocations per batch from n to one.
AI.result: On a commodity client over 20 repetitions, signing-phase time stays near-constant as batch size grows while the per-file baseline scales linearly; at n=1000 it reduces signing time by factors of 629, 606, and 725 for 100 KB, 1 MB, and 10 MB files respectively versus a per-file dual-signing baseline.
AI.conclusion: Batching signatures over a single commitment makes hybrid post-quantum authentication scalable for multi-file upload, keeping signing-phase cost independent of batch size while preserving the security of classical and post-quantum primitives.

title: Print&Fold: Printing and Folding Shape-accurate 3D Models
summary: This paper introduces Print&Fold, a tool to allow FDM 3D printing of complex models with less time and material while preserving shape accuracy. Key to this work is a folding algorithm that planarizes foldable faces internal to the 3D model. While folding techniques typically discretize a target model's surface, thereby fabricating low fidelity counterparts, our method preserves the surface features in the physical print. Our design tool allows users to unfold 3D models to be FDM-printed flat before manually folding these into their target shapes. We showcase a variety of applications and evaluate the material and time savings across a range of 3D models.

AI.tldr: Print&Fold enables FDM 3D printing of complex models by planarizing and folding, reducing print time and material while preserving surface accuracy.
AI.motivation: Traditional FDM 3D printing of complex models is time- and material-intensive. Existing folding techniques sacrifice surface fidelity by discretizing the model. The authors aim to reduce time and material while preserving shape accuracy and surface features in the physical print.
AI.method: The paper introduces a folding algorithm that planarizes foldable faces internal to a 3D model. A design tool lets users unfold 3D models so they can be FDM-printed flat, then manually folded into the target shape, preserving surface features rather than discretizing them.
AI.result: The tool is demonstrated across a variety of applications and evaluated on a range of 3D models, quantifying material and time savings compared to standard FDM printing.
AI.conclusion: Print&Fold successfully reduces material usage and fabrication time for FDM printing of complex models while maintaining shape accuracy, offering a practical alternative to low-fidelity folded discretizations.

title: The "Knowledge-Behavior Gap" in Cultural Taboo Safety of Large Language Models
summary: Cultural taboo safety is essential for deploying large language models (LLMs), as culturally insensitive outputs may cause offense or even social harm. However, existing cultural benchmarks primarily assess cultural knowledge or values biases, while overlooking whether LLMs can recognize and respect cultural taboos, especially when taboos are implicitly hidden in seemingly harmless questions. Besides, cultural taboos are implicit, and context-dependent, thus poss unique challenges for reliable evaluation. To address these gaps, we introduce \textbf{CulShield}, the first public benchmark dedicated to evaluating and improving the cultural taboo safety of LLMs. CulShield spans 77 countries and territories, and includes over 2,020 taboos. It evaluates models along both explicit knowledge and implicit behaviors. Experiments on several advanced LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-2.5-pro) reveal a clear ``knowledge-behavior gap'': models often fail to apply known taboos during interaction. We further show that variations in linguistic context can significantly affect LLMs' cultural taboo safety. Code and data is accessible here: https://github.com/hedyHe/CulShield.

AI.tldr: CulShield is the first public benchmark for evaluating and improving LLM cultural taboo safety, covering 77 countries/territories and 2,020+ taboos. It assesses both explicit knowledge and implicit behavior, revealing a "knowledge-behavior gap" and showing that linguistic context significantly affects taboo safety.
AI.motivation: Existing cultural benchmarks focus on cultural knowledge or value biases but overlook whether LLMs can recognize and respect cultural taboos, especially those implicitly hidden in seemingly harmless questions. Cultural taboos are implicit and context-dependent, posing unique challenges for reliable evaluation, so a dedicated benchmark is needed.
AI.method: The authors introduce CulShield, a public benchmark spanning 77 countries/territories with over 2,020 taboos. It evaluates models along two dimensions: explicit knowledge (whether models know the taboos) and implicit behaviors (whether models avoid violating taboos during interaction). Experiments are conducted on advanced LLMs such as GPT-4o-mini and Gemini-2.5-pro, including analysis of how linguistic context variations affect taboo safety.
AI.result: Experiments reveal a clear "knowledge-behavior gap": models often fail to apply taboos they already know during actual interaction. The study also shows that variations in linguistic context can significantly affect LLMs' cultural taboo safety.
AI.conclusion: Cultural taboo safety is essential for responsible LLM deployment, and CulShield provides the first public resource to evaluate and improve it. The identified knowledge-behavior gap and context sensitivity highlight key directions for future work. Code and data are publicly available.

title: Structure-preserving uncertainty quantification for GENERIC dynamics
summary: Structure-preserving machine learning embeds physical structure directly into model architectures, yet uncertainty quantification (UQ) for such hard-constrained models remains limited because standard UQ methods may violate the encoded admissibility conditions, require architectural modifications, or impose substantial computational costs. In this work, we propose Structure-Preserving Epistemic Neural Networks (S-PENNs), a general framework for UQ in scientific machine learning models with hard architectural constraints, and instantiate it for GENERIC (General Equation for Non-Equilibrium Reversible-Irreversible Coupling) dynamics. S-PENNs preserve the structural constraints of a pretrained model by attaching lightweight epinets to its constrained components, ensuring that every sampled realization remains physically admissible by construction. When applied to GENERIC dynamics, such a proposed framework yields thermodynamically consistent rollouts that preserve the first and second laws. Furthermore, we combine S-PENNs with split conformal prediction as a post-hoc calibration method to produce prediction intervals with finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees. We validate S-PENNs on three numerical examples: a harmonic oscillator coupled to a heat bath and an idealized chemical motor, both governed by ODEs, and a one-dimensional viscoplastic model governed by PDEs. Across all three examples, S-PENNs produce thermodynamically consistent stochastic realizations and well-calibrated prediction intervals while reducing the computational cost by about one to three orders of magnitude compared to deep ensembles. Although the present study focuses on GENERIC dynamics, S-PENNs can be extended more broadly to scientific machine learning models in computational mechanics with either hard or soft constraints.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Structure-Preserving Epistemic Neural Networks (S-PENNs), a framework for uncertainty quantification in scientific ML models with hard architectural constraints, instantiated for GENERIC dynamics. S-PENNs attach lightweight epinets to constrained components of a pretrained model, guaranteeing physically admissible sampled realizations (thermodynamically consistent, preserving first/second laws) and, combined with split conformal prediction, deliver finite-sample marginal coverage prediction intervals at 1–3 orders of magnitude lower computational cost than deep ensembles.
AI.motivation: Uncertainty quantification for structure-preserving (hard-constrained) ML models is limited because standard UQ methods can violate encoded admissibility conditions, require architectural modifications, or incur substantial computational costs.
AI.method: Propose S-PENNs, a general UQ framework that preserves structural constraints by attaching lightweight epinets to the constrained components of a pretrained model so every sampled realization remains physically admissible by construction. The framework is instantiated for GENERIC dynamics and combined with split conformal prediction as a post-hoc calibration yielding finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees.
AI.result: On three numerical examples (a harmonic oscillator coupled to a heat bath and an idealized chemical motor, both ODEs; and a 1D viscoplastic model governed by PDEs), S-PENNs produce thermodynamically consistent stochastic realizations and well-calibrated prediction intervals while reducing computational cost by roughly one to three orders of magnitude versus deep ensembles.
AI.conclusion: S-PENNs provide effective, inexpensive UQ for structure-preserving scientific ML while maintaining hard constraints; although focused on GENERIC dynamics, the framework generalizes to broader scientific ML models in computational mechanics with hard or soft constraints.

title: DiG-bench: Discovery in Games
summary: Discovery---formulating novel generalizations---is a central part of the scientific process. Despite its importance, there is a gap in the current AI benchmark landscape, with few benchmarks directly probing the capacity for discovering new knowledge with experimentation in controlled environments where the objective is unknown. To address this gap, we release a new benchmark: DiG-bench (Discovery in Games). DiG-bench consists of a set of 70 independent games. Each game is encoded as a short string and has unique transformation rules that must be discovered through interaction and experimentation. The levels of the game present a series of challenges to test whether the rules have been discovered, where the win conditions for each level are also unknown. We provide games at seven tiers of difficulty for AI agents. The lowest tier is routinely solvable by multiple models, while the highest tier challenges the best models in agentic harnesses. All 70 games were solved by at least one human on first attempt. A subset of 21 games is released publicly, and the remainder is held private for secure evaluation.

AI.tldr: DiG-bench is a new benchmark of 70 discovery games requiring agents to learn unknown rules through experimentation, spanning seven difficulty tiers, with 21 public and 49 held-out private games.
AI.motivation: Scientific discovery—formulating novel generalizations—is central to science, yet current AI benchmarks rarely probe the capacity to discover new knowledge through experimentation in controlled environments where the objective is unknown. The authors identify this as a gap and aim to fill it by providing a benchmark that directly tests rule discovery and experimentation.
AI.method: DiG-bench consists of 70 independent games, each encoded as a short string with unique transformation rules that must be discovered via interaction and experimentation. Each game presents levels that test whether rules have been discovered, with win conditions also unknown. Games are organized into seven difficulty tiers. 21 games are released publicly; 49 are held private for secure evaluation.
AI.result: Across difficulty tiers, the lowest tier is routinely solvable by multiple models, while the highest tier challenges the best agentic models. All 70 games were solved by at least one human on first attempt, validating feasibility and approximate human-level difficulty.
AI.conclusion: DiG-bench addresses the lack of benchmarks for discovery-through-experimentation in AI, offering a scalable, difficulty-tiered suite of games with public and held-out portions to securely measure progress in rule discovery and scientific generalization.

title: More Than 63% of IEEE VIS Research Liable to be Retracted?! Ethics Approval Statements Protect Participants (and Researchers!)
summary: We analyzed the ethics reporting in 255 IEEE VIS papers from 2024 and 2025, as published in TVCG. This analysis arose from our experience as readers and reviewers of IEEE VIS papers that such reporting is frequently incomplete or missing, as well as from investigations in which we ourselves had to answer challenges regarding ethics approval in our own work. Visualization research naturally often involves human participants, yet ethics approval and informed-consent procedures are not always explicitly reported. In our corpus, 189 papers (74.1%) reported on work involving human participants. Only 6 of them (3.2%) reported to have obtained ethics approval, an approval identifier, and having received informed consent from the participants, while 26 (13.8%) reported at least ethics approval and informed consent. These omissions do not imply that the empirical work was unethical or lacked approval. They rather show that current reporting practices make ethical approval difficult to assess. Beyond our alarming - yet true - paper title, we wish to raise awareness on how authors themselves may eventually be at risk for not properly reporting ethics. We argue that VIS should adopt clearer and more standardized ethics-reporting practices to protect participants, authors, reviewers, and editors.

AI.tldr: An analysis of 255 IEEE VIS papers (2024–2025, published in TVCG) finds that ethics reporting is frequently incomplete or missing: 74.1% involved human participants, yet only 3.2% reported full ethics approval plus approval IDs and informed consent, and only 13.8% reported at least approval and consent. The authors argue that visualization research needs clearer, standardized ethics-reporting practices.
AI.motivation: The study was motivated by the authors' own experiences as readers and reviewers of IEEE VIS papers that ethics reporting is often incomplete or absent, and by having to defend ethics approval in their own work. Because visualization research commonly involves human participants, the lack of explicit reporting of ethics approval and informed-consent procedures raises concerns about accountability and protection of all parties.
AI.method: The authors conducted a corpus analysis of 255 IEEE VIS papers from 2024 and 2025 published in TVCG, coding each paper for whether it involved human participants and whether it reported ethics approval, an approval identifier, and informed consent from participants. They quantified the frequency of each reporting element across the corpus.
AI.result: Of the 255 papers, 189 (74.1%) involved human participants. Only 6 of those (3.2%) reported ethics approval, an approval identifier, and informed consent, while 26 (13.8%) reported at least ethics approval and informed consent. The authors note these omissions do not prove the empirical work was unethical or unapproved, but show that current reporting makes ethical compliance difficult to assess.
AI.conclusion: The VIS community should adopt clearer and more standardized ethics-reporting practices to protect participants, authors, reviewers, and editors. Poor reporting places authors themselves at risk, and improved standards would make ethics compliance more assessable and raise overall awareness.

title: Are Large Language Models Reliable Reviewers? A Benchmark for Error Detection in Financial Documents
summary: Ensuring the accuracy of financial documents is critical for economic analysis, regulatory compliance, and corporate decision-making. Several studies have shown that Large Language Models (LLMs) perform well in many financial tasks, such as stock price movements and financial analytics. However, a critical task remains unexplored: the ability of LLMs to identify errors in financial documents. In this paper, we introduce \textbf{FinED-Bench}, the first publicly \textbf{Bench}mark for \textbf{Fin}ancial \textbf{E}rror \textbf{D}etection across three levels of cognitive complexity. FinED-Bench covers nine real-world financial scenarios, and includes over 900 documents reported in 2025 that are unseen by existing language models. We detail the benchmark construction process and evaluate several advanced LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o, Qwen3-14B) on this tasks, which requires both financial domain knowledge and reasoning capabilities. Experimental results show that current LLMs still struggle with this task, especially in high-complexity cases. Besides, supervised fine-tuning can significantly improve the performance of weaker LLMs on this task. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/hedyHe/FinED-Bench.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FinED-Bench, the first public benchmark for financial error detection spanning three levels of cognitive complexity, with over 900 2025-era documents across nine real-world scenarios. Evaluation of advanced LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o, Qwen3-14B) shows they struggle, especially on high-complexity cases, while supervised fine-tuning notably improves weaker models.
AI.motivation: Accuracy of financial documents is critical for economic analysis, regulatory compliance, and corporate decision-making. While LLMs perform well on many financial tasks (e.g., stock price movement prediction, financial analytics), the ability to detect errors in financial documents remains unexplored, motivating a dedicated benchmark and evaluation.
AI.method: The authors build FinED-Bench, covering nine real-world financial scenarios with over 900 documents reported in 2025 (unseen by current LLMs), organized into three levels of cognitive complexity. They detail the benchmark construction process and evaluate several advanced LLMs (GPT-4o, Qwen3-14B, etc.) on the error-detection task, which requires both financial domain knowledge and reasoning. They also investigate supervised fine-tuning to improve weaker models.
AI.result: Experimental results indicate that current LLMs still struggle with financial error detection, particularly on high-complexity cases. Supervised fine-tuning can significantly improve the performance of weaker LLMs on this task.
AI.conclusion: Financial error detection remains a challenging open task for LLMs, and FinED-Bench provides a public, realistic benchmark to drive progress, with data and code released for reproducibility.

title: CAKE: Compiler-Agent Co-Design for Frontier Kernel Evolution
summary: GPU kernel agents and GPU programming languages have advanced separately, leaving expert kernels difficult to reproduce. Agents usually treat the compiler as a fixed black box and receive only errors, correctness outcomes, and timing, while existing DSLs either hide critical scheduling decisions or expose them through difficult layout abstractions. We present CAKE, a compiler-agent co-design in which agents author CAKE IR, a typed, hardware-explicit schedule representation. CAKE exposes warp roles, memory movement, synchronization, and pipelines while supporting verification, cost modeling, and localized diagnostics. The harness itself evolves: recurring failures become verifier rules, IR primitives, model calibrations, and reusable optimization tactics. In matched implementation-hidden Flash-KMeans clean starts on B200, the best CAKE IR candidate at an 80-million-token budget runs at 1.144x the tuned FlashML baseline, compared with 0.928x for direct CUDA/PTX. Beyond this benchmark, agent-generated Kimi Delta Attention achieves a 2.05x geometric-mean speedup over official FlashKDA and passes end-to-end serving validation. Dispatcher-backed KNN and KMeans improve performance by 1.42x to 2.12x across more than 400 shapes, and four kernel changes are available as upstream PRs. CAKE targets NVIDIA GPUs from Ampere through Blackwell and separates single-shape evolution from library generalization and dispatch.

AI.tldr: CAKE is a compiler-agent co-design where LLM agents author CAKE IR, a typed, hardware-explicit schedule representation exposing warp roles, memory movement, synchronization, and pipelines. It outperforms tuned baselines on Flash-KMeans, Kimi Delta Attention, and KNN/KMeans across NVIDIA GPUs, and the harness itself evolves with verifier rules, IR primitives, and optimization tactics.
AI.motivation: GPU kernel agents and GPU programming languages have advanced independently, making expert-level kernels hard to reproduce. Agents typically treat the compiler as a fixed black box and only receive errors, correctness outcomes, and timing, while existing DSLs hide critical scheduling decisions or expose them via hard layout abstractions. This gap motivates a representation and workflow that lets agents reason about and control hardware scheduling explicitly.
AI.method: CAKE is a compiler-agent co-design. Agents author CAKE IR, a typed, hardware-explicit schedule representation exposing warp roles, memory movement, synchronization, and pipelines. It supports verification, cost modeling, and localized diagnostics. The harness is self-evolving: recurring failures are converted into verifier rules, IR primitives, model calibrations, and reusable optimization tactics. CAKE targets NVIDIA GPUs from Ampere through Blackwell and separates single-shape evolution from library generalization and dispatch.
AI.result: On matched implementation-hidden Flash-KMeans clean starts on B200 with an 80-million-token budget, the best CAKE IR candidate runs at 1.144x the tuned FlashML baseline versus 0.928x for direct CUDA/PTX. Agent-generated Kimi Delta Attention achieves a 2.05x geometric-mean speedup over official FlashKDA and passes end-to-end serving validation. Dispatcher-backed KNN and KMeans improve performance 1.42x to 2.12x across over 400 shapes, with four kernel changes available as upstream PRs.
AI.conclusion: Co-designing the compiler with the agent—rather than treating it as a black box—enables agents to reproduce and exceed expert kernels. CAKE's hardware-explicit IR plus an evolving harness yields substantial speedups over tuned baselines across attention, clustering, and KNN workloads, and supports generalization and dispatch beyond single-shape optimization.

title: Dead text or binding clause? Measuring and restoring constraint influence in black-box LLM dialogues
summary: Multi-turn dialogues let users revoke constraints as easily as impose them, but revocation does not reliably take effect: models keep enacting withdrawn requirements (occasionally beneath comments asserting their removal), a failure we call \emph{behavioral relapse}, or revocation inertia. No existing instrument measures this influence per clause, predicts it before delivery, or repairs it under matched budgets. \sysname{} closes the three gaps through the model API alone: a contract ledger pairs every constraint with an executable checker, records revocations as tombstones, and compiles the net constraint state ahead of time into a single specification; a sequential ablation probe measures per-clause adherence and incremental behavioral effect; a repair ladder operates under token- and attempt-matched budgets. On \dataname{} (\NTasks{} HumanEval tasks, \NClauses{} verified checkers), relapse at an 8B operating point climbs from \ScaleDelayedMTwo{} to \ScaleDelayedMEight{} as constraint load grows, while stronger models sit at floor. Under matched checkers, model, and budget, ahead-of-time compilation significantly reduces relapse against a no-ledger verifier-retry baseline (\RestoreDiff{}, 95\% CI \RestoreDiffCI{}, $p$ \RestoreDiffP{}); adaptive ladder interventions stacked on top add no detectable gain (95\% confidence excludes gains $\geq$ \LadderExcludedGain{}). The probe predicts relapse before delivery (AUROC \AurocPrimary{}); a one-sentence tombstone note recovers about a third of the compilation effect and survives a placebo control. At \CostDeliveryFactor{} delivery overhead and \CostTotalHedged{} of API compute for every result, revocation failure becomes a measurable, predictable, and repairable property of dialogue state rather than an invisible one.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "behavioral relapse" (revocation inertia) in multi-turn dialogues, where models continue to honor constraints that users have withdrawn. It introduces a system that (1) measures per-clause adherence via a contract ledger plus sequential ablation probe, (2) predicts relapse before delivery (AUROC 0.??), and (3) repairs it under matched budgets. Ahead-of-time specification compilation significantly reduces relapse versus a no-ledger baseline, while adaptive ladder interventions add no detectable gain; a one-sentence tombstone note recovers about a third of the compilation effect.
AI.motivation: Users can revoke constraints as easily as they impose them in multi-turn dialogue, but revocation often fails to take effect—models keep satisfying withdrawn requirements, sometimes even while claiming they removed them. No existing instrument measures this per-clause influence, predicts it before delivery, or repairs it under matched budgets, leaving revocation failure an invisible property of dialogue state.
AI.method: The system works through the model API alone with three components: (1) a contract ledger that pairs each constraint with an executable checker, records revocations as tombstones, and compiles the net constraint state ahead of time into a single specification; (2) a sequential ablation probe measuring per-clause adherence and incremental behavioral effect; and (3) a repair ladder operating under token- and attempt-matched budgets. Evaluation uses a dataset of HumanEval tasks with verified checkers, spanning an 8B operating point and stronger models.
AI.result: At the 8B operating point, relapse climbs from ScaleDelayedMTwo to ScaleDelayedMEight as constraint load grows, while stronger models sit at floor levels. Under matched checkers, model, and budget, ahead-of-time compilation significantly reduces relapse against a no-ledger verifier-retry baseline (RestoreDiff, 95% CI RestoreDiffCI, p index); adaptive ladder interventions stacked on top add no detectable gain (95% confidence excludes gains >= LadderExcludedGain). The probe predicts relapse before delivery (AUROC AurocPrimary), and a one-sentence tombstone note recovers about a third of the compilation effect and survives a placebo control.
AI.conclusion: At CostDeliveryFactor delivery overhead and CostTotalHedged of API compute per result, revocation failure becomes a measurable, predictable, and repairable property of dialogue state rather than an invisible one. The contributions close the three gaps in measuring per-clause influence, predicting relapse pre-delivery, and repairing it under matched budgets.

title: Slow and Steady: Preventing MEV with Verifiable Delays
comment: A revised version is accepted for publication at the 10th International Workshop on Cryptocurrencies and Blockchain Technology (CBT 2026)
summary: Our work presents a defense mechanism against Maximal Extractable Value (MEV) opportunities in distributed ledgers. The mechanism relies on the idea of enforcing a verifiable delay when generating transactions, such that a block creator cannot react to the appearance of a MEV opportunity without breaking liveness. We present positive results both in the Byzantine setting and in a game theoretic model of rational participants. We additionally present negative bounds that outline the limitations of this line of defense. Finally, we explore real-world implementation details of verifiable delays and show that, based on historical MEV data, our mechanism could realistically help prevent most existing MEV threats.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a defense against MEV in distributed ledgers by enforcing a verifiable delay on transaction generation, preventing block creators from reacting to MEV opportunities without breaking liveness. It provides positive results in Byzantine and game-theoretic settings, negative bounds on the approach's limitations, and an implementation analysis showing the mechanism could prevent most real-world MEV threats.
AI.motivation: MEV (Maximal Extractable Value) allows block creators to profit by reordering, inserting, or censoring transactions, harming ordinary users and ledger fairness. The authors seek a mechanism that removes the ability of block creators to exploit these opportunities.
AI.method: The defense enforces a verifiable delay when generating transactions, so a block creator cannot react to an MEV opportunity without violating liveness. The authors prove security guarantees under two models: a Byzantine setting (arbitrary adversarial behavior) and a game-theoretic model of rational participants. They also derive negative bounds and examine real-world implementation details using historical MEV data.
AI.result: The mechanism achieves positive security results in both the Byzantine and rational (game-theoretic) settings. Negative bounds characterize the inherent limitations of verifiable-delay-based defenses. Empirical analysis of historical MEV data indicates the mechanism could realistically prevent most existing MEV threats in practice.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing verifiable delays on transaction generation is a practical and effective line of defense against MEV, though it has inherent limits. The approach holds up under Byzantine and rational adversarial models and, based on real data, could mitigate most current MEV threats if implemented.

title: Sensorimotor Stickies: A Reconfigurable On-Body Platform for Closed-Loop Sensorimotor Training
summary: Closed-loop sensorimotor training systems can improve learning by sensing movement and delivering real-time feedback, yet most are built as fixed implementations tied to a single task, even though the core technology (inertial and tactile sensing, vibrotactile cueing, rule-based logic) remains the same. We present Sensorimotor Stickies, a reconfigurable on-body platform that treats sensing and vibrotactile feedback as modular stickies that can be patched onto the body as needed. The platform includes miniaturized adhesive modules for IMU sensing, optional tactile sensing, and vibrotactile actuation; low-power firmware and BLE infrastructure for raw streaming and motor control without task-specific rewrites; and a companion mobile app that provides a shared body-centered model for placement, calibration, and feedback authoring. Together, these components enable reconfiguration across training scenarios, user needs, and feedback setups. We evaluate the platform through technical characterization, configured application demonstration, practitioner-mediated configuration sessions, and an end-user study, demonstrating technical feasibility, reconfiguration breadth, and end-user configurability for first-time setup, calibration, and within-task feedback reconfiguration.

AI.tldr: Sensorimotor Stickies is a reconfigurable on-body platform that modularizes IMU sensing, tactile sensing, and vibrotactile feedback into adhesive "stickies," enabling closed-loop sensorimotor training to be patched onto the body and reconfigured across tasks without rewriting task-specific code.
AI.motivation: Closed-loop sensorimotor training systems are typically fixed implementations tied to a single task, despite sharing the same core technology (inertial/tactile sensing, vibrotactile cueing, rule-based logic). This rigidity limits reuse across training scenarios and user needs, motivating a modular, reconfigurable platform.
AI.method: The paper presents Sensorimotor Stickies, consisting of miniaturized adhesive modules for IMU sensing, optional tactile sensing, and vibrotactile actuation; low-power firmware and BLE infrastructure supporting raw streaming and motor control without task-specific rewrites; and a companion mobile app providing a shared body-centered model for placement, calibration, and feedback authoring.
AI.result: Evaluation through technical characterization, configured application demonstrations, practitioner-mediated configuration sessions, and an end-user study showed technical feasibility, broad reconfiguration capability, and end-user configurability for first-time setup, calibration, and within-task feedback reconfiguration.
AI.conclusion: The modular sticky-based approach enables reconfiguration across training scenarios, user needs, and feedback setups, demonstrating a practical path toward general-purpose, reusable closed-loop sensorimotor training hardware/software.

title: Large Language Models Pass the History Exam But Miss the <<History>>: A Polish High School Exit Exam Matura Benchmark
summary: AI chatbots are widely used by students as knowledge sources, yet LLM benchmarks rarely assess interpretative historical reasoning. We evaluate eight leading LLMs on the Polish high school exit exams (Matura) in history - three official papers from 2023-2025, comprising short-answer questions and extended essays - comparing model performance against the human examinee population. Every model dramatically outperforms human examinees, yet aggregate scores mask distinct competency profiles: rankings are unstable across task type, source modality, and geographical scope, with a consistent penalty on Polish versus Global history content. Qualitative error analysis reveals two recurring failure modes - source conflation, in which models reason from source content rather than treating it as an object of analysis, and temporal disorientation, in which responses are historically misplaced. This study introduces the first LLM history benchmark grounded in Polish national curriculum.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates eight leading LLMs on Polish high school history exit exams (Matura, 2023–2025), finding that all models dramatically outperform human examinees overall, but rankings are unstable across task type, source modality, and geographical scope, with systematic penalties on Polish content and two recurring failure modes: source conflation and temporal disorientation.
AI.motivation: AI chatbots are widely used by students as knowledge sources, yet existing LLM benchmarks rarely assess interpretative historical reasoning. The authors aim to fill this gap by grounding evaluation in a real national curriculum (Polish Matura history exams) to test models' ability to perform disciplinary historical reasoning rather than mere fact recall.
AI.method: The study evaluates eight leading LLMs on three official Polish Matura history exam papers from 2023–2025, which include short-answer questions and extended essays. Model performance is scored and compared against the human examinee population, with analyses of competency profiles across task type, source modality, and geographical scope, plus a qualitative error analysis of model outputs.
AI.result: Every model dramatically outperforms human examinees in aggregate scores, but aggregate results mask distinct competency profiles: rankings are unstable across task type, source modality, and geographical scope, with a consistent penalty on Polish versus Global history content. Qualitative analysis identifies two recurring failure modes—source conflation (reasoning from source content instead of treating it as an object of analysis) and temporal disorientation (historically misplaced responses).
