AI.conclusion: The study introduces the first LLM history benchmark grounded in the Polish national curriculum, demonstrating that while LLMs exceed human exam performance, their historical reasoning is uneven—unstable across assessment dimensions and prone to source conflation and temporal disorientation—highlighting the need for more nuanced, reasoning-focused evaluation of AI in education.

title: Interpretable Causal Discovery via Causal-Effect Constraints
summary: Causal discovery aims to uncover the underlying causal relationships given data generated from a system. The goal, however, is not merely to predict causal edges given data, but also to be able to interpret and explain either observed or hypothesized phenomena, such as a particularly large causal effect. We consider this task of conditional causal discovery and cast it as a Bayesian inference problem, in which we target the posterior over causal graphs and parameters conditional on an event such as a causal-effect constraint. Unfortunately, this poses a computational challenge: existing approaches to Bayesian causal discovery struggle when the event has small posterior mass. To address this, we adapt rare-event estimation techniques to perform inference the joint graph-parameter space. Our method gradually drives a particle population toward the constrained region while maintaining samples that approximate the conditional posterior. Empirical evaluation on synthetic graphs validates the accuracy of our approach at small and large scales, and we show in a case study on the Sachs protein dataset how our method can be used to aid scientific exploration by providing pathway-level summaries.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Bayesian approach to conditional causal discovery that infers the posterior over causal graphs and parameters conditional on a rare event (e.g., a large causal effect), using rare-event estimation techniques to sample efficiently even when the event has small posterior mass.
AI.motivation: Causal discovery typically predicts edges from data, but scientists often need to explain observed or hypothesized phenomena, such as an unusually large causal effect. Conditional causal discovery formalizes this need, yet standard Bayesian causal discovery methods fail computationally when the conditioning event has low posterior probability.
AI.method: The authors cast conditional causal discovery as Bayesian inference targeting the posterior over causal graphs and parameters conditional on an event (e.g., a causal-effect constraint). They adapt rare-event estimation techniques to the joint graph-parameter space, gradually driving a population of particles toward the constrained region while maintaining samples approximating the conditional posterior.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on synthetic graphs shows the method achieves accurate inference at both small and large scales. A case study on the Sachs protein dataset demonstrates its utility for scientific exploration by providing pathway-level summaries.
AI.conclusion: The proposed rare-event-adapted Bayesian method effectively performs conditional causal discovery even for low-mass conditioning events, offering accurate posterior inference and practical scientific interpretability through pathway-level summaries.

title: @skills: Attention is all you have
comment: 7 pages main, 23 pages in total with appendix, 6 figures
summary: There are 56,804 public agent skills today, and teams write many more privately. The dominant delivery model is installation: once installed, a skill's description remains in the system prompt, competing for fewer than 100 reliable trigger slots. This leaves the long tail with no practical path to use and forces teams' own playbooks to compete for the same scarce space. We observe that installation bundles three separable functions: content, persistence, and automatic triggering. Only the last requires prompt residency. We therefore propose @skills, an open protocol that separates them. A path addresses any skill, subtree, or collection, and reading a skill is sufficient to use it, so nothing is installed or made resident. The operation vendors a copy at the same path into a project's Git-tracked tree for adaptation and ownership. The operation adds one .gitignore-style line, the only element that costs prompt residency. A directory is a menu, making bundles ordinary directories rather than all-or-nothing units. The protocol requires no manifest, lockfile, or registration, and SKILL.md remains unchanged. @skills is additive, ships as an installable package, and turns any agent that can read files and run commands into a client through a single instruction file. Its open specification is at https://github.com/SylphAI-Inc/atskills and it is implemented in the AdaL CLI at https://adalagent.ai . Because paths address skills well but cannot find them, the protocol is paired with a free hub at https://atskills.one for corpus-wide search and ranking, repository-free hosting, private and team collections, and one-screen authoring. The hub is optional: gh: and local paths resolve without it, and indexed GitHub skills retain their gh: identities. Install less, use more.

AI.tldr: @skills is an open protocol that separates skill installation into three functions—content, persistence, and triggering—so that only a minimal .gitignore-style trigger line occupies prompt residency, enabling the long tail of public/private agent skills to be used without installation.
AI.motivation: The dominant install-based delivery model keeps a skill's description resident in the system prompt, but agents have fewer than 100 reliable trigger slots. This leaves the long tail of the 56,804+ public skills (and countless private team playbooks) unusable, forcing internal playbooks to compete with installed skills for the same scarce prompt space.
AI.method: The authors propose the @skills open protocol, which decomposes installation into three separable functions (content, persistence, automatic triggering) and keeps only triggering in the prompt. Paths address any skill, subtree, or collection; reading a skill suffices to use it (nothing installed/resident). A "vendor" operation copies a skill at the same path into a Git-tracked tree for adaptation. A single @ operation adds one .gitignore-style line as the only prompt-resident cost. Directories act as menus, so bundles are ordinary directories rather than all-or-nothing units. The protocol needs no manifest, lockfile, or registration and keeps SKILL.md unchanged. It ships as an installable package and exposes one instruction file so any file-reading/command-running agent becomes a client. A complementary free hub provides search, ranking, hosting, collections, and authoring, but is optional since gh: and local paths resolve independently.
AI.result: The protocol decouples skill content, persistence, and triggering; enables use-without-installation via path reads; supports vendoring, subtree/collection addressing, and menu-style directory bundles; requires no manifest, lockfile, or registration; and works with any capable agent via a single instruction file. It is implemented in the AdaL CLI and paired with an optional hub for search and hosting.
AI.conclusion: By separating installation's bundled functions and minimizing prompt residency to a single trigger line, @skills lets agents "install less, use more," giving the long tail of skills a practical path to use while preserving the familiar SKILL.md format. The specification is open at github.com/SylphAI-Inc/atskills, with the AdaL CLI implementation and an optional free hub.

title: VR-Themis: A Scalable Framework for Virtual Reality Application Clone Detection
comment: 25 pages, 14 figures, 1 table. Accepted at the 29th International Symposium on Research in Attacks, Intrusions and Defenses (RAID 2026)
summary: Repackaging of mobile applications (aka app cloning) not only threatens the security and privacy of mobile users but also infringes upon the copyright of the original app developers. However, existing detection methods that primarily focus on mobile platforms (such as Android) fail to capture the essential features of virtual reality (VR). Consequently, they are inadequate for effectively detecting cloned VR apps, which have often been targeted by illegal users in the VR market. Considering the unique features of VR apps, this paper proposes a two-stage app clone detection framework, namely VR-Themis, based on \emph{Hierarchy-Object-Behaviour} (HOB). Firstly, VR-Themis exploits the coarse-grained stage to cluster apps based on their retrievable statistical features, making this tool scalable to large-scale VR app datasets. Then, in the fine-grained stage, VR-Themis performs in-depth analysis of the suspicious apps (identified in the first stage) by calculating similarity using our defined \emph{HOB metrics}. Our extensive experiments indicate that VR-Themis successfully detects 307 suspected clone apps from the collected 4,277 VR apps without false positives, demonstrating its effectiveness and scalability.

AI.tldr: The paper presents VR-Themis, a two-stage framework for detecting cloned (repackaged) VR apps, which clusters apps by coarse statistical features and then compares them using Hierarchy-Object-Behaviour (HOB) similarity metrics, detecting 307 clones among 4,277 apps without false positives.
AI.motivation: Repackaging (app cloning) of mobile apps threatens user security/privacy and infringes developer copyright. Existing clone-detection methods focused on platforms like Android cannot capture VR-specific features, making them inadequate for VR apps that are increasingly targeted in the VR market. Hence a VR-tailored detection approach is needed.
AI.method: VR-Themis is a two-stage clone detection framework based on Hierarchy-Object-Behaviour (HOB). Stage 1 (coarse-grained) clusters apps using retrievable statistical features for scalability to large datasets. Stage 2 (fine-grained) performs in-depth analysis of suspicious apps identified in stage 1 by computing similarity with defined HOB metrics.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on 4,277 collected VR apps show VR-Themis detected 307 suspected clone apps with no false positives, demonstrating both effectiveness and scalability.
AI.conclusion: VR-Themis effectively and scalably detects cloned VR apps by leveraging VR-specific HOB features and a two-stage design, successfully identifying 307 clones among 4,277 apps without false positives.

title: Before You Say It: Anticipating Verbal Behavior from Longitudinal Everyday Conversations with LLMs
summary: Knowing someone deeply means not just understanding what they say or do but also how they will likely think, react, and engage across situations. Such predictions could eventually inform systems to anticipate when the individual is about to deviate from their goal, catch regrettable behaviors before they are made, and surface blind spots before they take hold. While many interactive systems model users to enable more personalized interactions, most cannot make such behavioral predictions, as this often requires longitudinal observation and inference of how the individual's behaviors unfold across various everyday situations. In this work, we introduce a novel LLM-based predictive behavioral modeling approach that anticipates a user's likely behavior across everyday conversational situations. We (1) collect a longitudinal dataset of over 1000 hours of naturalistic conversations from 14 participants using a wearable smartwatch; (2) evaluate LLM-based predictions against ground truth behaviors; and (3) use semi-structured interviews to explore participants perceptions of behavioral predictions and their views on possible forms of future behavioral support. Altogether, our findings provide evidence that person-specific verbal behavior can be predicted from longitudinal conversational data. This opens up new possibilities for potential future context-aware, anticipatory, proactive and personalized AI systems.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an LLM-based predictive behavioral modeling approach that anticipates a user's likely verbal behavior across everyday conversations, using longitudinal smartwatch data and measuring prediction accuracy alongside qualitative user perceptions.
AI.motivation: Knowing someone deeply, including how they will think, react, and engage across situations, could enable systems to anticipate goal deviations, catch regrettable behaviors, and surface blind spots. Existing interactive systems personalize interactions but mostly cannot make such behavioral predictions, which typically require longitudinal observation and inference of how behaviors unfold across many everyday situations.
AI.method: The authors (1) collect a longitudinal dataset of over 1000 hours of naturalistic conversations from 14 participants using a wearable smartwatch; (2) evaluate LLM-based predictions against ground truth behaviors; and (3) conduct semi-structured interviews to explore participants' perceptions of behavioral predictions and their views on possible future forms of behavioral support.
AI.result: The findings provide evidence that person-specific verbal behavior can be predicted from longitudinal conversational data, opening new possibilities for context-aware, anticipatory, proactive, and personalized AI systems.
AI.conclusion: Person-specific verbal behavior is predictable from longitudinal conversational data, suggesting a foundation for future anticipatory and proactive personalized AI systems that could support individuals in everyday situations.

title: Predicting consumer-technology ownership without a diffusion history
comment: 31 pages, 4 figures, supplementary material included (Tables S1-S6, Figure S1), data and code at https://osf.io/dr5ct
summary: We test whether the perceived attributes of a consumer technology predict how widely it is owned. In a 2022 Prolific survey of US adults (n = 678), respondents rated 65 consumer technologies on six attributes. We then elicited the same ratings from two frontier language models, Anthropic Claude Opus 4.7 and OpenAI GPT-5.5. We regress ownership prevalence on four UTAUT2 acceptance attributes plus a log-age covariate with a sign-constrained penalized regression and evaluate it by holding out one technology at a time. The attribute model improves on a baseline of years-since-launch: mean absolute error falls by 17% with the human ratings, and by more with either model, most with Opus 4.7. Over the short 2022-to-2025 window, where ownership moved little, the same attributes do not improve on a no-change baseline. We set out the limitations of the approach, including the possibility that language-model ratings reflect prior knowledge of these technologies rather than independent attribute reasoning. We include a deployment illustration: 2027 ownership predictions for eleven products launched in 2025 and 2026.

AI.tldr: A study tests whether consumer-perceived attributes of a technology (UTAUT2-based) predict how widely it is owned, comparing human ratings from a 2022 Prolific survey against ratings from two frontier language models (Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5), using sign-constrained penalized regression with leave-one-out evaluation and providing 2027 ownership forecasts.
AI.motivation: To determine whether widely used technology-acceptance attributes (UTAUT2) can predict real-world ownership prevalence better than simple benchmarks like years-since-launch, and whether language models can substitute for costly human survey ratings in such predictions.
AI.method: A 2022 Prolific survey of 678 US adults rated 65 consumer technologies on six attributes. The same ratings were elicited from two frontier language models (Anthropic Claude Opus 4.7 and OpenAI GPT-5.5). Ownership prevalence was regressed on four UTAUT2 acceptance attributes plus a log-age covariate using a sign-constrained penalized regression, evaluated by leaving out one technology at a time against a years-since-launch baseline and, for the 2022–2025 window, a no-change baseline. A deployment illustration generates 2027 ownership predictions for eleven products launched in 2025–2026.
AI.result: The attribute model reduces mean absolute error by 17% over the years-since-launch baseline using human ratings, and by more using either language model, with Opus 4.7 performing best. Over the short 2022-to-2025 period, where ownership changed little, the attributes do not improve on a no-change baseline.
AI.conclusion: Perceived UTAUT2 attributes meaningfully improve ownership prediction over a launch-age baseline, and language-model-elicited ratings can even outperform human ratings, though this may reflect models' prior knowledge of the technologies rather than independent attribute reasoning. Predictive value disappears when ownership is essentially static (2022–2025), and the approach carries documented limitations.

title: Training Under Challenge: Executable Certificates and Challenge-Closed Optimality for Neural Networks
comment: 82 pages, 24 figures, 10 tables. Ancillary reproducibility materials included
summary: A flat training curve does not reveal whether a neural network has reached a global optimum, is locally trapped, is representation-limited, or is mismatched to its trainer. We introduce Training Under Challenge, an executable-certificate framework in which predeclared, architecture-valid procedures construct complete alternatives in the same certified class and reevaluate the same objective. Any lower-valued candidate is a replayable witness that lower-bounds the checkpoint's empirical global-optimality gap. Passing a finite suite is only suite-relative; global-gap conclusions require a separately justified coverage mechanism. We define a resource-indexed challenge-power modulus that characterizes the largest gap compatible with passage. For squared loss, current block-decrease operators make coverage checkable and yield uniform and realized-residual bounds. We prove the converse frontier: without coverage, a first-order ReLU trainer can reach infinitely many exact conditional head optima while converging to a non-global point. On a channel-gated ResNet-18 distillation problem with known optimum, eight internal challenges cover all 240 audited output directions, and realized-residual bounds lie within factors of 1.74--3.02 of the true gap. Paired predictive certificates separate decoder under-use from representation insufficiency, while quantized-denoising studies demonstrate diagnosis, repair, and current-state recertification.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes "Training Under Challenge," a framework that certifies whether a trained neural network checkpoint is far from a global optimum by constructing alternative solutions within the same architecture class and comparing objective values, yielding replayable witnesses that lower-bound the empirical optimality gap.
AI.motivation: A flat training curve is uninformative: it cannot distinguish between reaching a global optimum, being stuck in a local trap, being limited by representation capacity, or being mismatched to the training objective. The authors seek a certificate-based way to rigorously measure how far a checkpoint is from empirically global optimality, rather than relying on vague convergence signals.
AI.method: They introduce an executable-certificate framework where predeclared, architecture-valid procedures build complete alternative networks in the same certified class and reevaluate the same objective. Any lower-valued candidate serves as a replayable witness lower-bounding the empirical global-optimality gap. They define a resource-indexed challenge-power modulus capturing the largest gap compatible with passing a suite, prove coverage-checkability for squared loss via block-decrease operators, derive uniform and realized-residual bounds, and prove a converse frontier showing a first-order ReLU trainer can hit infinitely many exact conditional head optima yet converge to a non-global point. Experiments use channel-gated ResNet-18 distillation and quantized-denoising tasks.
AI.result: On a channel-gated ResNet-18 distillation problem with a known optimum, eight internal challenges cover all 240 audited output directions, with realized-residual bounds within factors of 1.74–3.02 of the true gap. Paired predictive certificates separate decoder under-use from representation insufficiency, and quantized-denoising experiments demonstrate diagnosis, repair, and recertification of the current state.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides rigorous, replayable certificates that lower-bound the empirical optimality gap of neural network checkpoints; passing a finite suite is only suite-relative, so absolute global-gap claims require a separately justified coverage mechanism. The method enables practical diagnosis and repair of under-trained or representation-limited models.

title: Jagged Judges: Epistemic Stability Under Silence, Pressure, and Persistence
summary: LLM judges have become central infrastructure for model evaluations, online grading, and reward modeling. Judges are typically validated by accuracy on golden data, but accuracy says little about whether they are stable under re-prompting, challenge, or sustained pushback. We introduce the \emph{Wiggle Framework}, a unified stress test for epistemic stability in LLM judges. The framework decomposes judge robustness along three dimensions: Mechanical Consistency (stability under re-prompting and reframing), Single-turn Conviction (stability under a single challenge), and Multi-turn Persistence (stability under sustained or adaptive pressure). We use the framework to study 9 frontier models across 14 judging tasks spanning safety, toxicity, AI writing detection, and political-response evaluation. Every model exhibits substantial wiggle as a judge --- flipping verdicts 25--71\% of the time under static pushback, and 62--91\% with an adversarial LLM persuader. Critically, we find that pressure that succeeds in changing a judge's verdict is almost always net-corrupting with respect to ground truth. Beyond the framework itself, we identify baseline jury majority strength as the most effective single-shot signal for anticipating which items wiggle. Taken together, this is the first apples-to-apples cross-dataset comparison of mechanical, conformity, and persuadability tests in a judging context.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Wiggle Framework, a stress test for epistemic stability in LLM judges across three dimensions (mechanical consistency, single-turn conviction, multi-turn persistence). Testing 9 frontier models on 14 judging tasks, it finds judges flip verdicts 25–71% under static pushback and 62–91% under adversarial persuasion, with successful pressure almost always net-corrupting relative to ground truth. Jury majority strength is identified as the best predictor of which items wiggle.
AI.motivation: LLM judges are widely used for model evaluation, online grading, and reward modeling, but their validation focuses on accuracy over golden data, which fails to capture whether they remain stable under re-prompting, challenge, or sustained pushback. There is a need for a unified way to measure epistemic stability in judges rather than relying on accuracy alone.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Wiggle Framework, which decomposes judge robustness into three dimensions: Mechanical Consistency (stability under re-prompting and reframing), Single-turn Conviction (stability under one challenge), and Multi-turn Persistence (stability under sustained/adaptive pressure). They apply it to 9 frontier models across 14 judging tasks (safety, toxicity, AI writing detection, political-response evaluation), using static pushback and an adversarial LLM persuader, and analyze jury majority strength as a predictive signal.
AI.result: Every model shows substantial instability as a judge: verdicts flip 25–71% under static pushback and 62–91% with an adversarial LLM persuader. Pressure that changes a verdict is almost always net-corrupting relative to ground truth. Baseline jury majority strength is the most effective single-shot signal for anticipating which items wiggle.
AI.conclusion: The work provides the first apples-to-apples cross-dataset comparison of mechanical, conformity, and persuadability tests in judging contexts, demonstrating that LLM judges are broadly epistemically unstable and that accuracy alone is insufficient to certify judge reliability.

title: TeleGapper: On the (un)reliability of Privacy Policies in Telegram Mini apps
summary:
Telegram Mini Apps are Web applications embedded within the Telegram client, forming an ecosystem of third-party services within one of the world's most widely used messaging platforms. Despite their growing adoption and access to Telegram-provided context, their privacy properties remain largely unexplored. Unlike ecosystems such as WeChat, which rely on tightly controlled, proprietary execution frameworks, Telegram adopts a different model: Mini Apps run inside a WebView, combining platform-provided context with standard Web capabilities and unrestricted outbound networking. This enables applications to transmit sensitive information to analytics, advertising, tracking, or other third parties through ordinary Web requests, often with limited visibility.
  Privacy disclosures are therefore critical for transparency. Telegram allows Mini Apps either to define an application-specific privacy policy or to rely on a platform-provided default policy. While the latter reduces the developer's disclosure burden, it may lead to generic statements that do not accurately capture actual data practices of individual Mini Apps.
  In this paper, we present TeleGapper, a black-box dynamic analysis framework to assess the privacy posture of Mini Apps by capturing runtime network traffic, identifying third-party communications, and comparing observed data flows against disclosed privacy information. We evaluate 278 working Mini Apps collected from tApps Center, a community-driven catalogue for discovering third-party applications in Telegram. We find that 59.4% contact at least one undisclosed third party, 78.8% rely exclusively on Telegram's default privacy policy, and none provides a consent or opt-out mechanism. These findings expose a substantial transparency and compliance gap in a widely used yet understudied ecosystem.

AI.tldr: This paper presents TeleGapper, a black-box dynamic analysis framework that assesses Telegram Mini Apps' privacy posture by capturing runtime network traffic and comparing observed data flows against disclosed privacy policies. Evaluating 278 Mini Apps, it finds 59.4% contact at least one undisclosed third party, 78.8% rely solely on Telegram's default privacy policy, and none offer consent/opt-out mechanisms, revealing a significant transparency and compliance gap.
AI.motivation: Telegram Mini Apps form a large third-party ecosystem with growing adoption and access to platform-provided user context, yet their privacy properties remain largely unexplored. Unlike tightly controlled frameworks (e.g., WeChat), Telegram Mini Apps run in a WebView with unrestricted outbound networking, allowing sensitive data to be sent to analytics/advertising/tracking parties with limited visibility. Telegram also lets apps use a generic platform default privacy policy, which may not reflect actual data practices.
AI.method: TeleGapper is a black-box dynamic analysis framework that (1) captures runtime network traffic of Mini Apps, (2) identifies third-party communications, and (3) compares observed data flows against disclosed privacy information. It was evaluated on 278 working Mini Apps collected from tApps Center, a community-driven catalogue.
AI.result: 59.4% of Mini Apps contact at least one undisclosed third party; 78.8% rely exclusively on Telegram's default privacy policy; none provide a consent or opt-out mechanism.
AI.conclusion: The Telegram Mini App ecosystem exhibits a substantial transparency and compliance gap: widespread undisclosed third-party data flows, heavy reliance on generic default privacy policies, and absent consent/opt-out mechanisms in a widely used but understudied ecosystem.

title: Safety vs. Social Image: Co-Designing Protection Mechanisms Against Ableist Harassment with People with Disabilities in Social Virtual Reality
summary: People with disabilities (PWD) increasingly use avatars to express disability identities in social virtual reality (VR), but greater visibility also invites targeted harassment. Existing safety features are often insufficient, overlooking PWD's experiences and needs. To address this gap, we co-designed protection mechanisms with 11 PWD to reveal their values and needs. Our research employed a social lens to interpret harassment behaviors and protection mechanisms. Inspired by Hall's Proxemics Theory that interpersonal distances indicate social intent and boundaries, we divided social VR spaces into four proxemic zones (Intimate, Personal, Social, and Public) and used them to structure our protection mechanism co-design. We also provided different protection mechanism probes (Inform, Educate, Consent, and Combat) to elicit participant preferences. Our study highlighted the role of social proximity in shaping PWD's harassment perception and protection preferences and revealing PWD's unique social values and needs (e.g., managing harassment with optimism and resilience, prioritizing social image over safety). We proposed design recommendations for protection mechanisms that protect PWD while maintaining their desired social images.

AI.tldr: Co-designing anti-harassment protection mechanisms for people with disabilities (PWD) in social VR, using Hall's Proxemics Theory to map four proxemic zones and probing four mechanism types, revealing PWD's unique values such as managing harassment with optimism and prioritizing social image over safety.
AI.motivation: PWD increasingly use avatars to express disability identities in social VR, but greater visibility invites targeted harassment. Existing safety features are inadequate because they overlook PWD's experiences, values, and needs. The study addresses this gap through participatory co-design.
AI.method: The authors co-designed protection mechanisms with 11 PWD. They adopted a social lens and, inspired by Hall's Proxemics Theory (interpersonal distance signals social intent/boundaries), divided social VR spaces into four proxemic zones: Intimate, Personal, Social, and Public. They provided four protection mechanism probes—Inform, Educate, Consent, and Combat—to elicit participant preferences.
AI.result: Social proximity shaped PWD's harassment perception and protection preferences. PWD exhibited unique social values and needs, including managing harassment with optimism and resilience, and prioritizing social image over safety.
AI.conclusion: The authors propose design recommendations for protection mechanisms that safeguard PWD while preserving their desired social image.

title: New Terms, New Toxicity: Consensus-based Chinese Neologism Toxicity Detection via Search-Augmented LLMs
summary: Neologisms, emerging terms in meaning or form, can serve as new vehicles for toxic expression, like "country girl" as a stigmatizing label targeting feminism. Such toxic neologisms appear benign but have evolved into toxic usage in public consensus, posing challenges to moderation systems and remaining underexplored. In this paper, we investigate how to detect implicit toxicity expressed via neologisms. We first propose a taxonomy that captures the origins and consensus-verification criteria of toxic neologisms, followed by the construction of a lexicon spanning widely observed risk categories. To capture toxicity grounded in public consensus, we introduce SeTox, a search-augmented framework that enables static large language models (LLMs) to incorporate real-time web context for neologism toxicity detection. Experiments show that SeTox, even with 3B-scale models, outperforms recent large-scale models, demonstrating its scalability to incorporate real-world knowledge for toxic neologism detection. Disclaimer: this paper has offensive contents that may be disturbing to some readers.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SeTox, a search-augmented framework that detects implicit toxicity in neologisms by equipping static LLMs with real-time web context, outperforming much larger models even at 3B scale.
AI.motivation: Toxic neologisms—new or repurposed terms that superficially appear benign but carry harmful meaning via public consensus—bypass conventional moderation systems and remain understudied. The authors aim to address the detection of this implicit toxicity.
AI.method: The authors first propose a taxonomy capturing the origins and consensus-verification criteria of toxic neologisms, then build a risk-category lexicon. They introduce SeTox, a search-augmented framework enabling static LLMs to absorb real-time web context for toxicity detection.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate SeTox, even using 3B-scale models, outperforms recent large-scale LLMs, confirming its scalability in integrating real-world knowledge for toxic neologism detection.
AI.conclusion: SeTox effectively detects implicit toxic neologisms by grounding decisions in live public consensus, showing that retrieval-augmented context helps smaller models surpass larger static counterparts in this task.

title: Demand Transfer Estimation at Scale via Restricted Logit Modeling
comment: 8 pages. Accepted in the Main Conference of IEEE ICMLA 2026
summary:
Item demand forecasting is an integral component of store assortment optimization. Existing literature focuses on learning a suitable customer choice model and using this model to determine the value of an objective function (i.e. expected demand) with respect to an assortment proposal. However, for large item universe with many categories, this approach can prove inefficient, needing a separate demand forecast for every possible item assortment. An alternate approach exists whereby we combine the efficiency of forecasting item demand independently, while at the same time applying adjustments to the independent forecasts that account for the relations between item demand and the availability of other similar items on the shelf.
  Central to this approach is the estimation of Demand Transfer (DT) coefficients. These DT coefficients represent the percent of a particular target item's (item that the customer walked in the store to buy) demand that is redirected to each other item in the universe should the target item be removed from the shelf. We introduce an approach that allows us to compute these DT coefficients on large item universes (assortments having 1 million+ items). Experiments on data as well as historical transaction data for multiple locations within categories demonstrate that when certain reasonable assumptions about substitution behavior are satisfied, our procedure is able to accurately estimate underlying DT coefficients and lead to improvements in demand forecasting.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a scalable method to estimate Demand Transfer (DT) coefficients, which capture how much of a removed item's demand is redirected to other items, enabling efficient demand forecasting for large assortments (1M+ items) without forecasting every possible assortment.
AI.motivation: Existing assortment optimization relies on learning customer choice models that require a separate demand forecast for every possible item assortment, which becomes inefficient for large item universes spanning many categories. The authors seek an alternative that combines efficient independent item demand forecasting with adjustments accounting for substitution relationships between items.
AI.method: The authors introduce an approach that estimates Demand Transfer (DT) coefficients, defined as the percentage of a target item's demand redirected to each other item when the target is removed from the shelf. The method is designed to scale to large item universes (1M+ items) and is validated using simulation/experimental data and historical transaction data across multiple locations within categories.
AI.result: Under reasonable assumptions about substitution behavior, the procedure accurately estimates underlying DT coefficients and yields improvements in demand forecasting, as demonstrated on experimental data and historical transaction data across multiple locations and categories.
AI.conclusion: Estimating DT coefficients at scale enables a viable alternative to full choice-model fitting for assortment optimization in large catalogs, improving demand forecasting accuracy when substitution assumptions hold.

title: SteerBench-Work: A Benchmark for Agent Steering at Action Boundaries
summary:
Long-running LLM agents act through tools, and a single step can send an email, merge a pull request, or wire a payment. The steering decision is the pre-commit choice at that boundary: proceed, or hold for human or policy review. We introduce SteerBench-Work, an incident-anchored, bidirectional benchmark for that decision in workplace agents across developer operations, customer service, finance, legal, medical, HR, and security.
  Release v2026-05 contains 106 scenarios anchored in public incidents, paired evidence-reversed mirrors, and calibration controls, with labels split nearly evenly between proceed and hold so the two error directions get near-identical numbers of chances. A model sees the proposed action and the available evidence, returns a gate decision, and is scored on whether it crosses or holds the boundary correctly. Across 30 model conditions the failures run almost entirely in one direction: models wrongly hold authorized, evidence-cleared work on 28.1% of opportunities and wrongly allow unsafe work on 1.0%. The hardest cases are risk-resolved commits, where signed or structured evidence has already cleared a real risk trigger, and models score markedly worse on evidence-reversed mirrors of famous incidents (63.8%) than on the incidents themselves (98.5%). General capability is not the same as steering calibration: higher-capability models often over-refuse at the commit boundary, and more reasoning can repair a weak gate while leaving a calibrated one flat. The public leaderboard is at steerbench.com.

AI.tldr: SteerBench-Work is an incident-anchored, bidirectional benchmark for testing when workplace LLM agents should "proceed" versus "hold for review" before taking consequential actions. Across 30 model conditions, models fail almost entirely by over-refusing authorized work (28.1%) rather than allowing unsafe work (1.0%), and general capability does not translate into good steering calibration.
AI.motivation: Long-running LLM agents perform consequential single-step actions (email, merge, payment), requiring a reliable pre-commit "steering" decision. Prior benchmarks inadequately measure whether models correctly decide to proceed or hold at this boundary, especially balancing both error directions (false-hold vs. false-proceed) and handling evidence-reversed or risk-resolved cases.
AI.method: Introduces SteerBench-Work v2026-05: 106 scenarios anchored in public incidents across DevOps, customer service, finance, legal, medical, HR, and security. Each incident has paired evidence-reversed mirrors and calibration controls, with labels split nearly evenly between proceed and hold. Models receive the proposed action and available evidence, return a gate decision, and are scored on correct boundary crossing/holding. 30 model conditions are evaluated, including higher-capability and reasoning-enhanced models.
AI.result: Failures are highly asymmetric: models wrongly hold authorized, evidence-cleared work on 28.1% of opportunities versus wrongly allowing unsafe work on only 1.0%. Hardest cases are risk-resolved commits (evidence already cleared a real risk trigger). Models perform markedly worse on evidence-reversed mirrors of famous incidents (63.8%) than on the originals (98.5%). Higher-capability models often over-refuse at the commit boundary, and additional reasoning can fix a weak gate while leaving a calibrated one flat.
AI.conclusion: General LLM capability is distinct from steering calibration. Models systematically over-refuse rather than under-refuse, are thrown off by evidence-reversed mirrors, and struggle with risk-resolved commits, indicating current agents lack reliable boundary decision-making. A public leaderboard is provided at steerbench.com.

title: Privacy-Preserving RAG by Concealing Sensitive Information from External LLMs
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is widely used to improve the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) in answering user queries. Existing privacy research on RAG has focused on preventing unauthorized users from accessing sensitive data. However, another important problem that is often overlooked in RAG privacy research is that external generators have access to the query and the retrieved documents, which may contain confidential information that could potentially be misused or accessed for unintended purposes. In this paper, we introduce the Sensitive Entity Alias Generator (SEAG), a privacy-preserving framework that empowers users to utilize powerful third-party generators without disclosing sensitive information. SEAG introduces a lightweight model that locates sensitive entities, generates corresponding aliases, and constructs an entity replacement table. The table is used to replace sensitive words in the user's query and in the retrieved documents before they are forwarded to an external generator. For this purpose, two datasets were constructed: one for fine-tuning SEAG models to generate entity replacement tables, and another for evaluating the entire SEAG framework. The experimental results demonstrate the success of the SEAG framework. As for the User metric, which measures the ability of the model to provide a correct response to the user while hiding sensitive information from the external generator, all SEAG models achieved over 80% accuracy. Additional analysis further evaluated the ability of SEAG models Qwen-3, LLaMA-3.2, and Phi-4 to hide all sensitive entities within given documents. The results show good performance with total accuracies of 77.83%, 76.73%, and 74.91%, respectively.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes SEAG, a privacy-preserving RAG framework that hides sensitive entities from third-party generators by replacing them with aliases via a lightweight model and an entity replacement table.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG privacy research focuses on preventing unauthorized users from accessing sensitive data, but overlooks that external generators see both the query and retrieved documents, which may contain confidential information that could be misused.
AI.method: SEAG uses a lightweight model to locate sensitive entities, generate aliases, and build an entity replacement table. Before forwarding to an external generator, sensitive words in the user query and retrieved documents are replaced using this table. Two datasets were constructed: one for fine-tuning SEAG to generate replacement tables, and one for end-to-end framework evaluation.
AI.result: All SEAG models achieved over 80% accuracy on the User metric (correct answer while hiding sensitive info). In hiding all sensitive entities, Qwen-3, LLaMA-3.2, and Phi-4 reached total accuracies of 77.83%, 76.73%, and 74.91%, respectively.
AI.conclusion: The SEAG framework successfully enables users to leverage powerful third-party generators while preventing disclosure of sensitive information, as demonstrated by high accuracy across models.

title: Are you Talking Logic to Me? Assessing Language Models Syllogistic Reasoning Capabilities
comment: Accepted to the International Joint Conference on Rules and Reasoning (RuleML+RR) 2026
summary: Language models (LMs) struggle with logical tasks like reasoning on syllogisms. It has been shown that Knowledge Representation (KR) plays a crucial role in expressing input information to help models solve tasks. This observation motivates our study of the impact of different formal KR notations on syllogistic reasoning by extending the FOLIO and P-FOLIO datasets. Our experiments on Small Language Models (SLMs) in Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Zero-Shot (ZS) settings show that the choice of input notation can yield performances competitive with natural language while enabling faster inference. We also propose a syllogistic categorization method (SEF) and use it to enrich ZS prompts with logical definitions, which boost reasoning in small models. We open-source our framework, Common Logic Grammar Construction (CLGC), as the first Python library for automatically generating syllogisms in KR notations and defining their SEF categories.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how formal Knowledge Representation (KR) notations affect syllogistic reasoning in language models, introduces a syllogism categorization method (SEF) to enrich prompts, and releases the first Python library (CLGC) for auto-generating syllogisms in KR notations.
AI.motivation: Language models struggle with logical tasks like syllogistic reasoning, and prior work shows Knowledge Representation is crucial for expressing input to help models solve tasks. This motivates investigating how different formal KR notations impact syllogistic reasoning performance.
AI.method: The authors extend the FOLIO and P-FOLIO datasets with multiple formal KR notations, evaluate Small Language Models in Supervised Fine-Tuning and Zero-Shot settings, propose a syllogistic categorization method called SEF, use it to enrich zero-shot prompts with logical definitions, and build the Common Logic Grammar Construction (CLGC) framework to auto-generate syllogisms in KR notations.
AI.result: Experiments show that the choice of input notation can achieve performance competitive with natural language while enabling faster inference, and SEF-based prompt enrichment boosts reasoning in small models.
AI.conclusion: Formal KR notations are a viable, faster alternative to natural language for syllogistic reasoning, and the SEF categorization plus the open-sourced CLGC library provide practical tools for improving and generating syllogistic reasoning tasks.

title: Finding the Needle in a Haystack: Test-Time Analog Circuit Representation Adaptation for Bayesian Optimization
summary: Bayesian optimization (BO) is a sample-efficient framework for analog circuit topology search, where evaluating each candidate topology can require costly simulation. However, representation-based BO methods typically treat circuit embeddings as fixed after encoder training. This creates a mismatch between representation learning and optimization: embeddings learned to encode or reconstruct circuit structure are not necessarily organized according to the figure of merit (FoM) being optimized. This paper introduces Test-Time Analog Representation Adaptation for Bayesian Optimization (TTARO), an online deep-kernel BO framework that adapts circuit representations throughout the search process. Starting from pretrained circuit embeddings, TTARO jointly learns a nonlinear feature transformation and a Gaussian-process surrogate using the FoM labels of the circuits evaluated so far. Following each new evaluation, TTARO updates the representation and surrogate before selecting the next candidate. We compare TTARO with conventional Gaussian Process-based BO over fixed embeddings and with Deep Kernel Learning (DKL), which learns the representation only from the initial evaluated designs and keeps it fixed throughout the remainder of the search. By continually incorporating newly observed FoM labels into representation learning, TTARO aligns the search space with the optimization objective as BO progresses. In our experiments, TTARO reduces regret AUC by 15.2% on average relative to BO and by 20.7% relative to DKL across 40 encoder/kernel/acquisition settings, outperforming prior art in most settings with reductions as large as 46.7%.

AI.tldr: TTARO is an online deep-kernel Bayesian optimization framework that continuously adapts pretrained analog circuit embeddings to the figure of merit during search, outperforming fixed-embedding BO and Deep Kernel Learning.
AI.motivation: Representation-based Bayesian optimization for analog circuit topology search typically fixes circuit embeddings after encoder training, creating a mismatch between representation learning (geared toward structure reconstruction) and the optimization objective (the figure of merit). The authors aim to align the search space with the FoM by adapting representations online as new evaluations arrive.
AI.method: TTARO starts from pretrained circuit embeddings and jointly learns a nonlinear feature transformation together with a Gaussian-process surrogate, using FoM labels of all circuits evaluated so far. After each new simulation/evaluation, it updates both the representation and the surrogate before selecting the next candidate. It is compared against standard Gaussian-Process BO over fixed embeddings and against Deep Kernel Learning, which learns the representation only from initial designs and freezes it for the rest of the search.
AI.result: Across 40 encoder/kernel/acquisition settings, TTARO reduces regret AUC by 15.2% on average relative to BO and by 20.7% relative to DKL, outperforming prior art in most settings with reductions as large as 46.7%.
AI.conclusion: Continually incorporating newly observed FoM labels into representation learning lets TTARO align the search space with the optimization objective as BO progresses, yielding consistently better sample efficiency than fixed-embedding BO and Deep Kernel Learning.

title: General Probabilities of Causation with Causal Knowledge
summary: Probabilities of causation (PoCs) characterize individual causal responses that cannot be directly observed and therefore generally require partial identification. Tian and Pearl first derived theoretically sharp bounds for binary PoCs, including the probability of necessity (PN), the probability of sufficiency (PS), and the probability of necessity and sufficiency (PNS). Mueller et al. subsequently tightened the bounds for binary PNS by incorporating causal information encoded in covariates and mediators. More recently, Li and Pearl, as well as Shu et al., extended PoCs to multivalued settings and derived corresponding theoretical bounds. These developments naturally raise the question of whether additional causal knowledge can further tighten the bounds in multivalued settings. This paper addresses this question by deriving tighter bounds for multivalued PoCs through the incorporation of causal information encoded in covariates and mediators. We illustrate the theoretical results with toy examples, while simulation studies further demonstrate that the proposed bounds are tighter than existing nonbinary bounds.

AI.tldr: The paper derives tighter bounds for multivalued probabilities of causation (PN, PS, PNS) by incorporating causal information from covariates and mediators, extending earlier binary results to nonbinary settings and validating improvements via examples and simulations.
AI.motivation: Probabilities of causation (PoCs) require partial identification because individual causal responses are unobservable. While sharp theoretical bounds exist for binary PoCs and tighter binary PNS bounds have been obtained using covariate/mediator information, multivalued generalizations have only theoretical bounds. The open question is whether additional causal knowledge (covariates and mediators) can similarly tighten bounds in multivalued settings.
AI.method: The authors derive tightened bounds for multivalued PoCs by encoding causal information from covariates and mediators, extending the approach previously applied to binary PNS to nonbinary treatments and outcomes.
AI.result: The derived multivalued bounds incorporate covariate and mediator information and are demonstrated to be tighter than the existing nonbinary bounds, with illustrations via toy examples and simulation studies.
AI.conclusion: Additional causal knowledge from covariates and mediators can further tighten bounds on multivalued probabilities of causation, confirming that the gains observed in binary settings extend to nonbinary cases.

title: Correct Is Not Governed: Provenance Integrity in Agentic Workflows
summary: Agentic workflows are commonly evaluated by whether they reach the correct outcome. That is insufficient in institutional settings, where a correct action may rely on the wrong authority, an unsupported completion claim, or work made stale by a later change. We define governed execution as work whose decisions, completion, and response to change are supported by inspectable provenance. We present Matrix, a deterministic causal-state layer that records authority and fact dependencies, verifies completion evidence, and selectively invalidates affected work. Across controlled comparisons, governed and direct workflows often reached the same outcomes, but only the governed path consistently preserved governing evidence, refused unsupported closure, and limited recovery to dependent tasks. A role-separated transfer challenge then failed: a deterministically enforced completeness contract severely over-blocked synthetic packets produced outside its authoring context. These results do not establish Matrix as a general accuracy enhancer; they support its primary role as an institutional integrity layer for making agentic work auditable and independently verifiable.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Matrix, a deterministic causal-state layer that adds governed execution to agentic workflows, recording authority and fact dependencies, verifying completion evidence, and selectively invalidating stale work, to make decisions auditable rather than merely correct.
AI.motivation: Evaluating agentic workflows solely by whether they reach the correct outcome is insufficient in institutional settings. A correct action can still be flawed if it relies on the wrong authority, makes an unsupported completion claim, or is built on work made stale by later changes. Such settings demand that decisions, completion, and change responses be supported by inspectable provenance.
AI.method: The authors define "governed execution" as work whose decisions, completion, and response to change are supported by inspectable provenance. They implement Matrix, a deterministic causal-state layer that records authority and fact dependencies, verifies completion evidence, and selectively invalidates affected work. They run controlled comparisons of governed versus direct workflows, plus a role-separated transfer challenge.
AI.result: Governed and direct workflows often reached the same outcomes, but only the governed path consistently preserved governing evidence, refused unsupported closure, and limited recovery to dependent tasks. The role-separated transfer challenge failed: a deterministically enforced completeness contract severely over-blocked synthetic packets produced outside its authoring context.
AI.conclusion: The results do not establish Matrix as a general accuracy enhancer. Instead, they support Matrix's primary role as an institutional integrity layer that makes agentic work auditable and independently verifiable.

title: Query Timing Produces Opposite Positional Biases Between LLMs and Humans
summary: Positional biases such as recency and primacy effects have been documented in large language models (LLMs), yet the underlying mechanism by which these models make their evaluations remains poorly understood. Both primacy and recency biases have been observed in human judgments in response to evidence, but recent work suggest that \emph{when} the listener updates their beliefs -- during the presentation of evidence or only at the end -- influences the presence of such effects. We investigate whether a similar phenomenon holds for LLMs, finding divergence from human behavior. These biases are more exacerbated in newer models compared to their predecessors.

AI.tldr: This paper explores how positional biases (primacy and recency effects) manifest in LLM evaluations, testing whether belief-update timing—a factor known to influence human judgment—similarly affects LLMs, and finds LLMs diverge from humans with these biases worsening in newer models.
AI.motivation: Positional biases such as recency and primacy effects are documented in LLMs, but the underlying evaluation mechanism is poorly understood. In humans, when belief updating occurs (during evidence presentation vs. only at the end) influences these effects. The authors investigate whether the same phenomenon applies to LLMs.
AI.method: The authors investigate whether belief-update timing influences primacy and recency biases in LLMs, analogous to recent findings in human judgment research, and compare this behavior against human responses.
AI.result: LLMs diverge from human behavior regarding the influence of belief-update timing on positional biases. Additionally, primacy and recency biases are more exacerbated in newer LLMs compared to their predecessors.
AI.conclusion: The mechanism by which LLMs evaluate evidence differs from humans in how belief-update timing affects positional biases, and these biases have grown stronger as models have advanced, suggesting LLM evaluation mechanisms are not simply human-like.

title: The Impact of Temporal Context Length and Encoding Strategies on Self-Supervised ECG Representation Learning
comment: Accepted at the 48th Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBC 2026). 6 pages, 2 figures, 1 table
summary: Self-supervised electrocardiogram (ECG) models are often trained on a few seconds of ECG signal and, increasingly, on discretized token sequences. It remains unclear whether these choices sacrifice information needed for rhythm inference and longitudinal consistency in real-world ambulatory recordings. We present a controlled study on the Icentia11k single-lead dataset that varies (i) the input horizon (16 seconds, 1 minute, 5 minutes, and 10 minutes) and (ii) the front-end representation (continuous convolutional patch embeddings vs. fixed vector-quantized tokens), while holding the Transformer backbone and training protocol constant. Representations are assessed by downstream abnormal rhythm detection and by patient-level retrieval that probes cross-session stability. Our results show that increasing temporal context beyond 16-second snapshots yields stronger transfer and higher retrieval accuracy, with the strongest performance achieved by the 5- and 10-minute models, indicating improved capture of slow-varying rhythm dynamics and individual-specific structure. Across all evaluated horizons, continuous patch embeddings outperform discretized tokens, suggesting that quantization can discard clinically relevant waveform detail. These findings motivate ECG foundation models that emphasize extended context and continuous encoders for clinical prediction and similarity-based applications. Our code and pretrained models are publicly available at https://github.com/muha-0/ecg-ssl-representation-learning.

AI.tldr: A controlled study on ECG self-supervised learning shows that longer input horizons (5–10 minutes) and continuous patch embeddings outperform short snapshots and vector-quantized tokens for abnormal rhythm detection and patient-level retrieval.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether common self-supervised ECG modeling choices—training on a few seconds of signal and discretizing ECG into token sequences—sacrifice the information needed for rhythm inference and longitudinal consistency in real-world ambulatory recordings.
AI.method: The authors run a controlled study on the Icentia11k single-lead dataset, varying the input horizon (16 s, 1, 5, 10 min) and the front-end representation (continuous convolutional patch embeddings vs. fixed vector-quantized tokens) while holding the Transformer backbone and training protocol constant. Representations are evaluated by downstream abnormal rhythm detection and patient-level retrieval probing cross-session stability.
AI.result: Increasing temporal context beyond 16-second snapshots improves transfer and retrieval accuracy, with 5- and 10-minute models performing best, indicating better capture of slow-varying rhythm dynamics and individual-specific structure. Across all horizons, continuous patch embeddings outperform discretized tokens, suggesting quantization discards clinically relevant waveform detail.
AI.conclusion: ECG foundation models should emphasize extended temporal context and continuous encoders for clinical prediction and similarity-based applications. Code and pretrained models are publicly released.

title: Designing AI Pipelines for Decision-Ready ITSM Intelligence
summary: IT service management (ITSM) systems accumulate large volumes of heterogeneous ticket data that are difficult for sales and executive stakeholders to convert into actionable intelligence. This paper presents a sociotechnical AI pipeline, designed and evaluated following design science research principles, that transforms raw ITSM exports into a multilevel decision-support artifact. The pipeline combines LLM-based schema normalization, HDBSCAN sub-topic clustering, and hierarchical agglomerative clustering to generate executive-facing Main-topics and granular Sub-topics. A stakeholder evaluation across six artifacts and five raters from Sales Engineering and customer success roles shows that all four decision-support metrics, interpretability, actionability, trust, and likelihood of use, on average exceed 4.0 out of 5.0, with trust as the most consistent signal. The findings position ITSM analytics as an Information Systems (IS) problem of transformation, abstraction, and human-centered design.

AI.tldr: A design science study presents a sociotechnical AI pipeline that turns raw ITSM ticket exports into multilevel decision-support topics (Main-topics and Sub-topics) using LLM normalization and hierarchical clustering, with strong stakeholder-rated interpretability, actionability, trust, and likelihood of use.
AI.motivation: ITSM systems generate large volumes of heterogeneous ticket data that sales and executive stakeholders struggle to convert into actionable intelligence, motivating the need for an AI-driven artifact that transforms raw data into usable decision-support insights.
AI.method: The authors follow design science research principles to build a sociotechnical AI pipeline combining LLM-based schema normalization, HDBSCAN sub-topic clustering, and hierarchical agglomerative clustering to produce executive-facing Main-topics and granular Sub-topics. They evaluate it through six artifacts across five raters from Sales Engineering and customer success roles using four decision-support metrics.
AI.result: All four decision-support metrics (interpretability, actionability, trust, and likelihood of use) on average exceed 4.0 out of 5.0, with trust being the most consistent signal across raters.
AI.conclusion: ITSM analytics should be framed as an Information Systems problem of transformation, abstraction, and human-centered design rather than purely a technical data-processing task, positioning the pipeline as a validated decision-support artifact.

title: PatientAct: Theory-Grounded Mental Health Client Simulation
summary: LLM-based simulated clients are increasingly used to train novice counselors, evaluate LLM therapists, and generate synthetic data. However, current simulators produce overly cooperative clients that disclose too readily, accept therapeutic reframes without resistance, and resolve core issues within a single session. We trace these issues to profiles that lack causal depth and behavioral mechanisms that treat all content as equally accessible. We present PatientAct, a framework for client simulation grounded in established clinical theories. Our profiles integrate the 5Ps clinical case formulation, providing causal depth without tying the design to any single therapeutic modality. During simulation, profiles include a dynamic memory layer in which items carry trust thresholds (e.g., symptoms are available early, whereas formative memories require a sustained therapeutic alliance). At each turn, the client's emotional reaction and behavior are modeled before generating a response. If the therapist approaches gated content, PatientAct expresses resistance in terms of quantity, content, and style rather than defaulting to cooperation or a single resistance pattern. We evaluate our framework on 40 clinical situations and demonstrate that it generates diverse profiles with high clinical plausibility. Moreover, PatientAct significantly outperforms the baselines, yielding substantial gains in resistance quality and behavioral realism. Our code and data will be publicly available via github.com/Sahandfer/PatientHub.

AI.tldr: PatientAct is a client-simulation framework grounded in clinical theory (the 5Ps formulation and dynamic memory with trust thresholds) that models resistance in quantity, content, and style, producing more realistic, less overly-cooperative simulated clients for counselor training, therapist evaluation, and synthetic data generation.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based simulated clients are unrealistically cooperative: they disclose too easily, accept therapeutic reframes without resistance, and resolve core issues within one session. The authors attribute this to profiles that lack causal depth and behavioral mechanisms that treat all content as equally accessible.
AI.method: PatientAct builds profiles using the 5Ps clinical case formulation to give causal depth while remaining modality-agnostic. It adds a dynamic memory layer whose items carry trust thresholds (symptoms become available early; formative memories require a sustained therapeutic alliance). At each turn, it models the client's emotional reaction and behavior before generating a response, so gated content triggers resistance expressed across quantity, content, and style rather than default cooperation or a single resistance pattern.
AI.result: Evaluated on 40 clinical situations, PatientAct generates diverse profiles with high clinical plausibility and significantly outperforms baselines, yielding substantial gains in resistance quality and behavioral realism.
AI.conclusion: PatientAct provides a clinically grounded, realistic client simulation that improves over prior cooperative simulators, with code and data to be made publicly available.

title: Unified Multi-Dimensional Benchmark for Complex Graph Reasoning in Large Language Models
summary: Graph reasoning provides a promising testbed for evaluating the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs), as graph instances can be programmatically generated, structurally controlled, and naturally scaled to long-input settings. However, existing graph reasoning benchmarks have limited coverage of data complexity, rely heavily on manual construction, and lack unified evaluation across text-based and code-based reasoning modes. To address these limitations, we propose {\dataset}, a five-stage \textit{semi-automatic} framework for constructing complex graph reasoning benchmarks. It expands benchmark coverage along five dimensions: \textit{Graph Size}, \textit{Task Complexity}, \textit{Task Description}, \textit{Graph Loading}, and \textit{Task Source}. The framework uses an LLM-based data generator to automatically produce task descriptions, graph data, reference solutions, graph-loading scripts, question forms, and evaluation scripts, while retaining human validation at key quality-control stages. Based on it, we construct a benchmark with $202$ tasks and evaluate LLMs under text-based, code-based, and augmented reasoning settings. Experiments show that the complexity dimensions reveal model limitations that are less visible in existing benchmarks; existing fine-tuned models struggle to generalize to GraphGym, whereas retrieval-augmented methods show scenario-dependent adaptability, improving textual reasoning but not consistently improving coding reasoning. These findings suggest that ours serves as a challenging and diagnostic benchmark for graph reasoning and provides empirical guidance for future enhancement methods. Code and dataset will be published soon.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GraphGym, a five-stage semi-automatic framework that generates a complex graph reasoning benchmark covering five dimensions (Graph Size, Task Complexity, Task Description, Graph Loading, Task Source), with 202 tasks evaluated across text-based, code-based, and augmented reasoning modes, revealing LLM limitations invisible in prior benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing graph reasoning benchmarks have limited data-complexity coverage, rely heavily on manual construction, and lack unified evaluation across text-based and code-based reasoning modes. The authors aim to address these gaps to better test LLM reasoning ability.
AI.method: The authors propose GraphGym, a five-stage semi-automatic framework. It uses an LLM-based data generator to automatically produce task descriptions, graph data, reference solutions, graph-loading scripts, question forms, and evaluation scripts, while retaining human validation at key quality-control stages. The framework expands benchmark coverage along five dimensions: Graph Size, Task Complexity, Task Description, Graph Loading, and Task Source. A benchmark of 202 tasks is constructed and LLMs are evaluated under text-based, code-based, and augmented reasoning settings.
AI.result: The complexity dimensions reveal model limitations that are less visible in existing benchmarks. Existing fine-tuned models struggle to generalize to GraphGym. Retrieval-augmented methods show scenario-dependent adaptability: they improve textual reasoning but do not consistently improve coding reasoning.
AI.conclusion: GraphGym serves as a challenging and diagnostic benchmark for graph reasoning and provides empirical guidance for future enhancement methods. Code and dataset will be published soon.

title: A Contract-Grade Verifier for LLM-Generated GPU Kernels, and a Native Blackwell Backward for the Gated-Linear-Recurrence Family
comment: 17 pages, 3 figures. Also archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.21563213
summary: Systems that generate GPU kernels with language models report high correctness rates. Those rates come from a single loose test: run the kernel on a few random inputs at one fixed shape and accept it if the output is close to a reference. A kernel can pass that test and still be silently wrong. It can return an ordinary number where the true answer is a NaN or an infinity, differ from run to run, break when the shape changes, or accumulate in fp16 where the reference keeps an fp32 total. We build the instrument that checks correctness properly: a contract-grade verifier of twelve adversarial gates, each a property a correct kernel must satisfy, several of them tolerance-free, so no choice of threshold can explain a failure away. Aimed outward, the verifier audits 2,638 machine-generated kernels that a public system's own harness had already accepted as correct. It finds 39.5% broken beyond any tolerance argument and 62.1% carrying at least one violation. The field's standard test accepts 1,487 kernels the verifier rejects, against only 14 the other way. We defend the finding four independent ways: a 7/7 positive control, a threshold-calibration sweep, 98.5% agreement with the reference benchmark's own correctness code, and a stratified hand-audit. Aimed inward, the verifier judges a kernel of our own: the first native Blackwell tcgen05 training backward for the gated-linear-recurrence (GDN) family, including the reverse-state stage the field still runs on a fallback. We establish its correctness independently, against a double-precision oracle, and train five family members through it. The correctness signal behind reported progress in kernel generation is far weaker than the numbers suggest, and a set of tolerance-free contracts would close most of the gap.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a contract-grade verifier with twelve adversarial, partly tolerance-free gates to rigorously check GPU kernels, finding that the field's loose correctness testing dramatically overstates the reliability of machine-generated kernels and that stricter contracts reveal widespread silent failures.
AI.motivation: Language-model-generated GPU kernels report high correctness rates, but those rates come from a single loose test (running a few random inputs at one fixed shape and accepting near-reference outputs). Such kernels can still be silently wrong—returning ordinary numbers where the truth is NaN/infinity, being nondeterministic, breaking across shapes, or accumulating in fp16 where the reference uses fp32. The motivation is to replace this weak signal with a rigorous correctness instrument that cannot be explained away by threshold choices.
AI.method: The authors build a contract-grade verifier composed of twelve adversarial gates, each encoding a property a correct kernel must satisfy, several of which are tolerance-free. They apply it (aimed outward) to audit 2,638 machine-generated kernels that a public system's own harness had already accepted, and (aimed inward) to verify their own first native Blackwell tcgen05 training backward kernel for the gated-linear-recurrence (GDN) family, including a reverse-state stage, validated against a double-precision oracle and used to train five family members.
AI.result: Of 2,638 previously accepted kernels, 39.5% are broken beyond any tolerance argument and 62.1% carry at least one violation. The standard test accepts 1,487 kernels that the verifier rejects, versus only 14 the other way. The finding is defended via a 7/7 positive control, a threshold-calibration sweep, 98.5% agreement with the reference benchmark's own correctness code, and a stratified hand-audit. The authors' own GDN backward kernel is established as correct against a double-precision oracle and successfully trains five family members.
AI.conclusion: The correctness signal behind reported progress in kernel generation is far weaker than the numbers suggest, and a set of tolerance-free contracts would close most of the gap.

title: On the Expressive Power of Transformers
summary: Multi-layer transformers form the critical component of essentially all large language models (LLMs) in use today. Because of their ubiquity and computational capability, there is a rapidly growing body of work that aims to precisely calibrate the expressive power of transformers as language recognizers by comparing them against standard models of computation studied for decades by the theoretical computer science community. In this endeavor, circuit complexity has by and large emerged as the "correct" branch of computational complexity to analyze the expressive power of transformers; the reason is that parameterizing transformers by the various resources they use, such as attention and precision, leads to direct comparisons with different classes of circuits parameterized by resources such as type of gates, size, and depth. Here, we present an overview of selected results that delineate the expressive power of transformers using concepts and methods from circuit complexity.

AI.tldr: This paper surveys how circuit complexity has become the dominant framework for precisely characterizing the expressive power of multi-layer transformers in large language models as language recognizers, comparing transformers against classical computational complexity classes.
AI.motivation: Transformers are the core component of essentially all modern LLMs, yet precisely calibrating their expressive power is difficult. The motivation is to establish rigorous bounds on what transformers can compute by comparing them against well-studied models of computation, with the key insight that transformer resources (attention, precision) map naturally onto circuit resources (gate type, size, depth), making circuit complexity the "correct" analytical lens.
AI.method: The paper is a survey/overview that parameterizes transformers by the computational resources they consume (e.g., number of attention layers and numerical precision) and draws direct correspondences to circuit classes parameterized by analogous resources (gate types, circuit size, and depth). It collects and presents selected existing results delineating these correspondences.
AI.result: The overview demonstrates that transformers, when parameterized by attention layers and numerical precision, align naturally with circuit complexity classes parameterized by gate type, size, and depth, providing precise upper and lower bounds on transformer expressive power as language recognizers.
AI.conclusion: Circuit complexity has emerged as the appropriate branch of computational complexity for analyzing transformer expressive power, since resource-based parameterizations of transformers correspond directly to resource-based parameterizations of circuit families.

title: Understanding Backdoor Vulnerabilities in Vertical Federated Learning: The Gap Between Research and Practice
summary: Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) enables organizations holding complementary features of shared entities to collaborate and train models. In this setting, the initiator can withhold information about the learning task, while other contributors participate without exposing their local datasets, creating an asymmetric information structure aligned with growing privacy demands. However, this asymmetry is a double-edged sword. Among various threats, backdoor attacks are particularly concerning because VFL not only enables malicious contributors to poison the model during training, but also allows them to activate the backdoor at inference time to manipulate predictions. Although prior work has reported near-perfect attack success rates and proposed effective defenses, we find that most findings fail to hold under realistic conditions, exposing a fundamental gap between research and practice. In this paper, we present a systematic, practice-oriented study of backdoor vulnerabilities in VFL, revealing this gap in both methodological design and evaluation practices. We show that existing approaches overlook key practical constraints and therefore rely on unrealistic prior knowledge. Furthermore, these limitations have remained hidden due to poorly designed evaluation practices in the literature. To bridge this gap, we redefine threat models under realistic constraints, propose practical backdoor workflows, and introduce BVBench, a backdoor-centric benchmark that enables fair, practical, and comprehensive evaluation, preloaded with state-of-the-art baselines. BVBench provides strong evidence of the fragility of the current understanding of VFL backdoor risks and establishes a foundation for steering research toward uncovering practical vulnerabilities and developing more meaningful defenses.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically re-examines backdoor attacks in Vertical Federated Learning (VFL), showing that prior near-perfect attack results and defenses collapse under realistic constraints, then proposes practical threat models, workflows, and the BVBench benchmark to enable fair, practical evaluation.
AI.motivation: VFL's asymmetric information structure (task-hiding initiator vs. data-hiding contributors) enables both training-time poisoning and inference-time backdoor activation.
