Although prior work reported near-perfect attack success and effective defenses, the authors find these results fail under realistic conditions, exposing a gap between research and practice caused by unrealistic prior-knowledge assumptions and poorly designed evaluation practices.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic, practice-oriented study of VFL backdoor vulnerabilities, identifying overlooked practical constraints in prior methodological design and evaluation practices. They redefine threat models under realistic constraints, propose practical backdoor workflows, and introduce BVBench, a backdoor-centric benchmark preloaded with state-of-the-art baselines to enable fair, practical, and comprehensive evaluation.
AI.result: The study reveals that existing approaches rely on unrealistic prior knowledge and that their reported near-perfect performance stems from flawed evaluation practices. BVBench provides strong evidence of the fragility of current understanding of VFL backdoor risks.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes BVBench as a foundation for steering VFL backdoor research toward uncovering practical vulnerabilities and developing more meaningful defenses, bridging the gap between research and practice.

title: Multi-Layer Context Camouflaging: A Semantic Superposition and Contextual Lamination Framework for Malpractice-Resilient Online Assessment
summary: Contemporary online assessment systems rely primarily on browser lockdown, webcam monitoring, and behavioural analytics, yet remain vulnerable to attacks that extract the assessment content itself through screenshots, screen sharing, optical character recognition, and automated scraping. This paper extends the Multi-dimensional Spatio-Temporal Context Camouflaging Model (MSCCM) within the MARS (Multi-modal Assessment Resilience Suite) by introducing the Multi-Layer Context Camouflaging Theory (MCCT), a mathematical framework that protects rendered assessment content through semantic superposition. Authentic assessment content and synthetically generated camouflage are represented as a unified rendering while remaining recoverable only by legitimate candidates. The framework models the adversarial extraction process through an explicit extraction-channel operator and develops six coupled constructs: the Context Inversion Operator, Contextual Lamination Operator, Separation Channel, Human Readability Functional, Computational Ambiguity Functional, and Context Camouflage Tensor. Computational ambiguity is formulated using conditional entropy, yielding a closed-form expression that quantifies uncertainty during unauthorized extraction, while legitimate recovery is guaranteed through an exact filtering identity. We further establish theoretical properties governing ambiguity, camouflage density, semantic preservation, multi-observation leakage, and temporal multiplexing, and present a rendering algorithm with computational complexity and a pre-registered evaluation protocol. MCCT provides a mathematically rigorous foundation for behaviorally adaptive, accessibility-aware, and computationally resilient digital assessment by securing rendered assessment content while preserving readability for legitimate users.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the MSCCM model within the MARS suite by introducing the Multi-Layer Context Camouflaging Theory (MCCT), a mathematical framework that protects rendered online assessment content via semantic superposition, making it recoverable only to legitimate candidates while quantifying extraction uncertainty through conditional entropy.
AI.motivation: Existing online assessment protections (browser lockdown, webcam monitoring, behavioral analytics) fail against attacks that directly extract assessment content — screenshots, screen sharing, OCR, and automated scraping. The need is a defense that secures the rendered content itself, not just the environment around it.
AI.method: Introduces MCCT, which unifies authentic assessment content with synthetically generated camouflage into a single rendering recoverable only by legitimate candidates. It models adversarial extraction via an extraction-channel operator and develops six coupled constructs: Context Inversion Operator, Contextual Lamination Operator, Separation Channel, Human Readability Functional, Computational Ambiguity Functional, and Context Camouflage Tensor. Computational ambiguity is formalized using conditional entropy with a closed-form expression, and legitimate recovery is guaranteed via an exact filtering identity. The paper establishes theoretical properties on ambiguity, camouflage density, semantic preservation, multi-observation leakage, and temporal multiplexing, and presents a rendering algorithm with complexity analysis and a pre-registered evaluation protocol.
AI.result: A mathematically rigorous framework (MCCT) that secures rendered assessment content while preserving readability for legitimate users, with closed-form ambiguity quantification, guaranteed legitimate recovery via filtering identity, and established theoretical properties governing the constructs.
AI.conclusion: MCCT provides a rigorous mathematical foundation for behaviorally adaptive, accessibility-aware, and computationally resilient digital assessment by securing rendered content against extraction attacks while maintaining readability for legitimate candidates.

title: DIVE: Unlocking Self-Improvement in Frozen Language Models Through Diversity-Driven Skill Evolution
summary: Large language models (LLMs) cannot retain post-deployment experience without parameter updates. We introduce DIVE, a diversity-driven framework that enables frozen LLMs to improve by evolving persistent natural-language skills from task experience and verifier feedback. These skills encode reusable reasoning procedures, verification strategies, common failure modes, and output constraints and are both executed and revised by the same underlying model without access to a teacher model. Since natural-language skill evolution is a stochastic, non-convex search process, optimizing a single skill trajectory can overfit to sampled experience or converge to a suboptimal solution. DIVE mitigates this optimization variance by independently evolving multiple skill populations from bootstrapped experience, adaptively refining them through diverse transformations, and jointly selecting a complementary set of skills. Across six mathematical and logical reasoning tasks and multiple model families, DIVE consistently outperforms existing reasoning methods, prompt-optimization approaches, skill-development frameworks, and memory-based baselines. It achieves rapid self-improvement from accumulated experience, obtaining substantially larger performance gains with fewer rollouts than parameter-based methods such as SFT and GRPO, and prompt optimization with GEPA. Further, the resulting skills transfer across model scales and families, enabling smaller models such as GPT-5-nano to match or outperform larger counterparts, i.e., GPT-5, under conventional prompting. These results establish diversity-driven skill evolution as an effective, interpretable, and parameter-free approach to LLM self-improvement.

AI.tldr: DIVE is a diversity-driven framework that lets frozen LLMs self-improve by evolving multiple populations of natural-language skills from task experience and verifier feedback, then selecting a complementary skill set. It outperforms reasoning, prompt-optimization, skill-development, and memory baselines, achieving larger gains with fewer rollouts than parameter-based methods (SFT, GRPO) and transferring across model scales/families.
AI.motivation: LLMs cannot retain post-deployment experience without parameter updates. Converting experience into reusable natural-language skills is a promising fix, but skill evolution is a stochastic, non-convex search process, so optimizing a single skill trajectory risks overfitting to sampled experience or converging to a suboptimal solution. This motivates a diversity-driven approach that reduces optimization variance.
AI.method: DIVE evolves persistent natural-language skills (reusable reasoning procedures, verification strategies, common failure modes, and output constraints) that are both executed and revised by the same frozen model, without a teacher model. To counter optimization variance, it independently evolves multiple skill populations from bootstrapped experience, adaptively refines them through diverse transformations, and jointly selects a complementary set of skills.
AI.result: Across six mathematical and logical reasoning tasks and multiple model families, DIVE consistently outperforms existing reasoning methods, prompt-optimization approaches (e.g., GEPA), skill-development frameworks, and memory-based baselines. It achieves rapid self-improvement with substantially larger performance gains using fewer rollouts than SFT and GRPO, and its skills transfer across model scales and families (e.g., GPT-5-nano matching or beating GPT-5 under conventional prompting).
AI.conclusion: Diversity-driven skill evolution is an effective, interpretable, and parameter-free approach to LLM self-improvement, establishing a viable route for frozen models to retain and exploit post-deployment experience.

title: Federated Compositional Muon Optimizer for Matrix-Wise Models
summary: Muon, a more recently developed optimizer, is useful for matrix-wise models in AI areas. Although many works have studied Muon and its variants, these methods are still not particularly well-suited for hierarchical structured problems. To fill this gap, we propose an effective federated compositional Muon (FedCoMuon) optimizer to solve distributed matrix-wise compositional optimization problems. Specifically, our FedCoMuon optimizer builds on compositional gradient tracking and orthogonalized momentum. Moreover, we propose a variance reduced variant of FedCoMuon (FedCoMuon-VR) based on a momentum-based variance reduced technique. In theory, we analyze the convergence properties of our algorithms under the non-i.i.d. and non-convex settings. In particular, we prove that our FedCoMuon-VR obtains a lower sample complexity of $O(ε^{-3})$ for finding an $ε$-stationary solution than the existing FedMuon algorithms. Extensive numerical experiments on robust federated learning and task-distributed risk-sensitive meta learning show that our proposed methods are competitive with existing compositional baselines and achieve the best reported accuracy in several settings.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes FedCoMuon, a federated Muon-based optimizer for distributed matrix-wise compositional optimization, along with a variance-reduced variant FedCoMuon-VR. It proves an O(ε⁻³) sample complexity under non-i.i.d. non-convex settings and shows strong empirical performance on robust federated learning and risk-sensitive meta learning.
AI.motivation: Muon optimizers work well for matrix-wise models but are not well-suited to hierarchical structured problems. Existing federated Muon methods also lack efficient handling of compositional (two-level) optimization structures, motivating a new optimizer that bridges Muon's orthogonalized momentum with compositional gradient tracking in a distributed setting.
AI.method: FedCoMuon combines compositional gradient tracking with orthogonalized momentum for federated matrix-wise compositional optimization. The authors further develop FedCoMuon-VR, which incorporates a momentum-based variance reduction technique to lower variance and improve sample efficiency. Convergence is analyzed theoretically under non-i.i.d. and non-convex conditions, and both methods are evaluated on robust federated learning and task-distributed risk-sensitive meta learning.
AI.result: FedCoMuon-VR is proven to achieve a sample complexity of O(ε⁻³) for finding an ε-stationary solution, improving upon existing FedMuon algorithms. Extensive experiments show that the proposed methods are competitive with existing compositional baselines and attain the best reported accuracy in several settings.
AI.conclusion: The proposed FedCoMuon and FedCoMuon-VR effectively extend Muon-style optimization to distributed compositional problems, with theoretical guarantees and improved sample complexity, and demonstrate strong empirical performance, suggesting their suitability for robust federated learning and meta learning tasks.

title: Lines and Ladders: A Context-Aware Multi-Agent Framework for Large-Scale Retail Price Taxonomy
comment: 8 pages. Accepted in the Main Conference of IEEE ICMLA 2026
summary: Maintaining price consistency and executing an Every Day Low Price strategy is critical for global retailers. However, with catalogs spanning millions of active items, manual governance of price relationships is infeasible. Inconsistent pricing across item variants distorts customer value perception and cannibalizes sales. To address this, we present a scalable, context-aware Multi-Agent Framework designed to automate the construction of "Lines and Ladders" pricing taxonomies. Our framework employs specialized LLM agents to construct these coherent pricing structures by identifying key attributes, extracting multi-modal values, and applying hierarchical grouping logic. Evaluated on real-world enterprise data and deployed in production, our 3-Agent system achieves an F1-score of 0.83 for Lines, outperforming single-agent baselines by mitigating cognitive overload. The system achieves >90% precision and >75% recall in Food & Consumables, and 80.2% assignment accuracy in the unstructured General Merchandise catalog.

AI.tldr: A production-deployed, multi-agent LLM framework automates building "Lines and Ladders" pricing taxonomies for retailers, achieving F1=0.83 for Lines and high precision/recall across catalogs.
AI.motivation: Global retailers pursuing Every Day Low Price strategies must keep prices consistent across millions of items. Manual governance of price relationships is infeasible, and inconsistent pricing across item variants distorts customer value perception and cannibalizes sales, motivating automation of pricing taxonomy construction.
AI.method: A scalable, context-aware Multi-Agent Framework uses specialized LLM agents to construct "Lines and Ladders" pricing taxonomies by identifying key attributes, extracting multi-modal values, and applying hierarchical grouping logic. A 3-Agent system mitigates cognitive overload compared to single-agent baselines.
AI.result: The 3-Agent system achieves an F1-score of 0.83 for Lines, >90% precision and >75% recall in Food & Consumables, and 80.2% assignment accuracy in the unstructured General Merchandise catalog, outperforming single-agent baselines.
AI.conclusion: The multi-agent LLM framework effectively automates pricing taxonomy construction at scale, achieves strong production performance, and outperforms single-agent approaches by reducing cognitive overload, demonstrating viability for real-world enterprise retail governance.

title: EEG Decoding Using CNN and LSTM Network
summary: Motor imagery (MI) brain--computer interfaces (BCIs) have emerged as a promising approach for establishing flexible communication pathways between the human brain and external devices , particularly for individuals affected by stroke or neurodegenerative disorders. Reliable decoding of motor-imagery electroencephalography (MI-EEG) remains challenging because EEG recordings contain substantial noise and exhibit complex, weakly informative relationships with the underlying brain activity. Although deep learning provides an effective means of learning representations directly from EEG signals, its application to MI-EEG feature learning remains comparatively limited. This study introduces a hybrid deep-learning architecture that integrates a convolutional neural network (CNN) with a bidirectional long short-term memory (bi-LSTM) network. The CNN is used to learn high-level spatial and temporal representations directly from raw MI-EEG recordings, whereas the bi-LSTM models temporal dependencies and relationships among the extracted features. The proposed approach is evaluated using both a publicly available dataset and a privately acquired dataset obtained with an EEG acquisition system. The experimental results indicate that the CNN\&bi-LSTM architecture provides robust performance for both two- and three-class motor-imagery classification and demonstrates promising subject-independent decoding capability across the evaluated methods.

AI.tldr: A hybrid CNN + bidirectional LSTM deep-learning architecture is proposed for robust motor-imagery EEG decoding, showing strong performance on two- and three-class tasks and promising subject-independent generalization.
AI.motivation: MI-BCIs offer flexible brain-to-device communication for stroke and neurodegenerative patients, but reliable MI-EEG decoding is hard because EEG signals are noisy and have complex, weakly informative relationships with underlying brain activity. Deep learning can learn representations directly, yet its use for MI-EEG feature learning is still relatively limited.
AI.method: Introduces a hybrid deep-learning architecture combining a CNN with a bidirectional LSTM. The CNN learns high-level spatial and temporal representations directly from raw MI-EEG recordings, while the bi-LSTM captures temporal dependencies and relationships among the extracted features. Evaluated on a public dataset and a privately acquired dataset from an EEG acquisition system.
AI.result: The CNN+bi-LSTM architecture achieves robust performance for two- and three-class motor-imagery classification and demonstrates promising subject-independent decoding capability across the evaluated methods.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid CNN+bi-LSTM is a robust and effective approach for MI-EEG decoding, including cross-subject scenarios, advancing reliable brain-computer interface applications.

title: Intensional Anaphora
comment: 49 pages. Published in Semantics and Pragmatics
summary: Intensional operators are often treated as quantifiers over possible worlds, parallel to the treatment of determiners as quantifiers over individuals. Yet individuals introduced in intensional contexts cannot serve as antecedents to later pronouns as easily as those introduced in merely quantificational contexts. For instance, "Everyone is eating a cheeseburger" may be followed by "They are large", where "they" refers to the cheeseburgers being eaten. However, as Stone (1999) points out, the similar "Andrea might be eating a cheeseburger" does not support later anaphoric references such as "It is large" or "They are large". Stone (1999), Stone and Hardt (1999), and Brasoveanu (2010) address this by requiring a pronoun's value (its referents) to exist in the world of evaluation, ruling out anaphora from non-veridical intensional contexts. We show, however, both cases where such anaphora is disallowed even when the pronoun's referents clearly exist and cases where it is allowed even though they might not exist. We argue that intensional anaphora is best captured using a description-based rather than value-based account. A pronoun presupposes that its corresponding antecedent description is instantiated in each world of the context set. Thus, there must be a cheeseburger being eaten by Andrea in every candidate world for "It is large" to be felicitous after "Andrea might be eating a cheeseburger". We implement our proposal via a new logic, building on Keshet (2018) and Abney and Keshet (2022), called Plural Intensional Presuppositional predicate calculus (PIP). Each PIP formula translates directly into standard first-order predicate calculus with set abstraction, providing a classical foundation for this work.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a description-based (rather than value-based) account of intensional anaphora, arguing that a pronoun presupposes its antecedent description is instantiated in every world of the context set, and implements this via a new logic called Plural Intensional Presuppositional predicate calculus (PIP).
AI.motivation: Existing accounts (Stone 1999; Stone & Hardt 1999; Brasoveanu 2010) rule out anaphora from non-veridical intensional contexts by requiring a pronoun's referents to exist in the world of evaluation. The authors show this is empirically inadequate: there are cases where such anaphora is disallowed even when the referents clearly exist, and cases where it is allowed even though the referents might not exist.
AI.method: A description-based account is proposed: a pronoun presupposes that its corresponding antecedent description is instantiated in each world of the context set. This is implemented in a new logic, Plural Intensional Presuppositional predicate calculus (PIP), building on Keshet (2018) and Abney & Keshet (2022), where each PIP formula translates directly into standard first-order predicate calculus with set abstraction.
AI.result: The contrast between quantificational anaphora ("Everyone is eating a cheeseburger... They are large") and intensional anaphora ("Andrea might be eating a cheeseburger... It is large") is explained by instantiation of the antecedent description across candidate worlds rather than by mere existence of referents in the evaluation world. The description-based account correctly captures both the disallowed and allowed cases identified in the paper.
AI.conclusion: Intensional anaphora is best captured by a description-based account: a pronoun presupposes its antecedent description is instantiated in every world of the context set. The PIP logic provides a classical first-order foundation for this proposal, with each formula translating directly into standard predicate calculus with set abstraction.

title: Perturbation-based Regional Interpretability through Subtraction Mapping (PRISM): naming-error dissociations in language models and post-stroke aphasia
comment: 49 pages, 6 figures, 1 table. Supplementary methods, 6 tables and 5 figures included
summary: Mechanistic interpretability of large language models lacks spatially resolved, falsifiable tools for testing whether internal components are specialized for distinct cognitive operations. We adapt subtraction analysis, the standard framework of human neuroimaging, from biological brains to perturbed transformers, and apply the same logic to both substrates in parallel. Building on the Brain-LLM Unified Model (BLUM), which showed that layer-perturbed LLaVA-1.6-Vicuna-13B error profiles match the lesion patterns of aphasic patients, we develop PRISM (Perturbation-based Regional Interpretability through Subtraction Mapping). PRISM maps the seven clinical Philadelphia Naming Test categories, subtracts error classes pairwise, and treats each perturbation seed as a subject in a group analysis with threshold-free cluster enhancement along the layer axis. We run a structurally matched analysis on 213 chronic post-stroke aphasia patients using correlation-difference lesion-symptom mapping, and replicate both sides on held-out splits. The designs match in subject dimension (seeds, patients), spatial dimension (layers, atlas-parcellated cortex) and thresholding, but the contrast operator differs: a within-subject error-proportion difference for the LLM, a between-subject correlation difference for the cortex. Both substrates recover a robust phonemic-favoring dissociation, a deep layer cluster and a frontal-perisylvian cortical cluster, both replicating; the semantic-favoring direction is a consistently signed but non-significant trend on both. PRISM thus gives a falsifiable, spatially resolved test of functional-specialization claims in transformer language models. A confirmatory ROI-level intervention (PRISM Stage 3) licensing the strongest causal-mechanism claim is left to subsequent work.

AI.tldr: The authors adapt subtraction-based lesion-symptom mapping from human neuroimaging to transformers, developing PRISM to test whether specific LLM layers are specialized for distinct cognitive operations, obtaining a replicable phonemic-favoring dissociation paralleling aphasia imaging results.
AI.motivation: Mechanistic interpretability of LLMs lacks spatially resolved, falsifiable methods for testing whether internal components (layers) are specialized for distinct cognitive operations. The work builds on BLUM, which showed layer-perturbed LLaVA error profiles match aphasic lesion patterns, and aims to develop a rigorous, neuroimaging-style subtraction framework applicable in parallel to both brains and models.
AI.method: PRISM maps the seven Philadelphia Naming Test categories in a layer-perturbed LLaVA-1.6-Vicuna-13B, subtracts error classes pairwise, and treats each perturbation seed as a "subject" in a group analysis using threshold-free cluster enhancement along the layer axis. A structurally matched human analysis runs correlation-difference lesion-symptom mapping on 213 chronic post-stroke aphasia patients, with cortex parcellated by atlas and both sides replicated on held-out splits. Key difference: within-subject error-proportion difference for the LLM vs. between-subject correlation difference for cortex.
AI.result: Both substrates recover a robust, replicating phonemic-favoring dissociation: a deep layer cluster (LLM) paralleling a frontal-perisylvian cortical cluster (humans). The semantic-favoring direction is a consistently signed but non-significant trend in both. The designs matched on subject dimension (seeds/patients), spatial dimension (layers/cortical parcels), and thresholding.
AI.conclusion: PRISM provides a falsifiable, spatially resolved test of functional-specialization claims in transformer language models, yielding biologically consistent dissociations. A confirmatory ROI-level causal intervention (PRISM Stage 3) to license the strongest causal-mechanism claim is deferred to future work.

title: Sovereign by necessity? Frontier AI export controls, cyber security, and the limits of national AI capability
summary: A small number of firms based in two states produce the most capable frontier AI models. The governments of those states have shown both the legal power and the political will to decide which other countries may use these systems. In June 2026 the United States required a leading developer to obtain licences before releasing its most advanced models to any foreign person, including foreign nationals resident in the United States. The affected models were withdrawn worldwide at short notice, partly because the restriction proved impractical to administer. This followed within months of the first documented case of a largely autonomous, AI-run cyber espionage campaign, and coincided with mounting evidence that frontier models alter the economics of both cyber attack and cyber defence. This article examines how these two developments interact, and situates them within the unusual market dynamics now driving large-scale AI development. It argues that access to frontier AI is becoming part of national cyber defence, that such access can be revoked, and that the obvious remedy of sovereign capability remains only partly feasible for all but a handful of states. Drawing on evidence about training costs, the concentration of computing power and the support offered by national AI programmes, it asks what sovereignty can realistically mean for small and middle powers, and for large powers as well. The article proposes a layered strategy: negotiated access guarantees, sovereignty at the level of inference, hedging with open-weight models, pooled regional capability, sustained talent development and continued investment in basic cyber resilience. The open-weight hedge proves at once more capable and more politically exposed than is commonly assumed. Much of the near-term risk lies in how capable models are deployed and contained rather than in their apparent performance.

AI.tldr: Access to frontier AI is becoming a core component of national cyber defence, and is controlled by a small number of firms in two states that can revoke access. The article argues that full sovereign AI capability is feasible for only a handful of states and proposes a layered strategy involving negotiated access, inference-level sovereignty, open-weight hedging, pooled regional capability, talent development, and basic cyber resilience.
AI.motivation: Recent developments — a June 2026 U.S. licensing requirement that forced withdrawal of a leading developer's most advanced models from foreign users, the first documented autonomous AI-run cyber espionage campaign, and evidence that frontier models shift the economics of cyber attack and defence — show that access to frontier AI is becoming national cyber defence infrastructure that can be withdrawn. This raises the question of what sovereignty over AI can realistically mean for small, middle, and large powers.
AI.method: The article is a qualitative, policy-oriented analysis. It examines the interaction between frontier AI access and cyber defence, situates these dynamics within the unusual market structure of large-scale AI development (training costs, concentration of computing power, national AI programme support), and evaluates the feasibility of sovereign AI capability for different classes of states before proposing a layered strategy.
AI.result: The analysis finds that full sovereign frontier-AI capability is only partly feasible for all but a handful of states. It identifies a layered strategy as the remedy: negotiated access guarantees, inference-level sovereignty, open-weight hedging, pooled regional capability, talent development, and investment in basic cyber resilience. The open-weight hedge is both more capable and more politically exposed than commonly assumed, and much near-term risk lies in deployment and containment of capable models rather than their apparent performance.
AI.conclusion: Access to frontier AI has become integral to national cyber defence and can be revoked by a few controlling states; sovereignty in the traditional sense is unrealistic for most nations. States should pursue layered strategies combining negotiated access, inference-level and open-weight options, regional pooling, and resilience, while recognising that governance and containment of deployed models pose the greatest near-term risk.

title: When Explanations Betray Backdoors: Black-Box Auditing for Language Model Classifiers
summary: Language model classifiers with explanations are used for moderation, routing, topic triage, and low-resource annotation. We study black-box auditing when the defender has only clean calibration data without trigger information but can ask the classifier for a label plus a short rationale or quoted evidence. We introduce Groundedness Drift, a lightweight score measuring whether the answer summary remains grounded in the input. Across two 7B backbones, five datasets, and four common non-adaptive OpenBackdoor-style attack families, Groundedness Drift achieves higher AUROC and lower residual target ASR than every compared detector in all cases at a nominal 5\% clean-FPR budget. We then evaluate Unsupported Groundedness, a multi-probe escalation for explanation-camouflage stress cases. Unsupported Groundedness improves signals but does not close the adaptive gap.

AI.tldr: A lightweight score measuring whether a classifier's answer summary remains grounded in its input detects backdoor attacks on explanation-augmented language model classifiers more effectively than prior detectors, though adaptive attacks remain challenging.
AI.motivation: Backdoored language model classifiers that provide explanations are increasingly used for high-stakes tasks like moderation and triage, but existing black-box auditing methods rely on trigger information or clean-calibration assumptions that are unrealistic. The paper seeks a defense that works when only clean calibration data is available and the auditor can query labels plus short rationales or quoted evidence, without access to trigger details.
AI.method: The authors introduce Groundedness Drift, a lightweight score that measures whether the classifier's answer summary remains grounded in the input text. They evaluate it across two 7B-parameter backbones, five datasets, and four common non-adaptive OpenBackdoor-style attack families, comparing AUROC and residual target attack success rate (ASR) against prior detectors at a nominal 5% clean-FPR budget. They also introduce Unsupported Groundedness, a multi-probe escalation designed for explanation-camouflage stress cases, to assess adaptive attack robustness.
AI.result: Groundedness Drift achieves higher AUROC and lower residual target ASR than every compared detector in all tested cases at the 5% clean-FPR budget. Unsupported Groundedness improves detection signals for explanation-camouflage cases but does not fully close the adaptive adversarial gap.
AI.conclusion: Groundedness Drift provides a strong, practical black-box defense against common backdoor attacks on explanation-augmented classifiers without requiring trigger information, but adaptive attackers exploiting explanation camouflage still pose an open challenge that multi-probe escalation only partially mitigates.

title: MAG: MAnifold Guided Semi-Supervised Multi-modal In-Context Learning
summary: Few-shot in-context learning (ICL) with multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) enables task adaptation without parameter updates, but its performance is highly sensitive to the quality and coverage of the selected demonstrations. While unlabeled multi-modal data is abundant, it remains elusive how to exploit them for ICL. We propose MAG (MAnifold-Guided semi-supervised in-context demonstra- tion selection), an efficient framework that leverages unlabeled data to improve multi-modal ICL. MAG formulates demonstration selection as a semi-supervised propagation problem on a multi-modal graph and adopts a two-stage strategy: (i) relevance score propagation identifies a compact set of high-impact unlabeled samples for pseudo-labeling, reducing MLLM inference cost; (ii) multi-modal relevance is used to select the final demonstrations. We show that textual represen- tations are more effective for relevance propagation, while both visual and textual modalities are crucial for high-quality demonstration selection. Experiments on eight multi-modal benchmarks demonstrate that MAG consistently outperforms strong baselines in label-scarce regimes, achieving significant gains with a limited pseudo-labeling budget.

AI.tldr: MAG is a manifold-guided semi-supervised demonstration selection framework that leverages abundant unlabeled multi-modal data to improve few-shot in-context learning for multi-modal large language models, using graph-based propagation and a two-stage pseudo-labeling/selection strategy.
AI.motivation: Few-shot in-context learning with MLLMs is highly sensitive to the quality and coverage of selected demonstrations, yet existing approaches do not exploit abundant unlabeled multi-modal data. The paper aims to leverage this unlabeled data efficiently to enhance demonstration selection under label scarcity.
AI.method: MAG formulates demonstration selection as a semi-supervised propagation problem on a multi-modal graph with a two-stage strategy: (1) relevance score propagation identifies a compact set of high-impact unlabeled samples for pseudo-labeling, minimizing MLLM inference cost; (2) multi-modal relevance guides final demonstration selection. Textual representations are used for propagation effectiveness, while both visual and textual modalities inform final selection.
AI.result: Experiments on eight multi-modal benchmarks show MAG consistently outperforms strong baselines in label-scarce regimes, achieving significant gains even with a limited pseudo-labeling budget.
AI.conclusion: Unlabeled multi-modal data can be effectively exploited for in-context learning through manifold-guided semi-supervised demonstration selection, with textual representations being most effective for relevance propagation and both modalities being crucial for high-quality demonstration selection.

title: The Role of Natural Language Understanding in Multimodal Video-Based Dengue Diagnosis
summary: Detecting infection-related behavioral changes in mosquitoes from video data is challenging because mosquitoes are small, move rapidly and irregularly, and are affected by environmental factors such as background, lighting, and shadows, which can make reliable feature extraction difficult. In this study, a YOLO- and Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP)-based vision-language framework is proposed to classify mosquito flight frames of uninfected and Dengue virus serotype 2 (DENV2)-infected mosquitoes. First, YOLO is used to isolate mosquito regions from the background. Then, visual features extracted from video frames are aligned with biologically meaningful textual prompts in a shared embedding space. The multimodal model was fine-tuned using supervised bidirectional contrastive learning and evaluated through frame-level image-text similarity-based classification. The results show that the proposed method achieved 98.54% accuracy and 99.91% sensitivity at the frame level. After temporal aggregation of frame-level information, the model achieved complete video-level performance. The ablation results showed that fine-tuning and CLIP-based representations were essential for this domain, while the textual branch provided semantic image-text alignment rather than an accuracy advantage over the vision-only model. These findings suggest that vision-language models can provide a useful framework for analyzing infection-related biological behaviors from video data.

AI.tldr: A YOLO + CLIP vision-language framework is proposed to detect DENV2 infection-related behavioral changes in mosquitoes from video, achieving 98.54% frame-level accuracy and complete video-level performance, with fine-tuning and CLIP features being essential while the textual branch mainly enables semantic alignment.
AI.motivation: Detecting infection-related behavioral changes in mosquitoes from video is difficult because mosquitoes are small, move rapidly and irregularly, and are affected by environmental factors (background, lighting, shadows) that hinder reliable feature extraction.
AI.method: A YOLO- and CLIP-based vision-language framework is proposed. YOLO isolates mosquito regions from the background; visual features from frames are aligned with biologically meaningful textual prompts in a shared embedding space. The multimodal model is fine-tuned with supervised bidirectional contrastive learning and evaluated via frame-level image-text similarity-based classification, followed by temporal aggregation for video-level decisions.
AI.result: The method achieved 98.54% accuracy and 99.91% sensitivity at frame level, and complete video-level performance after temporal aggregation. Ablations showed fine-tuning and CLIP-based representations were essential, while the textual branch provided semantic image-text alignment without an accuracy advantage over the vision-only model.
AI.conclusion: Vision-language models provide a useful framework for analyzing infection-related biological behaviors from video data, with fine-tuning and CLIP representations being key to performance in this domain.

title: TopoIntent: Compiling Security Intent into Executable, Compliance-Checked Network Topologies
summary: Enterprise security topology design requires translating business intent, regulatory requirements, and risk assumptions into zones, boundary devices, inter-zone paths, and access-control policies. Existing NetOps automation tools mainly operate after this design is fixed, providing limited support for generating structured security topologies from underspecified natural-language requirements. We present TopoIntent, a system that compiles security intent into executable, compliance-checked network topologies. It uses a schema contract to constrain generation, retrieves reference architectures from a curated template library via dense-vector search, and applies staged fusion for intent-template alignment and security completion. The generated topology is checked against CIS Controls v8.1.2 safeguards visible at the topology layer, while unresolved cases are marked for manual review. Structural gaps are repaired through additive schema-preserving edits. The final topology is exported to Mininet scripts with kernel-level iptables ACLs, enabling executable reachability and allow/deny tests. Because no public benchmark exists for this requirement-to-topology task, we construct an evaluation set from reference security architecture diagrams. The retrieval set contains 22 templates and 44 synthetic intents across five scenarios, while the held-out set contains 7 templates and 14 intents from finance and government scenarios excluded from retrieval. On the held-out set, additive repair improves topology-visible CIS satisfaction from 0.78 to 1.00 in fewer than 1.5 rounds on average, and one feedback round raises the post-ACL policy pass rate from 0.78 to 0.88.

AI.tldr: TopoIntent compiles underspecified natural-language security requirements into executable, compliance-checked network topologies using schema-constrained generation, dense-vector template retrieval, staged intent-template fusion, CIS Controls compliance checking, and additive schema-preserving repair, exporting to Mininet with iptables ACLs for reachability testing.
AI.motivation: Existing NetOps automation tools operate after a security topology design is fixed and provide limited support for generating structured security topologies from underspecified natural-language requirements. The authors aim to bridge the gap between business intent, regulatory requirements, and risk assumptions, and the final zone/boundary/path/access-control design.
AI.method: TopoIntent uses a schema contract to constrain generation, retrieves reference architectures from a curated template library via dense-vector search, and applies staged fusion for intent-template alignment and security completion. Generated topologies are checked against CIS Controls v8.1.2 safeguards visible at the topology layer, with unresolved cases flagged for manual review. Structural gaps are repaired via additive schema-preserving edits. The final topology is exported to Mininet scripts with kernel-level iptables ACLs for executable reachability and allow/deny tests.
AI.result: Since no public benchmark exists, the authors constructed an evaluation set from reference security architecture diagrams: a retrieval set of 22 templates and 44 synthetic intents across five scenarios, plus a held-out set of 7 templates and 14 intents from finance and government scenarios excluded from retrieval. On the held-out set, additive repair improved topology-visible CIS satisfaction from 0.78 to 1.00 in fewer than 1.5 rounds on average, and one feedback round raised the post-ACL policy pass rate from 0.78 to 0.88.
AI.conclusion: TopoIntent demonstrates that security intent can be compiled into executable, compliance-checked network topologies, with additive repair and a single feedback round substantially improving both topology-level CIS compliance and post-ACL policy correctness on unseen scenarios.

title: A Cloud-Edge System for Multimodal Clinical Screening in Resource-Constrained Rural Settings
comment: 31 pages, 3 figures. In Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, Volume 340, 2026 (Machine Learning for Healthcare Conference)
summary: Medical AI has demonstrated specialist-level diagnostic accuracy, yet these capabilities remain largely inaccessible in resource-constrained rural settings where bandwidth is scarce, compute is limited, and clinical decision-making requires integrating heterogeneous modalities. We introduce a cloud--edge collaborative architecture that addresses these constraints: lightweight, domain-specific models on the edge transform raw medical data into compact structured outputs, while a cloud LLM synthesizes these outputs into clinical summaries. An LLM-based orchestrator dynamically selects diagnostic tools based on patient context, promoting comprehensive modality coverage without processing irrelevant inputs. We evaluate on 20 multimodal clinical cases spanning cardiac, obstetric, trauma, and screening scenarios under three simulated network profiles (500,kbps--5,Mbps). The hybrid system achieves 98--99% diagnostic tool recall with 92--96% precision, matches or exceeds cloud-only baselines on clinical accuracy, and maintains bandwidth-invariant latency (25--35,s) at 4--15x lower token cost. These results highlight the role of architectural design in enabling efficient multimodal integration and improving factual grounding compared to cloud-only approaches under deployment constraints.

AI.tldr: A cloud–edge collaborative architecture uses lightweight edge models to compress multimodal medical data and an LLM orchestrator to select relevant diagnostic tools, achieving near-cloud accuracy with far lower bandwidth and token costs under constrained rural network conditions.
AI.motivation: Specialist-level medical AI is largely inaccessible in resource-constrained rural settings due to scarce bandwidth, limited compute, and the need to integrate heterogeneous modalities for clinical decision-making.
AI.method: The system combines lightweight, domain-specific edge models that convert raw medical data into compact structured outputs, a cloud LLM that synthesizes these outputs into clinical summaries, and an LLM-based orchestrator that dynamically selects diagnostic tools based on patient context. Evaluation covers 20 multimodal clinical cases across cardiac, obstetric, trauma, and screening scenarios under three simulated network profiles (500 kbps–5 Mbps).
AI.result: The hybrid system achieves 98–99% diagnostic tool recall with 92–96% precision, matches or exceeds cloud-only baselines on clinical accuracy, and maintains bandwidth-invariant latency (25–35 s) at 4–15x lower token cost.
AI.conclusion: Architectural design plays a key role in enabling efficient multimodal integration and improving factual grounding compared to cloud-only approaches under deployment constraints.

title: Beyond the Best Guess: Improving LLM Solution Coverage with Evolution Strategies
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in discovery domains such as math and science. The usual approach is to present the problem to the model and use its answer as the proposed solution. However, beyond this best guess, discovery can be enhanced by increasing test-time compute. In a process called pass@k, the model is allowed to explore the solution space and generate diverse candidate solutions. Unfortunately, the standard approach to post-training LLMs through Reinforcement Learning (RL) may limit pass@k: the model's output distribution narrows around high-reward outputs, causing the solution coverage to collapse. The alternative is to use Evolution Strategies (ES), a population-based, gradient-free post-training method that optimizes directly in weight space through random perturbations. As this paper shows, ES achieves consistently higher pass@k than RL and produces a broader output distribution with greater solution coverage. This coverage in turn makes it possible to achieve better results in e.g. standard math benchmarks. Thus, ES provides a better foundation for post-training in discovery problems and other domains where diverse solution coverage is critical.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that Evolution Strategies (ES) outperform Reinforcement Learning (RL) for post-training LLMs when diverse solution coverage matters, as RL narrows the output distribution and collapses pass@k diversity, while ES preserves breadth and yields higher pass@k.
AI.motivation: LLMs used in discovery domains (math, science) benefit from exploring diverse candidate solutions via test-time compute (pass@k). Standard RL post-training optimizes toward high-reward outputs, which narrows the output distribution and reduces solution coverage, limiting pass@k performance.
AI.method: Use Evolution Strategies (ES), a population-based, gradient-free post-training method that optimizes directly in weight space through random perturbations, and compare it against RL. Evaluation focuses on pass@k and output distribution coverage, including on standard math benchmarks.
AI.result: ES achieves consistently higher pass@k than RL and produces a broader output distribution with greater solution coverage. This coverage translates into better results on standard math benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: ES provides a better foundation for post-training LLMs in discovery problems and other domains where diverse solution coverage is critical.

title: Novels generated by language models show compressed formal variation
summary: While large language models can generate entire novels, there is little information about the level of formal variation in their output over many generations. Rather than asking whether individual passages can be identified as AI-generated, this study asks whether repeated AI generation can produce the same range of diversity which is found across human corpora. This paper contrasts six corpora based on generation source and target style: twenty novels generated using GPT-5.5 Thinking in a nineteenth-century British realist style, twenty novels generated using Qwen3-14B in a nineteenth-century British realist style, twenty novels generated using each of these models in a contemporary zero style, 205 nineteenth-century human-written British novels, and sixty-five contemporary human-written Zero-Style novels. At the document level, the research includes MATTR-500, Shannon entropy, average sentence length, readability, and punctuation rate measurements. The most robust and reliable result is compression of sentence structure. Repeated generations produce novels that vary far less from one another in sentence structure than human novels do. Compression is also present in the measures of readability, punctuation, and sentence length variability within novels. Lexical measures tend to be similarly compressed, with the exception of Qwen Zero-Style MATTR. Despite having distinct mean stylistic profiles, GPT and Qwen lack a stable pattern of cross-measure correlation. This article therefore distinguishes between variance overclosure, which represents a limited formal range between novels, and a more specific phenomenon of correlational overclosure. This means that an individual AI-generated novel may resemble human fiction stylistically, while a collection of AI-generated novels occupies a much narrower formal range.

AI.tldr: This study tests whether repeatedly generating novels with LLMs (GPT-5.5 Thinking and Qwen3-14B) can reproduce the formal stylistic diversity found across human novel corpora. Key finding: despite distinct mean styles, AI-generated collections are stylistically "compressed"—they vary far less among themselves than human novels, especially in sentence structure—leading the authors to propose the concepts of variance overclosure and correlational overclosure.
AI.motivation: Prior work focuses on whether individual passages can be detected as AI-generated, but little is known about the range of formal variation across many AI generations. The study addresses whether repeated LLM generation can match the diversity observed across human-written corpora, moving beyond single-text detection to corpus-level stylistic variation.
AI.method: The paper contrasts six corpora defined by generation source and target style: 20 novels each from GPT-5.5 Thinking and Qwen3-14B in a nineteenth-century British realist style, 20 novels each from both models in a contemporary "zero" style, plus 205 nineteenth-century human British novels and 65 contemporary human Zero-Style novels. Document-level metrics include MATTR-500 (lexical diversity), Shannon entropy, average sentence length, readability, punctuation rate, and sentence-length variability. Analysis examines between-novel variance and cross-measure correlations within each corpus.
AI.result: The most robust finding is compression of sentence structure: AI-generated novels vary far less from one another in sentence structure than human novels. Compression also appears in readability, punctuation, and within-novel sentence-length variability. Lexical measures are similarly compressed except for Qwen Zero-Style MATTR. GPT and Qwen have distinct mean stylistic profiles but lack a stable pattern of cross-measure correlation. This motivates distinguishing variance overclosure (limited formal range between novels) from correlational overclosure.
AI.conclusion: An individual AI-generated novel may stylistically resemble human fiction, but a collection of AI-generated novels occupies a much narrower formal range. The authors distinguish between variance overclosure (limited between-novel formal range) and correlational overclosure, arguing that corpus-level diversity—not just single-text similarity—is the key limitation of repeated LLM generation.

title: Decentralized Multi-Player Q-Learning in Episodic Markov Decision Processes with Information Asymmetry
summary: We study decentralized multi-player reinforcement learning in episodic tabular Markov decision processes (MDPs) under three forms of information asymmetry: (A) unobserved actions with common rewards, (B) observed actions with independent rewards, and (C) unobserved actions with independent rewards. Players cannot communicate during learning but may agree on a protocol a priori. For Problems A and B we propose \texttt{mQ-learning} and \texttt{mQ-learning-intervals}, achieving $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{H^4 S A_{\text{joint}}\, T})$ regret, where $H$ is the horizon, $S$ the state count, $T = KH$ the total steps, and $A_{\text{joint}} = \prod_{i=1}^M |\mathcal{A}_i|$ the joint action space across $M$ players. For Problem C we give \texttt{mEXC} and \texttt{mEXC-Bellman}, two-phase explore-then-commit algorithms with regret $\tilde{O}(H (S A_{\text{joint}})^{1/3} T^{2/3})$. Against the centralized joint-action benchmark, decentralized learning under information asymmetry matches the single-agent Q-learning rate of \cite{jin2018q} up to logarithmic factors. Because $A_{\text{joint}}$ grows exponentially in $M$, the bounds are most meaningful for small $M$ or small per-player action sets.

AI.tldr: The paper studies decentralized multi-player RL in episodic tabular MDPs under three information-asymmetry settings and proposes algorithms achieving regret rates comparable to centralized single-agent Q-learning.
AI.motivation: Players in a multi-agent Markov decision process cannot communicate during learning but can agree on a protocol beforehand. The goal is to understand how different forms of information asymmetry—whether actions are observed and whether rewards are common or independent—affect the achievable regret against a centralized joint-action benchmark, and to design algorithms that match centralized performance despite decentralization.
AI.method: The authors consider episodic tabular MDPs with M players under three settings: (A) unobserved actions with common rewards, (B) observed actions with independent rewards, and (C) unobserved actions with independent rewards. For A and B they propose mQ-learning and mQ-learning-intervals, optimistic Q-learning-style algorithms with confidence intervals, achieving regret ~O(√(H⁴ S A_joint T)). For C they propose mEXC and mEXC-Bellman, two-phase explore-then-commit algorithms with regret ~O(H (S A_joint)^(1/3) T^(2/3)), where A_joint is the product of per-player action spaces and T = KH.
AI.result: Against the centralized joint-action benchmark, the proposed decentralized algorithms match the single-agent Q-learning rate of Jin et al. (2018) up to logarithmic factors. For Problems A and B the regret is ~O(√(H⁴ S A_joint T)); for Problem C it is ~O(H (S A_joint)^(1/3) T^(2/3)).
AI.conclusion: Decentralized learning under information asymmetry can match centralized single-agent Q-learning regret rates, provided players coordinate via an agreed protocol. The bounds depend on the joint action space, which grows exponentially in the number of players, so the results are most meaningful for small M or small per-player action sets.

title: Spatial Memory Agent: Experience-Grounded Procedure Memory for Spatial Intelligence
summary: Spatial intelligence is becoming a foundation for embodied agents, robotic planning, and multimodal assistants. To improve the spatial reasoning ability of VLM agents, existing work has mainly followed two lines. One line uses post-training methods, such as supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Another line adopts an agentic paradigm in which the model calls external spatial tools, such as depth estimation and 3D reconstruction tools, to gather intermediate spatial evidence. We study a complementary and underexplored route: Can a frozen VLM agent improve its spatial reasoning through \textbf{parameter-update-free self-evolution}, without depending on external expert spatial tools at inference time? We present \textbf{Spatial Memory Agent (SMA)}, an \textbf{experience-grounded runtime framework} that converts verified spatial experience into reusable transferable lessons. In a verifiable spatial environment, SMA queries the frozen VLM, obtains a predicted answer and reward, and uses \textbf{verifier-guided reflection} to distill compact transferable lessons from spatial experience. SMA further assigns each lesson a \textbf{Transfer Reliability Score (TRS)}, which is initialized uniformly and calibrated from later retrieval outcomes as visit evidence of future transfer reliability. During \textbf{read-only deployment}, SMA retrieves lessons by semantic filter and similarity-TRS combined ranking, allowing the retrieved memory to guide frozen model inference. Across five representative spatial benchmarks and four base VLMs, SMA achieves the highest macro average in every base-model block and the best accuracy among the evaluated methods in most of the 20 evaluations, establishing a practical parameter-update-free path for spatial self-evolution across the evaluated frozen model scales and environments.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Spatial Memory Agent (SMA), a parameter-free self-evolution framework that lets frozen VLM agents improve spatial reasoning by converting verified spatial experience into reusable, transferable lessons, without relying on external spatial tools at inference time.
AI.motivation: Spatial intelligence is foundational for embodied agents and robotics, yet existing approaches to improve VLM spatial reasoning rely either on post-training (SFT/RL) or on external spatial tools at inference. The authors target an underexplored, complementary route: enabling a frozen VLM to self-evolve its spatial reasoning through experience, parameter-update-free and without depending on external expert spatial tools during inference.
AI.method: SMA is an experience-grounded runtime framework. In a verifiable spatial environment, it queries a frozen VLM for a predicted answer and reward, then applies verifier-guided reflection to distill compact, transferable lessons from spatial experience. Each lesson is assigned a Transfer Reliability Score (TRS), initialized uniformly and calibrated from later retrieval outcomes (visit evidence) to reflect future transfer reliability. During read-only deployment, SMA retrieves lessons using a semantic filter combined with similarity-TRS ranking, and the retrieved memory then guides the frozen model's inference.
AI.result: Across five representative spatial benchmarks and four base VLMs, SMA achieves the highest macro average in every base-model block and the best accuracy among evaluated methods in most of the 20 evaluations, establishing a practical parameter-update-free path for spatial self-evolution across frozen model scales and environments.
AI.conclusion: SMA demonstrates that frozen VLM agents can improve spatial reasoning through parameter-update-free self-evolution grounded in verified experience, offering a practical and effective alternative to post-training and external-tool-based approaches across model scales and environments.

title: Excess Separability: Nuisance-Controlled Residual-Stream Probing for Benchmark Contamination Detection
comment: 22 pages, 11 figures, 7 tables. Code and artefacts: https://github.com/mabushi-lab/residual-stream-contamination-probing
summary:
Benchmark contamination is diagnosed today with n-gram overlap, with likelihood-based membership inference, or with canary strings, and each needs something usually unavailable: the training corpus, a well-chosen test statistic, or foresight at dataset release. A recent alternative reads contamination off a linear probe on internal activations. We show that the natural way to do this does not work, and specify one that survives measurement.
  The protocol reports a zero-sum contrast on the depth profile of probe accuracy, recentred on a level-matched placebo baseline, tested against a label-permutation null, with the reference set twice the size of the suspect set. Each choice replaces a simpler alternative we measured and rejected. Reporting the level of excess separability rather than its shape makes the false positive rate track the size of the analyst's own control set, from 0.03 to 0.99 under a true null. Contrasting against a flat depth profile fails in both directions, rejecting a true null 0.72 of the time when surface decodability rises with depth and losing all power when it falls. An item bootstrap holds the fitted probe fixed and rejects up to 0.09 of the time where a permutation null that refits it holds 0.02. A half-size baseline triples the error rate.
  On real transformers, baseline depth profiles are measurably not flat, spanning up to 29.1 accuracy points on a temporal split, and their non-flatness tracks the surface difference between the item sets (correlation 0.87 over 6 audits), so the correction is largest exactly where it is needed. All 4 well-matched Pile arms return null, and the protocol refuses a verdict on the temporal split rather than reporting one. What this does not establish is whether transformers carry a familiarity direction at all: the only positive sits on the split where exchangeability fails. Implementation, tests and audits are released.

AI.tldr: A linear-probe method for detecting benchmark contamination must use a zero-sum depth-profile contrast against a level-matched placebo, with a label-permutation null and a 2x reference set; simpler alternatives (flat baseline, fixed-probe bootstrap, half-size baseline) all fail under measurement.
AI.motivation: Existing contamination diagnostics (n-gram overlap, likelihood-based membership inference, canary strings) each require something rarely available: the training corpus, a well-chosen test statistic, or foresight at dataset release. A recent alternative reads contamination off a linear probe on internal activations, but the natural way to do this is flawed, so the authors seek a variant that survives measurement.
AI.method: The protocol reports a zero-sum contrast on the depth profile of probe accuracy, recentred on a level-matched placebo baseline and tested against a label-permutation null, with a reference set twice the size of the suspect set. Each design choice replaces a measured-and-rejected simpler alternative, and the method is validated on real transformers with audits of the Pile and a temporal split.
AI.result: Reporting excess separability level (not shape) makes the false positive rate track the analyst's control-set size (0.03–0.99 under a true null). Contrasting against a flat depth profile fails in both directions (rejects a true null 0.72 of the time when surface decodability rises with depth; loses all power when it falls). An item bootstrap (fixed probe) rejects up to 0.09 vs 0.02 for the refitting permutation null. A half-size baseline triples the error rate. On real transformers, baseline depth profiles are not flat (up to 29.1 accuracy points on a temporal split), and non-flatness tracks the surface difference between item sets (correlation 0.87 over 6 audits). All 4 well-matched Pile arms return null, and the protocol refuses a verdict on the temporal split.
AI.conclusion: The corrected protocol successfully avoids the failure modes of the natural linear-probe approach and returns null on well-matched Pile audits, but it does not establish whether transformers carry a familiarity direction at all, since the only positive sits on the split where exchangeability fails.

title: Beyond Outcome Rewards: Step-Level Self-Distilled Policy Optimization for Deep Search Agents
summary: Deep search agents operate over trajectories spanning dozens of steps, yet standard reinforcement learning provides only a single outcome reward per trajectory, which is far too sparse for effective credit assignment. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) addresses this by using the model's own logits as dense token-level teachers, but extending it to search agents introduces a fundamental tension: the teacher, having access to privileged information such as the correct answer, produces a distribution that differs systematically from the student's exploration-based reasoning, and naive distillation causes the student to inherit this information asymmetry rather than learn better search strategies. We resolve this tension through two contributions. First, we construct Evidence Anchors, which are concise, step-level evidence snippets extracted from the web, as privileged information that captures key reasoning steps without revealing the entire answer path. Second, we propose Step-Level Self-Distilled Policy Optimization (SSPO), which converts teacher-student disagreement into step-level advantage weights within GRPO, applied exclusively to incorrect trajectories. This design decouples what to update from how much to update: the outcome reward determines the direction of policy change, while the teacher modulates its magnitude at each step. Correct trajectories are left untouched, preserving their diversity. On Qwen3-8B, SSPO consistently outperforms GRPO across BrowseComp, GAIA, and FRAMES, surpassing or matching GRPO trained with twice as many gradient steps while adding only about 5 percent overhead per step from a single additional forward pass.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Step-Level Self-Distilled Policy Optimization (SSPO), which uses the model's own evidence-anchored logits as dense step-level teachers to improve credit assignment in deep search agents, outperforming GRPO on BrowseComp, GAIA, and FRAMES with only ~5% extra overhead.
AI.motivation: Deep search agents have trajectories spanning dozens of steps, but standard RL gives only one sparse outcome reward per trajectory, making credit assignment difficult. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers dense token-level teachers via the model's own logits, but extending it to search agents creates a tension: the teacher has privileged information (e.g., the correct answer) and produces a distribution that systematically differs from the student's exploration-based reasoning, so naive distillation causes the student to inherit information asymmetry rather than learn better search strategies.
AI.method: Two contributions: (1) Evidence Anchors—concise, step-level snippets extracted from the web that serve as privileged information capturing key reasoning steps without revealing the entire answer path; (2) Step-Level Self-Distilled Policy Optimization (SSPO), which converts teacher-student disagreement into step-level advantage weights within GRPO, applied only to incorrect trajectories. The outcome reward determines the direction of policy change while the teacher modulates its magnitude at each step; correct trajectories are left untouched to preserve diversity. Evaluation on Qwen3-8B across BrowseComp, GAIA, and FRAMES.
AI.result: SSPO consistently outperforms GRPO on Qwen3-8B across BrowseComp, GAIA, and FRAMES, surpassing or matching GRPO trained with twice as many gradient steps while adding only about 5% overhead per step from a single additional forward pass.
AI.conclusion: The tension between teacher privilege and student exploration in self-distillation for search agents can be resolved by evidence-anchored privileged information and step-level advantage weighting restricted to incorrect trajectories, yielding efficient and effective policy optimization that matches GRPO while using half the gradient steps at minimal extra cost.

title: Concept Drift Detection and Adaptive Retraining of Malware Classification Models
comment: To appear as a chapter in the book "Artificial Intelligence for Cyber Defense in Emerging Threats", to be published by Springer by early 2027
summary: Concept drift refers to changes over time in the statistical properties of data, as compared to the data that was used to train a learning model. Machine learning models for malware detection or classification are particularly susceptible to performance degradation caused by concept drift, as attackers constantly modify existing malware. In this chapter, we analyze two machine learning-based approaches to automated concept drift detection-a novel approach based on One-Class Support Vector Machines (OCSVM) and a previously-studied technique based on Minibatch K-Means (MK-Means). For comparison we also consider Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), a statistical technique for detecting changes in multidimensional data. We conduct an extensive series of experiments comparing the effectiveness of four learning models, namely, Multilayer Perceptron, Random Forest, Support Vector Machines, and eXtreme Gradient Boosting. For each of these models, we consider three distinct scenarios: A static scenario where no model retraining occurs, a periodic scenario where models are constantly retrained irrespective of concept drift, and a drift-aware scenario where models are only retrained when concept drift is detected. Under the drift-aware scenario, we analyze the tradeoff between accuracy and training efficiency using Pareto Front analysis. We find that all three concept drift detection techniques achieve classification accuracy comparable to periodic retraining, while offering substantially greater efficiency in terms of the number of models that must be retrained. In addition, drift-aware retraining based on our OCSVM technique generally outperforms the MK-Means and MMD approaches. Overall, these results provide strong evidence that we can accurately detect concept drift in malware classification models.

AI.tldr: The paper compares three concept drift detection techniques (OCSVM, MK-Means, MMD) for malware classification, across four learning models and three retraining scenarios. Drift-aware retraining matches the accuracy of periodic retraining while being far more efficient, and the novel OCSVM approach generally outperforms the others.
AI.motivation: Malware classifiers degrade over time due to concept drift caused by attackers constantly modifying malware. Retraining models constantly is computationally expensive, so there is a need to detect when retraining is actually necessary to maintain accuracy efficiently.
AI.method: The authors analyze three concept drift detection techniques: a novel One-Class Support Vector Machine (OCSVM) method, a previously-studied Minibatch K-Means (MK-Means) technique, and Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD). They evaluate four learning models (Multilayer Perceptron, Random Forest, Support Vector Machines, eXtreme Gradient Boosting) under three scenarios: static (no retraining), periodic (constant retraining), and drift-aware (retrain only when drift is detected). Accuracy vs. training efficiency is analyzed using Pareto Front analysis.
AI.result: All three drift detection techniques achieve comparable classification accuracy to periodic retraining while requiring substantially fewer model retrainings. The drift-aware approach based on OCSVM generally outperforms MK-Means and MMD approaches.
AI.conclusion: The results provide strong evidence that concept drift in malware classification models can be accurately detected, enabling efficient drift-aware retraining without sacrificing classification accuracy.

title: ERSkill: Evolving for Skill-Guided Adaptive Memory Retrieval
summary: While Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on long-term memory for persistent interactions, the retrieval mechanisms governing this memory are rarely treated as evolvable components. This static approach limits performance on heterogeneous memory queries, which often demand diverse evidence construction strategies. To address this, we introduce \textbf{ERSkill}, a retrieval-centric framework for self-evolving, skill-guided memory access. ERSkill compiles interaction histories into a structured memory store and represents retrieval behaviors as executable skills composed of fundamental primitives. At inference time, a trained router dynamically matches each query to the optimal skill to construct tailored evidence for answer generation. To enable continuous improvement, ERSkill co-evolves the skill set and the router during training. It employs an experience trie to efficiently record explored retrieval paths, alongside a double-frontier mechanism that safely decouples the expansion of new skill capabilities from stable, router-facing deployment. Experiments across multiple agent memory benchmarks demonstrate that ERSkill substantially outperforms strong non-evolving and self-evolving baselines. Notably, it improves the overall average across F1, BLEU-1, and LLM-judge scores by 31.3\% with Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct and by 28.1\% with GPT-5.4-nano.

AI.tldr: ERSkill is a retrieval-centric framework that treats memory retrieval as self-evolving, skill-guided processes. It compiles interaction histories into a memory store, represents retrieval behaviors as executable skills built from primitives, and uses a trained router to match queries to skills. A co-evolution of skill set and router, supported by an experience trie and a double-frontier mechanism, enables continuous improvement, yielding large gains over baselines on agent memory benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLM agents increasingly depend on long-term memory for persistent interactions, but existing retrieval mechanisms are static and not treated as evolvable components. This limits performance on heterogeneous memory queries that require diverse evidence construction strategies.
AI.method: ERSkill compiles interaction histories into a structured memory store and represents retrieval behaviors as executable skills composed of fundamental primitives. At inference, a trained router dynamically matches each query to the optimal skill to construct tailored evidence. During training, the skill set and router co-evolve, using an experience trie to efficiently record explored retrieval paths and a double-frontier mechanism to decouple expansion of new skill capabilities from stable, router-facing deployment.
AI.result: Across multiple agent memory benchmarks, ERSkill substantially outperforms strong non-evolving and self-evolving baselines, improving the overall average of F1, BLEU-1, and LLM-judge scores by 31.3% with Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct and by 28.1% with GPT-5.4-nano.
AI.conclusion: Treating retrieval as a self-evolving, skill-guided component enables LLM agents to dynamically construct tailored evidence for heterogeneous memory queries, leading to substantial and robust performance improvements over static and non-evolving retrieval approaches.

title: CoMedBench: A Multi-Source Benchmark of Synthetic Medical Data Fidelity and Downstream Utility
summary: Access to clinical data is essential for developing reliable healthcare machine learning systems, but direct use of electronic health records is constrained by privacy regulation, institutional review, data-use agreements, and the risk of re-identification. Synthetic data promises a practical alternative: it can preserve useful statistical and clinical structure while reducing exposure of sensitive patient records. Prior studies often evaluate a single generator, one dataset, or a narrow downstream task, making it difficult to know when synthetic data can support model development and when it fails to preserve task-critical signal. We introduce CoMedBench, a reproducible benchmark that evaluates a family of generators under a common clinical-validity framework and one shared training and evaluation engine, spanning static tabular and temporal downstream tasks on established critical-care datasets. In total the benchmark spans 37 dataset-task pairs across two modalities consists of 20 static tabular and 17 temporal ICU time-series-drawn from seven public data sources: three intensive-care databases (MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU) together with the UCI Machine Learning Repository, the CDC BRFSS diabetes cohort (2015), NHANES (1999-2014), and the pycox survival datasets (GBSG and METABRIC). The benchmark evaluates both statistical fidelity and task utility by comparing models trained and tested across real and synthetic data. In these settings, synthetic training data preserves most of the downstream signal: on tabular tasks the reference generator CoMed-CTGAN retains a mean AUROC utility (the synthetic-to-real performance ratio) of 90.6%, rising to 97.3% for the strongest generator, CoMed-TVAE. Temporal ICU tasks are harder and more generator-sensitive: CoMed-CTGAN retains 81.6% (AUROC) and only 64.0% under the imbalance-sensitive AUPRC, whereas CoMed-TVAE still retains ~95% (AUROC).

AI.tldr: CoMedBench is a reproducible benchmark evaluating synthetic clinical data generators across 37 dataset-task pairs (20 static tabular, 17 temporal ICU) from 7 public data sources, assessing both statistical fidelity and downstream task utility. It finds synthetic data retains most downstream signal, with CoMed-TVAE strongest (up to ~97% AUROC utility on tabular, ~95% on temporal), while temporal tasks are harder and more generator-sensitive, especially under AUPRC.
AI.motivation: Direct use of EHRs for ML is limited by privacy, IRB, data-use agreements, and re-identification risk. Synthetic data offers a way to preserve structure while reducing privacy exposure, but prior work evaluates single generators, single datasets, or narrow tasks, making it unclear when synthetic data can support model development and when it loses task-critical signal.
AI.method: Introduce CoMedBench, a reproducible benchmark evaluating a family of synthetic data generators under a common clinical-validity framework with one shared training/evaluation engine. It spans 37 dataset-task pairs (20 static tabular, 17 temporal ICU time-series) from seven public sources: MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, eICU, UCI repository, CDC BRFSS diabetes (2015), NHANES (1999-2014), and pycox survival datasets (GBSG, METABRIC). It evaluates statistical fidelity and task utility by comparing models trained and tested across real and synthetic data, using AUROC/AUPRC utility ratios.
AI.result: Synthetic training data preserves most downstream signal. On tabular tasks, CoMed-CTGAN retains 90.6% mean AUROC utility, rising to 97.3% for CoMed-TVAE. Temporal ICU tasks are harder and more generator-sensitive: CoMed-CTGAN retains 81.6% AUROC but only 64.0% AUPRC, while CoMed-TVAE retains ~95% AUROC.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic data can largely substitute for real clinical data in downstream ML tasks, but utility depends on generator choice and task type.
