AI.method: The authors model each human's personal space as a radial Gaussian-mixture field based on Hall's proxemics theory, then compute a robot-centric local cost over the robot's field of view. This proxemics-based reward is integrated into established DRL navigation methods and evaluated in simulation across multiple crowd scenarios, reward baselines, and crowd densities.
AI.result: The proposed reward consistently improves social metrics in simulation while maintaining competitive navigation performance relative to the compared reward models.
AI.conclusion: A proxemics-based, dense, interpretable reward formulation effectively enhances social compliance in DRL-based robot navigation in crowded environments without degrading navigation efficiency, supporting its practical applicability.

title: Polish Medical Visual Question Answering: Vision-Language Models Underutilize Visual Evidence
summary: We introduce a Polish-language medical visual question answering (VQA) benchmark, built from Polish Board Certification Examination questions for licensed physicians and dentists pursuing specialist certification. The benchmark comprises image-containing questions spanning diverse medical specialties and visual domains, together with a text-only question answering (QA) control set. We evaluate Polish-oriented, general-purpose open-weight, and commercial vision-language models. The task remains challenging: the best model achieves 79.0\% accuracy on the full VQA set, and only GPT-5.6 surpasses the approximate human reference on the subset with available candidate responses; all other evaluated models perform worse than humans. To assess visual grounding, we compare complete inputs with configurations omitting the image, the question, or both, and categorize questions by image importance. Models derive more useful information from the question text than from the image and perform worse on image-dominant questions. Across both QA and VQA, they nevertheless achieve above-chance accuracy from the answer choices alone, showing that non-trivial performance can persist even when key task components are missing.

AI.tldr: A new Polish medical VQA benchmark derived from Board Certification Examination questions is introduced; the best model reaches 79.0% accuracy, with only GPT-5.6 exceeding human-level performance on a subset, and ablations show models rely more on question text than images and can still score above chance without key components.
AI.motivation: There is a lack of medical visual question answering benchmarks in Polish, limiting the evaluation of multimodal models for non-English clinical languages. The authors aim to provide a challenging, multilingual-resource-poor benchmark spanning medical specialties and visual domains, and to diagnose whether models truly use visual information or merely exploit text and answer-choice biases.
AI.method: The benchmark is built from Polish Board Certification Examination questions for physicians and dentists, containing image-based questions across specialties plus a text-only QA control set. They evaluate Polish-oriented, general-purpose open-weight, and commercial vision-language models. Visual grounding is assessed through ablations: comparing full inputs against configurations that omit the image, the question, or both, and categorizing questions by image importance.
AI.result: The task is hard: the best model achieves 79.0% accuracy on the full VQA set. Only GPT-5.6 surpasses the approximate human reference on the subset with available candidate responses; all other models underperform humans. Models extract more useful information from the question text than from the image and do worse on image-dominant questions. Across both QA and VQA, models still achieve above-chance accuracy from answer choices alone, indicating non-trivial performance even when key components are missing.
AI.conclusion: Polish medical VQA remains a challenging task with a large gap between models and human performance for most systems. The reliance on question text over images and above-chance performance from answer choices alone highlight shortcuts and biases in current models, underscoring the need to verify genuine visual reasoning and language coverage in clinical multimodal evaluation.

title: When Your Agent Opens the Chat App: Agent-Controlled Search over Raw Chat Logs Rivals Structured Memory
summary: Agent-memory systems increasingly buy retrieval quality with structure, transforming raw conversation histories into summaries, embeddings, trees, or knowledge graphs before any question is asked. We ask how much of that benefit comes from the structure itself, rather than from competent retrieval over the raw history. We present ReFind, an agent-controlled search interface that builds no semantic structure at all: it leaves the conversation archive unmodified, indexes it lexically at turn granularity, and combines a generic iterative keyword-search loop with four chat-native controls grounded in empirical refinding work: session-aware rank fusion, local context expansion, temporal narrowing, and skipping already-inspected sessions. A separate reasoning stage answers from the collected evidence. Across a broad suite of conversational-memory tasks (single- and multi-hop QA, event ordering, and fact consolidation), roughly 2,800 questions on precise-retrieval and fact-tracking capabilities evaluated under the incremental multi-turn setting of MemoryAgentBench, ReFind attains the highest mean accuracy (58.2) of any system compared, above the strongest graph- and tree-based memory systems (HippoRAG 2, 53.2), all under a GPT-4o-mini backbone matched to every reused baseline. Controlled comparisons to single-shot BM25, a matched generic-agentic BM25 control, component removals, and agentic dense/hybrid variants separately support the roles of agent control, chat-native controls, and lexical retrieval. On LongMemEval-S/M, the same interface reaches 93.2 +/- 3.3 and 89.3 +/- 6.0 with GPT-5-mini. The results indicate that for precise, evidence-grounded questions over chat archives, much of the benefit credited to elaborate memory structures is recoverable by giving an agent controllable search over the unmodified record, with no LLM-based index construction at all.

AI.tldr: ReFind achieves state-of-the-art conversational-memory retrieval accuracy with zero semantic structure, using agent-controlled lexical search over raw chat histories — beating graph/tree-based systems — suggesting much of structured memory's benefit is recoverable through controllable search alone.
AI.motivation: Agent-memory systems increasingly rely on elaborate structures (summaries, embeddings, trees, knowledge graphs) built before questions arise. The authors ask how much of that benefit stems from the structure itself versus competent retrieval over the raw, unmodified history.
AI.method: ReFind is an agent-controlled search interface with no semantic structure: it leaves the conversation archive unmodified, indexes it lexically at turn granularity, and combines a generic iterative keyword-search loop with four chat-native controls (session-aware rank fusion, local context expansion, temporal narrowing, skipping already-inspected sessions). A separate reasoning stage answers from collected evidence.
AI.result: Across ~2,800 questions (single-/multi-hop QA, event ordering, fact consolidation) on MemoryAgentBench's incremental multi-turn setting, ReFind attains the highest mean accuracy (58.2), surpassing HippoRAG 2 (53.2), all under a GPT-4o-mini backbone. Ablations support agent control, chat-native controls, and lexical retrieval; dense/hybrid agentic variants underperform. On LongMemEval-S/M it reaches 93.2 ± 3.3 and 89.3 ± 6.0 with GPT-5-mini.
AI.conclusion: For precise, evidence-grounded questions over chat archives, much of the benefit credited to elaborate memory structures is recoverable by giving an agent controllable search over the unmodified record, requiring no LLM-based index construction.

title: Momentum as Residual-Driven Multiplier Correction for Deep Learning Optimization
summary: Momentum-based optimizers are widely used in modern deep learning, yet the relations among momentum recursion, update geometry, and acceleration remain only partially understood. We develop an $\textbf{A}$DMM-$\textbf{I}$nspired $\textbf{M}$omentum (AIM) framework based on residual-penalty variable splitting, which interprets momentum as a multiplier-like correction driven by the splitting residual. AIM recovers the exponential moving average of gradients from an ADMM-style multiplier update and separates two mechanisms that are usually intertwined in practical optimizers: the residual penalty determines the update geometry, whereas the approximation of the objective-related subproblem determines the acceleration form. Building on AIM, we propose $\textbf{R}$elativistic $\textbf{A}$daptive gradient $\textbf{D}$escent with $\textbf{A}$ccelerated $\textbf{R}$esidual (RADAR), which combines relativistic adaptive geometry, decoupled residual correction, and second-order momentum filtering to improve the update direction and momentum estimation. We establish stochastic convergence through a variance-perturbed Lyapunov drift analysis. Experiments on supervised vision learning, language modeling, and reinforcement learning show that RADAR achieves consistent improvements over strong adaptive optimizer baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper presents AIM, an ADMM-inspired framework that interprets momentum as a multiplier-like correction driven by a splitting residual, and uses it to derive RADAR, an optimizer combining relativistic adaptive geometry, decoupled residual correction, and second-order momentum filtering, with convergence guarantees and strong empirical results.
AI.motivation: Momentum-based optimizers are ubiquitous in deep learning, but the relationships among momentum recursion, update geometry, and acceleration are only partially understood. The authors aim to disentangle these intertwined mechanisms through a principled optimization-based interpretation rather than treating practical optimizers as ad hoc heuristics.
AI.method: They develop the ADMM-Inspired Momentum (AIM) framework using residual-penalty variable splitting. AIM recovers the exponential moving average of gradients from an ADMM-style multiplier update and separates two mechanisms: the residual penalty controlling update geometry and the subproblem approximation controlling acceleration form. Building on AIM, they propose RADAR (Relativistic Adaptive gradient Descent with Accelerated Residual), which integrates relativistic adaptive geometry, decoupled residual correction, and second-order momentum filtering. Convergence is established via a variance-perturbed Lyapunov drift analysis.
AI.result: RADAR achieves consistent improvements over strong adaptive optimizer baselines across supervised vision learning, language modeling, and reinforcement learning tasks.
AI.conclusion: The AIM framework provides a unifying lens connecting momentum to ADMM-style multiplier updates, cleanly separating update geometry from acceleration. RADAR operationalizes these insights and delivers robust empirical gains, suggesting the framework is a promising direction for designing and understanding adaptive optimizers.

title: FlashDrive: Flash Vision-Language-Action Inference for Autonomous Driving
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models promise to bring end-to-end reasoning to autonomous driving, but their computational cost remains far too high for real-time control. The core challenge is structural: VLA inference is not a single bottleneck but a cascade of four. Visual encoding wastes compute on overlapping video frames; language-model prefill recomputes context that could be carried over from the previous timestep; reasoning tokens are generated serially despite low entropy; and flow-matching denoising applies uniform compute to a non-uniform velocity field. Addressing any one stage in isolation leaves the others untouched. We propose FlashDrive, an algorithm-system co-design framework that targets all four stages simultaneously. Our key insight is that each bottleneck admits a distinct, lightweight algorithmic shortcut: temporal overlap enables streaming KV-cache reuse across frames; the low per-token entropy and strong intra-block correlations of driving-domain reasoning make a non-autoregressive diffusion drafter highly effective for speculative decoding; and the velocity field's structure---sharp at the endpoints, flat in the middle---permits adaptive step caching that concentrates compute where it matters. Layered on system-level CUDA Graph compilation and kernel fusion, these techniques compound. Applied to Alpamayo 1.5-10B with W4A8 quantization, FlashDrive reduces end-to-end latency from 717ms to 151ms (4.7x) while leaving accuracy essentially unchanged: minADE6@6.4s shifts by only 0.08m, minADE1 improves, and closed-loop collision and off-road rates improve in simulation. By raising a 10B-parameter reasoning VLA from 1.4~Hz to 6.6~Hz on a single GPU, FlashDrive moves end-to-end autonomous driving substantially closer to real-time deployment.

AI.tldr: FlashDrive is an algorithm-system co-design framework that accelerates Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for autonomous driving by targeting all four inference bottlenecks simultaneously, cutting end-to-end latency from 717ms to 151ms (4.7x) on a 10B model while preserving driving accuracy.
AI.motivation: VLA models promise end-to-end reasoning for autonomous driving but are too computationally expensive for real-time control. The problem is structural, not a single bottleneck: inference suffers from a cascade of four bottlenecks (visual encoding, language-model prefill, serial reasoning token generation, and flow-matching denoising), so addressing any one stage alone leaves the rest untouched and fails to deliver real-time performance.
AI.method: FlashDrive targets all four bottlenecks simultaneously with distinct, lightweight algorithmic shortcuts: (1) streaming KV-cache reuse across temporally overlapping frames for visual encoding; (2) a non-autoregressive diffusion drafter for speculative decoding, exploiting low per-token entropy and strong intra-block correlations in driving-domain reasoning; (3) adaptive step caching for flow-matching denoising, concentrating compute at the velocity field's sharp endpoints and skipping the flat middle; layered with system-level CUDA Graph compilation and kernel fusion. Evaluated on Alpamayo 1.5-10B with W4A8 quantization.
AI.result: FlashDrive reduces end-to-end latency from 717ms to 151ms (a 4.7x speedup), raising a 10B-parameter reasoning VLA from 1.4 Hz to 6.6 Hz on a single GPU. Accuracy remains essentially unchanged: minADE6@6.4s shifts by only 0.08m, minADE1 improves, and closed-loop collision and off-road rates improve in simulation.
AI.conclusion: By exploiting structural shortcuts across all four VLA inference bottlenecks, FlashDrive moves end-to-end autonomous driving substantially closer to real-time deployment, demonstrating that algorithm-system co-design can deliver near-7x speedups on a 10B reasoning VLA without sacrificing accuracy.

title: BavGround: A Benchmark for Regional Cultural Grounding and Dialect Competence in Bavarian
summary: Cultural evaluation of large language models (LLMs) often focuses on high-resource standard languages, leaving regional culture and dialect communities underrepresented. We introduce BavGround, a benchmark for evaluating Bavarian regional cultural grounding and dialect competence across English, German and Bavarian. BavGround contains 206 multiple-choice source questions across eight cultural domains per language, yielding 618 multi-parallel instances, with items covering both broadly accessible cultural knowledge and source-grounded regional knowledge from journalism, historical sources, and specialist literature. We evaluate fifteen 7B-10B open-weight instruction-tuned models and one closed-model reference. Strong multilingual models perform best overall, but performance drops on Bavarian items and source-grounded questions, indicating persistent difficulty with dialectal and localized cultural knowledge. We further show that conclusions depend strongly on evaluation protocol: raw answer-letter scoring, shuffled-letter scoring, option-text likelihood, generated-answer parsing, and semantic matching can produce different absolute scores and rankings, especially for regionally adapted models. Finally, an exploratory analysis of GENBA-10B checkpoints suggests that continued pretraining improves answer-content likelihood unevenly across domains, while dialect competence remains comparatively weak. BavGround supports localized, protocol-aware evaluation of cultural representation in LLMs.

AI.tldr: BavGround is a multilingual, multi-domain benchmark (English, German, Bavarian) for evaluating regional cultural grounding and dialect competence in LLMs. Evaluating 16 models (15 open-weight 7B–10B plus a closed reference) reveals performance drops on Bavarian and source-grounded items, strong sensitivity to evaluation protocol, and uneven gains from continued pretraining.
AI.motivation: Cultural evaluation of LLMs typically targets high-resource standard languages, underrepresenting regional cultures and dialect communities. The authors seek to fill this gap for Bavarian cultural knowledge and dialect, which are locally significant but under-resourced.
AI.method: BavGround comprises 206 multiple-choice source questions across eight cultural domains in each of three languages (English, German, Bavarian), totaling 618 multi-parallel instances. Items mix broadly accessible knowledge with source-grounded regional content drawn from journalism, historical sources, and specialist literature. Fifteen 7B–10B open-weight instruction-tuned models and one closed model were evaluated using five distinct protocols: raw answer-letter scoring, shuffled-letter scoring, option-text likelihood, generated-answer parsing, and semantic matching. An exploratory analysis of GENBA-10B checkpoints examined the effect of continued pretraining on answer-content likelihood and dialect competence.
AI.result: Strong multilingual models performed best overall, but scores dropped on Bavarian items and source-grounded questions, showing persistent difficulty with dialectal and localized cultural knowledge. Model rankings and absolute scores varied substantially across the five evaluation protocols, especially for regionally adapted models. Continued pretraining of GENBA-10B improved answer-content likelihood unevenly across domains, while dialect competence remained comparatively weak.
AI.conclusion: BavGround enables localized, protocol-aware evaluation of cultural representation in LLMs, demonstrating that dialectal and regional cultural knowledge remain challenging and that evaluation conclusions are highly protocol-dependent.

title: H-VAEP and H-xT: Valuing Offensive On-the-Ball Actions in Handball by Estimating Probabilities
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, 1 table. Accepted at the 13th Workshop on Machine Learning and Data Mining for Sports Analytics (MLSA 2026), co-located with ECML PKDD 2026
summary: Traditional player evaluation in professional handball relies on basic box-score metrics or heuristic indices, which fail to credit the multi-player build-up chain. While football (soccer) analytics has adopted Expected Threat (xT) and Valuing Actions by Estimating Probabilities (VAEP), these event-based action valuation frameworks have not yet been adapted to handball. In this paper, we present the first comprehensive adaptation and evaluation of xT and VAEP for handball, utilizing five seasons of tracking-derived event data from the Handball Bundesliga. We develop Handball-xT (H-xT) using a handball-native court zoning layout, demonstrating via simulations that it is systematically more robust than standard rectangular grids. We optimize Handball-VAEP (H-VAEP) by tailoring its feature space and selecting the context length to limit team-identity leakage. Our evaluation shows that H-VAEP yields exceptionally stable, discriminative, and intuitive player ratings that highlight build-up play. Finally, we release our complete code repository to help professional clubs deploy these models.

AI.tldr: This paper adapts two event-based action valuation frameworks (xT and VAEP) from football (soccer) to handball, using five seasons of tracking-derived event data from the Handball Bundesliga, introducing Handball-xT and Handball-VAEP, demonstrating improved robustness and player ratings, and releasing the code.
AI.motivation: Traditional player evaluation in handball relies on basic box-score metrics or heuristic indices that fail to credit the multi-player build-up chain, and no event-based action valuation framework (like xT or VAEP from football analytics) has been adapted to handball.
AI.method: The authors develop Handball-xT (H-xT) using a handball-native court zoning layout and validate via simulations that it is more robust than standard rectangular grids. They optimize Handball-VAEP (H-VAEP) by tailoring the feature space and selecting context length to limit team-identity leakage. Both models are built and evaluated on five seasons of tracking-derived event data from the Handball Bundesliga.
AI.result: H-xT is systematically more robust than standard rectangular grid zoning in simulations, and H-VAEP yields exceptionally stable, discriminative, and intuitive player ratings that highlight build-up play, with team-identity leakage limited by feature/context selection.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides the first comprehensive adaptation of xT and VAEP to handball, showing H-xT and H-VAEP offer superior robustness and player evaluation; the authors release a complete code repository to help professional clubs deploy these models.

title: Decomposition of Evidence, Contradiction, and Fragility in Perturbation Responses
summary: Perturbation methods explain model decisions by measuring prediction changes under altered inputs, but response magnitude tells us only how much a model reacts, not what that reaction means. The same magnitude can support the final factual-counterfactual difference, oppose it, or arise strongly along the perturbation path yet vanish at the endpoint. We therefore track how the contrast develops as paired inputs are progressively revealed, using the final contrast to interpret the trajectory. We introduce DECAF (Decomposition of Evidence, Contradiction, And Fragility), which routes aligned, opposed, and endpoint-null responses into evidence E, contradiction C, and fragility F. The decomposition preserves ordinary magnitude exactly, Abs = E + C + F, and is unique under endpoint-relative axioms. Across controlled vision and tabular settings, the three components track independently measured behavior. In a 72-model ImageNet-9 audit, we compare cases with nearly identical response magnitude but different independently measured behaviors. The largest DECAF component agrees with an observed behavior in 96.4% of cases, compared with 35.0% for magnitude alone. Changing only the reveal path increases total response by nearly 80%, yet evidence barely changes while fragility grows by more than 4x. On FunnyBirds and ImageNet-1k, short forward-only DECAF trajectories outperform the tested general-purpose attribution baselines. On a 1B-scale DINOv2 model, a short trajectory matches a strong gradient-based baseline with 4.75x lower wall time and 2.36x lower peak memory.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DECAF, a method that decomposes an input perturbation's effect on a model's prediction contrast into Evidence (E), Contradiction (C), and Fragility (F), summing exactly to the ordinary magnitude (Abs = E + C + F). DECAF distinguishes aligned, opposed, and endpoint-null responses along progressive input-reveal trajectories, enabling more meaningful attribution than raw magnitude alone.
AI.motivation: Response magnitude under input perturbation only indicates how much a model reacts, not what the reaction means: equal magnitudes can support, oppose, or vanish relative to the final factual-counterfactual contrast. Attribution needs to capture the semantic direction and endpoint relevance of a model's reaction, not just its size.
AI.method: DECAF tracks how the prediction contrast evolves as paired inputs are progressively revealed, then uses the final contrast to classify trajectory responses into Evidence (aligned with final contrast), Contradiction (opposed to it), and Fragility (strong during the path but endpoint-null). The decomposition satisfies Abs = E + C + F and is unique under endpoint-relative axioms. Evaluations span controlled vision/tabular settings, a 72-model ImageNet-9 audit, FunnyBirds, ImageNet-1k, and a 1B-scale DINOv2 model.
AI.result: The three DECAF components track independently measured behavior. In a 72-model ImageNet-9 audit, the largest DECAF component matches an observed behavior in 96.4% of cases versus 35.0% for magnitude alone. Changing only the reveal path raises total response by ~80%, yet evidence is nearly unchanged while fragility grows >4x. Short forward-only DECAF trajectories outperform tested general-purpose attribution baselines on FunnyBirds and ImageNet-1k; on 1B DINOv2, a short trajectory matches a strong gradient baseline with 4.75x lower wall time and 2.36x lower peak memory.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing perturbation response magnitude into Evidence, Contradiction, and Fragility yields a more accurate and efficient explanation of model decisions than magnitude alone, with strong empirical agreement, robustness to path choice, and substantial computational savings at scale.

title: Prompts in the Wild: A Large Analyzed Collection of Transactional Prompts in Code
summary: The behavior of contemporary generative Large Language Models (LLMs) is directly shaped by prompts, unstructured texts that describe the desired output and model behavior. In this paper we argue that prompts are linguistic objects that merit investigation in their own right. To this end, we collect 57.5K unique samples of prompts from GitHub. Specifically, we focus on transactional prompts: reproducible natural language instructions that are integrated into software. To enable the empirical, quantitative study of prompts, we introduce a structured ontology, capturing the properties of prompts as well as their formal and semantic components. Based on this ontology, we transform prompts from unstructured raw texts into richly structured linguistic objects. Analysis of these structured data reveals significant diversity of usage patterns across languages, domains, tasks, and modalities, in a typical Zipf-like distribution where some clearly prevail and others, more diverse, appear in the long tail. To validate the reliability of the ontology-based annotation of the prompts, we perform a comprehensive error analysis across all fields, providing a detailed assessment of annotation quality. We release the dataset together with a browsing and exploration interface (https://github.com/OnlpLab/transactionalPromptsCollection ).

AI.tldr: The paper treats prompts as linguistic objects worthy of dedicated study, collecting 57.5K transactional prompts from GitHub, defining an ontology to structure them, and analyzing their usage diversity across languages, domains, tasks, and modalities.
AI.motivation: Prompts directly shape modern LLM behavior but are under-studied as linguistic artifacts in their own right. The authors argue for empirical, quantitative study of prompts, especially transactional prompts (reproducible instructions embedded in software), which are currently lacking structured data and analytical frameworks.
AI.method: The authors collect 57.5K unique transactional prompt samples from GitHub, introduce a structured ontology capturing prompt properties and their formal/semantic components, transform raw unstructured prompts into richly structured linguistic objects using this ontology, and analyze the resulting data across dimensions including language, domain, task, and modality. They also perform a comprehensive error analysis to validate annotation reliability.
AI.result: Analysis reveals a Zipf-like distribution of prompt usage patterns, where some languages, domains, tasks, and modalities clearly dominate while more diverse patterns appear in the long tail. The ontology-based annotation is validated through error analysis, with the dataset and a browsing/exploration interface publicly released.
AI.conclusion: Prompts are legitimate linguistic objects deserving systematic empirical study. The released dataset and ontology provide a foundation for the quantitative analysis of transactional prompts, enabling deeper understanding of how prompts are used to shape LLM behavior in real-world software.

title: Multi-perspective Imbalance-Conscious 6G Beamforming Optimization and Performance
summary: The study presents a systematic machine learning (ML) study of 6G-IoT beamforming optimization (6GBO) using supervised and unsupervised approaches. We compared the predictive power of network, environmental, device, and vision feature groups for 6GBO. Additionally, it addressed other unsupervised perspectives that can enhance 6GBO, including clustering network scenarios using methods such as K-means, DBSCAN, and hierarchical clustering. Several imbalance-aware experiments revealed that network features possess better prediction power than device, environmental, and vision feature groups, as evidenced by their recall, F1-score and ROC-AUC values. For unsupervised ML exploration (assessed using Elbow, Silhouette score, and Davies-Bouldin Index methods), the results indicate that the deployment environment and type of device primarily influence clustering, rather than mobility-based attributes. Furthermore, the explainability analysis showed that bandwidth, IoT sensors, and mobility possess higher global feature importance across the feature groups. In the future, we would apply deep and reinforcement learning techniques to predict throughput/latency or to optimize rewards determined by performance indicators like SNR enhancement

AI.tldr: A systematic machine learning study of 6G-IoT beamforming optimization compares supervised and unsupervised methods, finding network features most predictive, with environment and device type driving clustering, and plans future deep/reinforcement learning work.
AI.motivation: The work seeks to systematically understand which feature groups (network, environmental, device, vision) best predict 6G-IoT beamforming optimization (6GBO) performance, and to explore unsupervised perspectives (clustering) that can further enhance 6GBO.
AI.method: Supervised ML comparing the predictive power of four feature groups (network, environmental, device, vision), evaluated via recall, F1-score, and ROC-AUC, including imbalance-aware experiments. Unsupervised ML using K-means, DBSCAN, and hierarchical clustering, assessed with Elbow, Silhouette score, and Davies-Bouldin Index. Explainability analysis of global feature importance across feature groups.
AI.result: Network features showed the best predictive power over device, environmental, and vision groups based on recall, F1-score, and ROC-AUC. Clustering was primarily influenced by deployment environment and device type rather than mobility-based attributes. Bandwidth, IoT sensors, and mobility had higher global feature importance across groups.
AI.conclusion: Network features dominate prediction for 6GBO, environment and device type drive clustering, and key features (bandwidth, IoT sensors, mobility) matter most. Future work will apply deep learning and reinforcement learning to predict throughput/latency or optimize rewards from performance indicators such as SNR enhancement.

title: Moose: Latent concept learning with reasoning-shortcut awareness in $\mathcal{EL}^{++}$
summary: The OWL 2 EL profile is used in some of the largest production ontologies, including the Gene Ontology and SNOMED CT. Existing neuro-symbolic (NeSy) learning methods accept propositional theories or Datalog, and reasoning-shortcut (RS) awareness has not been investigated in ontology settings. We present Moose, a method that compiles an $\mathcal{EL}^{++}$ TBox and finite ABox to a Sentential Decision Diagram (SDD). The SDD acts as a differentiable weighted-model-counting layer, and we add closure clauses outside the $\mathcal{EL}^{++}$ profile on declared exhaustive families to overcome the limited expressivity of $\mathcal{EL}^{++}$ under partial supervision. We show termination, soundness, completeness, and polynomial intermediate sizes, and validate the proofs in Lean. We then define the first formal partial-supervision latent-concept-learning task over an OWL EL ontology, i.e., learning per-individual classifiers for latent concepts from observed ABox literals, and evaluate Moose on MNIST-with-ontology and Pizzaïolo. Moose improves over propositional-NeSy, fuzzy-logic, and ontology embedding baselines, and presents the first reasoning-shortcut analysis in an OWL EL setting.

AI.tldr: Moose compiles an OWL 2 EL (EL++) ontology into a Sentential Decision Diagram (SDD) usable as a differentiable weighted-model-counting layer, enabling neuron-symbolic learning of latent concepts over ontologies with formal guarantees and improved performance.
AI.motivation: OWL 2 EL is widely used in large production ontologies (e.g., Gene Ontology, SNOMED CT), but existing neuro-symbolic (NeSy) methods only support propositional theories or Datalog, and reasoning-shortcut awareness has not been studied in ontology settings. The paper aims to bridge this gap by enabling latent-concept learning directly over EL ontologies under partial supervision.
AI.method: Moose compiles an EL++ TBox and a finite ABox into an SDD, which serves as a differentiable weighted-model-counting layer. It adds closure clauses (outside the EL++ profile) on declared exhaustive families to overcome EL++'s limited expressivity under partial supervision. The authors prove termination, soundness, completeness, and polynomial intermediate sizes, with proofs validated in the Lean theorem prover. They define the first formal partial-supervision latent-concept-learning task over an OWL EL ontology and evaluate on MNIST-with-ontology and Pizzaïolo benchmarks.
AI.result: Moose outperforms propositional-NeSy, fuzzy-logic, and ontology-embedding baselines, and presents the first reasoning-shortcut analysis in an OWL EL setting.
AI.conclusion: Moose successfully extends neuro-symbolic learning to OWL 2 EL ontologies with formal correctness guarantees, overcoming expressivity limits via closure clauses, and demonstrates superior performance and the first reasoning-shortcut analysis in this setting.

title: Decoupled Contrastive Decoding via Expert-Aligned Drafting
summary: Contrastive Decoding (CD) improves generation quality, but its amateur-model pass makes decoding expensive. Accelerating CD with speculative decoding raises a proposal-alignment question: should the contrastive signal shape the drafter, or should it remain only in verification? We study this question in the lightweight feature-level drafter regime. Two controlled diagnostics, matched Cross-alpha training and an Approximate Dual-Drafter decomposition, give the same diagnosis: contrastive-aware drafting does not consistently improve over expert-aligned drafting because the contrastive correction is usually weaker than drafter error, and reconstruction can amplify that error. We introduce Decoupled Contrastive Decoding (DCD), which drafts with an expert-aligned lightweight proposer and applies the amateur only in unchanged CD verification. Standard speculative verification preserves the vanilla-CD output distribution. Across the main 8B settings, EAGLE3-based DCD achieves average greedy speedups of 1.65 to 1.95x over vanilla CD and reduces MMLU proposal-path latency by about 5 to 12x relative to amateur-coupled proposal paths.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies that integrating the contrastive (amateur) signal into the drafter for fast Contrastive Decoding is unnecessary and often harmful. It proposes Decoupled Contrastive Decoding (DCD), which drafts with an expert-aligned lightweight proposer and applies the amateur model only during unchanged CD verification, yielding 1.65–1.95x speedups over vanilla CD.
AI.motivation: Contrastive Decoding improves generation quality but is expensive due to the amateur-model pass. Accelerating CD with speculative decoding raises an open design question: should the contrastive signal shape the drafter (contrastive-aware drafting) or remain only in verification? The authors aim to determine which option works better in the lightweight feature-level drafter regime.
AI.method: Two controlled diagnostics are used: (1) matched Cross-alpha training and (2) an Approximate Dual-Drafter decomposition, both yielding the same diagnosis. Based on this, the authors introduce Decoupled Contrastive Decoding (DCD), which uses an expert-aligned lightweight proposer for drafting and applies the amateur model only in the unchanged CD verification step. Standard speculative verification is shown to preserve the vanilla-CD output distribution.
AI.result: The diagnostics show contrastive-aware drafting does not consistently beat expert-aligned drafting because the contrastive correction is usually weaker than drafter error, and reconstruction can amplify that error. On main 8B settings, EAGLE3-based DCD achieves average greedy speedups of 1.65–1.95x over vanilla CD and reduces MMLU proposal-path latency by about 5–12x compared to amateur-coupled proposal paths.
AI.conclusion: For lightweight feature-level drafters, the contrastive signal should remain in verification rather than shape the drafter. Decoupled Contrastive Decoding (DCD) provides substantial speedups over vanilla Contrastive Decoding while preserving its output distribution and avoiding the error amplification seen in contrastive-aware drafting.

title: Diagnosing JEPA World Models with Action-Conditioned Predictive Consistency
summary: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models that predict in a compact latent space rather than in pixels, reducing the pressure to model nuisance appearance. Yet this provides no guarantee against visual perturbations: they can still alter the encoded representation and affect subsequent action-conditioned predictions. Bisimulation captures this requirement precisely: two observations should be treated as the same state only when their action-conditioned consequences agree. Guided by this criterion, we introduce Action-Conditioned Predictive Consistency (ACPC), a diagnostic that measures how far a clean history and a visually perturbed view of it diverge after being rolled forward under the same action sequence. We prove that this divergence bounds the perturbation-induced change in multi-step prediction error and planner cost. Building on pairwise ACPC, we define two complementary measures: the Invariance Radius (IR) summarizes clean-perturbed rollout spread, while the Separation Rate (SR) checks whether different states remain distinguishable after rollout. Experiments on four visual control tasks show that pairwise ACPC predicts perturbation-induced prediction and cost changes. On LeWM, the IR-SR screen transfers across tasks, and the joint diagnostic remains informative under blur and resize. PLDM exhibits similar diagnostic trends under a different architecture.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Action-Conditioned Predictive Consistency (ACPC), a diagnostic that measures divergence between a clean history and a visually perturbed view after both are rolled forward under the same action sequence. It proves this divergence bounds perturbation-induced changes in prediction error and planner cost, and defines two derived measures, Invariance Radius (IR) and Separation Rate (SR), validated on four visual control tasks.
AI.motivation: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models in compact latent space, reducing pressure to model nuisance appearance, but they provide no guarantee against visual perturbations, which can still alter encoded representations and affect action-conditioned predictions. Bisimulation formalizes the needed requirement: two observations should map to the same state only when their action-conditioned consequences agree. The work seeks a principled diagnostic to quantify this perturbation robustness.
AI.method: The authors define ACPC, a diagnostic measuring how far a clean history and a perturbed view diverge after being rolled forward under identical action sequences. They prove that this divergence upper-bounds the perturbation-induced change in multi-step prediction error and planner cost. From pairwise ACPC they derive two complementary measures: Invariance Radius (IR), summarizing clean-perturbed rollout spread, and Separation Rate (SR), checking whether different states remain distinguishable after rollout. Experiments run on four visual control tasks, evaluating LeWM and PLDM architectures under blur and resize perturbations.
AI.result: Pairwise ACPC successfully predicts perturbation-induced prediction error and cost changes on four visual control tasks. On LeWM, the IR-SR screen transfers across tasks, and the joint diagnostic stays informative under blur and resize. PLDM exhibits similar diagnostic trends despite a different architecture.
AI.conclusion: ACPC provides a theoretically grounded, bisimulation-inspired diagnostic for evaluating visual perturbation robustness in joint-embedding world models, with IR and SR offering complementary summary statistics that hold predictive value across tasks and architectures.

title: Unifying Depth and Width Pruning for LLMs via Binary Knapsack Optimization
summary: Structured pruning is a promising approach for compressing large language models (LLMs), yet existing methods rely heavily on greedy heuristics that produce myopic decisions, and often fail to precisely meet target compression budgets. We present SNIPER, a two-stage structured pruning framework that solves a knapsack optimization over coarse-granularity components to yield conditionally optimal parameter allocations with respect to fixed importance estimates, followed by a fine-grained pruning stage to meet strict budget constraints. We introduce the Compression Ratio Adherence Factor (CRAFT) to quantify budget fidelity, showing that while existing pruners deviate from target compression ratios by up to 33%, SNIPER achieves near-exact adherence with a CRAFT score of 0.98. Evaluations across four diverse architectures over a set of 18 tasks spanning five domains demonstrate SNIPER's consistent improvements in average performance retention and task-level stability over six state-of-the-art pruners. Across all pruning configurations, SNIPER achieves an excellent mean rank of 1.25, indicating its robust cross-architectural generalizability and excellent reliability.

AI.tldr: SNIPER is a two-stage structured pruning framework for LLMs that uses knapsack optimization for coarse allocation and fine-grained pruning for strict budget adherence, outperforming six SOTA pruners across 18 tasks and four architectures.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM structured pruning methods rely on greedy heuristics that make myopic (locally optimal but globally suboptimal) decisions and frequently fail to precisely meet target compression budgets, reducing reliability and downstream performance.
AI.method: SNIPER is a two-stage framework: (1) it solves a knapsack optimization over coarse-granularity components to produce conditionally optimal parameter allocations given fixed importance estimates; (2) it applies a fine-grained pruning stage to satisfy strict budget constraints. It also introduces CRAFT (Compression Ratio Adherence Factor) to measure budget fidelity.
AI.result: Existing pruners deviate from target compression ratios by up to 33%, while SNIPER achieves near-exact adherence (CRAFT = 0.98). Across four architectures, 18 tasks, and five domains, SNIPER shows consistent gains in average performance retention and task-level stability over six SOTA pruners, with a mean rank of 1.25 across all configurations.
AI.conclusion: SNIPER provides robust cross-architectural generalization and reliability, precisely meeting compression budgets while delivering stable performance, making it a strong alternative to greedy heuristic-based pruning methods.

title: CardioState-JEPA: Delay-Aware Cross-Modal Learning of a Shared Cardiac Representation
summary: Electrocardiography (ECG), photoplethysmography (PPG), and phonocardiography (PCG) provide complementary views of the same cardiac cycle, yet existing cardiac foundation models are trained for a single sensing modality, leaving the shared physiology across sensors unexploited. We introduce CardioState-JEPA, a cardiac foundation model to learn a single shared representation jointly across ECG, PPG, and PCG, built on a physiology-aware joint-embedding predictive architecture. The model maps heterogeneous waveforms into a common token space, processes them with a single shared Transformer encoder, and learns by predicting masked latent cardiac states, placing the pretraining target on shared physiology rather than sensor-specific waveform appearance. To handle the temporal offsets between electrical, mechanical, and hemodynamic events, cross-modal prediction uses a learned delay aligner that matches signals at the corresponding cardiac time. Because synchronized multi-sensor recordings are scarce, CardioState-JEPA first learns within-modality structure from abundant unimodal data and then uses paired data to align modalities in latent cardiac time. Evaluated as a frozen encoder across 25 downstream tasks spanning ECG, PPG, and PCG, our encoder improves average PPG classification by 8.2 AUROC points, PCG murmur detection by 18.8 AUROC points, and ECG classification by 15.5 AUROC points over the best self-supervised signal baseline and matches or exceeds cardiac models trained with privileged clinical text or supervised labels on several ECG benchmarks. These results establish that heterogeneous cardiac signals can mutually supervise a single foundation model of cardiac physiology.

AI.tldr: CardioState-JEPA is a multimodal cardiac foundation model that learns one shared representation across ECG, PPG, and PCG using a physiology-aware joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), training on abundant unimodal data plus limited paired data to align modalities in latent cardiac time.
AI.motivation: ECG, PPG, and PCG capture complementary views of the same cardiac cycle, but existing cardiac foundation models are single-modality, leaving shared cross-sensor physiology unexploited. The authors aim to exploit this shared physiology to build a unified cardiac representation.
AI.method: CardioState-JEPA maps heterogeneous waveforms into a common token space, processes them with a single shared Transformer encoder, and trains by predicting masked latent cardiac states (JEPA), placing the pretraining target on shared physiology rather than sensor-specific waveform appearance. A learned delay aligner handles temporal offsets between electrical, mechanical, and hemodynamic events during cross-modal prediction. Training proceeds in two stages: first learning within-modality structure from abundant unimodal data, then using scarce synchronized paired data to align modalities in latent cardiac time.
AI.result: As a frozen encoder evaluated across 25 downstream tasks, CardioState-JEPA improves average PPG classification by 8.2 AUROC points, PCG murmur detection by 18.8 AUROC points, and ECG classification by 15.5 AUROC points over the best self-supervised signal baseline. It matches or exceeds cardiac models trained with privileged clinical text or supervised labels on several ECG benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Heterogeneous cardiac signals can mutually supervise a single foundation model of cardiac physiology, demonstrating that a shared cross-modality representation learned via JEPA achieves strong transfer performance across ECG, PPG, and PCG tasks.

title: Foundations of MT-PDCL: Measure-Theoretic Probabilistic Definite Clause Logic
summary: Standard probabilistic logic programming frameworks typically rely on grounding logic programs into discrete propositional representations. This operational requirement restricts exact inference to finite domains and discrete probability distributions. In this paper, we introduce Measure-Theoretic Probabilistic Definite Clause Logic (MT-PDCL), a generalized foundational framework that eliminates this finite-domain restriction. By explicitly defining stochastic variables over bounded index domains and equipping the interpretation space with standard Borel $σ$-algebras, MT-PDCL allows logical variables to operate natively over continuous measurable spaces. Building on Continuous Distribution Semantics, MT-PDCL models probabilistic rules as mutually independent causal events. However, rather than aggregating these derivations via finite boolean circuits, declarative entailment is formally defined through exact Lebesgue integration over the continuous measure space. We introduce a continuous immediate consequence operator that unifies the integration of continuous prior distributions with the evaluation of exact continuous observations. We demonstrate that this approach replaces the combinatorial bottleneck of discrete grounding with exact, algebraic, and structurally differentiable inference. While this transition trades discrete combinatorics for the geometric curse of dimensionality, it achieves the expressive power of continuous probabilistic models while preserving the pure declarative syntax of definite clause logic.

AI.tldr: MT-PDCL generalizes Probabilistic Definite Clause Logic from finite, discrete propositional grounding to continuous measurable spaces, defining entailment via exact Lebesgue integration and a continuous immediate consequence operator.
AI.motivation: Standard probabilistic logic programming frameworks require grounding to discrete propositional representations, which restricts exact inference to finite domains and discrete probability distributions. The paper aims to remove this finite-domain restriction and support continuous distributions while maintaining declarative definite clause syntax.
AI.method: Introduces Measure-Theoretic Probabilistic Definite Clause Logic (MT-PDCL), defining stochastic variables over bounded index domains and equipping the interpretation space with standard Borel σ-algebras. It builds on Continuous Distribution Semantics, modeling probabilistic rules as mutually independent causal events, and defines entailment through exact Lebesgue integration over the continuous measure space rather than finite boolean circuits. A continuous immediate consequence operator unifies integration of continuous priors with evaluation of exact continuous observations.
AI.result: The approach replaces the combinatorial bottleneck of discrete grounding with exact, algebraic, and structurally differentiable inference, achieving expressive power of continuous probabilistic models while preserving pure declarative definite clause syntax.
AI.conclusion: The transition trades discrete combinatorics for the geometric curse of dimensionality, but still achieves continuous probabilistic modeling expressiveness while retaining the declarative syntax of definite clause logic.

title: LycheeMemory V2: Efficient Long-Term Memory for LLM Agents via Semantic Segment-Level Consolidation
summary: Long-horizon LLM agents must preserve information from past interactions to support future tasks. Existing memory systems typically rely on eager consolidation, invoking LLMs after each interaction to extract, summarize, or update memories. This design makes memory construction increasingly costly as conversations grow. Coarse summarization can reduce construction cost but risks discarding fine-grained contextual evidence, whereas larger retrieval contexts or multi-hop LLM reasoning shift the overhead to query time. We present LycheeMemory V2, an efficient long-term memory framework that replaces turn-level consolidation with semantic segment-level consolidation. Instead of consolidating every interaction, LycheeMemory batches multiple exchanges into segments and encodes each finalized segment into context-independent typed memory records. Segment-level batching lowers LLM encoding frequency, while semantic boundary detection helps preserve coherent event-level and temporal evidence compared with fixed-window batching. The resulting records are organized with lightweight structured indexes for query-planned evidence retrieval. Experiments using GPT-4.1-Mini show that LycheeMemory achieves state-of-the-art performance, reaching 89.22% on LoCoMo and 92.20% on LongMemEval-S. Compared with A-Mem, it reduces construction tokens by 86.0% on LoCoMo and 75.9% on LongMemEval-S without increasing query-time token usage. More broadly, our results suggest that the accuracy--cost trade-off of long-term agent memory depends not only on what information is retained, but also on the granularity at which it is consolidated.

AI.tldr: LycheeMemory V2 proposes a semantic segment-level consolidation approach for long-horizon LLM agent memory, batching exchanges and encoding them into typed memory records to cut construction cost while preserving accuracy, achieving state-of-the-art results with ~76–86% lower token usage than A-Mem.
AI.motivation: Existing long-term memory systems use eager turn-level consolidation that invokes LLMs after every interaction, making memory construction increasingly costly as conversations grow. Coarse summarization reduces cost but loses fine-grained evidence, while larger retrieval contexts or multi-hop reasoning push overhead to query time. The authors seek to optimize the accuracy–cost trade-off by changing the granularity of consolidation.
AI.method: LycheeMemory V2 replaces turn-level consolidation with semantic segment-level consolidation: it batches multiple exchanges into segments, detects semantic boundaries to preserve coherent event-level and temporal evidence, and encodes each finalized segment into context-independent typed memory records. Records are organized with lightweight structured indexes supporting query-planned evidence retrieval.
AI.result: Using GPT-4.1-Mini, LycheeMemory achieves 89.22% on LoCoMo and 92.20% on LongMemEval-S, reaching state-of-the-art. Compared with A-Mem, it reduces construction tokens by 86.0% on LoCoMo and 75.9% on LongMemEval-S without increasing query-time token usage.
AI.conclusion: The accuracy–cost trade-off of long-term agent memory depends not only on what information is retained but also on the granularity at which it is consolidated. Semantic segment-level batching offers an efficient balance between construction cost and retrieval quality.

title: I-SDPO: Instance-Level Adaptive Self-Distillation Policy Optimization
summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) learns from reward differences within a rollout group, but receives no useful relative signal when every sampled response is incorrect. Privileged self-distillation can fill this gap with dense token supervision, yet applying it throughout training creates a different failure mode: the teacher is a biased, low-variance surrogate for the reward objective, so persistent imitation can oppose reward-improving updates after the policy becomes capable of producing successful trajectories. We introduce I-SDPO (Instance-Level Adaptive Self-Distillation Policy Optimization), which treats teacher reliance as capability-dependent. I-SDPO makes one routing decision per input instance and shares it across that instance's rollout group: all-incorrect groups use a privileged self-distillation objective, whereas any-success groups remain intact for GRPO. This design uses imitation only where group-relative rewards are uninformative. A local analysis characterizes when teacher and reward directions align and shows that a non-vanishing biased distillation weight induces an optimization bias floor. The routing rule automatically reduces the expected distillation rate as success probability rises, withdrawing teacher influence without a hand-designed schedule. On SciKnowEval, I-SDPO obtains the best result in all four scientific domains and improves average mean@16 accuracy from 56.67% with GRPO to 70.31%, with a maximum domain gain of 18.24 points.

AI.tldr: I-SDPO adaptively uses privileged self-distillation only when a rollout group has no correct responses, otherwise applying GRPO, which improves scientific QA accuracy by up to 18.24 points over GRPO while avoiding the optimization bias of persistent imitation.
AI.motivation: GRPO learns from within-group reward differences but provides no useful signal when all sampled responses are incorrect. Privileged self-distillation offers dense token-level supervision to fill this gap, but applying it throughout training is harmful: the teacher is a biased, low-variance surrogate, so persistent imitation can oppose reward-improving updates once the policy can already produce successful trajectories. The paper seeks a method that uses teacher supervision only where rewards are uninformative.
AI.method: I-SDPO makes a single, per-input routing decision shared across the instance's rollout group. Groups where all responses are incorrect use a privileged self-distillation objective; groups with at least one success remain intact for GRPO. The routing rule automatically reduces the expected distillation rate as success probability rises. A local analysis characterizes when teacher and reward directions align and shows that a non-vanishing biased distillation weight induces an optimization bias floor.
AI.result: On SciKnowEval, I-SDPO achieves the best results in all four scientific domains, raising average mean@16 accuracy from 56.67% (GRPO) to 70.31%, with a maximum domain gain of 18.24 points.
AI.conclusion: Treating teacher reliance as capability-dependent resolves the trade-off between uninformative group rewards and biased teacher imitation: I-SDPO applies self-distillation only to all-incorrect groups and withdraws teacher influence automatically as success probability rises, yielding substantial gains over GRPO on scientific evaluation.

title: From Local Mismatch to Global Impact: Optimizing Cache Reuse Policy for Efficient Diffusion
summary: Diffusion models have achieved dominant performance in visual generation but suffer from substantial inference overhead. While cache-based acceleration has emerged as a promising solution, existing policies rely on local similarity heuristics, which we identify as being significantly misaligned with final generation quality. This discrepancy stems from the non-uniform propagation and accumulation of errors along the denoising trajectory. To address this, we propose Global-Impact Cache (GCache). We first establish a rigorous theoretical characterization of the error propagation upper bound. Recognizing that this bound can be overly conservative for complex, highly non-convex diffusion models, we further reparameterize the propagation exponent with a Bernstein form and reformulate cache policy search as a bilevel optimization problem. In detail, GCache identifies an optimal reuse policy in the inner objective while aligning the error-weighting function with generation quality loss in the outer objective. This framework effectively reconciles theoretical rigor with empirical performance, learning to prioritize computation where it most impacts visual fidelity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GCache consistently outperforms prior caching strategies on both video and image generation. Notably, on the state-of-the-art Wan2.1 video diffusion model, GCache maintains a 2.17x speedup while significantly enhancing generation quality, reducing LPIPS from 0.1095 to 0.0316.

AI.tldr: GCache replaces local-similarity caching heuristics in diffusion models with a theoretically grounded, bilevel-optimized reuse policy that aligns caching decisions with final generation quality, yielding a 2.17x speedup on Wan2.1 while cutting LPIPS from 0.1095 to 0.0316.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models are inference-expensive, and existing cache-based acceleration relies on local similarity heuristics that are misaligned with final generation quality because errors propagate and accumulate non-uniformly along the denoising trajectory. This motivates a caching policy that accounts for global error impact rather than local similarity.
AI.method: The authors propose Global-Impact Cache (GCache). They first derive a rigorous upper bound on error propagation along the denoising trajectory. Since the bound is overly conservative for complex, non-convex diffusion models, they reparameterize the propagation exponent using a Bernstein form and formulate cache policy search as a bilevel optimization problem: the inner objective finds an optimal reuse policy, while the outer objective aligns the error-weighting function with generation quality loss. This lets the model prioritize computation in regions that most affect visual fidelity.
AI.result: GCache consistently outperforms prior caching strategies on both video and image generation. On the Wan2.1 video diffusion model, it achieves a 2.17x speedup while significantly improving generation quality, reducing LPIPS from 0.1095 to 0.0316.
AI.conclusion: By reconciling theoretical rigor with empirical performance through a bilevel optimization framework and error-propagation-aware policy, GCache effectively learns to allocate computation where it most impacts visual fidelity, advancing cache-based acceleration for diffusion models.

title: The Objective Is the Bottleneck: Latent World Models Encode What Their Planners Cannot Use
comment: Follow-up to arXiv:2608.10145. All experiments run on a laptop CPU; no model was trained or fine-tuned. Code, checkpoints and every measurement: github.com/joyjeet-singh/tinylab
summary:
Latent world models are judged by how well they predict, so when planning fails at long horizons the natural reading is that the predictor degrades. On a reproduction of LeWorldModel on TwoRoom we show the binding constraint is the planner's objective instead.
  The predictor is not the limit: its imagined state seventy-five environment steps ahead is still only 0.189 as wrong as assuming the world froze, while the planner never imagines beyond twenty-five. The objective is. Cross-entropy-method planning minimises squared latent distance, which tracks true distance at r = 0.426, saturates by about eighty arena units and decreases beyond a hundred and twenty, so moving away from the goal can lower the cost. The information is present throughout: a ridge probe recovers position from the frozen embedding at R^2 0.9922.
  The pathology is the method's, not one reimplementation's. It is present in the authors' released weights, and across four checkpoints long-horizon success rank-orders exactly with metric quality and inversely with prediction accuracy.
  Replacing only the objective, with nothing retrained and no GPU, lifts goals reached at offset 100 from 26.0% to 98.0%, equals the 98.0% at offset 25, and reaches 92.0% under a third of the budget: planning stops depending on the horizon. The best cost is not the most accurate. A head learned from frame separation alone predicts spatial distance worse than a position probe (r = 0.819 against 0.9897) yet plans better, charging 24% more to cross the environment's dividing wall where squared latent distance charges 4% less. It has learned reachability, not proximity.

AI.tldr: A reproduction of the LeWorldModel on TwoRoom shows that long-horizon planning failures are caused by the planner's squared-latent-distance objective, not by predictor degradation. The predictor's imagined states remain accurate far beyond the planner's horizon, and replacing only the objective (no retraining, no GPU) raises goal-reaching at long offsets from 26% to 98%, matching short-horizon performance and making planning horizon-independent.
AI.motivation: Challenge the natural assumption that long-horizon planning failures in latent world models stem from predictor degradation. The authors suspect the planner's objective—not the imagined rollouts—is the true binding constraint, and set out to isolate and prove this.
AI.method: Reproduce LeWorldModel on the TwoRoom environment and diagnose the failure. They measure predictor quality (imagined state error vs. a frozen-world baseline at 75 steps), correlate squared latent distance with true distance (r=0.426) and show it saturates and even decreases beyond ~120 arena units. They recover position from the frozen embedding via a ridge probe (R²=0.9922), verify the pathology in the authors' released weights and across four checkpoints, and finally replace only the planning objective with a reachability head learned from frame separation alone—retraining nothing and using no GPU. They compare costs for crossing the dividing wall.
AI.result: The predictor is not the limit: imagined state at 75 steps is only 0.189 as wrong as freezing the world, while the planner never imagines beyond 25 steps. Squared latent distance tracks true distance weakly (r=0.426), saturates by ~80 units and decreases past ~120, so moving away from the goal can lower cost. A ridge probe recovers position at R²=0.9922, showing the information is present throughout. Replacing only the objective lifts goals reached at offset 100 from 26.0% to 98.0% (equaling the 98.0% at offset 25) and reaches 92.0% under a third of the budget. The reachability head predicts spatial distance worse than a position probe (r=0.819 vs 0.9897) yet plans better, charging 24% more to cross the dividing wall where squared latent distance charges 4% less—it has learned reachability, not proximity.
AI.conclusion: The failure is not predictor degradation but a flawed objective: squared latent distance is a poor proxy for true navigation cost and breaks down at long horizons. The best cost is not the most accurate; a learned reachability objective dramatically improves long-horizon planning and decouples performance from the horizon, implying world-model planners should prioritize learned reachability over proximity.

title: BoardroomAI: Dependency-Aware Human-Steerable Multi-Agent Deliberation through Evolving Decision Graphs
summary: Organizational decisions are co-created while evidence, constraints, and human priorities continue to evolve. In conventional transcript-based multi-agent systems, humans typically provide an initial problem, agents deliberate internally, and the system returns a final response. BoardroomAI instead treats the human as a persistent participant who can intervene by challenging assumptions, modifying constraints, changing priorities, introducing evidence, or redirecting the decision process. We operationalize this human--agent coexistence through four components: (i) a typed decision graph representing evidence, assumptions, constraints, claims, objections, alternatives, risks, decisions, semantic dependencies, and specialist responsibility; (ii) an intervention compiler that converts confirmed human actions into explicit graph updates; (iii) dependency-aware propagation that identifies affected subgraphs, preserves unaffected artifacts, and selectively reactivates relevant specialists; and (iv) an evaluation framework measuring intervention impact, repair coverage, preservation, recomputation, and decision validity. Across 600 generated decision-DAG interventions, propagation matched exhaustive impact computation while inspecting only 14.59% of nodes. In a 12-case exploratory pilot, selective repair recomputed 62.11% of canonical nodes, preserved all gold-unaffected nodes, and produced valid updated decisions in six cases while abstaining in the remaining six. These abstentions show that correct intervention routing may still provide insufficient context for synthesis, motivating a \emph{decision-sufficient context closure} for human-steered multi-agent deliberation. All results are synthetic and prototype-level.

AI.tldr: BoardroomAI introduces a human-in-the-loop multi-agent system where humans persist as active participants who can intervene in ongoing decisions, using a typed decision graph and dependency-aware selective repair; evaluation shows efficient propagation (14.59% node inspection) and valid decisions in half of exploratory cases, motivating "decision-sufficient context closure."
AI.motivation: Conventional transcript-based multi-agent systems treat humans as one-shot providers of an initial problem, returning only a final response, while real organizational decisions are co-created amid evolving evidence, constraints, and priorities. The work aims to support persistent human intervention (challenging assumptions, modifying constraints, changing priorities, introducing evidence, redirecting the process) within agent deliberation.
AI.method: Operationalizes human-agent coexistence via four components: (i) a typed decision graph encoding evidence, assumptions, constraints, claims, objections, alternatives, risks, decisions, semantic dependencies, and specialist responsibility; (ii) an intervention compiler converting confirmed human actions into explicit graph updates; (iii) dependency-aware propagation that identifies affected subgraphs, preserves unaffected artifacts, and selectively reactivates relevant specialists; and (iv) an evaluation framework measuring intervention impact, repair coverage, preservation, recomputation, and decision validity.
AI.result: Across 600 generated decision-DAG interventions, propagation matched exhaustive impact computation while inspecting only 14.59% of nodes. In a 12-case exploratory pilot, selective repair recomputed 62.11% of canonical nodes, preserved all gold-unaffected nodes, and produced valid updated decisions in six cases while abstaining in the remaining six.
AI.conclusion: Correct intervention routing can still leave insufficient context for synthesis, as shown by the six abstentions, motivating a "decision-sufficient context closure" for human-steered multi-agent deliberation. Note that all results are synthetic and prototype-level.

title: DMDIntel: Interpreting Large Language Models via Dynamic Mode Decomposition
summary: In this work, we introduce DMDIntel which uses dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) to make the predictions made by LLMs in a classification task interpretable. It develops an input attribution pipeline, that first decomposes the hidden states of an LLM into prominent patterns, also known as modes, and then associates ranks to the input tokens based on the projection values on those modes. Rigorous experiments across three datasets and three model families consistently show that the ranked attribution of input tokens obtained using DMDIntel by far outperforms state-of-the-art techniques such as principal component analysis, integrated gradients and SHAP.

AI.tldr: DMDIntel uses dynamic mode decomposition to interpret LLM classification decisions by attributing importance to input tokens based on their projections onto dominant modes of hidden states, outperforming PCA, integrated gradients, and SHAP.
AI.motivation: Making LLM predictions in classification tasks interpretable is challenging; existing input-attribution methods (e.g., PCA, integrated gradients, SHAP) are insufficient, motivating a DMD-based approach that exploits the temporal dynamics of hidden states to identify prominent patterns driving predictions.
AI.method: DMDIntel introduces an input-attribution pipeline that (1) applies dynamic mode decomposition to the sequence of hidden states of an LLM to extract prominent dynamic patterns (modes), and (2) assigns importance ranks to input tokens according to their projection values onto these modes.
AI.result: Experiments across three datasets and three model families show that DMDIntel's ranked token attributions consistently and substantially outperform state-of-the-art methods, including principal component analysis, integrated gradients, and SHAP.
AI.conclusion: DMD-based decomposition of LLM hidden states yields a highly effective and interpretable input-attribution method, establishing DMDIntel as a superior alternative to established interpretability techniques across diverse datasets and model families.

title: Comment on "Modeling rapid language learning by distilling Bayesian priors into artificial neural networks"
summary: McCoy & Griffiths (2025, henceforth M&G) suggest that a Bayesian prior can be distilled into Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) through Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML, Finn et al., 2017). They support this empirically by showing that meta-trained networks demonstrate formal language learning abilities comparable to Yang & Piantadosi (2023)'s Bayesian learner, significantly outperforming standard ANNs. We point out that under the standard interpretation of a prior, M&G's procedure does not actually instill one; it merely initializes network weights favorably, leaving the objective function unchanged. We then consider a more permissive interpretation, where the system as a whole can be seen as implementing a Bayesian learner even without an explicit prior in the objective. We show that this interpretation faces nontrivial challenges. Finally, we assess how well MAML approximates the empirical results of Bayesian learning, showing that unlike genuine Bayesian learners, M&G's model overfits and generalizes poorly to unseen data.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques McCoy & Griffiths (2025)'s claim that MAML distills a Bayesian prior into ANNs, arguing it only improves weight initialization without changing the objective, and that the MAML model overfits and generalizes poorly compared to a genuine Bayesian learner.
AI.motivation: To challenge the claim that Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning can distill a Bayesian prior into artificial neural networks, and to clarify the distinction between favorable weight initialization and an actual prior in the learning objective.
AI.method: The authors analyze M&G's procedure under the standard interpretation of a prior (arguing MAML only initializes weights without altering the objective function), then consider a more permissive interpretation where the whole system implements a Bayesian learner, and finally empirically evaluate how well MAML approximates Bayesian learning, focusing on overfitting and generalization to unseen data.
AI.result: Under the standard interpretation, MAML does not instill a prior but merely initializes weights favorably. The more permissive interpretation faces nontrivial challenges. Unlike genuine Bayesian learners, M&G's MAML model overfits and generalizes poorly to unseen data.
AI.conclusion: M&G's claim that MAML distills a Bayesian prior into ANNs is not supported; MAML does not alter the objective function and the resulting model exhibits poorer generalization than genuine Bayesian learners.

title: VALG: An Agentic System for ML Theory Research
summary:
Machine learning theory studies learning procedures through mathematical setups in which the data model, training protocol, oracle access, loss, metric, and randomness define the phenomenon that a theorem is meant to explain. Solving an open problem therefore requires the problem formulation, theorem target, and proof mechanism to be developed in concert. Researchers formulate hypotheses, test them through preliminary theoretical or empirical analysis, and refine both assumptions and proofs. We investigate whether this process can be organized as an autonomous agentic workflow for ML theory research.
  We develop VALG, an agentic system that combines multi-level Verification, Adaptive formulation of Learning-theory problems, and Graph-structured proof development. Within each source-relative theorem branch, VALG maintains a fixed mathematical specification, checks the theorem-level composition of a typed proof-dependency graph, and constructs and reviews local proofs in dependency order. When a proof attempt fails, VALG identifies whether the obstruction lies in a derivation, the proof structure, or the theorem formulation and routes the next attempt accordingly. Formulation-level obstructions initiate an explicitly related variant or relaxation, preserving the mathematical relation between the resulting theorem and the source problem.
  We evaluate VALG on nine subproblems from five COLT 2026 open problems. Two runs produce internally finalized theorem candidates that match the scope of their source briefs; the remaining seven yield restricted-method results, special cases, or conditional theorems. These case studies show how VALG keeps source-scope matches, relaxations, conditional results, and blocked attempts mathematically distinct. VALG is open source at https://github.com/DechenZhang/VALG-ML-Theory-Agent.

AI.tldr: VALG is an autonomous agentic system for machine learning theory research that integrates multi-level verification, adaptive problem formulation, and graph-structured proof development. It was tested on nine COLT 2026 open subproblems, producing two source-scope-matching theorem candidates and seven restricted, special-case, or conditional results.
AI.motivation: Solving ML theory open problems requires jointly developing the problem formulation, theorem target, and proof mechanism through iterative hypothesis testing and refinement. The authors investigate whether this research process can be organized as an autonomous agentic workflow.
AI.method: VALG combines multi-level Verification, Adaptive formulation of Learning-theory problems, and Graph-structured proof development. It maintains a fixed mathematical specification per source-relative theorem branch, checks theorem-level composition via a typed proof-dependency graph, and constructs and reviews local proofs in dependency order. On failures, it classifies obstructions as derivation-level, proof-structure-level, or formulation-level and routes retries accordingly; formulation-level issues spawn explicitly related variants or relaxations that preserve mathematical relation to the source problem.
AI.result: Evaluated on nine subproblems from five COLT 2026 open problems, two runs produced internally finalized theorem candidates matching source-brief scope, while seven produced restricted-method results, special cases, or conditional theorems. The case studies demonstrate that VALG keeps source-scope matches, relaxations, conditional results, and blocked attempts mathematically distinct.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates the feasibility of an autonomous agentic workflow for ML theory research, with VALG open-sourced at https://github.com/DechenZhang/VALG-ML-Theory-Agent.

title: CASA: Content-Acoustic Speaking Assessment with Speech Encoder and Large Language Model
comment: To be submitted to ICASSP 2027. Code is available at https://github.com/aalto-speech/casa
summary:
Research on automatic speaking assessment (ASA) has increasingly adopted multimodal speech large language models to assess learners' speaking performance. However, existing studies provide limited analysis of how acoustic and content information contribute to predictions and how stable the resulting performance is.
