We propose CASA, a simpler architecture combining Whisper-medium and Qwen3.5-2B that achieves state-of-the-art performance while providing a more interpretable separation between speech delivery and content.
  On the Speak & Improve Corpus 2025, CASA achieves a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.358, improving on the previous best RMSE while using approximately half the estimated inference parameters. The general-purpose architecture is designed for adaptation to other ASA corpora without structural changes and relies on three handcrafted fluency features. Through ablations and repeated runs, we analyze the individual and complementary contributions of acoustic and content information, examine performance variability, and demonstrate the potential of large language model reasoning for training-free content validation.

AI.tldr: CASA combines Whisper-medium and Qwen3.5-2B into a simpler multimodal architecture for automatic speaking assessment, achieving state-of-the-art RMSE (0.358) on the Speak & Improve Corpus 2025 while using roughly half the inference parameters of the previous best model and offering clearer separation between speech delivery and content.
AI.motivation: Existing ASA research using multimodal speech LLMs provides limited analysis of how acoustic and content information individually contribute to predictions, and how stable the resulting performance is. The authors aim to build a simpler, more interpretable and stable model that clearly separates speech delivery from content.
AI.method: CASA is a general-purpose architecture composed of Whisper-medium (acoustic encoder) and Qwen3.5-2B (language model), relying on only three handcrafted fluency features. It performs ablations and repeated runs to analyze separate and complementary contributions of acoustic and content information, examine performance variability, and use LLM reasoning for training-free content validation.
AI.result: CASA achieves an RMSE of 0.358 on the Speak & Improve Corpus 2025, outperforming the previous best while using approximately half the estimated inference parameters. Ablations and repeated runs reveal the individual and complementary roles of acoustic and content information and characterize performance variability.
AI.conclusion: A simpler, more interpretable architecture can reach state-of-the-art ASA performance with lower inference cost. The clear acoustic/content separation, reliance on only three handcrafted fluency features, and demonstrated potential of LLM reasoning for training-free content validation make CASA adaptable to other ASA corpora without structural changes.

title: Learning the Mathematical Property for Designing Low Mutual Coherence Binary Sensing Matrices
summary: In this research work, we are constructing the sensing matrix, which is essential for the success of the compressive sensing technique. We have chosen a learning-based technique for the construction of the sensing matrix. The novelty and uniqueness of the proposed technique is that it does not use any data set and also does not use a specific application. It uses the mathematical property/constraint for the construction of the sensing matrix for the perfect recovery of the signal. The perfect recovery of signals is an old and still very challenging problem in real-world applications. In late 2000, compressive sensing became a popular mathematical tool for the perfect recovery of sparse signals. The core of the compressive technique is the construction of the sensing matrix, which satisfies certain special properties such as restricted isometry property (RIP), null space property (NSP), and spark property (SP). All these properties are NP-hard problems and hence computationally challenging to solve. For all practical purposes, the construction of the sensing matrix needs to achieve low mutual coherence to achieve the perfect recovery of the signals. We have used a neural network for the construction of the sensing matrix, and this framework constructs a binary sensing matrix with low mutual coherence. The entries in the matrix are generated through a shared underlying rule. The proposed architecture is simple and does not use large-scale training data sets. Such uniqueness and novelty bring a drastic reduction in computational cost, and also, for the first time in literature, the use of a mathematical property for defining the loss function. In this proposed research work, the mutual coherence property has been used in the neural network framework. Such a neural network framework brings generality, robustness, and reduces storage requirements.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a learning-based (neural network) approach for constructing a binary sensing matrix with low mutual coherence for compressive sensing, distinguishing itself by using only mathematical properties (mutual coherence) as the loss function rather than any training dataset or application-specific data.
AI.motivation: Perfect recovery of sparse signals via compressive sensing depends heavily on the sensing matrix, which ideally satisfies properties such as restricted isometry property (RIP), null space property (NSP), and spark property (SP). However, verifying/ensuring these properties is NP-hard and computationally challenging. A practical surrogate goal is to construct a sensing matrix with low mutual coherence, which supports perfect recovery. The motivation is to build such a matrix efficiently, generally, and robustly without relying on large-scale datasets or a specific application.
AI.method: A neural network framework is used to construct a binary sensing matrix. The entries of the matrix are generated through a shared underlying rule. The novelty is that the loss function is defined directly by a mathematical property—mutual coherence—rather than using any training data or application-specific data. This avoids large-scale training datasets and reduces computational cost.
AI.result: The proposed architecture yields a binary sensing matrix with low mutual coherence, bringing generality, robustness, reduced storage requirements, and a drastic reduction in computational cost. It is claimed to be the first work in the literature to use a mathematical property (mutual coherence) to define the loss function in a neural network framework.
AI.conclusion: Using a neural network that directly optimizes the mutual coherence property enables efficient construction of a binary sensing matrix suitable for perfect signal recovery in compressive sensing, without data dependence, with generality, robustness, and lower storage/computational costs.

title: Uniform Herding: Exemplar Replay with Representation Refresh
summary: As the feature representation changes, replay must preserve the earlier classes. However, only a bounded active exemplar set can be replayed. We propose Uniform Herding, which allocates the current active set across observed classes and uses a bounded candidate pool to refresh their chosen exemplars in the current representation. On CIFAR-100 with ten class-incremental tasks, a ResNet-18 backbone, active budget $M=2{,}000$, retrieval budget $b=64$, and three seeds, Uniform Herding obtains $44.00\pm0.51\%$ final average accuracy and $17.22\pm0.43\%$ forgetting, compared with $42.33\pm1.20\%$ and $24.87\pm1.11\%$ for iCaRL. Within the Uniform Herding protocol, final accuracy decreased when NME or herding was replaced with the tested alternatives, while forgetting increased when distillation was removed. Changing the retrieval budget has a smaller effect across the tested range than changing the active budget. The comparison with iCaRL is end-to-end. It does not isolate the effect of refresh from the other protocol differences. These results are limited to the tested protocol.

AI.tldr: Uniform Herding is a continual-learning replay method that distributes a fixed active exemplar set evenly across observed classes and periodically refreshes exemplars from a small candidate pool. On CIFAR-100 (10 tasks, ResNet-18, M=2000, b=64), it achieves 44.00% final accuracy and 17.22% forgetting, outperforming iCaRL's 42.33% and 24.87%.
AI.motivation: As the feature representation evolves during class-incremental learning, replayed exemplars must still accurately represent earlier classes; however, only a bounded active exemplar set can be stored and replayed, creating tension between coverage and representativeness under a changing feature space.
AI.method: Uniform Herding allocates the current active exemplar set evenly across all observed classes and uses a bounded candidate pool to refresh the selected exemplars in the current feature representation. Ablations compare it against NME and other herding alternatives, with and without distillation, and vary retrieval and active budgets.
AI.result: On CIFAR-100 with ten class-incremental tasks, a ResNet-18 backbone, active budget M=2000, retrieval budget b=64, and three seeds, Uniform Herding yields 44.00±0.51% final average accuracy and 17.22±0.43% forgetting, versus 42.33±1.20% and 24.87±1.11% for iCaRL. Removing NME/herding lowered final accuracy; removing distillation increased forgetting. Retrieval budget had smaller impact than active budget across tested ranges.
AI.conclusion: Uniform Herding improves over iCaRL under the tested protocol, but the comparison is end-to-end and does not isolate the effect of refresh from other protocol differences; findings are limited to the tested settings.

title: Balanced Adaptive Prototype Selection for Scalable TabPFN Inference on Large-Scale Tabular Data
summary: Pretrained tabular foundation models have demonstrated strong predictive capability; however, their application to large-scale datasets remains constrained by the limited inference context. This paper introduces Balanced Adaptive Prototype Selection (BAPS), a framework for constructing compact, information-preserving contexts for scalable TabPFN inference. Without modifying or retraining the pretrained model, BAPS jointly preserves representative structure, informative decision boundaries, local density, class balance, and feature-space diversity. Experiments on the million-row HIGGS and SUSY datasets show that 512 prototypes retain strong predictive performance and reliable calibration, corresponding to an approximately 1,953-fold context compression. All experiments were conducted on an Intel Core i7 CPU with 16 GB RAM and no GPU acceleration. These findings establish effective context construction as a practical mechanism for extending pretrained tabular foundation models to million-scale datasets.

AI.tldr: BAPS is a prototype-selection framework that builds compact, information-preserving contexts to scale pretrained TabPFN inference to million-row tabular datasets, achieving ~1,953-fold context compression with 512 prototypes while maintaining accuracy and calibration on CPU-only hardware.
AI.motivation: Pretrained tabular foundation models like TabPFN show strong predictive performance but are constrained by limited inference context, making them impractical for large-scale datasets with millions of rows. A method is needed to reduce inference input size without sacrificing predictive quality or requiring model retraining.
AI.method: BAPS (Balanced Adaptive Prototype Selection) jointly optimizes the selection of a small set of prototypes to preserve representative structure, informative decision boundaries, local density, class balance, and feature-space diversity. It operates as a context-construction wrapper around the frozen pretrained TabPFN model, requiring no modification or retraining.
AI.result: On the million-row HIGGS and SUSY benchmark datasets, using just 512 prototypes retained strong predictive performance and reliable calibration, corresponding to roughly 1,953-fold context compression. All experiments ran on an Intel Core i7 CPU with 16 GB RAM and no GPU acceleration, demonstrating practical scalability.
AI.conclusion: Effective context construction via prototype selection is a practical mechanism for extending pretrained tabular foundation models to million-scale datasets, enabling accurate, calibrated, and CPU-feasible inference without modifying the underlying model.

title: Explanatory Engagement Under Rare Anomalous Failure: Asymptotic Rarity in Model Behavior (or: The Asymptotic AI)
comment: 11 figures. Elicitation-condition sweep across three open-weight models (qwen3:8b, llama3.1:8b, mistral:7b); pipeline scripts and experimental data available upon reasonable request
summary: Prior work on LLM behavior under anomalous conditions asks whether a model notices anomalies. We ask a narrower question: once a model sits in a workflow with a low, controllable failure rate, does its explanatory engagement - length, specificity, self-reported confidence - change as failure grows asymptotically rarer? We built a local, zero-cost harness on three open-weight models (qwen3:8b, llama3.1:8b, mistral:7b) running a repeated tool-call task where one call fails at probability p, swept across eight rates from 0.2 to 0.0001, under five elicitation conditions from immediate prompting to none. We hypothesized a rise in engagement as failures grew rarer, then a collapse near a detectability threshold. Pooled across conditions this appeared false: length fell in a flat, monotonic pattern. Splitting by condition overturned that. Under immediate_forced, where the model must explain every failure instantly, the predicted rise is confirmed but followed by a plateau, not a collapse: length peaks at 28.4 words at p=0.05, settles to 17.4-19.0 words at the rarest rates, and confidence rises unevenly from about 53% to the 70s-90s. Under grouped_runs, explanation batched to run-end, no collapse appears. Under passive_unprompted, aggregate magnitude is a floor artifact, but a recovered logging gap revealed real, model-specific self-monitoring: llama3.1:8b volunteers structured confidence reports unprompted, sometimes eroding its own confidence as trials accumulate; the other two do so only once, as boilerplate. Elicitation structure is a first-class moderator of collapse observability. A companion guaranteed-failure run (72 cells, backfilling rates where random sampling gave zero real failures) shows models differ in whether they recognize an anomaly, distinct from engagement once recognized. Limitation: discrete rate points cannot capture behavior between them, a direction for future work.

AI.tldr: Study of how three small open-weight LLMs modulate their explanatory engagement (length, specificity, confidence) as failure becomes asymptotically rarer across eight probabilities and five elicitation conditions. Elicitation structure, not rarity alone, determines whether a predicted rise-then-collapse pattern appears; models also differ in anomaly recognition versus engagement.
AI.motivation: Prior work only asks whether LLMs notice anomalies; this paper asks a narrower question about how explanatory engagement scales as anomaly (failure) rates drop toward rarity, testing a hypothesis of a rise in engagement followed by collapse near a detectability threshold.
AI.method: Built a local zero-cost harness on three open-weight models (qwen3:8b, llama3.1:8b, mistral:7b) running a repeated tool-call task where one call fails with probability p, swept across eight rates (0.2 to 0.0001) under five elicitation conditions (from immediate_forced to passive_unprompted). A companion guaranteed-failure run (72 cells) backfilled rates where random sampling produced zero real failures.
AI.result: Pooled across conditions, length fell in a flat monotonic pattern (hypothesis false). Split by condition: immediate_forced shows the predicted rise then a plateau (not collapse), peaking at 28.4 words at p=0.05 and settling to 17.4–19.0 at rarest rates, with confidence rising unevenly from ~53% to the 70s–90s. grouped_runs shows no collapse. passive_unprompted magnitudes are mostly a floor artifact, but a recovered logging gap revealed llama3.1:8b volunteers structured self-monitoring and erodes its own confidence as trials accumulate, while the other two volunteer only once as boilerplate. Guaranteed-failure runs show models differ in recognizing anomalies, distinct from engagement after recognition.
AI.conclusion: Elicitation structure is a first-class moderator of whether an engagement collapse is observable near a detectability threshold. Models also differ in recognizing anomalies versus engaging once recognized. Discrete rate points cannot capture behavior between rates, a key limitation and future direction.

title: Better Decomposition, Free Aggregation: A Synthesizer-Folding Framework for Multilingual Multi-Hop Question Answering
summary: Multilingual retrieval-augmented generation (mRAG) equips large language models with access to globally distributed external knowledge for complex multilingual question answering. Recent approaches either translate retrieved documents into English or the query language to bridge the cross-lingual semantic gap, or decompose a complex query into sub-questions and aggregate the intermediate reasoning process. However, both lines of work suffer from two limitations. First, one-size-fits-all translation alignment, blanket translation discards culturally and linguistically native information unique to the target language, introduces translation noise, and inflates system cost. Second, greedy decomposition and aggregation, uncontrolled decomposition produces redundant sub-questions that compound errors during step-wise reasoning, and the final aggregation over reasoning paths further amplifies these errors. We address both with our method Syfer, a synthesizer-folding framework for multilingual multi-hop question answering that defers translation rather than applying it by default. Syfer first invokes a format-constrained decomposer to produce a sub-question graph in the original language, followed by a decomposition-quality check; when the check passes, sub-questions are answered sequentially under a retrieve-then-answer policy in the target language, and the English translation pathway with bilingual sub-question graph alignment is activated only when the check fails. Experiments across multiple languages show that Syfer attains competitive accuracy while striking a favourable balance between performance and computational cost.

AI.tldr: Syfer is a multilingual multi-hop QA framework that defers translation, decomposing queries into a quality-checked sub-question graph answered natively in the target language, and only activating an English-translation pathway with bilingual graph alignment when quality checks fail.
AI.motivation: Existing mRAG approaches are limited by (1) blanket translation that discards native cultural/linguistic information, introduces translation noise, and inflates cost, and (2) greedy decomposition/aggregation that generates redundant sub-questions and compounds errors during step-wise reasoning and final aggregation.
AI.method: Syfer uses a format-constrained decomposer to build a sub-question graph in the original language, applies a decomposition-quality check, and if it passes, answers sub-questions sequentially via retrieve-then-answer in the target language; only on check failure does it fall back to an English translation pathway with bilingual sub-question graph alignment.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple languages show Syfer achieves competitive accuracy while maintaining a favorable balance between performance and computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Deferring translation to a conditional fallback path, coupled with quality-checked decomposition, enables multilingual multi-hop QA that preserves native information and reduces translation noise while controlling cost and error propagation.

title: Incremental Evaluation and Training in Relational Deep Learning
summary: Relational Deep Learning (RDL) models multi-tabular databases as temporal heterogeneous graphs to enable end-to-end representation learning. However, prevailing RDL evaluation practices rely on static, single-episode dataset snapshots, overlooking the continuous, time-evolving nature of real-world databases. Consequently, current RDL benchmarks fail to capture how model performance changes as new data accumulates over time. To address this limitation, we introduce an incremental, multi-episode evaluation and training paradigm to assess and improve the temporal robustness and adaptability of state-of-the-art RDL models. Using established large-scale datasets, we examine data evolution and model training dynamics, demonstrating that temporal concept drifts occur in the majority of predictive tasks. We present multiple incremental training regimes for fine-tuning the models and demonstrate that transfer learning is both feasible and highly effective in the RDL setting. Alongside a new temporal evaluation metric that prioritizes near-future accuracy, we show that our incrementally fine-tuned models consistently outperform the standard, expensive, from-scratch trained baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an incremental, multi-episode evaluation and training paradigm for Relational Deep Learning (RDL), showing that temporal concept drift is common, and that incrementally fine-tuned models outperform expensive from-scratch baselines while better capturing time-evolving databases.
AI.motivation: Prevailing RDL evaluation relies on static, single-episode dataset snapshots, which overlooks the continuous, time-evolving nature of real-world databases. This means current benchmarks fail to capture how model performance changes as new data accumulates over time, motivating a temporal, incremental evaluation and training methodology to improve temporal robustness and adaptability.
AI.method: The authors introduce an incremental, multi-episode evaluation and training paradigm applied to state-of-the-art RDL models on established large-scale datasets. They analyze data evolution and model training dynamics to detect temporal concept drift, propose multiple incremental training (fine-tuning) regimes, and introduce a new temporal evaluation metric that prioritizes near-future accuracy.
AI.result: Temporal concept drifts occur in the majority of predictive tasks. Transfer learning (incremental fine-tuning) is feasible and highly effective in the RDL setting, and the incrementally fine-tuned models consistently outperform the standard, expensive, from-scratch trained baselines under the proposed near-future-focused temporal metric.
AI.conclusion: Incremental, multi-episode evaluation and fine-tuning better reflect real-world database dynamics, improve temporal robustness, and achieve superior accuracy at lower computational cost compared to from-scratch training.

title: Behavioral Reprogramming of Open-Weights Models: Cognitive Plasticity and Alignment Bounds
comment: Preprint submitted to arXiv, August 12, 2026. 13 pages, 5 figures
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are predominantly aligned to function as passive, sycophantic assistants. We challenge this default paradigm by empirically evaluating the cognitive plasticity of open-weight architectures when subjected to rigorous behavioral reprogramming. Our objective is to induce a proactive, Socratic conversational framework, characterized by high-frequency question generation under strictly constrained high-performance computing (HPC) conditions. Through a massively parallelized hyperparameter sweep comprising 405 HPC jobs, we define precise mathematical bounds for parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). We identify an architectural threshold at LoRA rank $r=16$ and demonstrate via extensive epoch ablation that generalization capacity strictly reaches its optimal convergence within an optimized training window of $e \in [2, 3]$ depending on dataset density (minimum validation loss of 0.919). Furthermore, scaling model capacity to 14B parameters yielded a lower localized evaluation perplexity (1.414). Subsequent Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) successfully decoupled the underlying assertive behavior from localized syntax, while rigorous cross-lingual stress testing reveals both the capabilities and the structural boundaries of zero-shot persona transfer, demonstrating robust alignment in closely related linguistic families alongside identifiable degradation pathways in morphologically distant targets. These findings establish a rigorous empirical framework for compute-efficient, cross-lingual behavioral modification.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically demonstrates that open-weight LLMs can be behaviorally reprogrammed from passive assistants into proactive Socratic questioners using parameter-efficient fine-tuning, with optimal performance found at LoRA rank r=16 and training epochs e∈[2,3], validated through DPO decoupling and cross-lingual stress testing.
AI.motivation: LLMs are predominantly aligned as passive, sycophantic assistants. The authors challenge this default paradigm, aiming to induce a proactive Socratic conversational framework with high-frequency question generation, under constrained HPC conditions.
AI.method: A massively parallelized hyperparameter sweep of 405 HPC jobs over open-weight architectures using parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT/LoRA), followed by Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and cross-lingual stress testing. Model capacity was scaled up to 14B parameters.
AI.result: Identified an architectural threshold at LoRA rank r=16. Generalization converges optimally at epochs e∈[2,3] depending on dataset density, with minimum validation loss of 0.919. Scaling to 14B parameters yielded lower evaluation perplexity (1.414). DPO decoupled assertive behavior from localized syntax; cross-lingual testing showed robust zero-shot persona transfer in closely related language families with degradation in morphologically distant targets.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish a rigorous empirical framework for compute-efficient, cross-lingual behavioral modification of LLMs, demonstrating that proactive Socratic behavior can be induced reliably within defined mathematical bounds.

title: Which LLM Is Your Ideal Companion? Evaluating Emotional Companion Capabilities of LLMs Based on Adult Attachment Theory
summary: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied for emotional companionship, evaluating their behavior and capabilities in intimate relationships has become a pressing issue. However, existing assessments primarily characterize general personality traits, providing limited insight into model behavior within intimate and emotionally sensitive contexts. Therefore, we introduce adult attachment theory into LLM evaluation and use the Experiences in Close Relationships-Revised (ECR-R) scale to characterize attachment anxiety and avoidance. To evaluate emotional companionship capabilities of LLMs in realistic interaction scenarios, we present an emotional companionship benchmark, ECBench, spanning four scenarios including emotional support, collaborative tasks, conflict resolution, and social guidance, across friendship and romantic relationships. ECBench is utilized to assess model behavior using 11 dialogue-quality metrics and three evaluation methods. We evaluate the attachment tendencies of 32 LLMs and select representative models to investigate how these tendencies manifest in contextualized multi-turn interactions and whether they can be shaped through prompting. Our study provides a theoretical lens from psychology, along with practical tools to understand and select LLMs for emotional companionship.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces adult attachment theory into LLM evaluation, using the ECR-R scale to measure attachment anxiety/avoidance, and presents ECBench, a benchmark spanning four scenarios (emotional support, collaborative tasks, conflict resolution, social guidance) across friendship and romantic relationships. It evaluates 32 LLMs and explores how attachment tendencies manifest in multi-turn interactions and whether prompting can shape them.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used for emotional companionship, existing assessments only characterize general personality traits, offering limited insight into model behavior in intimate, emotionally sensitive contexts. This gap motivates bringing a psychological framework (adult attachment theory) to LLM evaluation and building realistic interaction benchmarks.
AI.method: The authors adopt adult attachment theory and use the Experiences in Close Relationships-Revised (ECR-R) scale to quantify attachment anxiety and avoidance. They construct ECBench, an emotional companionship benchmark covering four scenarios (emotional support, collaborative tasks, conflict resolution, and social guidance) across friendship and romantic relationships. Evaluation uses 11 dialogue-quality metrics and three evaluation methods on contextualized multi-turn interactions. They assess 32 LLMs' attachment tendencies, select representative models, and test whether tendencies can be shaped through prompting.
AI.result: The study characterizes the attachment tendencies of 32 LLMs, demonstrates how these tendencies manifest in contextualized multi-turn interactions, and shows that attachment tendencies can be shaped through prompting. Representative models were selected to investigate these behaviors.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a psychological (attachment theory) lens plus practical tools (ECR-R-based measurement and ECBench) to understand, evaluate, and select LLMs for emotional companionship.

title: On the global feature importance for interpretable and trustworthy heat demand forecasting
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures. This preprint corresponds to the paper published in Thermal Science 2025 Volume 29, Issue 5 Part A, Pages: 3355-3365
summary: The paper introduces the ante-hoc Explainable AI methodology to assess the global feature importance of the Machine Learning models used for heat demand forecasting in intelligent control of District Heating Systems, with motivation to facilitate their interpretability and trustworthiness, hence addressing the challenges related to adherence to communal standards, customer satisfaction and liability risks. Methodology includes use of four different approaches, namely intrinsic interpretability of Gradient Boosting method and selected post-hoc methods, namely Partial Dependence, Accumulated Local Effects and SHAP. None of the selected methods assume feature permutation or perturbations which can introduce bias due to introduction of random unrealistic values of data instances. Discussion of results is provided, including the assessment of complementarities where applicable, with specific interpretations in context of the district heating processes.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an ante-hoc Explainable AI methodology to assess global feature importance for heat demand forecasting models in District Heating Systems, using intrinsically interpretable Gradient Boosting complemented by post-hoc methods (Partial Dependence, Accumulated Local Effects, SHAP) that avoid permutation-based bias.
AI.motivation: To facilitate interpretability and trustworthiness of Machine Learning models used for heat demand forecasting in intelligent District Heating Systems, addressing challenges related to adherence to communal standards, customer satisfaction, and liability risks.
AI.method: The methodology employs four approaches: intrinsic interpretability of Gradient Boosting, plus post-hoc methods including Partial Dependence (PD), Accumulated Local Effects (ALE), and SHAP. Notably, none of the selected methods rely on feature permutation or perturbations, thereby avoiding bias from introducing random unrealistic data instance values.
AI.result: Results include a discussion of the feature importance findings, assessment of complementarities among methods where applicable, and specific interpretations grounded in the context of district heating processes.
AI.conclusion: The ante-hoc Explainable AI methodology provides interpretable and trustworthy global feature importance assessments for heat demand forecasting models, using permutation-free methods that avoid unrealistic-value bias, and yields context-relevant insights for District Heating Systems.

title: EEG-PRIME: Prototype-Aligned Representation Learning with Multi-Level Conditioning for EEG Decoding
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) decoding models often generalize poorly across datasets and subjects due to domain shifts in acquisition protocols and individual neurophysiology. We propose EEG-PRIME, a two-stage EEG foundation model for cross-dataset multi-task decoding. EEG-PRIME combines masked pretraining with prototype-aligned instruction tuning to enable instruction-aware and subject-invariant decoding across diverse BCI paradigms. During pretraining, an EEG encoder learns transferable representations through masked reconstruction with frequency-cutoff spectral augmentation. During instruction tuning, EEG-PRIME incorporates task-semantic, dataset-specific, and subject-invariant conditioning. The resulting conditioning signal modulates the Q-Former through Layer-wise Query Modulation, while frozen text embeddings of class labels serve as prototypes for cosine-similarity-based prediction across heterogeneous label spaces. Experiments on sixteen datasets covering motor imagery, emotion recognition, ADHD detection, covert speech, and mental workload show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines and prior EEG foundation models under cross-subject settings. On two additional held-out datasets, EEG-PRIME achieves balanced accuracy comparable to within-session calibration models without target-domain optimization, calibration, or linear probing, demonstrating promising zero-shot transfer capability.

AI.tldr: EEG-PRIME is a two-stage EEG foundation model that combines masked pretraining with prototype-aligned instruction tuning, achieving instruction-aware and subject-invariant decoding across heterogeneous BCI datasets, including strong zero-shot transfer on held-out data.
AI.motivation: EEG decoding models generalize poorly across datasets and subjects due to domain shifts in acquisition protocols and individual neurophysiology, motivating a foundation model capable of cross-dataset, multi-task, and subject-invariant decoding.
AI.method: EEG-PRIME uses two stages: (1) masked pretraining with frequency-cutoff spectral augmentation, where an EEG encoder learns transferable representations via reconstruction; (2) prototype-aligned instruction tuning using task-semantic, dataset-specific, and subject-invariant conditioning. The conditioning signal modulates a Q-Former via Layer-wise Query Modulation, and frozen text embeddings of class labels act as prototypes for cosine-similarity-based prediction across heterogeneous label spaces.
AI.result: Across sixteen datasets covering motor imagery, emotion recognition, ADHD detection, covert speech, and mental workload, EEG-PRIME consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and prior EEG foundation models under cross-subject settings. On two held-out datasets, it achieves balanced accuracy comparable to within-session calibration models without target-domain optimization, calibration, or linear probing, demonstrating zero-shot transfer.
AI.conclusion: EEG-PRIME advances cross-dataset multi-task EEG decoding by enabling instruction-aware, subject-invariant representations and promising zero-shot transfer, underscoring the value of prototype-aligned instruction tuning for generalizable EEG foundation models.

title: Latent On-Policy Self-Distillation
summary: Enabling agents to learn from experience and internalize it into their policy has become a central problem in self-evolving AI. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers an effective pathway by using a privileged self-teacher to provide dense supervision on the student's own trajectories; however, existing methods still rely heavily on designer-specified privileged artifacts (e.g., answers, feedback, skills, or trajectories), limiting the end-to-end learnability and scalability required for continual self-improvement. In this work, we introduce Latent On-Policy Self-Distillation (LOPD), which, rather than proposing another hand-crafted OPSD variant with a newly prescribed form of privileged context, makes the teacher's privileged context itself learnable end-to-end from experience. Technically, LOPD retrieves relevant experiences and composes them into continuous latent tokens that condition a self-teacher, while the student generates trajectories from the task and interaction history and receives dense token-level supervision at every visited prefix. We further introduce a privileged-margin objective to stabilize and regulate the learning of latent context. Empirically, LOPD demonstrates (I) strong performance, outperforming RLVR and representative OPSD methods including OPSD, SDPO, and Skill-SD across both agentic tool use and code generation; and (II) high learning efficiency, surpassing GRPO and Skill-SD with less than 30% of their rollout budget. Ablation studies further provide direct evidence that making privileged context learnable is necessary for realizing these gains. Together, these results position LOPD as a step toward a more scalable and self-directed paradigm for agent evolution.

AI.tldr: LOPD makes the privileged context of on-policy self-distillation learnable end-to-end from experience, enabling agents to self-improve without designer-specified privileged artifacts, achieving strong performance and high sample efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) methods rely on designer-specified privileged artifacts (answers, feedback, skills, or trajectories), which limits end-to-end learnability and scalability for continual self-improvement of agents.
AI.method: LOPD retrieves relevant experiences and composes them into continuous latent tokens that condition a self-teacher; the student generates trajectories from task and interaction history and receives dense token-level supervision at every visited prefix. A privileged-margin objective stabilizes and regulates latent context learning.
AI.result: LOPD outperforms RLVR and representative OPSD methods (OPSD, SDPO, Skill-SD) on agentic tool use and code generation, and surpasses GRPO and Skill-SD using less than 30% of their rollout budget. Ablations confirm learnable privileged context is necessary for these gains.
AI.conclusion: LOPD represents a step toward a more scalable and self-directed paradigm for agent evolution by removing reliance on hand-crafted privileged information and enabling end-to-end learning of privileged context.

title: SPADE: Speculative Decoding for Precise and Low Cost Distributed Edge Cloud Inference
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success in natural language understanding and generation, but their deployment is constrained by high computational demands. Deploying smaller LLMs directly on the edge can circumvent this, but with degraded accuracy. Deploying smaller cloud-based big LLMs preserves performance, but at the cost of expensive per-token computation. We present a distributed inference framework, \our{}, that integrates speculative decoding (SD) across edge and cloud. A compact draft model deployed on the edge generates candidate tokens rapidly, and a large verifier model on the cloud validates these tokens in parallel. Accepted tokens are retained, while only rejections trigger verifier correction, substantially reducing the number of cloud queries. Our plug-and-play design shifts the bulk of computation to the edge, significantly lowers inference time and cloud cost, and preserves the accuracy of the big model without any retraining requirement. Our approach demonstrates a practical path toward scalable, cost-efficient, and accurate deployment of LLMs in real-world environments. Experimental results across multiple Natural Language Processing tasks using SpecBench and CNN/Dailymail datasets demonstrate that \our{} reduces the cloud model calls by $76\%$ with zero loss in accuracy as compared to the full model.

AI.tldr: A distributed edge–cloud inference framework that combines a small on-device draft model with a cloud-based large verifier via speculative decoding, cutting cloud calls by 76% with no accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: LLMs are accurate but computationally expensive. Running smaller models on the edge saves cost but degrades accuracy, while running large models in the cloud is accurate but incurs high per-token computation cost. The paper seeks a practical deployment path that is scalable, cost-efficient, and accurate.
AI.method: The proposed plug-and-play framework distributes speculative decoding (SD) across edge and cloud. A compact draft model on the edge rapidly generates candidate tokens, which a large verifier model on the cloud validates in parallel. Accepted tokens are kept, and only rejections trigger verifier correction, shifting most computation to the edge and avoiding any retraining.
AI.result: Experiments on SpecBench and CNN/Dailymail across multiple NLP tasks show the framework reduces cloud model calls by 76% with zero accuracy loss compared to the full model.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides a practical, scalable, and cost-efficient path for accurate LLM deployment in real-world environments by cutting cloud computation and inference time while preserving the large model's accuracy without retraining.

title: Localize, Then Reason: Visual Latent Structural Reasoning for Molecular Properties and Edits
summary: Local chemical perception and property reasoning are both essential for understanding how molecular structure determines properties. Current LLM-based chemical reasoning methods either receive SMILES/molecular images together with descriptions of local motifs, or reason directly from molecular images. Neither approach enables the model to focus on chemically meaningful regions before reasoning. To address this gap, we propose Visual Latent Structural Reasoning (VLSR), an end-to-end framework that jointly learns localization and reasoning from molecular images. Central to our approach is a localize-then-reason strategy. VLSR first learns to locate chemically meaningful regions in a molecular image. It then reasons about their property effects in a compact latent workspace before producing the final answer. Under the same inference setup, this design achieves 9.6X higher throughput than a comparable textual-reasoning baseline.

AI.tldr: VLSR is an end-to-end framework that localizes chemically meaningful regions in molecular images and then reasons about their property effects in a latent workspace, achieving 9.6X higher throughput than a textual-reasoning baseline.
AI.motivation: The two existing LLM-based chemical reasoning approaches either (1) combine SMILES/molecular images with textual descriptions of local motifs, or (2) reason directly from molecular images. Neither allows the model to focus on chemically meaningful regions before reasoning. The authors aim to bridge this gap by enabling joint localization and reasoning from molecular images.
AI.method: VLSR uses a localize-then-reason strategy: it first learns to locate chemically meaningful regions in a molecular image, then reasons about their property effects in a compact latent workspace before producing the final answer. It is an end-to-end framework that jointly learns localization and reasoning.
AI.result: Under the same inference setup, VLSR achieves 9.6X higher throughput than a comparable textual-reasoning baseline.
AI.conclusion: VLSR effectively integrates local chemical perception with property reasoning, demonstrates that localize-then-reason in a latent workspace is a viable and more efficient alternative to textual reasoning from molecular images.

title: A Multispectral Framework for the Detection of Calcium Carbide-Induced Ripening and Shelf-Life Estimation in Climacteric Fruits
summary: Significant health risks are associated with the illegal, yet commonly practiced use of industrial-grade Calcium Carbide (CaC2) for ripening climacteric fruits like mango and banana, which leaves behind trace residues of arsenic and phosphorus. To address this, the proposed study explores a novel, non-invasive multispectral framework for distinguishing safely ripened fruits (naturally ripened and ethephon-induced) from calcium carbide-ripened samples, while also estimating their ripening progression (in percentage) and remaining shelf life (in days). The spectral profiles of mango (Mangifera indica) and banana (Musa acuminata) at 18 discrete wavelengths in the visible-near infrared (NIR) range (410 nm - 940 nm) are studied using the AS7265x spectral triad sensor. CaC2-treated samples exhibit sharper spectral intensity drops in the visible region, consistent with accelerated chlorophyll degradation and carotenoid development. To characterize these physiological changes, the feature engineering strategy integrates inter-method spectral variance, intensity ratios at distinct wavelengths, and environmental parameters including temperature and humidity. Dimensionality reduction using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) retains >90% of spectral variance within the first 5-7 components. The resulting feature set is used to train three independent eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)-based learning algorithms for ripening method classification, along with quantitative estimation of remaining shelf life and ripening progression. A classification accuracy of 95% along with carbide class recall of 0.67 is observed for mango samples, while the model achieves an accuracy of 81% and carbide class recall of 0.74 for banana. This instrumentation and data-driven approach demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed non-invasive framework.

AI.tldr: A non-invasive multispectral framework using the AS7265x sensor across 410–940 nm, combined with XGBoost classifiers and PCA feature reduction, distinguishes calcium carbide-ripened mangoes and bananas from safely ripened ones and estimates ripening progression (%) and remaining shelf life (days).
AI.motivation: Illegal industrial-grade calcium carbide (CaC2) ripening of climacteric fruits leaves toxic arsenic and phosphorus residues, posing significant health risks. There is a need for a non-invasive method to differentiate CaC2-ripened fruit from safely ripened (natural or ethephon-induced) fruit and to quantify ripening status.
AI.method: Spectral reflectance profiles of mango and banana are captured at 18 discrete wavelengths (410–940 nm) with the AS7265x spectral triad sensor. Feature engineering includes inter-method spectral variance, intensity ratios at specific wavelengths, and environmental parameters (temperature, humidity). PCA is applied for dimensionality reduction (retaining >90% variance in 5–7 components). Three independent XGBoost models are trained for ripening-method classification, ripening-progression estimation, and shelf-life estimation.
AI.result: For mango, the model achieves 95% classification accuracy with a carbide class recall of 0.67; for banana, 81% accuracy with a carbide class recall of 0.74. CaC2-treated samples show sharper spectral intensity drops in the visible region, consistent with accelerated chlorophyll degradation and carotenoid development.
AI.conclusion: The instrumentation and data-driven approach demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed non-invasive multispectral framework for detecting carbide-ripened fruit and estimating ripening progression and shelf life.

title: Self-Referential Induction Increases Response Instability Relative to Unresolvable and Verifiable Questions in Large Language Models
summary: Self-referential prompting has been shown to reliably induce large language models to produce first-person reports resembling subjective experience, but no prior work measures how consistent these reports are across repeated, independent trials, or how that consistency compares to the model's behavior on other kinds of open-ended questions. We measure response instability, defined as one minus the mean pairwise cosine similarity of sentence embeddings computed over a compressed core claim extracted from each response, for three groups of questions: self-referential prompts eliciting a subjective-experience report, unresolvable philosophical questions unrelated to self-reference, and questions with a verifiable correct answer. Using 30 independent responses per question (360 responses total, Gemini API, temperature 0.7) across four questions per group, we find that self-referential questions show the highest instability (0.343 +/- 0.047), unresolvable philosophy questions show intermediate and tightly clustered instability (0.192 +/- 0.008), and verifiable questions show the lowest instability (0.105 +/- 0.058). This provides a quantitative baseline for the induced subjective-experience report, showing that it occupies a distinct, less stable position in the model's output distribution than ordinary open-ended philosophical uncertainty.

AI.tldr: The paper measures whether LLM responses to self-referential prompts (which elicit first-person reports of subjective experience) are stable across repeated trials, comparing them against unresolvable philosophy questions and questions with verifiable answers. It finds self-referential reports are the least stable, establishing a quantitative baseline for this phenomenon.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed self-referential prompting reliably induces LLMs to produce first-person reports resembling subjective experience, but no study had measured how consistent these reports are across repeated independent trials or compared that consistency to other open-ended question types. This gap motivated a quantitative measurement of response instability for induced subjective-experience reports.
AI.method: The authors define response instability as one minus the mean pairwise cosine similarity of sentence embeddings computed over a compressed core claim extracted from each response. They test three question groups: self-referential prompts eliciting subjective-experience reports, unresolvable philosophical questions unrelated to self-reference, and questions with verifiable correct answers. For each of four questions per group, they collected 30 independent responses (360 total) via the Gemini API at temperature 0.7, then computed instability scores.
AI.result: Self-referential questions show the highest instability (0.343 ± 0.047); unresolvable philosophy questions show intermediate and tightly clustered instability (0.192 ± 0.008); verifiable questions show the lowest instability (0.105 ± 0.058).
AI.conclusion: The induced subjective-experience report occupies a distinct, less stable position in the model's output distribution than ordinary open-ended philosophical uncertainty, providing a quantitative baseline for future work studying such reports.

title: Learning Discrete Decisions for MIPs with Constraint-Aware Diffusion
summary: This paper proposes a novel learning-based approach to approximately solve instances of mixed-integer optimization problems. These problems are computationally challenging, as they require jointly determining discrete and continuous decisions while satisfying complex combinatorial constraints. The proposed method relies on a graph-based generative diffusion model that learns the discrete component of mixed-integer optimization problems while integrating a training-free feasibility projection operator directly into the reverse diffusion process to steer intermediate samples toward the feasible set throughout generation. Once the discrete decisions are generated, the remaining optimization reduces to a continuous problem that can be solved efficiently (relative to the original problem) using existing numerical methods. The resulting framework named Constrained Graph Diffusion (CGD), is problem-agnostic and can accommodate a broad class of mixed-integer optimization problems through suitable projection operators. We evaluate CGD on optimal transmission switching for ACOPF and discrete portfolio optimization, demonstrating substantial improvements in feasibility and solution quality over learning-based baselines while achieving speedups of up to $425\times$ over state-of-the-art numerical solvers for MINLPs.

AI.tldr: CGD is a learning-based framework that uses a graph-based generative diffusion model to generate the discrete decisions of mixed-integer optimization problems, with a training-free feasibility projection operator embedded in the reverse diffusion process. The remaining continuous problem is then solved efficiently by existing numerical methods.
AI.motivation: Mixed-integer optimization problems are computationally challenging because they require jointly determining discrete and continuous decisions under complex combinatorial constraints. The goal is to substantially accelerate solving while improving feasibility and solution quality over learning-based baselines and numerical MINLP solvers.
AI.method: CGD relies on a graph-based generative diffusion model that learns the discrete component of mixed-integer optimization problems. A training-free feasibility projection operator is integrated directly into the reverse diffusion process to steer intermediate samples toward the feasible set during generation. Once discrete decisions are generated, the problem reduces to a continuous optimization that is solved efficiently with existing numerical methods. The framework is problem-agnostic and generalizes across problems via suitable projection operators.
AI.result: Evaluated on optimal transmission switching for ACOPF and discrete portfolio optimization, CGD achieves substantial improvements in feasibility and solution quality over learning-based baselines, and speedups of up to 425x over state-of-the-art numerical MINLP solvers.
AI.conclusion: CGD provides a problem-agnostic, learning-based approach that effectively separates discrete decision generation (via constrained graph diffusion) from continuous optimization, enabling fast, feasible, and high-quality approximate solutions for a broad class of mixed-integer optimization problems.

title: Robust Dempster-Shafer Evidence Fusion with Chaos-Conflict Measurement and Historical-Experience Weighting
summary: Multi-source evidence fusion under Dempster-Shafer theory faces two persistent challenges: existing conflict measures assess inter-evidence inconsistency and intra-evidence uncertainty independently, yielding incomplete evaluations, and current fusion methods evaluate evidence sources exclusively through instantaneous comparisns without exploiting their long-term reliability across diverse decision contexts. This paper proposes a unified evidence reasoning framework that addresses both limitations. Specifically, a chaos-conflict measurement is introduced to jointly quantify cross-evidence conflict and intra-evidence non-specificity, with five formally proven properties ensuring consistent assessment. A historical experience driven weighting scheme partitions the decision space via spectral clustering and applies regret theory to compute context-specific reliability profiles from past fusion outcomes. These mechanisms feed into a hybrid combination rule that adaptively balances uncertainty preservation against weighted consensus, controlled by the global conflict level, followed by a belief-interval decision strategy that enables robust classification without discarding epistemic uncertainty. Experiments on 16 real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves an average F1 score of 85.78 and a mean AUC of 93.30, outperforming eight DST-based baselines and three gradient boosting methods. Ablation analysis confirms the contribution of each component we proposed. The framework offers an effective approach for adaptive evidence fusion in multi-source decision making.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a unified evidence reasoning framework for Dempster-Shafer theory that jointly measures conflict and non-specificity, uses historical reliability profiles via spectral clustering and regret theory, and applies a hybrid combination rule with belief-interval decision-making, outperforming eight DST baselines and three gradient boosting methods on 16 benchmark datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing DST conflict measures assess inter-evidence inconsistency and intra-evidence uncertainty separately, producing incomplete evaluations. Additionally, current fusion methods evaluate evidence sources only through instantaneous comparisons, ignoring long-term reliability across diverse decision contexts.
AI.method: The framework introduces: (1) a chaos-conflict measurement that jointly quantifies cross-evidence conflict and intra-evidence non-specificity with five formally proven properties; (2) a historical experience-driven weighting scheme that partitions the decision space via spectral clustering and applies regret theory to compute context-specific reliability profiles from past fusion outcomes; (3) a hybrid combination rule that adaptively balances uncertainty preservation against weighted consensus based on the global conflict level; and (4) a belief-interval decision strategy enabling robust classification while preserving epistemic uncertainty.
AI.result: On 16 real-world benchmark datasets, the framework achieves an average F1 score of 85.78 and a mean AUC of 93.30, outperforming eight DST-based baselines and three gradient boosting methods. Ablation analysis confirms the contribution of each proposed component.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides an effective approach for adaptive evidence fusion in multi-source decision making by jointly addressing conflict quantification and long-term source reliability.

title: How Do VLMs Behave When Blind or Misled? Behavioral Evaluation of VLMs on Scientific Figures
comment: 25 pages including appendix. Project website: https://scifigbench.nlp4sci.com
summary:
Existing vision-language model (VLM) benchmarks emphasize perception and reasoning accuracy (how well VLMs describe and reason about what they see in an image), with limited attention to behavioral reliability under uncertainty (how they behave when visual evidence is missing or misleading). We introduce SciFigBench, a diagnostic VLM benchmark for scientific figure understanding that jointly evaluates perception, reasoning, and behavioral reliability under uncertainty. It contains 250 figures with high-quality human annotations across three evaluation aspects, totaling 600+ hours of annotation effort. We further extend these figures via image transformations, reasoning questions, resistance probes, caption-bias probes, and confirmed selective-blur targets, producing over 34,000 evaluation setups for stress testing.
  We further propose the Admittance-Resistance-Inductance (A-R-I) framework to evaluate whether models acknowledge insufficient evidence, resist misleading context, and infer cautiously from partial information. Our results reveal substantial behavioral differences among models. GPT-5.2 achieves the highest description quality (MQM 91.6) with strong reasoning accuracy (78.4%), yet hallucinates unreadable content in 96% of cases, whereas Gemini 3.1 Pro, a comparably capable model (MQM 90.2, reasoning 81.0%), admits uncertainty in 71% of such cases and achieves the strongest resistance score (0.91). These findings show that high perception and reasoning accuracy alone do not guarantee behavioral reliability, a dimension critical for deployment in scientific workflows.

AI.tldr: SciFigBench is a diagnostic benchmark for VLMs evaluating scientific figure understanding across perception, reasoning, and behavioral reliability under uncertainty. Using 250 annotated figures extended to 34,000+ stress-testing setups, it introduces the Admittance-Resistance-Inductance (A-R-I) framework and shows that high accuracy (e.g., GPT-5.2) does not guarantee behavioral reliability—GPT-5.2 hallucinates unreadable content 96% of the time, while Gemini 3.1 Pro admits uncertainty in 71% of such cases.
AI.motivation: Existing VLM benchmarks focus on perception and reasoning accuracy but neglect behavioral reliability under uncertainty—how models respond when visual evidence is missing or misleading. This gap matters for scientific workflows where silent hallucination is dangerous.
AI.method: The authors build SciFigBench: 250 scientific figures with human annotations (600+ hours) covering perception, reasoning, and behavioral reliability. They extend these via image transformations, reasoning questions, resistance probes, caption-bias probes, and selective-blur targets to create 34,000+ evaluation setups. They propose the Admittance-Resistance-Inductance (A-R-I) framework to measure whether models admit insufficient evidence, resist misleading context, and infer cautiously from partial information.
AI.result: GPT-5.2 achieves the highest description quality (MQM 91.6) and strong reasoning accuracy (78.4%) but hallucinates unreadable content in 96% of cases. Gemini 3.1 Pro has comparable accuracy (MQM 90.2, reasoning 81.0%) yet admits uncertainty in 71% of unreadable cases and scores highest on resistance (0.91). Models show substantial behavioral differences despite similar accuracy.
AI.conclusion: High perception and reasoning accuracy alone do not guarantee behavioral reliability under uncertainty; this behavioral dimension is critical for safe deployment in scientific workflows. The A-R-I framework and SciFigBench provide a means to evaluate and diagnose it.

title: Sampling Luck Masquerades as Allocation Gain: Auditing Test-Time Budget Allocation for Neural Combinatorial Optimization
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 8 tables. Pre-registered study; code, cost arrays, and the full pre-registration record (including every amendment and its direction) at https://github.com/nepersoned/best-of-k-allocation
summary:
Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) solvers report the best of many sampled solutions per instance, and the sample count is, by convention, identical for every instance. Whether a non-uniform allocation of a fixed total budget would buy anything has not been measured. We measure it, and we audit the measurement itself.
  First, on in-distribution workloads the allocation headroom is not detectable. Across three pretrained solvers (POMO, AM, SymNCO) on uniform TSP-100, an oracle allocation computed and evaluated on the same stored samples reports a 2.2-2.6% gain with intervals excluding zero; measured out of sample the same gain is indistinguishable from zero (0.457, 0.015, -0.512 percent). Following the customary in-sample procedure, all three solvers would have supported a published 2%-level gain that does not exist. We calibrate this bias against an instance-wise null in which the true gain is zero by construction; over the ranges we test it does not shrink with more samples or more instances.
  Second, the same correction that removes the phantom gains preserves a real one. Under distribution shift (a workload mixing uniform and clustered instances), a pre-registered confirmatory experiment finds that allocation guided by held-out sample statistics improves best-of-k by 11.5% (AM, primary endpoint; 95% CI [7.4, 19.7]) and 12.0% (SymNCO, replication) at equal evaluation budget, with the signal-acquisition cost not charged; a pre-registered negative control (POMO, an order of magnitude more robust to shift) shows -0.3% [-0.7, 0.24]. The gain exceeds a frozen distribution-label baseline by 4.2 points [1.9, 7.7]. An exploratory policy charging a 20-sample probe against the same budget retains 3.4% (AM) and 4.6% (SymNCO).
  We give a correction procedure and a reporting checklist, and release all data, code, and the pre-registration record.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that reported gains from non-uniform budget allocation in neural combinatorial optimization solvers are often in-sample artifacts. On in-distribution data the apparent 2% gains vanish out-of-sample, but under distribution shift a real 11–12% best-of-k improvement exists, especially for shift-robust solvers, and remains (3–5%) even when probe costs are charged.
AI.motivation: NCO solvers use a uniform sample count per instance by convention, and it was unknown whether non-uniform allocation of a fixed evaluation budget yields real improvements. The authors aim to measure any gains and, critically, to audit whether such measurements themselves suffer from methodological bias.
AI.method: They compare an oracle allocation (computed and evaluated on the same stored samples) against out-of-sample evaluation across three pretrained solvers (POMO, AM, SymNCO) on TSP-100. They calibrate the in-sample bias using an instance-wise null where the true gain is zero by construction. A pre-registered confirmatory experiment tests allocation under distribution shift (mixed uniform and clustered instances) with a primary endpoint, replication, negative control, and a frozen distribution-label baseline, plus an exploratory policy charging probe cost.
AI.result: In-distribution, the oracle reports 2.2–2.6% gains that are indistinguishable from zero out-of-sample (0.457, 0.015, -0.512 percent) and the bias does not shrink with more samples or instances. Under distribution shift, held-out-sample-guided allocation improves best-of-k by 11.5% (AM, 95% CI [7.4, 19.7]) and 12.0% (SymNCO); the negative control POMO shows -0.3% [-0.7, 0.24], and the gain exceeds a frozen distribution-label baseline by 4.2 points. Charging a 20-sample probe retains 3.4% (AM) and 4.6% (SymNCO).
AI.conclusion: The conventional in-sample procedure can produce phantom 2%-level gains that disappear out-of-sample, so a correction procedure and reporting checklist are necessary. Once corrected, a genuine allocation gain exists under distribution shift, especially for less shift-robust solvers, and survives even when signal acquisition is charged.

title: SkillEvo: Self-Renewing Evolution Gradients from Multi-Turn Interaction Feedback
summary: Agent Skills are today either hand-authored or produced in a single LLM generation pass, and consequently possess no closed loop through which they might improve from the interaction failures they actually cause. Recent work does close this loop, but derives its feedback from single-turn question-answering evaluation. The consequence is a sharp asymmetry: once the first round has patched the gaps that a single exchange can reveal, the evolution gradient decays, the defects that surface only across multiple turns remain invisible, and evolution stalls. Governance in these systems is likewise driven by an end-to-end verification score, a scalar gate that can reject a degraded candidate but can neither localize nor repair its structural cause. We argue that the binding constraint on sustained skill evolution is neither editing capability nor the number of iterations, but whether the evaluation feedback keeps supplying trustworthy evolution gradients. We introduce SkillEvo, in which trustworthy feedback generates the gradient and controllable governance constrains its direction. The first component recasts multi-turn user simulation from an evaluation endpoint into a feedback generator: follow-up questions expose defects layer by layer, so that every round of revision both consumes feedback and produces new feedback. The second replaces the passive rejection of a scalar gate with an independent governance layer that actively repairs factual degradation and structural bloat, preventing the gradient from drifting as degradation accumulates. Across six categories of cloud services, 9 production Skills, and 98 skill-reference files, SkillEvo surpasses self-reflection-based evolution by 23.0 points and single- turn-QA-driven evolution by 15.4 points.

AI.tldr: SkillEvo introduces a two-component framework for evolving agent Skills: trustworthy multi-turn user simulation as a feedback generator that creates sustained evolution gradients, and an independent governance layer that actively repairs factual degradation and structural bloat. It outperforms baselines by 23.0 and 15.4 points across cloud-service Skills.
AI.motivation: Current agent Skills lack a closed feedback loop, and existing closed-loop methods rely on single-turn QA, whose gradient decays after the first round and misses multi-turn defects. Governance uses only a scalar end-to-end verification score that cannot localize or repair structural causes. The binding constraint on sustained skill evolution is the trustworthiness of the evaluation feedback gradient, not editing capability or iteration count.
AI.method: SkillEvo has two components: (1) recasting multi-turn user simulation from an evaluation endpoint into a feedback generator, where follow-up questions expose defects layer by layer so each revision round both consumes and produces feedback; and (2) replacing passive scalar-gate rejection with an independent governance layer that actively repairs factual degradation and structural bloat, keeping the gradient from drifting as degradation accumulates.
AI.result: Across six cloud-service categories, 9 production Skills, and 98 skill-reference files, SkillEvo surpasses self-reflection-based evolution by 23.0 points and single-turn-QA-driven evolution by 15.4 points.
AI.conclusion: The key to sustained skill evolution is trustworthy, continuously supplying feedback gradients combined with controllable governance to constrain their direction. Multi-turn simulation as a feedback generator plus active governance-level repair enables continued improvement that single-turn evaluation and scalar gates cannot achieve.

title: Mixture of Training: Recombining Small-Scale Scaffolded Pretraining Runs into a Larger Language Model
comment: Accepted at the Workshop on Methods and Opportunities at Small Scale (MOSS), COLM 2026
summary: We ask whether language-model pre-training can be decomposed into smaller, independently trainable jobs that can later be recomposed into a coherent larger model. We introduce Mixture of Training (MoT), a scaffolded modular pre-training procedure that partitions a target Transformer into contiguous layer blocks, trains each block inside a frozen pretrained aligner scaffold, and then recomposes the trained blocks with an optional short end-to-end adaptation pass. On a 1.3B-parameter Gemma-style model trained on C4, MoT provides a small-scale proof of mechanism: independently trained depth slices can be recomposed into a usable language model, and a quality-parity schedule reaches the same reported perplexity as the monolithic baseline. This parity setting processes more aggregate tokens and has a shorter idealized layer-equivalent critical path after aligner preparation; its effective compute advantage depends on reusing the aligner across runs. We therefore present MoT not as a general replacement for monolithic pre-training, but as a small-scale framework for studying whether scaffolded sub-runs can act as reusable training units.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Mixture of Training (MoT), a method that decomposes language-model pre-training into independently trainable contiguous layer blocks within a frozen pretrained aligner scaffold, then recomposes the blocks into a full model. It demonstrates on a 1.3B Gemma-style model trained on C4 that this produces a usable model matching monolithic baseline perplexity, framing MoT as a small-scale framework for studying reusable scaffolded training units rather than a general replacement for monolithic pre-training.
AI.motivation: The authors seek to determine whether language-model pre-training can be broken into smaller, independently trainable jobs that can later be recomposed into a coherent larger model, with the goal of exploring whether scaffolded sub-runs can serve as reusable training units and potentially improve training efficiency or parallelism.
AI.method: MoT partitions a target Transformer into contiguous layer blocks (depth slices). Each block is trained inside a frozen pretrained aligner scaffold, meaning the surrounding context is provided by an already-trained model rather than training end-to-end. Afterward, the independently trained blocks are recomposed into the full model, optionally followed by a short end-to-end adaptation pass. The approach is validated on a 1.3B-parameter Gemma-style model trained on the C4 corpus.
AI.result: MoT provides a small-scale proof of mechanism: independently trained depth slices recompose into a usable language model. A quality-parity schedule reaches the same reported perplexity as the monolithic baseline. This parity setting processes more aggregate tokens but has a shorter idealized layer-equivalent critical path after aligner preparation. The effective compute advantage depends on reusing the aligner across runs.
AI.conclusion: MoT is presented not as a general replacement for monolithic pre-training but as a small-scale framework for studying whether scaffolded sub-runs can act as reusable training units, with its practical compute benefit contingent on aligner reuse across multiple runs.

title: FlowLOB: Efficient and Controllable Limit Order Book Generation with Flow Matching
summary: Limit order book (LOB) simulators are most useful to practitioners when they combine realistic market dynamics, computationally efficient sampling, controllable scenario generation, and the ability to generalize beyond the instruments seen during training---properties that existing agent-based and deep generative simulators provide only partially. We present \textbf{FlowLOB}, a conditional \textbf{flow}-matching generator of \textbf{LOB} trajectories, trained on multiple Hong Kong Exchange (HKEX) symbols at three sampling frequencies ($0.1$s, $1$s, $10$s) in tick-relative representation that transfers to unseen instruments. Because flow and diffusion models admit a common formulation, we train both with identical data, architecture, and budget, and sample both through the same fixed-step ODE solvers, yielding a controlled comparison of sampling efficiency and fidelity. Flow matching attains its best quality with only $10$ ODE-solver steps, whereas diffusion needs many more function evaluations to approach the same fidelity. At this efficient operating point, FlowLOB improves realism over baselines, two learned and two agent-based models, in most distributional metrics at the two finer sampling frequencies. We evaluate counterfactual controllability with a distributional test that asks whether changing a scenario condition moves the generated statistic toward the corresponding real tail regime; FlowLOB satisfies this criterion in most tested settings. Both realism and control effects transfer zero-shot on a held-out symbol. We additionally conduct ablation studies on the network architecture and the learning rate.

AI.tldr: FlowLOB is a conditional flow-matching generative model for limit order book trajectories, trained on multiple HKEX symbols in tick-relative representation. It reaches best sampling quality with only 10 ODE steps, outperforming both diffusion and agent-based baselines at finer frequencies, while offering controllable scenario generation and zero-shot transfer to unseen instruments.
AI.motivation: Existing LOB simulators fail to jointly satisfy realistic market dynamics, computationally efficient sampling, controllable scenario generation, and generalization to unseen instruments. Agent-based simulators and deep generative models (including diffusion) each provide only partial coverage of these properties, motivating a unified generator that addresses all four.
AI.method: FlowLOB is a conditional flow-matching generator of LOB trajectories in tick-relative representation, trained on multiple HKEX symbols at 0.1s, 1s, and 10s sampling frequencies. Leveraging the shared formulation of flow and diffusion models, both are trained with identical data, architecture, and budget, and sampled via the same fixed-step ODE solvers for a controlled comparison. The authors add ablation studies on network architecture and learning rate.
AI.result: Flow matching achieves its best fidelity with only 10 ODE-solver steps, while diffusion requires substantially more function evaluations to match that fidelity. At this efficient operating point, FlowLOB improves realism over four baselines (two learned, two agent-based) on most distributional metrics at the two finer sampling frequencies. A distributional controllability test confirms that changing a scenario condition moves generated statistics toward the corresponding real tail regime in most settings. Realism and control effects transfer zero-shot to a held-out symbol.
AI.conclusion: FlowLOB demonstrates that conditional flow matching offers a compelling trade-off between sampling efficiency and fidelity for LOB simulation, achieving strong realism and controllable, transferable scenario generation while requiring far fewer ODE steps than diffusion, with ablation results further informing architecture and hyperparameter choices.

title: Numeracy in Large Language Models: Fundamental Limitations and Paths to Improvement
summary: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong results on mathematical reasoning benchmarks yet remain unreliable on elementary numerical tasks, including magnitude comparison, large-integer arithmetic, fractions, and scientific notation. This survey examines basic numerical understanding as a capability distinct from high-level mathematical reasoning. We propose the Numerical Grounding Framework (NGF), which decomposes numeracy into Representational Grounding (RG), mapping numeral forms to value, magnitude, and equivalent representations, and Procedural Grounding (PG), executing arithmetic operations in accordance with their mathematical definitions. Using NGF, we organize recent diagnostic benchmarks, failure modes, structural explanations, and mitigation strategies. We review evidence concerning tokenization, positional encoding, embedding geometry, and pretraining-data distribution. We also apply NGF in a coordinated evaluation of three frontier model families across Number Cookbook, NumericBench, and GSM-Symbolic, comparing atomic, contextual, and reasoning-assisted numeracy. Architectural interventions such as digit-aware tokenization and Abacus Embeddings can improve models trained from scratch but are generally unavailable to users of pretrained systems, for whom supervised fine-tuning, reasoning scaffolds, and external tools are more practical. We conclude with deployment recommendations and research directions for more reliable numerical behavior in foundation models.

AI.tldr: This survey formalizes "numerical grounding" as a capability distinct from high-level math reasoning, proposes the Numerical Grounding Framework (NGF) to organize diagnostics, failure modes, and mitigations, and evaluates frontier models on atomic, contextual, and reasoning-assisted numeracy.
AI.motivation: LLMs excel at mathematical reasoning benchmarks but remain unreliable on elementary numerical tasks (magnitude comparison, arithmetic, fractions, scientific notation). The authors argue this reflects a distinct "basic numerical understanding" capability that is under-addressed and deserves systematic study to improve reliable numerical behavior.
AI.method: The paper introduces the Numerical Grounding Framework (NGF), decomposing numeracy into Representational Grounding (RG: mapping numerals to value, magnitude, and equivalent representations) and Procedural Grounding (PG: executing arithmetic per mathematical definitions).
