NGF is used to organize recent benchmarks, failure modes, structural explanations (tokenization, positional encoding, embedding geometry, pretraining data), and mitigations. A coordinated evaluation of three frontier model families is conducted across Number Cookbook, NumericBench, and GSM-Symbolic, comparing atomic, contextual, and reasoning-assisted numeracy.
AI.result: Architectural interventions like digit-aware tokenization and Abacus Embeddings improve models trained from scratch, but are unavailable to users of pretrained systems. For pretrained models, supervised fine-tuning, reasoning scaffolds, and external tools are more practical. NGF organizes evidence on why and how numerical grounding fails across model families.
AI.conclusion: The survey concludes with deployment recommendations and research directions for improving reliable numerical behavior in foundation models, distinguishing between training-time architectural fixes and inference-time user-applicable mitigations.

title: Refusing Intent, Not Form: Wrapper-Based Intent-Group Supervision for LLM Safety
summary: Safety tuning can improve harmful refusal, but models may learn surface-form shortcuts: wrapped harmful prompts bypass safety, while similarly wrapped benign prompts are over-refused. We propose Wrapper-Based Intent-Form Augmentation (WIFA), an automatic intent-group augmentation method that pairs wrapped harmful examples with structurally matched wrapped benign counterexamples, requiring no external teacher or manual per-wrapper intent labels. We use WIFA as a common data layer for two complementary fine-tuning routes: WIFA-Boost, a two-stage high-safety recipe, and Anchored Group-Consistent Refusal Training (A-GCRT), which regularizes refusal/compliance decision scores across same-intent wrappers and anchors harmful and benign groups on opposite sides of a margin. In the Qwen setting, WIFA-Boost reaches the strongest transformed-harmful refusal, while A-GCRT reduces OR-Bench over-refusal from 25.7\% for the base model to 17.4\%; reproduced baselines do not match these operating points. Llama results and ablations over data structure, two-stage order, and A-GCRT components support this intent-group interpretation without claiming universal below-base over-refusal.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses safety tuning's vulnerability to "wrapper" attacks (wrapped harmful prompts bypassing refusal) and over-refusal of similarly wrapped benign prompts. It introduces WIFA, an automatic data augmentation method pairing wrapped harmful and benign examples by intent group, and uses it in two fine-tuning recipes (WIFA-Boost and A-GCRT) to improve harmful-refusal and reduce over-refusal.
AI.motivation: Safety-tuned models learn surface-form shortcuts: adversarially wrapped harmful prompts slip past safety filters, while benign prompts with similar wrappers get incorrectly refused. Existing fixes require external teachers or manual per-wrapper labels, which are costly and don't scale. The authors want an automatic, teacher-free way to teach models that refusal should depend on underlying intent, not on wrapper surface form.
AI.method: WIFA (Wrapper-Based Intent-Form Augmentation) automatically pairs wrapped harmful examples with structurally matched wrapped benign counterexamples within the same intent group, needing no external teacher or manual labels. It serves as a shared data layer for two fine-tuning routes: (1) WIFA-Boost, a two-stage high-safety recipe, and (2) A-GCRT (Anchored Group-Consistent Refusal Training), which regularizes refusal/compliance decision scores to be consistent across wrappers of the same intent and anchors harmful and benign groups on opposite sides of a margin.
AI.result: On Qwen, WIFA-Boost achieves the strongest transformed-harmful refusal, and A-GCRT lowers OR-Bench over-refusal from 25.7% (base model) to 17.4%; reproduced baselines fail to reach these operating points. Llama experiments and ablations over data structure, two-stage order, and A-GCRT components support the intent-group interpretation, though without claiming universal below-base over-refusal.
AI.conclusion: Augmenting safety data by intent-group pairing (harmful vs. structurally matched benign wrappers) lets models learn refusal driven by intent rather than surface form, improving harmful-refusal while cutting over-refusal. The approach is automatic, teacher-free, and validated across Qwen and Llama, though the authors avoid overclaiming universal below-base over-refusal.

title: Branch and Bound for Relational Verification of Neural Networks
comment: The full version of the paper accepted by EMSOFT 2026
summary:
Verification of neural networks against relational specifications, such as global robustness, is crucial for safety-critical applications of cyber-physical systems (CPS), given their increasing adoption of AI components. Compared to simple trace properties (e.g., local robustness), verifying relational specifications requires reasoning about the relationship between multiple network inferences, which brings significant technical challenges. Existing research has explored abstraction techniques based on sound and convex over-approximation of neural network outputs; however, since these approaches are inherently incomplete and may raise false alarms, they further underscore the need of effective abstraction refinement.
  In this paper, we propose a branch-and-bound (BaB) framework to mitigate the issue, which iteratively splits the problem until all sub-problems are verified. Specifically, our BaB framework features splitting of relational neurons rather than individual neurons as prior works do, and as the core of our technique, we devise a relational neuron selection strategy based on the dual formulation of the verification problem, which allows us to efficiently select the (most likely) optimal relational neuron that maximizes the refinement brought by problem splitting. We evaluate SaBRe on 817 verification problems across ACAS Xu, MNIST-F, MNIST-C, CIFAR and GTSRB. The results show that SaBRe outperforms different baseline approaches, in terms of the number of solved instances and verification efficiency, which demonstrates the effectiveness of our proposed techniques.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SaBRe, a branch-and-bound (BaB) framework for verifying neural networks against relational specifications (e.g., global robustness). It splits on "relational neurons" rather than individual neurons and selects the most promising relational neuron using a dual-formulation-based strategy, outperforming baselines on 817 ACAS Xu, MNIST, CIFAR, and GTSRB verification problems.
AI.motivation: Safety-critical cyber-physical systems increasingly use neural networks, making verification of relational specifications (like global robustness) essential. Unlike simple trace properties, relational specifications require reasoning about relationships between multiple network inferences, which is technically challenging. Existing sound convex over-approximation methods are incomplete and may generate false alarms, underscoring the need for effective abstraction refinement.
AI.method: The authors propose SaBRe, a branch-and-bound framework that iteratively splits verification problems until all sub-problems are verified. Its key innovations are: (1) splitting on relational neurons instead of individual neurons, and (2) a relational neuron selection strategy built on the dual formulation of the verification problem to efficiently choose the (most likely) optimal relational neuron that maximizes the refinement from splitting.
AI.result: SaBRe was evaluated on 817 verification problems spanning ACAS Xu, MNIST-F, MNIST-C, CIFAR, and GTSRB. It outperformed different baseline approaches in both the number of solved instances and verification efficiency, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed techniques.
AI.conclusion: The proposed branch-and-bound framework with relational-neuron splitting and dual-based neuron selection effectively mitigates the incompleteness and false-alarm issues of convex over-approximation, providing a more complete and efficient approach to verifying relational specifications of neural networks in safety-critical CPS.

title: Rethinking Normalization Placement for LLMs: Post-Norm under Curriculum Depth Growing
summary: Pre-norm is the standard normalization placement in modern Transformers because it facilitates joint optimization of full-depth models. We ask whether this preference persists when depth is introduced through a curriculum. In curriculum depth growth, each appended block receives the boundary representation produced by a trained prefix, making normalization placement relevant to forward conditioning. We therefore test whether placement and training curriculum interact. In a controlled distillation study with a Qwen3-8B teacher and a nine-layer student, pre-norm and post-norm are indistinguishable under joint training, differing by $0.0004$ validation CE, while post-norm improves over pre-norm by $0.0328$ under curriculum growth, an order of magnitude larger. A post-joint control matched by student active-layer tokens remains worse than post-grow, which rules out compute as the sole explanation. The ranking crosses over during the curriculum: post-norm takes the lead once blocks are appended. Single-block and freeze controls localize the ranking change to block appending rather than shallow-block quality or retraining. Boundary diagnostics associate post-norm with stable residual scales and pre-norm with structural-token scale drift; on a fixed batch, the final pre-grow block is also nearly identity-mapped. Together with the phase-wise crossover, these observations are consistent with boundary-scale conditioning after new blocks are appended. The results motivate treating normalization placement and training curriculum as coupled design choices in this distillation setting.

AI.tldr: Pre-norm and post-norm are indistinguishable under joint training, but post-norm significantly outperforms pre-norm when Transformers are trained with curriculum depth growth, indicating that normalization placement and training curriculum are coupled design choices.
AI.motivation: Pre-norm is standard in modern Transformers due to its compatibility with joint optimization of full-depth models. The authors question whether this preference holds when depth is introduced incrementally via a curriculum, since each new block receives boundary representations from a trained prefix, making normalization placement directly relevant to forward conditioning.
AI.method: A controlled distillation study with a Qwen3-8B teacher and a nine-layer student. The authors compare pre-norm vs. post-norm under joint training and curriculum depth growth, measure validation cross-entropy, and run controls: a post-joint model matched by active-layer tokens (to rule out compute), single-block and freeze controls (to isolate block appending), and boundary diagnostics of residual scales and structural-token scale drift.
AI.result: Under joint training, pre-norm and post-norm differ by only 0.0004 validation CE; under curriculum growth, post-norm improves by 0.0328 (an order of magnitude larger). The post-joint compute-matched control remains worse than post-grow, ruling out compute alone. The ranking crosses over during the curriculum, with post-norm taking the lead once blocks are appended. Boundary diagnostics show post-norm has stable residual scales while pre-norm suffers structural-token scale drift, and the final pre-grow block is nearly identity-mapped on a fixed batch.
AI.conclusion: Normalization placement and training curriculum interact; post-norm is superior when depth is grown via curriculum, consistent with boundary-scale conditioning after new blocks are appended. These findings motivate treating normalization placement and training curriculum as coupled design choices in this distillation setting.

title: Beyond Local Accuracy: A Protocol-Level Identifiability Audit for Controlled LLM Reasoning Evaluation
comment: 15 pages, 9 figures. Ning Huang, Ziqi Sha, and Wenxuan Tang contributed equally as second authors. Wei Deng is the corresponding author
summary: LLM benchmark scores can be precise even when the observation protocol does not identify the behavioral property they are intended to measure. In a controlled, solver-grounded setting, we formalize a protocol-level identifiability audit over a finite behavioral policy class: given policies H, observation support O, and estimand $τ$, we test whether O separates every pair with different $τ$. The audit requires zero model calls and resolves our diagnostic case: base-only observation collapses seven frozen deterministic policies into one equivalence class; full support yields seven classes and no cross-estimand collisions; every leave-one-out support retains a constructive collision witness. Empirically, both constrained-generation variants have pair-validity 1.0, yet base accuracy and selective-response fidelity diverge - 0.620 versus 0.324 across six balanced oracle-transition directions (cluster-bootstrap 95% CI [0.600, 0.642] vs. [0.304, 0.345]) - and the gap recurs on a second deterministic source (0.646 vs. 0.331). The audit also synthesizes a minimum identifying support $O^*$ for the frozen policy class: two cells instead of the full 36-cell tensor. This case shows how evaluation-design validity can be checked structurally before model inference and why base correctness does not determine intervention-response fidelity.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a structural, model-free "identifiability audit" for LLM benchmarks. It shows that a benchmark can score precisely while failing to identify the behavioral property it claims to measure, and it demonstrates the method on a solver-grounded case where base accuracy and intervention-response fidelity diverge sharply.
AI.motivation: Benchmark scores can be numerically precise yet observationally invalid: the observation protocol may not actually separate policies that differ on the estimand being measured. The authors want a way to verify, before any model inference, whether an evaluation design structurally identifies the intended property, rather than merely reporting scores.
AI.method: Over a finite behavioral policy class H, observation support O, and estimand τ, the protocol-level audit tests whether O separates every pair of policies with different τ values. It requires zero model calls. It is applied to frozen deterministic policies: base-only observations, full support, all leave-one-out supports, and a synthesized minimum identifying support O*.
AI.result: Base-only observation collapses seven frozen deterministic policies into one equivalence class. Full support yields seven distinct classes with no cross-estimand collisions, while every leave-one-out support retains a constructive collision witness. Empirically, constrained-generation variants both achieve pair-validity 1.0, but base accuracy (0.620) and selective-response fidelity (0.324) diverge with non-overlapping cluster-bootstrap CIs ([0.600,0.642] vs [0.304,0.345]); the gap recurs on a second source (0.646 vs 0.331). The audit synthesizes a minimum identifying support O* of only two cells instead of the full 36-cell tensor.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation-design validity can be checked structurally before spending compute on model inference, and base correctness does not determine intervention-response fidelity. The audit provides a cheap, principled prerequisite step for benchmark construction.

title: ProME: Prototype-Margin Environments with Repair-Aware Selection for Group-Robust Learning
summary: Group-robust learning is crucial for maintaining accuracy on rare subpopulations when training-group labels are unavailable. However, existing methods often infer environments from a separate reference model and select representations before fitting the classifier used at deployment, leaving both decisions misaligned with the deployed predictor. In this work, we formulate group robustness without training-group labels as the endogenous environments with repair-aware selection (ERAS) problem, and propose ProME (Prototype-Margin Environments) to align both decisions with the deployed predictor. ProME splits prototype margins at their median to construct approximately balanced environments along the training trajectory, and fits a group-balanced linear head on group-annotated validation data to rank the resulting predictors by validation worst-group accuracy. We theoretically bound the worst risk across the inferred environments for a fixed predictor and partition, showing that this bound transfers to the oracle groups under an explicit alignment condition. Extensive experiments show that prototype margins enrich shortcut-conflicting examples, classifier repair reshapes candidate evaluation, and ProME achieves the highest average worst-group accuracy among the compared methods with the same group-label access.

AI.tldr: ProME tackles group-robust learning without training-group labels by constructing environments from prototype margins and selecting the deployed predictor via repair-aware selection, achieving state-of-the-art average worst-group accuracy under limited group-label access.
AI.motivation: Existing group-robust methods infer environments using a separate reference model and select representations before fitting the deployed classifier, which misaligns environment inference and candidate selection with the final predictor, hurting worst-group performance when training-group labels are unavailable.
AI.method: The paper formulates the ERAS (endogenous environments with repair-aware selection) problem and designs ProME, which (1) splits prototype margins at their median to build approximately balanced environments along training, (2) fits a group-balanced linear head on group-annotated validation data to rank predictors by validation worst-group accuracy, and (3) provides a theoretical bound on worst risk across inferred environments that transfers to oracle groups under an explicit alignment condition.
AI.result: Experiments show prototype margins enrich shortcut-conflicting examples, classifier repair reshapes candidate evaluation, and ProME achieves the highest average worst-group accuracy among compared methods with the same group-label access.
AI.conclusion: Aligning environment inference and representation/classifier selection with the deployed predictor via ProME improves worst-group accuracy under limited group supervision, with theoretical and empirical support for endogenous environment construction and repair-aware selection.

title: SkillShapley: Boundary-Adaptive Shapley Valuation for Skill Step Attribution in LLM Agents
summary: Agent skills are crucial external instructions that enable language agents to execute long procedural tasks such as coding or document processing. Existing agent skills are primarily created through human manual crafting or agent execution traces, with limited understanding of how each step contributes to overall skill performance on specific tasks; i.e., there remains an open problem in quantifying the contribution of individual steps within an agent skill. To address this issue, we first model skill-step attribution as a Shapley value-based contribution estimation problem, and then propose SkillShapley, a step-level attribution framework for agent skills. Notably, SkillShapley operates in two phases, motivated by key empirical insights, i.e., discretized benchmark rewards that create sharp performance cliffs, and step interactions that are largely additive rather than synergistic. Specifically, it first identifies informative coalitional regions, and then adaptively samples new coalitions that can yield reusable marginal evidence. Experiments on skills from the widely adopted SkillsBench demonstrate that our SkillShapley can effectively and efficiently identify high- or low-value skill steps, providing several key takeaways for agent skill creation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SkillShapley, a Shapley value-based framework for attributing the contribution of individual steps within agent skills, using a two-phase adaptive sampling method to efficiently quantify step value.
AI.motivation: Agent skills (external instructions for long procedural tasks) are typically created manually or from execution traces, but there is no principled way to quantify how much each individual step contributes to overall skill performance on specific tasks. The paper aims to solve this open step-level attribution problem.
AI.method: SkillShapley models skill-step attribution as a Shapley value-based contribution estimation problem. Motivated by two empirical insights—(1) discretized benchmark rewards create sharp performance cliffs, and (2) step interactions are largely additive rather than synergistic—the framework operates in two phases: first identifying informative coalitional regions, then adaptively sampling new coalitions that yield reusable marginal evidence.
AI.result: Experiments on skills from the widely adopted SkillsBench show that SkillShapley can effectively and efficiently identify high- or low-value skill steps, yielding key takeaways for agent skill creation.
AI.conclusion: SkillShapley provides an effective and efficient step-level attribution method for agent skills, enabling practitioners to identify valuable or dispensable steps and informing better agent skill design and creation.

title: It's How You Ask: Gender-Associated Linguistic Bias in LLMs
summary: Professional communication is increasingly mediated by LLMs - but do these models serve all users equally? We show that when prompts contain linguistic features more commonly used by women (hedges, tag questions, collective reference), they systematically elicit shorter, less sophisticated, and less formal responses across three document types and four models. These effects persist after controlling for prompt complexity and feature carry-over. Explicit gender cues like sign-off names are encoded in the same representational space as linguistic dialect - suggesting shared underlying mechanisms - yet linguistic register is far more influential, producing large, consistent effects where names produce none. Our results further reveal that post-hoc mitigation is challenging: because these patterns are culturally embedded and outside conscious control, users cannot easily avoid them through strategic self-presentation, and mechanistic analysis reveals that linguistic features are encoded in early transformer layers and entangled with other features. Our work calls for upstream consideration of the influences of linguistic variation to mitigate disparate impacts of LLM-mediated workplace communication.

AI.tldr: LLMs systematically produce shorter, less sophisticated, and less formal responses when prompts use linguistic features more common among women, an effect that is robust, hard to mitigate, and encoded early in the models.
AI.motivation: Professional communication is increasingly mediated by LLMs, raising the question of whether these models serve all users equally. The authors investigate whether gendered linguistic variation (how women versus men tend to write) causes differential treatment by LLMs in workplace communication.
AI.method: The authors analyzed LLM responses to prompts containing gendered linguistic features (hedges, tag questions, collective references) versus those more common in men's language, across three document types and four models. They controlled for prompt complexity and feature carry-over, compared linguistic dialect against explicit gender cues (sign-off names), tested whether users could strategically avoid the effects, and performed mechanistic analysis of transformer layers to locate where linguistic features are encoded.
AI.result: Gendered linguistic features systematically elicit shorter, less sophisticated, and less formal responses, and these effects persist after controlling for complexity and carry-over. Explicit gender cues (names) are encoded in the same representational space but produce no effects, while linguistic register produces large, consistent effects. Post-hoc mitigation fails because the patterns are culturally embedded and outside conscious control, and features are encoded in early transformer layers, entangled with other features.
AI.conclusion: Because the disparate impact of linguistic variation cannot be easily avoided by users or fixed downstream, the work calls for upstream consideration of linguistic variation during model design and deployment to mitigate inequities in LLM-mediated workplace communication.

title: Beyond Simulated Benchmarks: Evaluating Motion Representations for Fall Detection Under Real-World Data Scarcity
summary: Falls are a major health concern for older adults, and wearable sensors have been widely explored for detecting falls and enabling timely intervention. However, real-world falls are extremely rare: collecting 100 of them requires an estimated 100,000 days of monitoring, resulting in severely limited labelled data for training machine learning models. Consequently, many approaches rely on simulated datasets, often reporting high laboratory performance but limited real-world generalisation. We present a systematic evaluation of motion representations for wearable fall detection under real-world data scarcity. Using accelerometer signals, we compare interval-based, kernel-based, symbolic, and foundation model representations. As an interpretable baseline, we additionally investigate a lightweight symbolic representation that converts short motion segments into symbolic sentences augmented with physically-grounded impact descriptors. Experiments use FallAllD, a simulated falls dataset, and FARSEEING, a clinically verified real-world falls dataset. Through cross-validation, controlled data scarcity, and cross-dataset transfer, we examine how representation choices affect robustness under realistic deployment. Our results reveal that highly parameterised kernel and foundation models excel on simulated data but degrade severely under both data scarcity and domain shift. Although the interval-based representation achieves the strongest absolute real-world performance, augmenting a symbolic representation with physically-grounded impact descriptors yields the smallest degradation under domain shift and retains detection sensitivity under extreme scarcity, albeit at lower precision. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating beyond simulated benchmarks and show that representation choice is critical for deployable fall detection given the scarcity of real-world data.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically compares four motion representation families (interval-based, kernel-based, symbolic, and foundation-model embeddings) for wearable accelerometer-based fall detection, using a simulated dataset (FallAllD) and a real-world dataset (FARSEEING). It finds that highly parameterised models excel on simulated data but degrade severely under data scarcity and domain shift, while a symbolic representation augmented with physically-grounded impact descriptors is most robust, showing the smallest degradation under shift and retaining sensitivity under extreme scarcity.
AI.motivation: Real-world falls are extremely rare (collecting 100 falls requires ~100,000 monitoring days), so labelled data is severely scarce and most approaches rely on simulated datasets with high lab performance but poor real-world generalisation. There is a need to understand how the choice of motion representation affects robustness under realistic deployment conditions.
AI.method: The authors compare interval-based, kernel-based, symbolic, and foundation-model representations of accelerometer signals. They also introduce a lightweight interpretable symbolic baseline that converts short motion segments into symbolic sentences augmented with physically-grounded impact descriptors. Evaluation uses cross-validation, controlled data scarcity, and cross-dataset transfer on FallAllD (simulated) and FARSEEING (clinically verified real-world) datasets.
AI.result: Highly parameterised kernel and foundation models achieve strong performance on simulated data but degrade severely under data scarcity and domain shift. The interval-based representation achieves the strongest absolute real-world performance. The symbolic representation augmented with physically-grounded impact descriptors shows the smallest degradation under domain shift and retains detection sensitivity under extreme data scarcity, albeit at lower precision.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating beyond simulated benchmarks is essential, and representation choice is critical for deployable fall detection given real-world data scarcity. Robust, interpretable representations with physically-grounded features can mitigate performance degradation under realistic conditions.

title: Teach the Magnitude, Not the Direction: Verifier-Bounded Credit Assignment for Multi-Turn Multi-step LLM Agents
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) offers a verifier-bounded performance ceiling for training multi-turn tool-use agents, yet its trajectory-level credit assignment conflates heterogeneous per-turn outcomes into a single reward signal. On-policy distillation provides dense per-token supervision but is either teacher-bounded or prone to gradient concentration collapse. We introduce $\textbf{CrEST}$, a hierarchical credit assignment framework that retains RL's verifier-bounded ceiling while incorporating dense token-level signals from a privileged self-teacher. $\textbf{CrEST}$ resolves credit at two levels: turn-segmented verified advantages address inter-turn dilution, while entropy-gated self-teacher modulation refines intra-turn token contributions. Experiments on BFCL V3 and WildToolBench show that $\textbf{CrEST}$ consistently outperforms both RL and distillation baselines across two model scales, with the largest gains on long-trajectory and strict session-level metrics. Our work demonstrates that the teacher's role in policy optimization can be reduced from determining update directions to modulating update magnitudes, unlocking dense credit assignment without sacrificing the verifier-bounded ceiling.

AI.tldr: CrEST is a hierarchical credit assignment framework for multi-turn tool-use agents that keeps RL's verifier-bounded ceiling while adding dense token-level signals from a privileged self-teacher, outperforming pure RL and distillation baselines on BFCL V3 and WildToolBench.
AI.motivation: RLVR is verifier-bounded but suffers from trajectory-level credit assignment that conflates heterogeneous per-turn outcomes into a single reward; on-policy distillation gives dense per-token supervision but is teacher-bounded or suffers gradient concentration collapse. The goal is to combine RL's ceiling with dense token-level signals without being limited by the teacher.
AI.method: CrEST resolves credit at two levels: turn-segmented verified advantages (to address inter-turn dilution) and entropy-gated self-teacher modulation (to refine intra-turn token contributions). A privileged self-teacher is used only to modulate update magnitudes, not to determine update directions.
AI.result: On BFCL V3 and WildToolBench, CrEST consistently outperforms both RL and distillation baselines across two model scales, with the largest gains on long-trajectory tasks and strict session-level metrics.
AI.conclusion: The teacher's role in policy optimization can be reduced from determining update directions to modulating update magnitudes, which unlocks dense credit assignment without sacrificing the verifier-bounded ceiling.

title: RippleMem: From Isolated Retrieval to Associative Recollection for Long-Term Agent Memory
summary: LLM-based agents increasingly rely on external memory to support long-horizon reasoning and interaction. However, the main bottleneck is not simply storing past experience, but recovering the right set of evidence when relevant information is distributed across many interactions. Existing approaches struggle with this access problem. Full-context methods require noisy long-context search, flat retrieval often returns isolated and incomplete records, and graph-based memory systems can be expensive to construct while compressing rich event context. We introduce RippleMem, a long-term memory system that replaces one-shot retrieval with adaptive associative recollection. Inspired by cue-dependent episodic retrieval and associative completion, RippleMem stores interaction history as cue-rich episodic memory units and organizes them in an event-centric memory graph. Given a query, it first recalls relevant memory anchors through hybrid cues, then expands from these anchors along semantic and structural associations to recover missing supporting evidence. In this way, initially recalled memories serve not only as answer context, but also as cues for completing the evidence needed to answer. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S show that RippleMem achieves the best overall performance across evaluated settings, improving LLM-as-a-Judge accuracy by 3.95% on LoCoMo and up to 11.87% on LongMemEval-S, while reducing graph construction cost by about 30x.

AI.tldr: RippleMem is a long-term memory system for LLM agents that replaces one-shot retrieval with adaptive associative recollection, using cue-rich episodic memory units in an event-centric graph. It recalls anchors via hybrid cues, then expands along semantic and structural associations to complete missing evidence, achieving the best overall performance on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S while cutting graph construction cost by ~30x.
AI.motivation: The key bottleneck in LLM-based agents using external memory is not storing past experience but recovering the correct set of evidence when relevant information is scattered across many interactions. Existing methods fail: full-context approaches need noisy long-context search, flat retrieval returns isolated incomplete records, and graph-based memory systems are costly to build and compress rich event context. This motivates a memory access mechanism that can reconstruct multi-hop, distributed evidence effectively and cheaply.
AI.method: RippleMem stores interaction history as cue-rich episodic memory units organized in an event-centric memory graph. Retrieval is modeled as adaptive associative recollection inspired by cue-dependent episodic retrieval and associative completion. For a given query, it first recalls relevant memory anchors using hybrid cues (combining semantic and structural signals), then expands from these anchors along semantic and structural associations to recover missing supporting evidence. Recalled memories thus act both as answer context and as cues for completing the full set of required evidence.
AI.result: On LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S, RippleMem achieves the best overall performance across evaluated settings: it improves LLM-as-a-Judge accuracy by 3.95% on LoCoMo and by up to 11.87% on LongMemEval-S, while reducing graph construction cost by approximately 30x.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive associative recollection in an event-centric memory graph effectively addresses the evidence-recovery bottleneck in long-term memory for LLM agents, outperforming full-context, flat-retrieval, and graph-based baselines in both accuracy and construction efficiency.

title: TANGCO: Learning Topology-Aware Capacity Allocation for Overload-driven Cascading Failures
summary: Networked systems, from power grids to traffic networks and cloud clusters, carry loads across nodes with limited capacity. A node whose load exceeds its capacity fails and sheds its load onto its neighbors, which can trigger a system-wide cascade. We study how to allocate a fixed capacity budget across nodes to resist these cascades under local load redistribution. The problem is difficult because no optimal allocation is known, and the fail-or-survive objective is non-differentiable and piecewise constant, so exact and gradient-based optimization methods do not directly apply. We introduce TANGCO (Topology-Aware Neural Graph-Guided Capacity Optimization), which uses a graph neural network policy trained through the cascade simulator with policy-gradient learning and a heuristic anchor. We evaluate TANGCO on five synthetic graph families and five real networks spanning power, road, air, and Internet topologies. The learned policy improves on the best of four hand-designed heuristics in all 450 synthetic instances and in 40 of 45 real-network conditions, with robustness gains ranging from 1.6% to 246%. The learned policies transfer to unseen graphs within a family and partially across related topologies, and TANGCO$^{pre}$, pre-trained on synthetic graphs, matches per-network training on unseen real networks. Training scales near-linearly with graph size, and TANGCO$^{pre}$ allocates on a new network with no per-target training, matching the deployment cost of a hand-designed heuristic. Free-vector variants without the GNN, stay close to the heuristics, so the graph representation carries the gain beyond numerical search. Finally, analysis of the learned allocations identifies when local risk is sufficient, leads to an improved closed-form heuristic, and reveals the regimes where a topology-aware learned policy remains necessary.

AI.tldr: TANGCO uses a graph neural network trained via policy-gradient against a cascade simulator to allocate a fixed capacity budget across network nodes, outperforming hand-designed heuristics on synthetic and real networks while remaining deployable without per-network training.
AI.motivation: Networked systems (power grids, traffic, clouds) carry load across capacity-limited nodes; overloaded nodes fail and shed load to neighbors, risking system-wide cascades. Allocating a fixed capacity budget to resist cascades is hard because no optimal allocation is known and the fail-or-survive objective is non-differentiable and piecewise constant, defeating exact and gradient-based optimization.
AI.method: TANGCO (Topology-Aware Neural Graph-Guided Capacity Optimization) trains a graph neural network policy through the cascade simulator using policy-gradient learning with a heuristic anchor. It is evaluated on five synthetic graph families and five real networks (power, road, air, Internet). Ablations include free-vector variants without the GNN, transfer tests across graph families/topologies, and a pre-trained variant TANGCO^pre on synthetic graphs applied to unseen real networks.
AI.result: TANGCO beats the best of four hand-designed heuristics in all 450 synthetic instances and 40 of 45 real-network conditions, with robustness gains of 1.6%–246%. Policies transfer to unseen graphs within a family and partially across related topologies. TANGCO^pre matches per-network training on unseen real networks. Training scales near-linearly with graph size, and TANGCO^pre allocates on a new network with no per-target training, matching hand-designed heuristic deployment cost. GNN-free variants stay close to heuristics, showing the graph representation drives the gain. Analysis yields an improved closed-form heuristic and identifies regimes where topology-aware learned policies remain necessary.
AI.conclusion: TANGCO provides a scalable, topology-aware learned approach to capacity allocation that substantially improves cascade robustness over hand-designed heuristics, transfers across networks, and exposes both when a simple local-risk heuristic suffices and when a learned topology-aware policy is required.

title: TsuGO: Probing Search Efficiency in LLM Reasoning via Go Life-and-Death Problems
summary: The evaluation of LLM reasoning is moving from final-answer accuracy to process-level assessment, yet existing methods still fail to capture how models plan reasoning paths and allocate reasoning resources--that is, how they organize search. Prior process-level methods focus on the coherence and redundancy of chain-of-thought (CoT), and most benchmark tasks have a single objective solvable by static capabilities such as derivation and tool use, leaving search organization unmeasured. We introduce TsuGO, a process-level reasoning benchmark for evaluating Search Efficiency in LLM reasoning through Go life-and-death problems. These problems provide closed and verifiable solution spaces with an inherent adversarial structure, making candidate generation, response checking, branch comparison, and backtracking necessary parts of reasoning rather than incidental trace patterns. By constraining the solution space, TsuGO disentangles domain knowledge from search organization, parses CoT into a structured search tree, and reports Search Efficiency together with Token Efficiency and other diagnostic metrics and visualizations. Experiments show that current LLMs remain far from stable tsumego solving: stronger models succeed by finding the correct candidate earlier and sustaining effort on productive branches, but most models still behave much closer to unguided search algorithms than to neural-guided KataGo. Longer CoT or higher Token Efficiency does not necessarily imply better search. Our results identify search organization and reasoning-resource allocation as missing dimensions in LLM reasoning evaluation.

AI.tldr: Introduces TsuGO, a process-level benchmark using Go life-and-death (tsumego) problems to evaluate how LLMs organize search and allocate reasoning resources, revealing that current models still fall short of stable, guided search.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM reasoning evaluation is shifting from final-answer accuracy to process-level assessment, but current methods only measure the coherence/redundancy of chain-of-thought and use single-objective tasks solvable by static capabilities (derivation, tool use). This leaves search organization—how models plan paths and allocate reasoning resources—unmeasured. The authors aim to fill this gap.
AI.method: Proposes TsuGO, a process-level benchmark built on Go life-and-death (tsumego) problems. These problems offer closed, verifiable solution spaces with inherent adversarial structure, making candidate generation, response checking, branch comparison, and backtracking necessary parts of reasoning. By constraining the solution space, TsuGO disentangles domain knowledge from search organization, parses chain-of-thought into a structured search tree, and reports Search Efficiency together with Token Efficiency, plus diagnostic metrics and visualizations.
AI.result: Experiments show current LLMs remain far from stable tsumego solving. Stronger models succeed by finding the correct candidate earlier and sustaining effort on productive branches, but most models behave much closer to unguided search algorithms than to neural-guided KataGo. Longer CoT or higher Token Efficiency does not necessarily imply better search.
AI.conclusion: Search organization and reasoning-resource allocation are missing dimensions in LLM reasoning evaluation, and TsuGO demonstrates that evaluating these dimensions is both feasible and revealing of current model limitations.

title: CROP: Task Relevance via Counterfactuals for Selective On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) supervises a student language model on trajectories sampled from its current policy, but assigns equal credit to response tokens with unequal supervision value. Selective OPD addresses this limitation by allocating supervision non-uniformly across response tokens according to their estimated training value. Most existing criteria, however, focus primarily on optimization need, such as uncertainty or teacher-student disagreement, while task relevance, namely whether the supervision is tied to the semantic content of the current input, remains less directly characterized as a complementary dimension. To address this gap, we introduce Counterfactual Relevance for On-Policy Distillation (CROP), which operationalizes task relevance through a paraphrase-calibrated counterfactual sensitivity margin. For each source prompt, CROP constructs a validated original-paraphrase-counterfactual triplet, holds the student rollout fixed, and measures each response position by its sensitivity to a task-relevant condition change calibrated by its sensitivity to a meaning-preserving rewrite. Matched selection controls show that CROP identifies more useful supervision positions than random or lowest-relevance selection, while component comparisons confirm the value of both counterfactual sensitivity and paraphrase calibration. Across two teacher-student settings, CROP improves aggregate performance by 1.92 and 2.96 points over the strongest non-CROP selector. These results support task relevance as a complementary criterion for selective OPD and establish CROP as a model-internal, contrast-specific method for allocating token-level supervision.

AI.tldr: CROP introduces task relevance as a complementary criterion for selective on-policy distillation, measuring token-level training value via a paraphrase-calibrated counterfactual sensitivity margin, and improves aggregate performance by 1.92–2.96 points over the strongest baseline selector.
AI.motivation: Existing selective on-policy distillation (OPD) criteria focus on optimization need (uncertainty, teacher-student disagreement) but do not directly characterize task relevance—whether supervision is tied to the semantic content of the current input. This gap motivates a model-internal method that quantifies task-relevant supervision value per token.
AI.method: CROP operationalizes task relevance via a paraphrase-calibrated counterfactual sensitivity margin. For each source prompt, it builds a validated original–paraphrase–counterfactual triplet, keeps the student rollout fixed, and scores each response position by its sensitivity to a task-relevant condition change, normalized/calibrated by its sensitivity to a meaning-preserving paraphrase rewrite.
AI.result: Matched selection controls show CROP identifies more useful supervision positions than random or lowest-relevance selection. Component comparisons confirm the value of both counterfactual sensitivity and paraphrase calibration. Across two teacher-student settings, CROP improves aggregate performance by 1.92 and 2.96 points over the strongest non-CROP selector.
AI.conclusion: Task relevance is a complementary criterion for selective OPD, and CROP provides a model-internal, contrast-specific approach for allocating token-level supervision that outperforms existing optimization-need-based selectors.

title: History-informed Lagrangian Neural Networks
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures. Accepted to the 9th Chinese Conference on Pattern Recognition and Computer Vision (PRCV 2026) as an oral paper
summary: Forecasting the long-horizon evolution of mechanical systems from position-only observations is a pivotal yet difficult task, as hidden velocities and trajectory-specific physical properties must be inferred simultaneously. Although physics-guided neural networks like Lagrangian Neural Networks (LNNs) guarantee physical plausibility, they generally require complete state inputs and lack adaptability to changing system parameters. To break these limitations, we introduce History-informed Lagrangian Neural Networks (HiLNN). Grounded in the insight that temporal position sequences implicitly encode underlying dynamics, HiLNN employs a recurrent encoder to extract a latent context from history. This context not only reconstructs the unobserved initial velocity but also adaptively modulates the mass matrix, potential energy, and damping coefficients of a structured Lagrangian system. By leveraging a differentiable RK4 rollout scheme, the entire pipeline is optimized end-to-end under multi-step trajectory supervision and energy-consistency regularization. Empirical evaluations across conservative, dissipative, and heterogeneous variable-parameter systems show that HiLNN delivers superior long-term prediction accuracy and maintains precise energy profiles compared to state-of-the-art baselines. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/yingtian22/History-informed-LNN.

AI.tldr: HiLNN is a physics-guided neural network that forecasts long-horizon mechanical system trajectories from position-only observations by using a recurrent encoder to recover hidden state and adapt physical parameters, trained end-to-end with RK4 rollout and energy regularization.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon forecasting from position-only data requires simultaneously inferring hidden velocities and trajectory-specific physical properties. Existing Lagrangian Neural Networks guarantee physical plausibility but need complete state inputs and cannot adapt to changing system parameters.
AI.method: HiLNN uses a recurrent encoder to extract a latent context from temporal position history. This context reconstructs the unobserved initial velocity and adaptively modulates the mass matrix, potential energy, and damping coefficients of a structured Lagrangian system. A differentiable RK4 rollout integrates the dynamics, and the pipeline is optimized end-to-end with multi-step trajectory supervision plus energy-consistency regularization.
AI.result: Across conservative, dissipative, and heterogeneous variable-parameter systems, HiLNN achieves superior long-term prediction accuracy and maintains precise energy profiles compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: By encoding temporal history into a latent context that reconstructs initial velocity and modulates system parameters, HiLNN overcomes the limitations of standard LNNs and enables accurate, energy-consistent long-horizon forecasting from position-only observations.

title: Capability Sheaves for Compositional Agent-Harness Repair: Controlled Quotients and a Real-Repository Stress Test
summary:
Agent harnesses combine retrieval, routing, state, provenance, and verification, but locally successful components may disagree on shared state. We model this failure with a finite \emph{capability sheaf}: stalks encode typed behavior signatures, restriction maps retain shared fields, and accepted runs are useful global sections. An exact finite constraint-satisfaction problem (CSP) defines acceptance, while a linearized relative cohomology class provides a diagnostic and search feature.
  A controlled experiment over 20 task clusters introduces hidden interior mediators whose raw states are nuisance variables. Quotienting their coboundaries reduces the candidate budget from 2,000 to 1,000 per cluster; aligning the hidden state removes the gap. Exact CSP matches the quotient, so the result demonstrates invariance to stale representatives, not superiority over exact reasoning.
  We then test the method on a discovery split from the SWE-bench Multilingual pool of PatchFuseBench: 160 issues from 20 repositories, 875 real candidate patches, 2,579 source-aware edit atoms, and 153 newly executed patches. A first pool-level construction is constant because $[b-Dx]=[b]$ in $\operatorname{coker}D$ and therefore cannot rank configurations. A candidate-indexed repair is nontrivial on 848/875 candidates and varies within 120/160 issues. It resolves 118 issues versus 116 for a matched noncohomological selector, but the difference is not supported across repositories (exact sign-flip $p=0.75$). A leave-one-repository-out abstention gate reaches 127/160, tying the strong anchor and exceeding its matched gate by one issue ($p=1.0$). The discovery gate therefore fails and the confirmatory split remains sealed. The study supports the controlled invariance mechanism and an identifiability correction, but not a real-world cohomological advantage.

AI.tldr: The paper models multi-component agent failure via a finite "capability sheaf," where acceptance is an exact CSP (constraint-satisfaction problem) and a relative cohomology class offers diagnostics/search. Experiments show the method matches exact CSP under controlled invariance but fails to demonstrate a real-world advantage on SWE-bench Multilingual data, with differences not statistically supported and the confirmatory split remaining sealed.
AI.motivation: Agent harnesses compose components (retrieval, routing, state, provenance, verification) that can locally succeed yet disagree on shared state. The authors seek a principled model of this coherence failure and a way to diagnose/repair it, posing the question whether cohomological reasoning yields a practical advantage over exact CSP-based reasoning.
AI.method: The paper models agent states as a finite capability sheaf: typed behavior signatures on stalks, shared-field restriction maps, and accepted runs as global sections. Acceptance is defined by an exact finite constraint-satisfaction problem (CSP); a linearized relative cohomology class serves as a diagnostic and search feature. A controlled experiment (20 task clusters) tests quotienting hidden interior mediators via coboundaries against exact CSP. A discovery test uses SWE-bench Multilingual (PatchFuseBench): 160 issues, 20 repositories, 875 candidate patches, 2,579 source-aware edit atoms, 153 newly executed patches. Variants include a pool-level (constant) construction, a candidate-indexed repair, and a leave-one-repository-out abstention gate compared against matched noncohomological selectors and a strong anchor.
AI.result: Controlled experiment: quotienting coboundaries of hidden mediators cuts candidate budget 2,000→1,000 per cluster while exact CSP matches the quotient, showing invariance to stale representatives but no superiority. Discovery: pool-level construction is constant ([b-Dx]=[b] in coker D) and cannot rank. Candidate-indexed repair is nontrivial on 848/875 candidates, varies in 120/160 issues, resolves 118 vs 116 issues for the matched noncohomological selector (exact sign-flip p=0.75), i.e., not supported. The abstention gate reaches 127/160, tying the anchor and exceeding the matched gate by one issue (p=1.0).
AI.conclusion: The discovery gate fails and the confirmatory split remains sealed. The controlled invariance mechanism and an identifiability correction are supported, but there is no demonstrated real-world cohomological advantage over matched/exact baselines.

title: Motor, Cognitive, or Corpus? What Survives Cross-Lingual Transfer in Speech-Based Parkinsons Disease Detection
summary: Self-supervised learning (SSL) speech representations achieve strong performance for Parkinson's disease (PD) detection within individual corpora. However, it remains unclear whether these models capture disease-related characteristics or exploit dataset-specific confounds, particularly since most SSL backbones are pretrained exclusively on healthy speech. To investigate this question, we perform a layer-wise analysis of nine SSL speech backbones using a low-capacity logistic regression probe across three languages. We structure the evaluation as multiple scenarios that progressively introduce distribution shifts in participant identity, recording conditions, language, and pathology. Our results reveal two key findings. First, layer selection is highly corpus-dependent: the optimal representation layer is determined primarily by the source dataset rather than by the SSL architecture itself. Second, the transferred discriminative signal lacks pathological specificity: classifiers trained to detect PD assign similarly high probabilities to both PD and dementia speech in the target corpus. These results highlight critical limitations that must be addressed before speech-based pathology recognition models can be reliably deployed in clinical settings.

AI.tldr: Analyzing nine self-supervised speech backbones with lightweight probes across three languages, the authors find that optimal representation layer choice depends on the corpus rather than the architecture, and that transferred PD-detection signal is not pathology-specific (it also fires on dementia speech), revealing limitations for clinical deployment.
AI.motivation: Determine whether SSL speech representations truly capture Parkinson's disease characteristics or merely exploit dataset-specific confounds, given that most SSL backbones are pretrained only on healthy speech.
AI.method: Layer-wise analysis of nine SSL speech backbones using a low-capacity logistic regression probe, across three languages, structured as multiple evaluation scenarios that progressively introduce distribution shifts in participant identity, recording conditions, language, and pathology.
AI.result: Two key findings: (1) optimal representation layer is highly corpus-dependent, driven primarily by the source dataset rather than the SSL architecture; (2) the transferred discriminative signal lacks pathological specificity, with PD-trained classifiers assigning similarly high probabilities to both PD and dementia speech in the target corpus.
AI.conclusion: Critical limitations must be addressed before speech-based pathology recognition models can be reliably deployed in clinical settings.

title: Knowledge-guided Pattern Discovery via Coupled Tensor Factorizations
summary: In order to understand complex systems such as the human metabolome or human brain, different sensing technologies are used, generating complex data. These datasets are often multiway, i.e., with more than two axes of variation such as a subjects by metabolites by time array. While tensor factorizations have successfully revealed interpretable patterns from such complex data, they have so far been mainly data-driven. On the other hand, there is more to data -- there are computational models (of these systems), which are rich sources of prior information. In this paper, we introduce a knowledge-guided approach that brings together data and computational models by jointly analyzing real data and simulated data (generated using a computational model) using coupled tensor factorizations with linear coupling. Our experiments on real metabolomics measurements demonstrate that guiding the analysis of such noisy data with simulated data improves the pattern discovery performance while also revealing potential discrepancies between data and computational models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a knowledge-guided tensor factorization approach that couples real and simulated data to improve interpretability and pattern discovery, while also uncovering model-data discrepancies.
AI.motivation: Complex systems (e.g., metabolome, brain) produce multiway datasets, and existing tensor factorizations are mostly data-driven, ignoring rich prior information available in computational models. The authors aim to combine real data with model-generated simulated data for better guided analysis.
AI.method: A knowledge-guided framework using coupled tensor factorizations with linear coupling to jointly analyze real data and simulated data (generated by a computational model) in a shared latent space.
AI.result: Experiments on real metabolomics measurements show that guiding the analysis of noisy data with simulated data improves pattern discovery performance and reveals discrepancies between the data and the computational model.
AI.conclusion: Coupling real and simulated data via tensor factorization effectively leverages computational models as priors, enhancing interpretability and supporting model validation.

title: vToken: Token-Level Virtualization for Reclaimable KV Caches
summary: Large language model serving faces a critical memory bottleneck: the KV cache grows with sequence length and batch size. PagedAttention uses fixed-size memory blocks to reduce allocator-level fragmentation, but recent KV eviction algorithms operate at a token granularity finer than block-level management. This mismatch causes intra-block fragmentation, leaving a large fraction of allocated KV memory unreclaimable. We present vToken, a lightweight token-level virtualization layer that decouples logical token liveness from physical block placement. vToken maintains a stable logical token view through token-table indirection and realizes physical reclamation by repacking live tokens asynchronously. The design preserves PagedAttention kernels and CUDA Graph compatibility. We implement vToken in vLLM and evaluate it with H2O, Random, and Scissorhands across models. Compared with a paired Naive-Evict baseline, vToken reduces retained KV blocks per request by 27.2\%--72.3\% and improves SLA-constrained throughput by up to 1.37$\times$. Under a constrained active-KV budget, it extends the maximum feasible concurrency by up to 2$\times$, while reducing the per-policy integration footprint from 500+ lines to under 50.

AI.tldr: vToken is a token-level virtualization layer for LLM serving that decouples logical token liveness from physical KV block placement, eliminating intra-block fragmentation caused by token-granular KV eviction in PagedAttention. It achieves large reductions in retained KV memory and improved throughput/concurrency with minimal integration effort.
AI.motivation: LLM serving is bottlenecked by KV cache memory growth. PagedAttention uses fixed-size blocks to cut allocator-level fragmentation, but recent KV eviction algorithms (e.g., H2O, Scissorhands) work at token granularity, finer than block-level management. This mismatch causes intra-block fragmentation, leaving much of the allocated KV memory unreclaimable even after eviction.
AI.method: vToken introduces a lightweight token-level virtualization layer: (1) a stable logical token view maintained via token-table indirection, decoupling logical token liveness from physical block placement; (2) asynchronous repacking of live tokens to realize physical reclamation. The design preserves PagedAttention kernels and CUDA Graph compatibility, and is implemented in vLLM.
AI.result: Evaluated with H2O, Random, and Scissorhands across models against a paired Naive-Evict baseline, vToken reduces retained KV blocks per request by 27.2%–72.3% and improves SLA-constrained throughput by up to 1.37×. Under a constrained active-KV budget, it extends maximum feasible concurrency by up to 2×, while cutting the per-policy integration footprint from 500+ lines to under 50.
AI.conclusion: vToken effectively bridges the granularity mismatch between token-level KV eviction policies and PagedAttention's block-level memory management, recovering otherwise unreclaimable KV memory. It delivers substantial memory savings, higher SLA-constrained throughput, and up to 2× higher concurrency under active-KV budgets, all with a dramatically reduced integration cost and without breaking existing PagedAttention kernels or CUDA Graph compatibility.

title: Are You Sure You're Sure? On the Impact of Instruction Tuning on Confidence and Lexical Diversity
summary: Instruction-tuned language models achieve strong performance across a range of generation tasks, but have also recently been shown to exhibit verbalized overconfidence. In question answering, verbalized model overconfidence may be associated with the consistency of the generated supporting rationales. In this paper, we study whether corresponding changes in the lexical diversity of generated answer rationales accompany changes in model confidence induced by instruction tuning. We evaluate three matched base and instruction-tuned models across question-answering benchmarks and find that instruction tuning consistently alters answer confidence, despite limited changes in predictive accuracy and decreases in likelihood-based calibration. Secondly, we observe a non-uniform effect of instruction tuning on rationale diversity: cross-rationale diversity consistently decreases, whereas surface-level lexical diversity varies in both direction and magnitude across models and benchmarks. Finally, we find that these differences persist after controlling for answer selection and rationale length, confirming that confidence and rationale diversity capture distinct effects of instruction tuning.

AI.tldr: Instruction tuning makes language models more overconfident in question answering, and this shift is accompanied by changes in rationale diversity. Cross-rationale diversity decreases, while surface-level lexical diversity varies across models and benchmarks, and both effects persist after controlling for answer selection and rationale length.
AI.motivation: Recent work has shown instruction-tuned language models tend to exhibit verbalized overconfidence, despite limited gains in predictive accuracy. The authors aim to investigate whether this overconfidence is linked to the consistency of generated supporting rationales, specifically examining whether changes in lexical diversity of rationales accompany changes in model confidence induced by instruction tuning.
AI.method: The authors evaluate three matched pairs of base and instruction-tuned models across question-answering benchmarks. They measure answer confidence, predictive accuracy, likelihood-based calibration, and two aspects of rationale lexical diversity: cross-rationale diversity (consistency across generated rationales) and surface-level lexical diversity. They also control for answer selection and rationale length to isolate the effect of instruction tuning on confidence and diversity.
AI.result: Instruction tuning consistently increases verbalized answer confidence despite limited changes in accuracy and decreases in likelihood-based calibration. It has a non-uniform effect on rationale diversity: cross-rationale diversity consistently decreases, while surface-level lexical diversity changes in both direction and magnitude depending on the model and benchmark. These differences persist after controlling for answer selection and rationale length, indicating confidence and rationale diversity capture distinct effects of instruction tuning.
AI.conclusion: Instruction tuning induces distinct and consistent changes in both model confidence and rationale diversity that are not reducible to changes in accuracy, calibration, answer selection, or rationale length. Confidence and rationale diversity therefore represent separate dimensions of instruction-tuning's impact on language models.

title: Novel Knowledge-Guided Generative Methods for Synthetic Transcriptomic Data
summary: As biomedical research increasingly relies on data-intensive tools, the quality and utility of datasets are critical. Challenges such as imbalances, biases, and ethical or legal constraints often limit access to high-quality data. Synthetic data generation can help overcome these limitations. Here, we present a comparative analysis of generative models for transcriptomic data, investigating strategies to incorporate prior biological knowledge via gene graphs. This ensures that synthetic data capture real-world gene patterns, maintaining their usefulness for downstream tasks. In particular, we introduce and benchmark three variants of the Generative Adversarial Network. Among the alternatives, MK-TGAN - an innovative multi-kernel, Graph Neural Network-based model - stands out for its performance in terms of both the realism and utility of the generated data. Unlike other methods, MK-TGAN leverages prior knowledge graphs by exploiting graph neural networks. Our results show that prior knowledge integration strategies improve performance, and that MK-TGAN consistently produces synthetic samples with superior realism and biological plausibility.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks generative models for transcriptomic (gene expression) data that integrate prior biological knowledge via gene graphs, and introduces MK-TGAN, a multi-kernel, Graph Neural Network-based Generative Adversarial Network that produces the most realistic and biologically plausible synthetic samples.
AI.motivation: Biomedical research increasingly depends on data-intensive tools, yet dataset quality is limited by imbalances, biases, and ethical or legal constraints. Synthetic data generation is proposed as a way to overcome these limitations, motivating the need to ensure synthetic transcriptomic data preserve real-world gene patterns for downstream use.
AI.method: The authors perform a comparative analysis of generative models for transcriptomic data, focusing on strategies that incorporate prior biological knowledge through gene graphs. They introduce and benchmark three Generative Adversarial Network variants, among them MK-TGAN, an innovative multi-kernel, Graph Neural Network-based model that leverages prior knowledge graphs via graph neural networks.
AI.result: MK-TGAN outperforms the alternatives in both realism and utility of generated data, consistently producing synthetic samples with superior realism and biological plausibility. The results show that prior knowledge integration strategies improve model performance.
AI.conclusion: Integrating prior biological knowledge through gene graphs improves synthetic data generation, and MK-TGAN is the most effective approach, generating transcriptomic samples with high realism and biological plausibility suitable for downstream tasks.

title: Toward a Gricean Retreat: Probing LLMs for Knowledge Boundaries and Referent Specificity
summary: When asked about entities outside their knowledge boundary, LLMs routinely fabricate plausible-sounding details rather than backing off to safer, more general claims. We frame this failure through a Gricean lens: a cooperative speaker who is uncertain about a referent retreats up the specificity hierarchy, trading informativeness for truthfulness. We ask whether LLMs have the ingredients to perform this retreat. Using a T-REx-based benchmark that varies entity familiarity and referent specificity, we probe models to answer two questions: (i) do their activations encode whether a referent falls inside the knowledge boundary, and (ii) do they anticipate the specificity of the referent they are about to generate? We find that the answer to both is yes, but the two signals are not reconciled in generation. Models overwhelmingly prefer specific referents even when the entity is unknown to them, and do so even when offered correct generic alternatives. The substrate for a Gricean retreat is present, but the policy that would act on it is not. We position our findings as a first step toward Gricean alignment, training or steering objectives that couple knowledge-boundary awareness to referent-specificity during generation.

AI.tldr: LLMs fabricate specific details for unknown entities instead of retreating to safer generic claims. The paper shows that models internally encode both whether a referent is inside their knowledge boundary and the specificity of the referent they will generate, yet fail to connect these signals, preferring overly specific referents even when correct generic alternatives are available.
AI.motivation: Large language models habitually hallucinate plausible-sounding specifics when asked about entities beyond their knowledge, rather than admitting uncertainty. The authors frame this as a Gricean failure: a cooperative speaker should retreat up the specificity hierarchy, trading informativeness for truthfulness. They investigate whether LLMs possess the necessary ingredients for such a retreat.
AI.method: The authors construct a T-REx-based benchmark that varies entity familiarity and referent specificity. Using probes on model activations, they ask two questions: (1) do activations encode whether a referent falls inside the knowledge boundary, and (2) do they anticipate the specificity of the referent about to be generated. They also test generation behavior, including whether models prefer specific referents over offered correct generic alternatives.
AI.result: Probing reveals that model activations do encode both knowledge-boundary status and anticipated referent specificity (both answers are "yes"). However, the two signals are not reconciled during generation: models overwhelmingly prefer specific referents even for unknown entities, and persist in this preference even when correct generic alternatives are explicitly offered.
AI.conclusion: The substrate for a Gricean retreat is present in LLMs, but the policy acting on it is missing. The authors propose "Gricean alignment" as a future direction: training or steering objectives that couple knowledge-boundary awareness with referent-specificity during generation.

title: Virtual Temperature Sensors in Power Transformers Using Neural Ordinary Differential Equations
summary: Accurate modeling and forecasting of power transformer thermal behavior are critical for reliability, asset lifetime, and optimized power system operation. Numerical approaches such as finite element methods (FEM) and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) offer high fidelity but are computationally expensive, require complex mesh generation, and are often impractical for real-time or large-scale applications, particularly when transformer geometries are unknown. Lumped-parameter thermal models are more practical but depend on transformer-specific thermal constants and may fail to capture dynamic responses under varying operating and environmental conditions. Purely data-driven machine learning methods, including artificial neural networks, convolutional neural networks, and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, have shown success in forecasting transformer temperatures but typically require large volumes of high-quality training data and may produce physically inconsistent or uninterpretable results. This paper develops a physics-aware Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (Neural ODE) framework for forecasting transformer thermal behavior from real-world time-series data. Neural ODEs model system dynamics in continuous time, providing smooth trajectory prediction and a natural representation of continuously evolving thermal dynamics. A key contribution is the integration of simplified heat-transfer equations directly into the Neural ODE formulation. The model is evaluated across datasets from fifteen transformers in different regions of Norway with varying designs and cooling mechanisms. The results demonstrate that the developed Neural ODE framework provides a standardized, physics-aware, and robust forecasting approach for heterogeneous transformer units.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a physics-aware Neural ODE framework to forecast transformer thermal behavior from real-world time-series data, integrating simplified heat-transfer equations into the continuous-time model. Evaluated on fifteen heterogeneous transformers in Norway, it offers a standardized, robust approach that bridges physics-based and data-driven methods.
AI.motivation: Existing thermal modeling approaches each have limitations: FEM/CFD are accurate but computationally expensive and impractical for real-time or large-scale use (especially with unknown geometries); lumped-parameter models need transformer-specific constants and struggle with dynamic responses; purely data-driven ML (ANN, CNN, LSTM) needs large training data and can yield physically inconsistent results. A method is needed that is standardized, physics-aware, and robust across heterogeneous transformer units.
AI.method: The authors develop a physics-aware Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (Neural ODE) framework that models thermal system dynamics in continuous time for smooth trajectory prediction. The key contribution is integrating simplified heat-transfer equations directly into the Neural ODE formulation, constraining the learned dynamics with physical knowledge.
AI.result: The framework was evaluated across datasets from fifteen transformers in different regions of Norway with varying designs and cooling mechanisms. Results demonstrate that the Neural ODE framework provides a standardized, physics-aware, and robust forecasting approach for heterogeneous transformer units.
AI.conclusion: Physics-aware Neural ODEs effectively combine physical heat-transfer principles with data-driven learning, enabling continuous-time, robust thermal forecasting of transformers without requiring detailed geometry or transformer-specific constants, and generalizing across diverse transformer designs and cooling systems.

title: Towards Context-Aware Clinical Motion Understanding in Daily Living at Home: Freezing of Gait Detection with Egocentric Vision
comment: Accepted to ECCV Workshop 2026 (Human Motion Challenges in Real-World and Clinical Settings)
summary: Understanding motion in daily living requires context beyond kinematics, because similar inertial patterns during activities of daily living (ADLs) can reflect intentional stopping, object interaction, or pathological movement impairment. Egocentric vision provides task-related context that may help disambiguate these cases. We investigate this challenge through freezing of gait (FOG) detection in Parkinson's disease (PD), a symptom strongly influenced by contextual factors during ADLs. Using synchronized egocentric video, wearable IMUs, and expert-annotated FOG labels collected from 13 PD participants in their homes, we evaluate frozen representations from pretrained ego-video and time-series foundation models, alongside an IMU-based TCN trained from scratch, under leave-one-subject-out evaluation. The IMU-based TCN achieved the strongest event-detection performance, reaching 42.3 F1 and 83.0 AUROC, compared with 32.6 F1 and 77.2 AUROC for V-JEPA2 ego-video features. Although ego-video alone did not outperform IMU-based sensing, it showed above-chance discrimination, and qualitative analyses suggest that egocentric vision may capture FOG-relevant information independent of IMUs. Together, these results support the use of pretrained ego-video representations to add contextual information to wearable-sensor-based clinical motion understanding in daily living.

AI.tldr: This paper studies whether egocentric video (pretrained foundation-model features) can add task context to IMU-based detection of freezing of gait (FOG) in Parkinson's disease during activities of daily living. In leave-one-subject-out evaluation, an IMU TCN outperformed ego-video features (42.3 vs 32.6 F1; 83.0 vs 77.2 AUROC), but video showed above-chance discrimination and captured FOG-relevant information independent of IMUs, supporting multimodal fusion.
AI.motivation: Inertial patterns during ADLs are ambiguous: similar movement signatures can reflect intentional stopping, object interaction, or pathological impairment. Freezing of gait in Parkinson's disease is strongly context-dependent, so egocentric vision may provide the task-related context needed to disambiguate these cases and improve clinical motion understanding.
AI.method: Using synchronized egocentric video, wearable IMUs, and expert-annotated FOG labels from 13 Parkinson's participants in their homes, the authors evaluate frozen representations from pretrained ego-video and time-series foundation models, plus an IMU-based temporal convolutional network (TCN) trained from scratch, under leave-one-subject-out evaluation. They also perform qualitative analyses to assess whether video captures FOG-relevant information independent of IMUs.
AI.result: The IMU-based TCN achieved the best event detection at 42.3 F1 and 83.0 AUROC, versus 32.6 F1 and 77.2 AUROC for V-JEPA2 ego-video features. Ego-video alone did not beat IMU sensing but performed above chance, and qualitative analysis indicated egocentric vision captures FOG-relevant information complementary to IMUs.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained ego-video representations are a promising source of contextual information to augment wearable-sensor-based clinical motion understanding in daily living, supporting their use alongside IMUs rather than as a replacement.
