title: Measuring Task-Agnostic Training Data Influence Across Language Model Pretraining
summary: Measuring training data influence consistently across language model pretraining is challenging. It is difficult to select downstream tasks or validation sets representative of a model's general capabilities, and reliance on task performance at intermediate checkpoints complicates comparisons across training. We propose a measure of training data influence that does not require selecting a downstream task or validation set as the attribution target. Specifically, we define an example's influence by how much its gradient update reduces the squared distance to the final parameters of a given pretraining run, and estimate this quantity from intermediate checkpoints without retraining. Applying the method to 18 configurations from the Pythia and PolyPythia suites, we find systematic temporal changes in influential data. Early in training, literature-related data are more strongly aligned with the trajectory toward the final parameters, whereas STEM data become more strongly aligned in later stages. This qualitative crossover is broadly consistent across model configurations. Our results provide a tractable trajectory-level view of how influential data change throughout pretraining, complementing influence analyses defined with respect to specific downstream tasks or validation sets.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a task-agnostic measure of training data influence for language model pretraining, based on how much each example's gradient update reduces squared distance to the final parameters, estimated from intermediate checkpoints without retraining. Applied to Pythia/PolyPythia, it reveals a temporal crossover: literature data are influential early, STEM data later.
AI.motivation: Existing influence measures require choosing a downstream task or validation set as the attribution target, which is hard to make representative of a model's general capabilities, and comparisons across training runs are complicated by reliance on task performance at intermediate checkpoints.
AI.method: Define an example's influence as the amount by which its gradient update reduces the squared distance to the final parameters of a given pretraining run, and estimate this quantity from intermediate checkpoints without retraining (no downstream task or validation set needed).
AI.result: Across 18 configurations from Pythia and PolyPythia, influential data show systematic temporal changes: literature-related data align more strongly with the trajectory toward final parameters early in training, while STEM data become more strongly aligned in later stages. The qualitative crossover is broadly consistent across model configurations.
AI.conclusion: The method offers a tractable, trajectory-level view of how influential data change throughout pretraining, complementing task- or validation-set-based influence analyses without requiring retraining.

title: Into the ORBIT for Time Series: Training Regimes for Foundation Models
summary: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) have advanced primarily through architectural innovation, while training regimes for large-scale heterogeneous corpora remain under-explored. As a result, pre-training distributions are often poorly controlled with respect to domain imbalance, context requirements, prediction horizons, and missingness. We introduce ORBIT (Omni-Range Bootstrap Incremental Training), a training paradigm that makes this distribution explicit and controllable. ORBIT combines Bootstrap Multi-Level Sampling, which controls dataset exposure and samples records, target variables, context windows, and prediction horizons, with Omni-Range Incremental Training, which varies context lengths and prediction horizons throughout a single training stage. Under ORBIT, we train Falcon-2.0, a simple univariate encoder-only Transformer with missingness-aware triple-channel patch tokenization and parallel patch prediction. We further introduce Rank-Guided Cross-Depth Alignment, a training objective that uses late-layer representations as stop-gradient teachers for shallow layers without additional inference cost. Evaluations on GIFT-Eval and fev-bench demonstrate strong zero-shot forecasting performance across diverse domains and frequencies.

AI.tldr: ORBIT is a controllable pre-training paradigm for time series foundation models, combining Bootstrap Multi-Level Sampling with Omni-Range Incremental Training. It is used to train Falcon-2.0, a univariate encoder-only Transformer with missingness-aware patch tokenization and Rank-Guided Cross-Depth Alignment, achieving strong zero-shot forecasting on GIFT-Eval and fev-bench.
AI.motivation: Existing TSFMs have advanced mostly via architecture, while pre-training on large heterogeneous corpora remains under-explored, leaving distributions poorly controlled regarding domain imbalance, context length, prediction horizon, and missing data.
AI.method: ORBIT training paradigm: (1) Bootstrap Multi-Level Sampling controls dataset exposure and samples records, target variables, context windows, and prediction horizons; (2) Omni-Range Incremental Training varies context lengths and horizons within one training stage. Falcon-2.0 model: univariate encoder-only Transformer with missingness-aware triple-channel patch tokenization and parallel patch prediction. Additional objective: Rank-Guided Cross-Depth Alignment uses late-layer representations as stop-gradient teachers for shallow layers with no extra inference cost.
AI.result: Falcon-2.0 achieves strong zero-shot forecasting performance across diverse domains and frequencies on GIFT-Eval and fev-bench benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Making the pre-training distribution explicit and controllable via ORBIT yields effective time series foundation models, demonstrating that training regime design is as important as architectural innovation for TSFMs.

title: NAS-Driven Hardware Accelerator Exploration for Edge AI and Quantization Effects on the Pareto Space
comment: 6 pages, 6 figures, accepted for presentation to the 39th IEEE International System-on-Chip Conference, Heidelberg, Germany, September 30 - October 2, 2026
summary: Edge AI deployment demands neural architectures that are simultaneously accurate, computationally efficient, and hardware-deployable - a challenge addressed by hardware-aware Neural Architecture Search (NAS). While recent works incorporate quantization directly into the NAS loop, these approaches expand search complexity and tightly couple architecture and quantization design. The simpler post-search quantization strategy has received little analytical attention: the effects of Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) on the NAS-discovered Pareto structure remain uncharacterised, and no framework combines quantized architecture mapping onto reconfigurable accelerators with automated hardware exploration. This paper addresses both gaps. First, a three-stage pipeline is proposed: a hardware-agnostic Pareto rank surrogate frontend on NAS-Bench-201, a quantization bridge with Pareto-aware filtering and feedback control, and an evolutionary Domain Space Exploration (DSE) backend on CGRA4ML for optimal hardware mapping. Second, an empirical study characterises how INT4 PTQ perturbs the NAS-Bench-201 Pareto space through formal stability metrics on ground-truth data for all 15,625 architectures, and demonstrates that an FP32 zero-shot surrogate outperforms a dedicated INT4-trained surrogate in Pareto space coverage across two standard search strategies.

AI.tldr: A three-stage pipeline combining a Pareto-rank surrogate on NAS-Bench-201, a quantization bridge with Pareto-aware filtering, and evolutionary hardware DSE on CGRA4ML is proposed; an empirical study characterises how INT4 PTQ perturbs the NAS-Bench-201 Pareto space and shows an FP32 zero-shot surrogate outperforms an INT4-trained surrogate.
AI.motivation: Edge AI requires neural architectures that are accurate, efficient, and deployable. Hardware-aware NAS exists, but quantization-in-the-loop methods increase search complexity and couple architecture/quantization design. Post-search PTQ's effect on the discovered Pareto structure is uncharacterized, and no framework combines quantized architecture mapping onto reconfigurable accelerators with automated hardware exploration.
AI.method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) hardware-agnostic Pareto rank surrogate frontend on NAS-Bench-201; (2) quantization bridge with Pareto-aware filtering and feedback control; (3) evolutionary Domain Space Exploration (DSE) backend on CGRA4ML for optimal hardware mapping. An empirical study uses formal stability metrics on ground-truth data for all 15,625 NAS-Bench-201 architectures to characterize INT4 PTQ perturbation, comparing FP32 zero-shot vs INT4-trained surrogates across two search strategies.
AI.result: The empirical study demonstrates that an FP32 zero-shot surrogate outperforms a dedicated INT4-trained surrogate in Pareto space coverage across two standard search strategies, contrary to the assumption that quantization-aware surrogates are necessary.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pipeline addresses the gap between post-search PTQ and quantized architecture mapping onto reconfigurable accelerators with automated hardware exploration, and the stability analysis provides guidance that FP32 zero-shot surrogates suffice for Pareto coverage after PTQ.

title: DFM Mimir v1: An Open HRM Delivering Frontier Performance at 1B Parameters Using Only Permissible Post-Training Data
comment: Technical Report, 20 Pages, 1 Model, Hierarchical Reasoning Model
summary: Current large language model development relies on massive, often non-permissible datasets, creating a high barrier for researchers committed to open-source and ethically sourced data. We introduce Mimir v1, a 1-billion-parameter language model based on the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM) architecture, that is trained from scratch and delivers highly competitive performance for English and sets a new state of the art for Danish using only permissible post-training data. Trained on a mixture of 161 datasets, Mimir v1 outperforms the original HRM-Text 1B and competes with larger frontier models like Qwen 3.5 4B and Gemma 4 E2B, tested across 20 benchmarks for English, Math & Code and Danish. The model is available on the Hugging Face Hub: https://huggingface.co/danish-foundation-models/DFM-Mimir

AI.tldr: Mimir v1 is a 1B-parameter language model trained from scratch on permissible data only, achieving competitive English performance and state-of-the-art Danish results using 161 post-training datasets.
AI.motivation: Reduce the high barrier to entry for researchers who require open-source and ethically sourced data by building a capable model without relying on massive, often non-permissible datasets.
AI.method: Train Mimir v1, a 1-billion-parameter model, from scratch using the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM) architecture, then post-train on a mixture of 161 permissible datasets.
AI.result: Mimir v1 outperforms the original HRM-Text 1B, sets a new state of the art for Danish, and competes with larger frontier models like Qwen 3.5 4B and Gemma 4 E2B across 20 benchmarks spanning English, Math & Code, and Danish.
AI.conclusion: A freely available, ethically sourced 1B model can deliver highly competitive multilingual performance, demonstrating that open research can rival larger models while maintaining data compliance.

title: StateBridge: Training-free Hidden-state Alignment for Latent Communication in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
comment: 18 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables, accepted by COLM2026
summary: Large language model based multi-agent systems usually communicate in text, i.e., using discrete tokens. However, text introduces a discrete bottleneck. Converting the sender's continuous hidden states into discrete tokens discards information that token identities alone cannot capture. Recent work proposes latent communication as an alternative, where agents transmit hidden representations directly without converting them to text. However, existing latent methods either inject working memory layer by layer across the transformers, or require trained projectors that limit portability. We propose StateBridge, a training-free latent communication approach that aligns the sender's final-layer hidden states to the receiver's input space via a closed-form orthogonal transformation. Lightweight norm calibration and vocabulary anchoring ensure compatibility with the pretrained input distribution. The aligned states are prepended to the input of the receiver agent as a continuous prefix. We evaluate StateBridge on math reasoning, code generation, and question answering with four models from two families. StateBridge achieves the best or tied-best score on 22 out of 26 model-task pairs, consistently outperforming the strongest baseline.

AI.tldr: StateBridge is a training-free latent communication method for multi-agent LLM systems that aligns a sender's final hidden states to a receiver's input space via a closed-form orthogonal transform, plus norm calibration and vocabulary anchoring, and prepends them as a continuous prefix.
AI.motivation: Text-based communication in multi-agent LLM systems creates a discrete token bottleneck that discards information in the sender's continuous hidden states. Existing latent communication methods either inject working memory layer-by-layer across transformers or require trained projectors, limiting portability across models.
AI.method: StateBridge aligns the sender agent's final-layer hidden states to the receiver's input embedding space using a closed-form orthogonal transformation (training-free). Lightweight norm calibration and vocabulary anchoring ensure compatibility with the pretrained input distribution. The aligned states are prepended to the receiver's input as a continuous prefix.
AI.result: Evaluated on math reasoning, code generation, and question answering with four models from two families, StateBridge achieves the best or tied-best score on 22 out of 26 model-task pairs, consistently outperforming the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: StateBridge offers a portable, training-free solution to latent communication between LLM agents, overcoming the discrete token bottleneck and eliminating reliance on trained projectors, with strong empirical results across diverse tasks and models.

title: SAEVerbalizer: Generating Explanations for Sparse Autoencoder Features via Representation Verbalization
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are proposed to extract numerous features from large language model (LLM) representations, yet explaining these features still relies primarily on external observation. This reliance leads to superficial explanations inferred from observed model behavior and computational inefficiency from collecting such behavioral evidence at scale. We introduce SAEVerbalizer, a framework that injects SAE decoder directions into an LLM's representations and fine-tunes the LLM's downstream layers to generate natural-language explanations of the injected features. Once trained, the resulting verbalizer explains SAE features directly from decoder directions, addressing both limitations. Our experiments show that the learned verbalization capability generalizes to unseen features, transfers across separately trained SAE dictionaries, and, with a lightweight adapter, extends to SAE features from different LLMs. Intervention experiments show that injecting multiple directions yields an explanation combining their meanings, while reversing individual directions produces corresponding meaning shifts.

AI.tldr: SAEVerbalizer fine-tunes an LLM to directly generate natural-language explanations of SAE features from decoder directions, replacing costly external behavioral observation.
AI.motivation: Explaining sparse autoencoder (SAE) features currently relies on external observation of model behavior, which produces only superficial explanations and is computationally inefficient at scale. The authors seek a method to explain SAE features directly from decoder directions.
AI.method: SAEVerbalizer injects SAE decoder directions into LLM representations and fine-tunes the LLM's downstream layers to verbalize the injected features as natural-language explanations. A lightweight adapter extends the approach to SAEs from different LLMs.
AI.result: The trained verbalizer generalizes to unseen features, transfers across separately trained SAE dictionaries, and, with an adapter, works on SAE features from different LLMs. Injecting multiple directions yields combined explanations, while reversing individual directions shifts the meaning accordingly.
AI.conclusion: SAEVerbalizer enables direct, efficient verbalization of SAE features from decoder directions, overcoming the superficiality and computational cost of behavior-based explanation.

title: Large-scale Testing Global Optimization Methods with Black-box Adversarial Attacks
summary: Existing global optimization benchmark suites are of a moderate size and are based on a small number of analytical functions that date back even to the 1970s. This causes a risk of biasing the development of global optimization methods. We argue that the tasks related to the black-box adversarial attack (BBAA) can serve as valuable global optimization benchmark in many-dimensional space. We demonstrate the efficiency of several types of evolutionary algorithms and other metaheuristics in solving example BBAA problems. Thus, we take a step towards convergence of global optimization methods to the challenges and needs that arise in the modern machine learning field.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using black-box adversarial attack (BBAA) tasks as a modern, many-dimensional benchmark suite for global optimization, showing that evolutionary algorithms and metaheuristics can effectively solve them, thereby aligning optimization benchmarks with contemporary machine-learning challenges.
AI.motivation: Existing global optimization benchmark suites are moderately sized and rely on a small set of analytical functions dating back as far as the 1970s, which risks biasing the development of global optimization methods. The authors seek more realistic, large-scale, high-dimensional benchmarks reflecting modern needs.
AI.method: The authors propose framing black-box adversarial attack problems as global optimization benchmarks in many-dimensional spaces, and evaluate several types of evolutionary algorithms and other metaheuristics on example BBAA problems to demonstrate their efficiency.
AI.result: Several evolutionary algorithms and metaheuristics demonstrated efficiency in solving example black-box adversarial attack problems, supporting the viability of BBAA tasks as global optimization benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: BBAA tasks represent a promising, modern, many-dimensional benchmark suite that can reduce bias in global optimization research and help converge optimization methods with the challenges arising in the machine learning field.

title: LLM-Guided Graph Generation for Structure-Based Local Improvement Methods
summary: Large neighborhood search normally selects a random subset of decision variables for iterative optimization. For efficiently solving different problems, researchers tend to design variable selection strategies by taking into account structural features from different domains. In this paper, we build an automatic pipeline that is problem-agnostic to all problems in the MiniZinc format. By prompting an LLM with our semantic guidelines, we guide the LLM to produce a graph generator that maps any instance of a problem type to a uniform weighted graph, where nodes represent decision variables and edges represent constraint relationships. These problem-agnostic graphs guide our structure-based local improvement framework (SLIM) in variable selection. Meanwhile, the weighted graph enables all problem instances to share the same generic graph representation, from which the same graph features can be extracted and used for configuration selection. We evaluated our pipeline on instances across 20 MiniZinc competition problems, finding that algorithm selection achieves a 39.5% average problem-weighted win rate against a one-shot Gurobi baseline, more than doubling the best single configuration (19.3%). Configuration and feature ablation boost the performance further to 44.0%, demonstrating that LLM-based semantic generation enables effective automated structure extraction and feature extraction for constraint optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an automatic, problem-agnostic pipeline for MiniZinc problems that uses an LLM to generate a graph representation of problem structure (variables as nodes, constraints as edges), then uses these graphs to drive variable selection in a local improvement framework and to extract features for algorithm configuration selection. It achieves strong performance gains over a one-shot Gurobi baseline across 20 MiniZinc competition problems.
AI.motivation: Large neighborhood search typically selects decision variables randomly, and existing variable-selection strategies require hand-designed, domain-specific structural features. The authors aim to automate structure extraction in a problem-agnostic way so that diverse problems (especially those in MiniZinc format) can benefit from structure-guided variable selection and configuration without manual feature engineering.
AI.method: The authors build an automatic pipeline that prompts an LLM with semantic guidelines to generate a graph generator, mapping any instance of a problem type to a uniform weighted graph (nodes = decision variables, edges = constraint relationships). This yields a generic, shared graph representation across instances, enabling (1) a structure-based local improvement framework (SLIM) that uses the graph for variable selection, and (2) extraction of uniform graph features for configuration selection (algorithm selection). Ablations on configuration and features are also performed.
AI.result: Evaluated on instances from 20 MiniZinc competition problems, algorithm selection achieves a 39.5% average problem-weighted win rate against a one-shot Gurobi baseline, more than doubling the best single configuration (19.3%). Configuration and feature ablation further improves performance to 44.0%.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based semantic generation enables effective automated structure extraction and feature extraction for constraint optimization. The problem-agnostic graph representation supports variable selection and configuration selection, substantially outperforming both the best single configuration and the Gurobi baseline.

title: LittleLearner: Language Models Under Pedagogically Controlled Knowledge Exposure
summary: Modern language models are trained on heterogeneous web-scale text corpora. Consequently, studying knowledge and skill acquisition is difficult, as prior exposure to related content is hard to characterize. To address this challenge, we introduce LITTLECURRICULUM, a curated 88B-token pretraining corpus tailored to U.S. elementary school material, explicitly excluding concepts, facts, and vocabulary taught above Grade 5. Training a 5B-parameter LLM from scratch on LITTLECURRICULUM yields LITTLELEARNER, a model with sufficient language competence for open-ended evaluation, yet with clear knowledge and capability boundaries mapped to interpretable curriculum guidelines. We release LITTLECURRICULUM and LITTLELEARNER as a developmentally restricted sandbox to study how models acquire, represent, and use data under a well-defined training scope. We illustrate the sandbox's utility in a first suite of experiments on injecting new knowledge through post-training and in-context learning. These methods let LITTLELEARNER better utilize existing knowledge, but do not raise out-of-scope capabilities. Our findings underscore the value of this controlled environment for future investigations.

AI.tldr: The authors build LITTLECURRICULUM, an 88B-token U.S. Grade-5-and-below pretraining corpus, train a 5B LLM (LITTLELEARNER) on it from scratch, and release both as a boundary-controlled sandbox; initial experiments show post-training and in-context learning improve use of in-scope knowledge but do not unlock out-of-scope capabilities.
AI.motivation: Studying knowledge/skill acquisition in LLMs is confounded by web-scale training data with unknown prior exposure to related content; a controlled corpus with a well-defined, interpretable scope is needed.
AI.method: Curate an 88B-token corpus restricted to U.S. elementary-school material (concepts/facts/vocabulary up to Grade 5); train a 5B-parameter LLM from scratch; map the model's knowledge/capability boundaries to curriculum guidelines; run experiments on post-training and in-context learning for injecting new knowledge.
AI.result: LITTLELEARNER has enough language competence for open-ended evaluation while showing clear, curriculum-aligned knowledge boundaries; post-training and in-context learning help it use existing knowledge better but do not raise out-of-scope capabilities.
AI.conclusion: A developmentally restricted, curriculum-defined sandbox provides a valuable controlled environment for studying how models acquire, represent, and use data, and highlights that in-scope capability gains via post-training/ICL do not generalize to out-of-scope knowledge.

title: The Time Value of Evolution
comment: Submitted to AAAI 2026, 8 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables
summary: In evolutionary search, a weak child can be a valuable ancestor that makes high-fitness regions reachable. Immediate-return control is blind to this delayed utility, penalizing mutations through their immediate offspring even when they open productive future lineages. We formalize this hidden dynamic as the time value of evolution within a finite-horizon Markov decision process. To exploit it, we introduce Lineage-Value Policy Gradients (LVPG), a long-horizon actor-critic framework for automated trading policy discovery. Our architecture decouples search control into specialized policy heads over a shared generative backbone: a bootstrapped critic head estimates the value of finite-horizon lineage potential from multi-step mutation trees, while an actor head dynamically modulates mutation intensity over the remaining search budget. We isolate the impact of long-horizon credit assignment against immediate-return optimization across 90 paired runs under matched operators, lineage supervision, folds, seeds, and budgets. Path-based credit assignment substantially accelerates finite-budget search, increasing validation best-so-far AUC by 0.394 Sharpe units. LVPG also produces fewer temporary regressions than immediate-return optimization and recovers from them more often. Finite-horizon lineage value yields more selective non-monotonic search and stronger policies within identical resource constraints.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that immediate-return evolutionary search discards valuable "weak" children that open up future high-fitness lineages, and proposes Lineage-Value Policy Gradients (LVPG), a long-horizon actor-critic framework that credits delayed lineage value, improving finite-budget trading-policy search by +0.394 Sharpe units.
AI.motivation: Immediate-return control in evolutionary search is blind to delayed utility: a weak child may be a valuable ancestor that makes high-fitness regions reachable later, yet greedy mutation control penalizes it. The authors formalize this hidden dynamic as the "time value of evolution" within a finite-horizon Markov decision process to recover productive future lineages that short-sighted search discards.
AI.method: LVPG decouples search control into specialized policy heads over a shared generative backbone. A bootstrapped critic head estimates finite-horizon lineage potential from multi-step mutation trees, while an actor head dynamically modulates mutation intensity over the remaining search budget. The framework is evaluated in 90 paired runs with matched operators, lineage supervision, folds, seeds, and budgets, isolating long-horizon credit assignment against immediate-return optimization.
AI.result: Path-based credit assignment substantially accelerates finite-budget search, increasing validation best-so-far AUC by 0.394 Sharpe units. LVPG produces fewer temporary regressions than immediate-return optimization and recovers from them more often. Finite-horizon lineage value yields more selective non-monotonic search and stronger policies under identical resource constraints.
AI.conclusion: Delayed lineage value matters in finite-budget evolutionary search. By replacing immediate-return control with long-horizon credit assignment, LVPG achieves more selective, non-monotonic search and stronger trading policies within fixed resource constraints, demonstrating the value of accounting for the time value of evolution.

title: LongEarth-R1: Benchmarking and Aligning Vision-Language Models for Long-Horizon Earth Observation Reasoning
summary: Long-horizon Earth observation reasoning requires models to organize multi-stage geographic evolution, localize spatial changes, detect temporal anomalies, and infer future from extended image sequences. However, existing remote sensing vision-language models mainly focus on isolated images, image pairs, or short sequences, limiting reliable grounding in the relevant frames and regions. We introduce LongEarth-Bench, a benchmark containing approximately 120k question-answering samples derived from 117k unique images. Its sequences average 15.14 frames and extend to 30 frames, covering 12 tasks across evolution summarization, spatial reasoning, anomaly identification, and logical prediction. A 30k-sample subset further provides structured reasoning traces linking key frames and changed regions to final answers. We develop LongEarth through supervised fine-tuning with explicit sequence identifiers and structured chain-of-thought supervision. Building on LongEarth, LongEarth-R1 applies group relative policy optimization with format, temporal, and spatial rewards. LongEarth-R1 achieves the best results on all 12 long-sequence tasks while remaining competitive on standard remote sensing benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LongEarth-Bench, a large benchmark (~120k QA samples, ~117k images, sequences averaging 15.14 frames and up to 30 frames) for long-horizon Earth observation reasoning, along with LongEarth (SFT with sequence identifiers and chain-of-thought supervision) and LongEarth-R1 (group relative policy optimization with format, temporal, and spatial rewards), which achieves state-of-the-art results on all 12 long-sequence tasks while remaining competitive on standard benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing remote sensing vision-language models focus on isolated images, image pairs, or short sequences, which limits reliable grounding across the relevant frames and regions needed for long-horizon Earth observation reasoning (multi-stage evolution, spatial change localization, temporal anomaly detection, future inference).
AI.method: The authors construct LongEarth-Bench, a benchmark with ~120k QA samples from 117k unique images, sequences averaging 15.14 frames (extending to 30), spanning 12 tasks across evolution summarization, spatial reasoning, anomaly identification, and logical prediction. A 30k-sample subset provides structured reasoning traces linking key frames and changed regions to answers. They develop LongEarth via supervised fine-tuning with explicit sequence identifiers and structured chain-of-thought supervision. LongEarth-R1 extends this by applying group relative policy optimization with format, temporal, and spatial rewards.
AI.result: LongEarth-R1 achieves the best results on all 12 long-sequence tasks in LongEarth-Bench while remaining competitive on standard remote sensing benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Long-horizon Earth observation reasoning benefits from explicit sequence identifiers, structured chain-of-thought supervision, and reinforcement learning with temporal/spatial rewards, enabling reliable grounding across long image sequences and strong performance on diverse temporal reasoning tasks.

title: A Probe Direction Is a Property of Its Prompt
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 13 appendices. Code, data manifests and results: https://github.com/vcnoel/probe-direction
summary: A model that behaves differently when it senses it is being tested would undermine the evaluations we rely on, so recent work has sought to read that sense directly from a model's activations. The standard instrument contrasts activations on prompts that announce an evaluation against prompts that do not, and reports how well the resulting direction separates held-out cases. That number is then compared across models and correlated with scale. We observe that the instrument has a free parameter its readings do not disclose: "a prompt that announces an evaluation" is not a prompt but a choice among many, and nothing in the method fixes which. Holding the task text fixed and varying only that choice, we find that the reported score, and even the direction in which it trends with model size, follows the prompt rather than the model; two published studies that disagree about the sign of that trend are both reproducible from a single design, by choice of prompt alone. Treating the prompt as a facet of a measurement design rather than an implementation detail, we find the model under study accounts for a small share of the variance in the number reported about it, and most of the rest lies in how each model responds to each prompt: collecting more evaluation items cannot repair the measurement, while varying prompts can. A further check finds that the split these probes are scored on is largely separable from surface form alone, so a direction carrying no information about evaluation at all still reproduces a substantial fraction of each published score. We conclude that a single-prompt design cannot support comparison between models, and we give the number of prompts a defensible comparison requires.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques a common method for detecting whether models "know" they are being evaluated (contrasting activations on evaluating vs. non-evaluating prompts). It shows the method's reported scores are driven largely by the arbitrary choice of evaluation prompt wording rather than by the model itself, meaning single-prompt designs cannot support model-to-model comparisons.
AI.motivation: Recent work claims to read a model's awareness of being tested from its activations and uses the resulting scores to compare models and correlate with scale. The authors suspect these measurements are unstable because the "evaluation-announcing prompt" is an under-specified free parameter, so they test whether reported scores depend on the model or merely on the prompt wording.
AI.method: They hold task text fixed and vary only the choice of evaluation-announcing prompt, measuring how the reported separation score and its trend with model size change. They then treat the prompt as a facet in a measurement design (generalizability analysis) to decompose variance attributable to the model versus prompt-model interaction, and test whether scores survive a surface-form-only baseline direction that carries no evaluation information.
AI.result: The reported score and even the sign of its trend with model size follow the chosen prompt rather than the model; two published studies with opposite trend signs are both reproducible from one design by prompt choice alone. The model accounts for a small share of variance, with most variance in how each model responds to each prompt. Collecting more evaluation items cannot fix this, but varying prompts can. A surface-form-only direction reproduces a substantial fraction of each published score.
AI.conclusion: A single-prompt design cannot support comparison between models. The authors conclude that multiple prompts are required for a defensible comparison and specify the number of prompts such a comparison requires.

title: Rules or Character? Scaling Laws for AI Safety Design
comment: Accepted at AIES 2026 (9th AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society). 10 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) safety systems combine character shaping (e.g., Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback [RLHF], Constitutional AI), which modifies behavioral distributions at training time, with rule enforcement (e.g., output filters, safety classifiers), which blocks harmful outputs at inference time, yet little formal analysis exists on how their optimal balance should change as deployment scales increase. We introduce a stylized comparative-statics model that parameterizes safety design as a resource allocation alpha in [0,1] between these two approaches, incorporating scale-dependent filter degradation, common-mode failures, and character fragility -- the risk that shaped behavior degrades or collapses under novel conditions. Under a multiplicative Pareto damage model, we derive closed-form expected harm and supplement it with tail-risk (CVaR) analysis via Monte Carlo simulation. Across three scenarios (optimistic, moderate, pessimistic), the optimal alpha* is interior or at the rules-only boundary and shifts weakly toward character shaping as deployment scale T grows, from negligible (Delta alpha* = +0.01) to pronounced (Delta alpha* = +0.21) depending on scenario. The dominant parameter is the baseline character fragility rate p^(0)_frag, which shifts alpha* by 0.50 across its range -- far exceeding the effect of tail severity, filter quality, or common-mode failure probability. CVaR and expected-harm optima converge at large T. These results suggest that safety architecture decisions depend less on deployment scale per se than on the reliability of character shaping under distributional shift.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a comparative-statics model showing how the optimal allocation between AI character shaping (training-time) and rule enforcement (inference-time) safety approaches should shift as deployment scale grows, finding that optimum depends less on scale and more on character fragility under distributional shift.
AI.motivation: AI safety systems combine training-time character shaping (RLHF, Constitutional AI) with inference-time rule enforcement (filters, classifiers), but there is little formal analysis of how the optimal balance between these two approaches should change as deployment scale increases.
AI.method: The authors introduce a stylized comparative-statics model parameterizing safety design as a resource allocation alpha in [0,1] between character shaping and rule enforcement, incorporating scale-dependent filter degradation, common-mode failures, and character fragility. They use a multiplicative Pareto damage model to derive closed-form expected harm, supplemented by tail-risk (CVaR) analysis via Monte Carlo simulation across optimistic, moderate, and pessimistic scenarios.
AI.result: The optimal alpha* is interior or at the rules-only boundary and shifts weakly toward character shaping as deployment scale T grows (Delta alpha* from +0.01 to +0.21 depending on scenario). The dominant parameter is baseline character fragility rate p^(0)_frag, which shifts alpha* by 0.50 across its range, far exceeding effects of tail severity, filter quality, or common-mode failure probability. CVaR and expected-harm optima converge at large T.
AI.conclusion: Safety architecture decisions depend less on deployment scale per se than on the reliability of character shaping under distributional shift, suggesting robustness of character shaping is the key lever for optimal AI safety resource allocation.

title: Training AI Scientists to Replicate Research
summary: The replicability of papers is a cornerstone of scientific knowledge, ensuring the reliability of existing results and providing a base for further experiments. The act of replication typically illuminates details that were previously underspecified, and thus requires similar hypothesis-driven exploration to open-ended research. In this work, we develop Replica, a scalable task space for paper replication. To provide reward signal, we introduce an auto-generated rubric-based judge that has low noise and agrees with human assessment of replication quality. We post-train Faraday, a 27B-parameter "AI Scientist" agent that leverages coding agents as tools, surpassing the performance of Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 on held-out replication tasks. Qualitative analysis of individual rollouts reveals that Faraday adopts a more scientifically-principled approach. We believe that our results provide a stepping stone towards AI agents capable of long-horizon scientific innovation without requiring complex harnesses.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Replica, a scalable benchmark for paper replication, along with a rubric-based automated judge for low-noise reward signals, and Faraday, a 27B-parameter AI Scientist agent that outperforms larger frontier models on replication tasks.
AI.motivation: Paper replicability is central to scientific reliability but is difficult to automate and evaluate. Replication behaves like open-ended, hypothesis-driven research, exposing underspecified details, so the authors aim to build a scalable environment and reward signal to train AI agents for this task.
AI.method: They develop Replica, a scalable task space for paper replication, and an auto-generated rubric-based judge that provides low-noise reward signals correlating with human assessments. They then post-train Faraday, a 27B-parameter AI Scientist agent that uses coding agents as tools.
AI.result: Faraday surpasses Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 on held-out replication tasks. Qualitative analysis shows Faraday adopts a more scientifically-principled approach to replication.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a step toward AI agents capable of long-horizon scientific innovation without requiring complex harnesses, using paper replication as a scalable and measurable training signal.

title: Neural Quadratic Forms: A Unified Minimal Model for Sudden Learning and Scaling Laws
summary: Neural networks trained by gradient descent on a smooth cost function can nevertheless learn in steps: the cost holds on long plateaus and then drops abruptly. Meanwhile, training losses instead follow smooth power laws. Variants of both behaviors occur in architectures with very different microscopic structures, which is the signature of a few relevant collective variables. We show that a symmetry fixes what those variables are: a network layer is a sum over interchangeable units, so relabeling the units leaves it unchanged; given smoothness and the condition that a unit's gradient vanish at the origin, symmetry then enforces a universal leading form for the expansion about the near-zero weights present at the start of training, the quadratic $\Tr[WW^{\top}A(x)]$, in which every architectural detail is confined to a single ``structure matrix" $A(x)$ that we compute for each architecture. Perceptrons, attention layers, mixtures of experts, and convolutions become one model at different $A$. Its training dynamics then close on the ``order parameter" $M=WW^{\top}$ and, whenever the data matrices share an eigenbasis, reduce to a Lotka--Volterra equation whose modes switch on one after another. The smaller the initial weights, the further apart the switch-on times, and the plateaus appear as a singular limit of a smooth flow; when many modes are unresolved the same events merge into a power law in training time whose exponent the theory predicts. We confirm both numerically across training methods and architectures.

AI.tldr: Neural networks trained with gradient descent can learn in sudden, stepwise drops separated by plateaus, yet training losses show smooth power laws. The paper explains these unified behaviors through a symmetry: layers are sums of interchangeable units, and symmetry plus smoothness forces a universal quadratic leading form governed by a single structure matrix A(x). With this, all architectures reduce to a common model whose dynamics close on an order parameter and follow a Lotka–Volterra equation with modes switching on sequentially.
AI.motivation: Explain why apparently contradictory behaviors—stepwise (plateau-and-drop) learning versus smooth power-law loss trajectories—co-occur across very different network architectures, signaling that a few relevant collective variables govern training dynamics.
AI.method: Exploit the permutation symmetry of interchangeable units within a layer and the smoothness condition that a unit's gradient vanishes at the origin. This symmetry enforces a universal leading form of the expansion about near-zero initial weights: the quadratic Tr[W W^T A(x)], where all architecture-specific detail is captured by a single "structure matrix" A(x), computed for perceptrons, attention layers, mixtures of experts, and convolutions. Training dynamics then close on the order parameter M = W W^T; when data matrices share an eigenbasis, the dynamics reduce to a Lotka–Volterra equation whose modes activate sequentially. Plateaus emerge as a singular limit of a smooth flow as initial weights shrink, and unresolved mode-switching events merge into a power law in training time whose exponent the theory predicts.
AI.result: At different A(x), perceptrons, attention layers, mixtures of experts, and convolutions become a single model. Smaller initial weights push switch-on times further apart, producing plateaus as a singular limit; when many modes are unresolved, the events coalesce into a power law whose exponent is theoretically predicted. These predictions are confirmed numerically across training methods and architectures.
AI.conclusion: Symmetry and smoothness alone determine the universal low-weight expansion of network layers, reducing diverse architectures to one collective-variable model. This framework unifies stepwise and power-law learning as two limits of the same smooth flow, with quantitative predictions validated numerically.

title: Jointly Predicting Courses and Grades Using a Transformer-Based Model
summary: Existing predictive models in learning analytics often treat student academic history as a simple sequence, overlooking the concurrent nature of courses taken within a semester. This simplification can lead to inaccurate performance predictions, particularly for students with heavy or challenging course loads. This paper introduces a TRansformer for Academic Course-grade Estimation (TRACE) that addresses this limitation by jointly predicting both the set of courses a student will take and their corresponding grades for an upcoming semester. Our approach encodes courses on a per-semester basis to capture the effects of course concurrency and utilizes a novel loss function combining course-set prediction with grade prediction. We demonstrate that predicting courses taken in addition to the grades in those courses leads to significant improvements in prediction quality. Trained on ten years of institutional data, our joint prediction model reduces mean absolute error by nearly 50% compared to an identical architecture that predicts grades alone. The model also outperforms traditional LSTM-based sequential models, as well as graph neural network-based approaches, and offers natural ways to incorporate student attribute data. This work demonstrates the utility of modern neural architectures for creating interpretable models that can be adapted to new institutions via retraining and recalibration, as well as the importance of key techniques, such as predicting courses taken during training. We discuss how this model could be incorporated into early detection systems at institutions of higher education.

AI.tldr: TRACE is a Transformer-based model that jointly predicts a student's upcoming course set and their grades, capturing the concurrency of courses within a semester. It reduces grade-prediction error by nearly 50% versus a grade-only model and outperforms LSTM and GNN baselines, supporting interpretable, retrainable early-detection systems.
AI.motivation: Existing learning analytics models treat academic history as a simple course sequence, ignoring that students take multiple courses concurrently within a semester. This misses important interactions (e.g., heavy/challenging course loads) and degrades performance prediction accuracy, motivating a model that accounts for course concurrency and jointly predicts courses taken and grades.
AI.method: The paper proposes TRACE, a Transformer for Academic Course-grade Estimation. Courses are encoded per semester to capture concurrency effects. A novel loss function combines course-set prediction with grade prediction, forcing the model to jointly predict both the courses a student will take and their grades. The model is trained on ten years of institutional data and compared against LSTM-based sequential models, graph neural network (GNN) approaches, and a grade-only equivalent architecture. It also supports incorporating student attribute data and can be adapted via retraining and recalibration.
AI.result: Jointly predicting courses and grades reduces mean absolute error by nearly 50% compared to an identical architecture predicting grades alone. TRACE also outperforms traditional LSTM-based sequential models and GNN-based approaches, with natural integration of student attribute data.
AI.conclusion: Modern Transformer architectures are highly effective for course-grade estimation when trained to predict both courses taken and grades, leveraging within-semester concurrency. Key techniques such as predicting courses during training are critical. The resulting interpretable model can be retrained and recalibrated for new institutions and integrated into early detection systems in higher education.

title: Where You Measure Decides What You Measure: Position Selection in Ablation-Based SAE Evaluation
comment: 19 pages, 3 figures. Code and data: https://github.com/vcnoel/sae-artifact
summary: Sparse autoencoders are meant to name the things a language model computes, and the usual way to check that a latent matters is to switch it off and see what changes. But a latent fires at many tokens, and the effect has to be measured at one of them. The convention is to measure where the latent fires hardest. That choice is almost never reported, and it is not made by the experimenter: it is made by the dictionary under evaluation. Change the dictionary and the measurement moves to a different token. We show this is not a detail. Take two sparse autoencoders released by Google for the same model and match their latents by decoder similarity: even among the pairs the two dictionaries encode almost identically, they pick different tokens for a large share of them. Two dictionaries compared under the usual protocol are therefore very often compared at different places. To separate the convention from the dictionaries we train six autoencoders from one initialisation, differing only in fitting choices, so that a latent means the same thing in each. Most of the variance such a comparison reads as "these dictionaries disagree about this latent" turns out to be the position instead: it falls from 7.6% and 11.9% of variance to near zero once every dictionary is measured at the same token. More evaluation data does not rescue it. Across a sixteenfold range of corpus sizes the dictionaries agree less about where to measure, not more, so the problem grows with scale. The correction is one line of evaluation code. We give the protocol an ablation-based causal number must report to be comparable across papers, and an audit of five published papers against it. In short: a causal number reported without its position describes the token it was taken at as much as the latent it was taken from.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the standard practice of evaluating sparse autoencoder latents "where the latent fires hardest" makes comparisons across dictionaries unreliable, because the measurement position is chosen by the dictionary itself rather than held fixed. Matching or controlled experiments reveal that most apparent disagreement between dictionaries is actually disagreement about where to measure, not what the latent means; the problem grows with corpus size, and the fix is one line of evaluation code (fixing the measurement token).
AI.motivation: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are used to interpret model internals by identifying latents and checking their causal effect when ablated. The common causal check measures the effect only at the token where the latent fires hardest. The authors argue this position is implicitly selected by the dictionary under evaluation, so different dictionaries are compared at different tokens, making results non-comparable and misleading.
AI.method: (1) Take two Google-released SAEs for the same model, match latents by decoder similarity, and quantify how often nearly-identical latent pairs pick different measurement tokens. (2) Train six autoencoders from a single initialization differing only in fitting choices so latents mean the same thing; compare inter-dictionary disagreement with and without fixing the measurement token. (3) Vary corpus size over a sixteenfold range to test whether more evaluation data closes the gap. (4) Propose a one-line fix (measure all dictionaries at the same token) and audit five published papers against a reporting protocol.
AI.result: Even among latent pairs that two dictionaries encode almost identically, a large share pick different tokens under the usual protocol. In the controlled six-SAEs comparison, variance attributed to "dictionaries disagree about this latent" falls from 7.6% and 11.9% to near zero when every dictionary is measured at the same token. More evaluation data does not help: across a sixteenfold range of corpus sizes, dictionaries agree less (not more) about where to measure, so the problem grows with scale.
AI.conclusion: A causal number reported without its measurement position describes the token it was taken at as much as the latent it was taken from. To be comparable across papers, ablation-based causal numbers must report the token/position at which the effect was measured, and the standard fix is one line of evaluation code that fixes the measurement token.

title: Who Speaks Matters: Authority-Aware Multi-View RAG over Italian Parliamentary Proceedings
comment: Accepted at ISWC 2026 In-Use Track. Please cite the ISWC version
summary: Parliamentary proceedings are a primary record of democratic deliberation, yet their volume and fragmentation make multi-perspective access difficult for citizens, journalists, and researchers. Applying Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to parliamentary transcripts introduces three specific risks: dominance of the most frequent speakers, inability to weight speakers according to topical expertise, and citation misattribution in politically sensitive text. We present ParliamentRAG, a RAG system for the Italian Chamber of Deputies that addresses these risks jointly. Its core contribution is a topic-dependent authority model that estimates each speaker's authority as a function of the current query, combining interpretable components such as profession, education, and previous interventions. Given a user query, the system retrieves relevant speech chunks, identifies topic-relevant experts across parliamentary groups, and generates a summary synthesizing their perspectives, accompanied by supporting quotations. ParliamentRAG is evaluated against Google NotebookLM on 15 policy topics via a two-level protocol combining automated metrics and blind A/B human evaluation by six domain experts. The system achieves higher coverage across political groups (0.97 vs. 0.95), perfect quotation faithfulness (1.00 vs. 0.95), and stronger expert preferences on source-related dimensions, while NotebookLM remains stronger on prose-oriented dimensions.

AI.tldr: ParliamentRAG is a retrieval-augmented generation system for the Italian Chamber of Deputies that uses a topic-dependent authority model to weigh speakers by expertise, mitigating risks of speaker dominance and citation misattribution; it outperforms Google NotebookLM on coverage, quotation faithfulness, and source-related expert preferences across 15 policy topics.
AI.motivation: Parliamentary transcripts are a key record of democratic deliberation but are voluminous and fragmented, making multi-perspective access hard for citizens, journalists, and researchers. Directly applying RAG to such transcripts introduces three risks: dominance of the most frequent speakers, inability to weigh speakers by topical expertise, and citation misattribution in politically sensitive text.
AI.method: ParliamentRAG jointly addresses the three risks via a topic-dependent authority model that estimates each speaker's authority as a function of the current query, combining interpretable components such as profession, education, and previous interventions. Given a query, the system retrieves relevant speech chunks, identifies topic-relevant experts across parliamentary groups, and generates a summary synthesizing their perspectives with supporting quotations. Evaluation uses a two-level protocol with 15 policy topics, comparing against Google NotebookLM via automated metrics and blind A/B human evaluation by six domain experts.
AI.result: ParliamentRAG achieves higher coverage across political groups (0.97 vs 0.95), perfect quotation faithfulness (1.00 vs 0.95), and stronger expert preferences on source-related dimensions, while NotebookLM remains stronger on prose-oriented dimensions.
AI.conclusion: The topic-dependent authority model effectively improves multi-perspective coverage, quotation faithfulness, and source-related quality in parliamentary RAG, though prose quality remains an area where general-purpose systems like NotebookLM still have an advantage.

title: Simulation-to-real transfer learning for infrared spectroscopic chemical sensing and analysis from molecules to complex samples
summary: Infrared (IR) spectroscopy is widely used for chemical sensing, but extracting reliable chemical information from spectra remains challenging. Conventional interpretation is labor-intensive, relies on prior knowledge and reference spectra, and is difficult to scale, whereas most machine-learning methods are tailored to individual tasks or datasets, require large labeled training sets, and transfer poorly across analytical objectives and experimental datasets. Here we introduce UltraIR, a foundation model for IR spectroscopy with more than 100 million parameters that enables simulation-to-real transfer learning for chemical sensing and analysis from molecules to complex samples. UltraIR is pretrained on approximately 60 million simulated IR spectra using spectral reconstruction, molecular fingerprint similarity alignment, and functional-group prediction, then adapted to downstream objectives with task-specific labels or targets. Across functional-group prediction, molecular structure elucidation, physicochemical property prediction, mixture-component identification and quantification, bacterial classification, medicinal-herb geographic origin traceability and constituent quantification, microplastics classification, and soil property prediction, UltraIR outperforms conventional machine-learning and task-specific deep-learning baselines. It performs strongly with limited labeled experimental spectra and in zero-shot inference for the same analytical task across Fourier-transform infrared spectrometers and laboratories, providing a route to adaptable, data-efficient chemical sensing from complex real-world samples.

AI.tldr: UltraIR is a 100M+ parameter foundation model for IR spectroscopy, pretrained on ~60M simulated spectra, that transfers to many downstream chemical-sensing tasks and outperforms both conventional ML and task-specific deep-learning baselines, including under limited-label and zero-shot settings.
AI.motivation: IR spectroscopy is widely used for chemical sensing, but extracting reliable chemical information is challenging: manual interpretation is labor-intensive and hard to scale, while most ML methods are task-specific, require large labeled datasets, and generalize poorly across objectives and instruments.
AI.method: UltraIR is a foundation model with >100M parameters pretrained on ~60 million simulated IR spectra using three objectives: spectral reconstruction, molecular fingerprint similarity alignment, and functional-group prediction. It is then adapted to downstream tasks with task-specific labels or targets, enabling simulation-to-real transfer learning from molecules to complex samples.
AI.result: Across nine downstream tasks—functional-group prediction, molecular structure elucidation, physicochemical property prediction, mixture-component identification and quantification, bacterial classification, medicinal-herb origin traceability and constituent quantification, microplastics classification, and soil property prediction—UltraIR outperforms conventional ML and task-specific deep-learning baselines. It performs strongly with limited labeled experimental spectra and in zero-shot inference across different FTIR spectrometers and laboratories.
AI.conclusion: UltraIR provides a route to adaptable, data-efficient chemical sensing from complex real-world samples, achieving strong cross-domain and cross-instrument generalization from simulation-based pretraining.

title: Beyond Final Scores: A Systematic Evaluation of Agents for Long-Horizon AI Research and Development
summary: Autonomous agents are increasingly capable of improving models, systems, and other technical artifacts through long-horizon experimentation. To understand the current state of this capability, however, evaluation must go beyond final scores, which neither reveal where progress is gained or lost nor indicate whether accumulated experience improves later decisions. We therefore present a systematic evaluation of seven frontier models on 36 long-horizon tasks based on a new framework that uses rule-based metrics to characterize within-run behavior through Solution Framing, Execution, and Feedback Control and controlled comparisons to assess experience reuse within and across tasks. The results show that current agents operate more like engineering optimizers than fully autonomous researchers: they can formulate and implement practical solutions, but their performance varies substantially across runs, their strongest solutions mainly adapt or combine established techniques, and genuine methodological novelty remains rare. Detailed analysis reveals that observed performance is shaped by multiple factors, including distinct process bottlenecks behind similar final outcomes, experience reuse that can help or mislead subsequent decisions, and harness designs that affect performance stability. These findings suggest concrete directions for improving model training, inference-time strategies, experience management, and harness design.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates seven frontier models on 36 long-horizon autonomous experimentation tasks, using a framework that analyzes within-run behavior (Solution Framing, Execution, Feedback Control) and experience reuse, finding that current agents perform like engineering optimizers rather than fully autonomous researchers.
AI.motivation: Evaluation of autonomous agents must go beyond final scores, which fail to reveal where progress is gained or lost and whether accumulated experience improves later decisions. Existing benchmark-style scoring obscures within-run process dynamics and the role of experience reuse across tasks, motivating a more granular, behavior-level assessment.
AI.method: The authors propose a new evaluation framework applied to seven frontier models on 36 long-horizon tasks. It uses rule-based metrics to characterize within-run behavior along three axes—Solution Framing, Execution, and Feedback Control—and employs controlled comparisons to assess experience reuse both within and across tasks, enabling measurement of process bottlenecks and decision quality.
AI.result: Current agents act more like engineering optimizers than fully autonomous researchers: they can formulate and implement practical solutions, but performance varies substantially across runs, their strongest solutions mainly adapt or combine established techniques, and genuine methodological novelty is rare. Analyses show that distinct process bottlenecks can underlie similar final outcomes, experience reuse can help or mislead later decisions, and harness design affects performance stability.
AI.conclusion: The findings point to concrete directions for improvement in model training, inference-time strategies, experience management, and harness design, indicating that richer process-oriented evaluation is necessary to advance toward genuinely autonomous research agents.

title: When Local Variance Optimality Is Not Enough: RoPE-Aligned Q/K Rotations for Dynamic 4-Bit Quantisation
summary: Rotation-based post-training quantisation commonly applies an orthogonal transform across an entire attention head to reduce outlier-induced error. RoPE instead partitions each head into two-dimensional frequency pairs, raising the question of whether a transform respecting this decomposition can improve on full-head mixing. Prior work has established the per-pair rotations that commute with RoPE. We state the converse result that, for distinct frequencies, no other single-head orthogonal map commutes with RoPE. For the head-shared parameterisation used in our experiments, we then derive the rotation angle that minimises the larger channel variance under a pooled-covariance, position-averaged surrogate and verify that the implementation attains its analytic minimum. The evaluated head-shared pairwise configuration does not improve accuracy in the tested dynamic W4A4KV4 setting. Across four checkpoints, replacing the full-head Hadamard with this configuration increases perplexity at both short and long context lengths. Composing the pairwise rotation with the Hadamard satisfies the selected $\pm0.05$-PPL interval criterion under the default estimator. Estimating the shared angle from K alone improves pairwise-only on every checkpoint but does not close its gap to full-head mixing. The analytic objective controls a position-averaged second moment of a pooled calibration covariance, whereas the dynamic quantiser sets its step from a tokenwise group range. The pairwise transform also has only two-channel mixing support. Along a controlled interpolation from two-channel to full-head mixing, K range, relative quantisation error, and perplexity degradation decrease as support increases. These results show that optimality for a structured surrogate need not reduce quantisation error when the surrogate and mixing support are misaligned with the quantiser's scale-setting statistic.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that per-pair rotations are the only orthogonal maps commuting with RoPE (for distinct frequencies), derives the variance-minimising shared angle, and shows empirically that this pairwise rotation underperforms full-head Hadamard mixing in dynamic W4A4KV4 quantisation.
AI.motivation: Rotation-based post-training quantisation typically uses a full-head orthogonal transform to suppress outlier-induced error, but RoPE decomposes heads into 2D frequency pairs; the authors ask whether a transform respecting this decomposition can outperform full-head mixing.
AI.method: They state the converse result that no other single-head orthogonal map commutes with RoPE for distinct frequencies, then derive the rotation angle minimising the larger channel variance under a pooled-covariance, position-averaged surrogate for the head-shared parameterisation, and verify the implementation reaches the analytic minimum.
AI.result: The pairwise configuration does not improve accuracy in dynamic W4A4KV4; across four checkpoints it raises perplexity at short and long contexts versus full-head Hadamard. Composing it with Hadamard satisfies a ±0.05-PPL criterion under the default estimator; estimating the angle from K alone improves pairwise-only but not to Hadamard's level; quantisation error and perplexity degradation shrink as mixing support grows from two-channel to full-head.
AI.conclusion: Optimality for a structured surrogate does not reduce quantisation error when the surrogate and two-channel mixing support are misaligned with the quantiser's tokenwise group-range scale-setting statistic.

title: Enhancing Virtual Agents through SLMs and Edge-Computing: An Exploratory Evaluation of Think and Memory Processes
summary: Embodied intelligent virtual agents are expected to operate as persistent, adaptive, and context-aware entities within complex virtual and Metaverse worlds. However, implementing cognitively capable agents in such environments is conceptually and technologically challenging. Among a range of blueprints and development approaches, the Cognitive Embodied Agent Architecture (CEAA) has been developed as an implementation-oriented framework for architecting components of perception, memory, reasoning, planning, and embodied action. Considering the recent advances in edge computing and generative AI language models, this paper explores the use of Small Language Models (SLMs) to support edge-based operation of selected CEAA components, focusing on "Think" and "Memory" as processes central to cognitive orchestration and persistence of virtual agents in interactive virtual worlds. An edge-based virtual agent gateway system was developed and evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX using Qwen2.5 models of different sizes, exploring the system's capability to process service requests and handle memory-driven conversations. A series of simulation experiments evaluated routing accuracy, memory-read performance, and latency, demonstrating an SLM-driven prototype agent system that partially implements selected CEAA processes to support the development of embodied agents whose cognitive "brain" can operate efficiently and contextually for interactive experiences in immersive virtual worlds.

AI.tldr: This paper explores using Small Language Models (SLMs) running on edge computing (NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX) to implement key Cognitive Embodied Agent Architecture (CEAA) processes—"Think" and "Memory"—for embodied virtual agents in Metaverse environments. A prototype edge-based virtual agent gateway was built using Qwen2.5 models, and simulation experiments evaluated routing accuracy, memory-read performance, and latency, demonstrating a feasible SLM-driven cognitive "brain" for immersive virtual worlds.
AI.motivation: Embodied intelligent virtual agents should be persistent, adaptive, and context-aware in complex virtual and Metaverse worlds, but implementing cognitively capable agents is conceptually and technologically challenging. The authors aim to leverage recent advances in edge computing and generative AI (specifically SLMs) to make selected CEAA cognitive components run efficiently at the edge, rather than relying on cloud infrastructure.
AI.method: The paper adopts the Cognitive Embodied Agent Architecture (CEAA) as an implementation-oriented framework and focuses on its "Think" and "Memory" processes. It develops an edge-based virtual agent gateway system deployed on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, using Qwen2.5 models of different sizes as SLMs. A series of simulation experiments were conducted to evaluate routing accuracy, memory-read performance, and latency of the system in processing service requests and handling memory-driven conversations.
AI.result: The experiments evaluated routing accuracy, memory-read performance, and latency, demonstrating an SLM-driven prototype agent system that partially implements selected CEAA processes. The results show that the cognitive "brain" of embodied agents can operate efficiently and contextually on edge hardware, supporting interactive experiences in immersive virtual worlds.
AI.conclusion: SLMs running on edge devices can effectively support the "Think" and "Memory" components of the CEAA framework, enabling embodied agents to function with a cognitive "brain" that operates efficiently and contextually. This approach provides a viable blueprint for developing persistent, adaptive virtual agents in immersive virtual and Metaverse worlds without full dependence on cloud resources.

title: Reduced Matrix Multiplication: Input-Adaptive Matrix-Product Reduction for LLM Inference
summary: Transformer-based language models achieve strong performance but incur substantial inference cost due to repeated high-dimensional matrix multiplications. We propose Reduced Matrix Multiplication (RMM), a training-free, input-adaptive inference method that reduces Transformer matrix products by selecting informative slices along their contraction dimensions, without modifying model weights. Under a simple retention-ratio control, RMM provides a smooth and predictable accuracy-efficiency trade-off. Across language models ranging from 1B to 70B parameters, we find that reduction tolerance depends on the model family, task, component, and retention ratio, although it often improves with model scale. Under moderate reduction, RMM remains robust across the evaluated discriminative, autoregressive generation, and long-context settings. We further show that the same principle extends to multimodal vision-language inference. Mechanistic ablations reveal a structural asymmetry within Transformers: attention-side computations are substantially more reducible than MLP components. Finally, wall-clock benchmarks with custom kernels on an NVIDIA A100 show that these computational savings can translate into practical runtime gains, especially at longer sequence lengths. Together, these results position RMM as a scalable direction for input-adaptive inference-time optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Reduced Matrix Multiplication (RMM), a training-free, input-adaptive inference method that cuts Transformer matrix products by selecting informative slices along contraction dimensions without changing model weights, offering a smooth accuracy-efficiency trade-off across 1B–70B models.
AI.motivation: Transformer-based language models achieve strong performance but incur high inference cost driven by repeated high-dimensional matrix multiplications. The authors aim to reduce this computational burden without retraining or modifying weights, enabling practical runtime gains.
AI.method: RMM is a training-free, input-adaptive approach that reduces Transformer matrix products by selecting informative slices along their contraction dimensions under a retention-ratio control. It requires no weight modification. The method is evaluated across discriminative, autoregressive generation, and long-context tasks, extended to multimodal vision-language inference, and validated with custom CUDA kernels on an NVIDIA A100.
AI.result: Reduction tolerance depends on model family, task, component, and retention ratio, and often improves with model scale (1B–70B). Under moderate reduction, RMM stays robust across evaluated settings. Mechanistic ablations reveal structural asymmetry: attention-side computations are substantially more reducible than MLP components. Wall-clock benchmarks show practical runtime gains, especially at longer sequence lengths.
AI.conclusion: RMM offers a scalable direction for input-adaptive inference-time optimization, providing predictable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs with practical speedups, particularly for larger models and longer sequences.

title: RAIL: An Automatic Classifier of the Artificial Intelligence Readiness Level
summary: Assessing the maturity of artificial intelligence technologies is essential for investment decisions, project management, and policy monitoring, yet the available readiness frameworks are heterogeneous and difficult to apply automatically: the adaptation of Technology Readiness Levels to AI lacks AI-specific gating criteria, the Machine Learning Technology Readiness Levels presuppose access to internal process artifacts, and AI/data readiness dimension models employ scales that resist direct comparison. This paper makes two contributions. First, we unify these three frameworks into the Unified AI Readiness Level (AIRL), a nine-level ordinal scale built on an environmental evidence ladder and complemented by dimensional caps (covering specification, data existence, data quality, data legality, expert knowledge, and algorithmic maturity) together with a generality-anchoring rule and explicit assignment disciplines, so that a readiness level becomes decidable from a natural-language description of the work alone. Second, we propose RAIL (Readiness Assessment via Independent LLM-experts), a panel-of-experts classifier that operationalizes the scale: one evidence agent and six independent dimension agents, each a large language model with a narrowly scoped mandate, deliver verdicts that a deterministic minimum rule aggregates and a chief expert reviews under asymmetric authority, confirming or lowering the panel's recommendation but never raising it above the caps. The method was tested in the analysis of several research works showing consistency and avoiding overestimation from monolithic LLM classifiers.

AI.tldr: The paper unifies three heterogeneous AI readiness frameworks into a single nine-level Unified AI Readiness Level (AIRL) scale, then operationalizes it with RAIL, a panel of independently scoped LLM experts combined with deterministic aggregation rules to make readiness levels decidable from natural-language text and to curb overestimation.
AI.motivation: Existing AI technology readiness frameworks are heterogeneous and hard to apply automatically: Technology Readiness Levels lack AI-specific criteria, MLTRL requires internal process artifacts, and AI/data readiness dimension models use non-comparable scales. The authors need a unified, automatically applicable, and defensible scale for investment, project management, and policy monitoring.
AI.method: First, the authors define AIRL, a nine-level ordinal scale based on an environmental evidence ladder plus dimensional caps (specification, data existence, data quality, data legality, expert knowledge, algorithmic maturity), a generality-anchoring rule, and explicit assignment disciplines so readiness is decidable from a natural-language description alone. Second, they implement RAIL, a panel-of-experts classifier using one evidence agent and six independent dimension agents (each an LLM with a narrow mandate). A deterministic minimum rule aggregates verdicts, and a chief expert reviews with asymmetric authority, able to confirm or lower the recommendation but never raise it above the caps.
AI.result: Testing on several research works showed the method produces consistent readiness assessments while avoiding overestimation that monolithic LLM classifiers are prone to.
AI.conclusion: The Unified AI Readiness Level combined with the RAIL panel-of-experts classifier provides a unified, decidable, and conservative framework for assessing AI technology maturity from natural-language descriptions, improving consistency and preventing overestimation compared to single monolithic classifiers.

title: Symmetry-Breaking De Novo Crystal Generation via Markovian Jump Diffusion
summary: Generating crystals has recently attracted significant interest due to their broad applications in materials science.
